When asked, the crackerjack professionals at the Flippo campaign told the Journal dang, whoopsy again (or words to that effect) and rejiggered the donation a second time, into a categorization that maybe/who knows?/might approximate legality.
Campaign finance violations tend to make voters yawn. That said, trying to make your campaign contribution amounts look on the up and up by reattributing some of them to a dead person is, as campaign finance allegations go, not uninteresting.
Meanwhile, led by Mark Amodei, the Nevada Republican who Flippo would like to replace in Congress, a bunch of Northern Nevada Republicans are publicly sharing their disgust with Flippo. Even if it means having to suffer a Democrat in that congressional seat for a couple years, they hope to rid the Nevada political landscape of Flippo now they needn’t bother to primary a Republican incumbent in 2028.
Lombardo didn’t post his endorsement of Flippo on social media until seven weeks after the primary. Probably had to make sure Flippo was property vetted first.
The Washington Post this week reported that a long-ago Nevada Republican Party chair filed a Federal Elections Commission complaint because Flippo’s aforementioned financial filings are an omnishambles (except the Post phrases it differently). 
And of course all this comes after the Post reporting last month that Flippo lied in campaign materials about his military honors because … that’s just the kind of chap David Flippo is.
All of which raises the obvious question: When Flippo hauled his carpet bag up to CD2, who had “Washington Post and Wall Street Journal both do stories about Flippo” on their bingo cards? I didn’t.
To be clear: If enough Republican voters in Nevada’s 2nd congressional district hold their noses and elect Flippo, upon his swearing in they will be represented by an immediate lame duck and the most impotent and irrelevant person in the U.S. Congress.
So Flippo should take a moment to reflect on and relish this moment. He may not realize it now, but both the Journal and the Post (twice!) writing about him likely marks the zenith of his political “career.”
And whatever happens, Flippo will always be able to say that when the chips were down, not only has Trump stuck by his endorsement of Flippo. So has Lombardo.
Portions of this column originally appeared in the Daily Current Newsletter, which is free and which you can subscribe to here.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Judge blocks DHS from conducting election-related sweeps in 9 states
text:
A federal judge on Wednesday night blocked the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations that could sweep up U.S. citizens in nine states.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden in U.S. District Court in the Northern District of California, issued a preliminary injunction after voting rights advocates alleged that Homeland Security was sending armed agents to homes to question residents about their voter status. 
The injunction bars operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin until polls close on Election Day, though the administration may appeal in the coming days.
The decision marks a legal setback to the Trump administration’s intensifying campaign this fall against noncitizen voting ahead of Election Day. It comes as the Department of Justice is suing California to force state and local election officials to not count the ballots of some 20,000 voters the federal government says it suspects are noncitizens.
President Donald Trump has long decried the threat of noncitizen voting, which studies have shown rarely occurs. He now faces political peril, as Democrats appear increasingly likely to retake the U.S. House and possibly the Senate in the midterm elections.
Martínez-Olguín found that the importance of the public voting free of intimidation outweighed the Trump administration’s interest in rooting out noncitizen voting. But she paused her order until Friday, presumably to give the Trump administration time to appeal.
The evidence in the case, she wrote, leads to an “objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote.”
The lawsuit was filed by San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. 
“Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens – whether born here or naturalized – should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them,” Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer at the legal advocacy group Protect Democracy, which represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement.
Martínez-Olguín wrote that the “ongoing intimidation that CNA/NNU members experience and the direct impediment it plays in their effort to engage voter outreach, education, and engagement efforts, are irreparable harms that are appropriately addressed by preliminary injunctive relief.”
A Homeland Security Investigations internal memo dated Aug. 31 describes a “surge initiative” beginning Sept. 1 that includes conducting field interviews. The memo, which was filed in court, identifies California, Georgia, Missouri, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin as targets of the surge during September. Additional locations are redacted in the document.
Homeland Security didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the decision.
In a previous court filing, Department of Justice lawyers representing DHS have argued that the federal government has the authority to investigate potential voting by noncitizens. 
“Enjoining the government from even investigating such criminal violations would damage the public interest, not serve it,” they wrote.
Democratic groups and top Democrats in Congress filed a lawsuit Tuesday seeking to block Trump intimidating election officials.
This story was first published Oct. 21, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Counseling helps students thrive. Are CT community colleges meeting the need?
text:
On the Tunxis campus of Connecticut State Community College, a sign in front of a building reads, “Keep going. You’ve got this!”
Inside, some students quietly pour over books.
But in a more boisterous corner, with big windows facing some red-leaved trees, the Healthy Minds Club gathers in a classroom for its regular meeting. Faculty advisor Kelly O’Brien Mann talks to the group about the importance of setting goals in order to have a sense of purpose.
“If you don’t know what is it you’re working for, what’s meaningful to you, what does your life look like in the future?” she asks.
The club’s goal is to normalize talking about mental health. It’s a support group of sorts, where students share what they’re going through.
O’Brien Mann is a professor of psychology — but she wears more hats than that.
“In any given day, we might be doing counseling on the fly, and social work, and case management, and de-escalating, and helping students just problem solve with really complicated life issues,” she said.
Across the country, studies show many students struggle with mental health. In a recent survey by the Healthy Minds Network, an organization that conducts research to help guide campus policies, about one third of U.S. college students reported symptoms of moderate or severe anxiety, and roughly the same share reported symptoms of moderate or severe depression.
At Tunxis, there are usually two wellness counselors on staff to provide mental health services. O’Brien Mann would like to see more counselors there, including a nurse practitioner for medication management.
Short-term counseling services on campus are free, though O’Brien Mann said students who have more chronic mental health conditions and need consistent counseling have to look outside CT State.
“Trying to find a therapist who has availability, who takes your insurance, is a tricky thing,” O’Brien Mann said.
Other professors at Tunxis like Michael Hinton have concerns about crisis services being available.
“I’m walking this student down the hall trying to keep them calm and redirect them a little bit until we can get to mental health people,” Hinton explained. “And I walk into a room just, fingers crossed, hoping that there’s somebody here that can help.”
‘Mental health is a priority’
In Connecticut, mental health resources differ across state-funded schools. The University of Connecticut — the state’s flagship four-year school — employs nearly three dozen mental health professionals, who serve about 32,400 undergraduate and graduate students across its campuses.
A UConn spokesperson said the school appointed a task force in 2020 to focus on students’ mental health needs, and it has expanded services and personnel.
CT State offers one to two counselors at each of its 12 community college campuses. The system enrolled almost 38,000 full- and part-time students in fall 2026, a spokesperson said.
Like UConn, the Connecticut State Colleges and Universities system has taken steps to enhance mental health services in recent years, including by joining JED Campus, a nationwide program of The Jed Foundation that helps schools evaluate and improve their support for students.
Nevertheless, this fall, CT State Tunxis started the semester with over 5,600 enrolled students and zero wellness counselors. The two counselors on campus left in the spring, and their positions weren’t filled by the start of this school year.
O’Brien Mann said it’s nobody’s fault — it’s just how things played out. But the lack of counselors speaks to a bigger problem for students in the community college system: an unmet need for more in-person mental health services.
“It would be great to say, ‘Here are the names of the two counselors, here’s how you get an appointment with them,'” O’Brien Mann said. “But I think understaffing for counseling has been a problem probably for every community college.”
The open jobs at Tunxis are being filled, according to Meredith Yuhas, director of mental health and wellness at CT State Community College. Staffing challenges are not a new issue, she said.
“This is the situation that we’ve faced continuously,” Yuhas said.
Yuhas said CT State is navigating a structural deficit and other financial pressures.
To help fill the gap for students, the college provides telehealth services with staff from a third-party contractor. The counseling and crisis support is free.
Yuhas acknowledged that having in-person counselors is important, and said the community college system is evaluating the needs on each campus.
“We have to be very intentional about staffing,” Yuhas said. “I think everybody agrees mental health is a priority.”
Ruth Pinto laughs as she talks with Eli Lund during the Healthy Minds Club meeting at CT State Community College Tunxis on Oct. 14, 2026. Pinto is studying to get a master’s in social work and attends the club with other students every week. Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public
The mental health staffing at Tunxis has other people concerned, like psychology student Ruth Pinto.
Pinto helped a classmate get mental health support through the college’s CARE referral system, which connects students in distress with a multidisciplinary group of campus partners, such as faculty members, the accessibility and disability coordinator, the wellness counselor and the dean of students.
“All I wanted to do was the most important thing … to save his life and to save my friend who I love,” Pinto said.
Pinto also became her friend’s health proxy. But then she started struggling herself, and had a difficult time keeping up with schoolwork.
Pinto remembers walking into the former counselor’s office and breaking down when they asked a simple question: But how are you?
“And I was so stressed,” Pinto said. “And I didn’t realize, because I hadn’t paused to think about myself.”
The counselor helped Pinto get accommodations — support she didn’t realize she needed.
Community college students face more barriers
The state has studied the lack of college mental health support before. A 2021 law required Connecticut higher education institutions to assess resources on campus and identify areas of improvement.
Through its partnership with JED Campus, the state community college system launched a multi-year project to support student mental health, which included soliciting input and collecting data from students.
State Rep. Greg Haddad, a Democrat representing Mansfield who co-chairs the Higher Education Committee, said that in the last 20 years, college campuses have seen more need to provide mental health services.
“And so we see these, you know, growing budgets on college campuses to provide more services to students,” Haddad said. “But the legislature’s portion of the state subsidy has not been following suit.”
Haddad wants the state to do more. He said it’s tough because of tight controls imposed by Connecticut’s fiscal guardrails — budget laws that limit growth in spending.
But investment can be meaningful to students. In one recent survey by the Association for University and College Counseling Center Directors, respondents said counseling services helped academic performance and ability to stay in school for about three quarters of clients.
For community college students, completing a degree program can make a significant difference over the course of their life. Earning an associate degree is a pathway to more job stability. Associate degree holders also earn an average of $400,000 more during their working years than people with a high school diploma alone, according to a 2002 study of U.S. Census Bureau data.
However, research shows many community college students also face more barriers to completing their education compared with students in a four-year program, such as balancing school with work and family, and paying for transportation, housing and food.
These students need different kinds of support because many come from different backgrounds than traditional four-year students, said Amy Rusch, a doctoral student at the Department of Health Behavior and Health Equity at the University of Michigan’s School of Public Health.
“The really big difference is that community college students are experiencing the same mental health crisis with fewer resources to address it,” Rusch said.
Student Monika Rozsa-Horvath navigates some of those challenges. Rozsa-Horvath studies part-time in the Tunxis paralegal program. She also works at a daycare, and helps her brother, who uses a wheelchair, get to campus. Rozsa-Horvath said she sometimes sleeps only four or five hours a night to complete everything she needs to.
She said her stress levels are “through the roof.”
Receiving counseling outside of CT State has been a part of her life, but she said it’s been tricky to stay on top of.
“I just started up therapy again recently because school was a lot,” Rozsa-Horvath said. “I had lost my job a while back, so then I didn’t have the funds to be driving from Bristol to Hartford.”
Rusch said her team’s research showed community college students benefit from a coordinated continuum of care, such as teletherapy, crisis supports and in-person professional counseling.
Ruth Pinto, the psychology student who sought help, said some people need that in-person support in order to heal. Pinto said the friend she connected with campus resources recently marked six months of sobriety, a major milestone.
“I’m so proud I could cry,” she said. “But it’s of happiness.”
This story was first published Oct. 21, 2026 by Connecticut Public.
Connecticut Public is part of the Mental Health Parity Collaborative, a group of newsrooms that are covering stories on mental health care access and inequities in the U.S. The partners on this project include The Carter Center and newsrooms in select states across the country.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah Legislature may take a look at accountability processes for tenured professors after audit
text:
The Capitol in Salt Lake City is pictured on Monday, May 6, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah lawmakers may soon evaluate how public universities hold tenured professors accountable after a legislative audit found the institutions struggle to correct instances in which faculty members are “persistently poor teachers.”
Auditors analyzed 666 performance reviews conducted in 2024 and 2025, which are required by law for all tenured faculty, and found that only eight of them were issued a teaching improvement plan. However, many had satisfactory scores despite having overwhelmingly low evaluations from students, the review showed. As a result, auditors said in a presentation to legislators this week that some students paid the price.
“Deans and department chairs described how much damage a single poor performer can inflict on a department when persistent underperformance is not corrected,” the audit says. “Poor instruction can contribute to students abandoning majors and academic programs, including in high-demand fields Utah needs. Even when students persisted through a course with poor instruction, they report being unprepared to succeed in their field.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In some cases of misconduct or violation of policy, universities avoided going through the established process for termination and instead negotiated separation agreements. That’s because apart from standards established in Utah law to terminate their employment, universities have their own sets of more complex policies that need to be followed, auditors said, which makes the termination process lengthy and expensive. 
But those agreements have also been pricey. A tenured faculty member who was found to have spent thousands of dollars on a university purchasing card for personal expenses bypassed the discipline protocol and was, instead, offered a separation agreement.
In exchange for leaving their post and not suing the university, the professor agreed to receive a $175,000 payment, a reference letter from the provost and the signature of a nondisclosure agreement to avoid discussing the circumstances of the separation case. 
That’s a case that left House Speaker Mike Schultz, R-Hooper, with questions about why it is so difficult to fire professors in the state.
“In some cases it’s the Legislature’s fault that we’ve what put into statute things and then allowed the universities to add policies on top of that that make it very difficult to get rid of somebody, even to the point to where I have clear violations of the law and policies, and taking advantage of the taxpayer, and we still had to pay them to leave,” Schultz said. “That’s what’s created this problem.”



Let us know what you think...


 


Senate Minority Leader Luz Escamilla, D-Salt Lake City, was also appalled by the practice.
“This is criminal, and I mean it’s also irresponsible of the institutions, if they think they can get away with this,” Escamilla said. “I mean, as a constituent, I’m very upset.”
The audit recommendation, Nick Varney, senior audit and operations supervisor said, is that the Legislature consider whether the minimum due process for removing tenured faculty specified in Utah code is excessive. Auditors also recommend the Utah Board of Higher Education consider requiring universities not establish processes for dismissing tenured faculty that go beyond what the law requires.
“As we looked at tenure as it’s been awarded throughout the institutions, we didn’t see any examples of academic freedom being harmed, where any faculty were terminated for academic freedom reasons, we didn’t see any of that,” Varney said. “Our primary concern is when it comes to an issue where faculty can and maybe should be terminated for cause.” 
The root cause for the lack of accountability among professors in less egregious cases, auditors said, is the traditional leadership model of academic departments, a rotating system that could undermine authority.
“Many of the department chairs that we spoke with described for us some structural barriers that limited their ability to lead effectively. Often, it was a matter of a lack of time, training, and authority,” Joe Hadfield, the supervisor of the audit told lawmakers. “But there were also some deeper issues where the incentives for performance for the leader were misaligned.”
Department chairs, for example, know that they are set to rotate back into the regular ranks of faculty after their leadership tenure, “so there’s an incentive to keep the peace” instead of making bold decisions to keep professors accountable, he said. Sometimes, a junior faculty member serving as department chair has to supervise the work of a higher ranked professor. 
“We recommend that the Board of Higher Education redefine department chair roles across institutions to position department chairs primarily as academic leaders, rather than faculty members with secondary leadership responsibilities,” the audit says. “Institutions should ensure that chairs have the time and support needed to carry out their leadership and supervisory responsibilities. This should enable chairs to provide stronger leadership and oversight within their departments.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Proposal for golf course at coastal WA state park draws furor
text:
(Larry Williams/Getty Images)A plan for a new Scottish links-style golf course at an oceanfront Washington state park has divided a community.
Proponents of the years-in-the-making proposal at Westport Light State Park say the course will be an economic boost for the small town, while opponents fear environmental disruption despite commitments from the developer to be a steward of the park’s habitat.
Over the course of a three-and-a-half-hour hearing in a nearly packed Aberdeen High School auditorium this week, the two sides aired their support and grievances.
On Wednesday, state parks commissioners expressed their skepticism, and for some downright opposition, of the project. They could decide its fate in November. 
The prognosis doesn’t look good for the developers to obtain the concession agreement they need to move forward.
Commission Chair Holly Williams said after seven years of conversations on the proposal, she’s reached a conclusion.
“Work on the project should be discontinued,” she said.
The city of Westport is neutral on the project, said Mayor Ed Welter. But Welter said this week that “delays, exhaustion and division have surrounded this.”
The proposal
The potential 18-hole public course would come with a short course, clubhouse, lodge with dozens of rooms, driving range and food options. By the mid-2030s, the project would bring in between $15 million and $18 million in revenue per year, according to the developers, Westport Golf Links, which is led by homebuilder Ryann Day. The company expects 26,000 visits in its first year of operation, a figure that would grow over time and be a boon for local restaurants, hotels and shops.
The course would be owned by Washington State Parks and constructed and run by the company. The revenue would be shared, with some going toward caring for state parks across the state. 
“We pay for it, and we address many of the public needs associated with the environment on site,” Day said.
The developers would also establish miles of new and improved trails and leave open the beach, which is popular among surfers. Day argues the links-style course, designed by Oregon’s Bandon Dunes architect David McLay Kidd, would be less disruptive to the habitat and use less water and fertilizer than traditional courses. 
Westport Golf Links will also try to bring dredged sand on Westport’s beaches and dunes to protect against coastal erosion without artificial armoring.

To make up for wetland fill for the golf course, the company notes it would restore or create 69 acres of wetlands elsewhere.
“Our goal with the Westport golf team is creating a vision of a healthier park in the future,” project manager Mark Merkelbach said, adding the company will continue to manage invasive species and monitor the habitat.
The Port of Grays Harbor supports the project. Port Commissioner Tom Quigg said it “offers a rare combination of economic, environmental, and recreational benefits.”
“Opportunities of this scale and potential are difficult to secure in a rural coastal community,” Quigg added.
The concept of a golf course here isn’t a new idea for locals. Another plan in the early 2000s fell through.
The problems
The state Department of Ecology labels the park’s interdunal wetlands as Category 1 due to the critical habitat they provide. The shore pine/slough sedge swamp forest there is considered “critically imperiled.”
The agency said Westport Golf Links leadership is underestimating the negative impacts its development would have on the wetlands. 
“We’re still seeing a net loss of ecological function from this project,” said Maria Sandercock, a regional section manager with the Department of Ecology.
The department estimates direct impact to over 30 acres of wetlands, and that’s higher than annual totals every year for the last 10 years, Sandercock told state parks commissioners. For reference, the Highway 167 expansion in Pierce County affected 25 acres of wetlands. The addition of a third runway at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport impacted 19 acres.
Sandercock said she doubts the project is permittable.
A judge last year tossed a lawsuit from local environmental groups seeking to stop the development over the proposed wetland fill.
The Quinault Indian Nation, which has a treaty right to fish in the area, opposes the development as proposed due to risks to nearby fish habitat.
Commissioner Laurie Connelly said that based on the environmental harms, focusing on potential economic benefit from the course development would mean “putting the cart before the horse.”
Given the natural resources concerns, Scott Merriman, the commission’s vice chair, said the project “doesn’t appear to comply with any of our policies,” and he hasn’t seen “any movement by the proponent to figure out how to honor and comply with our policies.”
“I don’t know how to move forward on this proposal as it’s currently configured,” Merriman said. “But I know we can’t spend much more time on it. We don’t have the staff resources. We don’t have the budget to do it.”
Day didn’t immediately provide comment for this story. He told commissioners this week that a lot of work remains to bring his idea to fruition: “Our sleeves are rolled up, and we’re ready to go.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: New Stage Theatre in Jackson hosts world premiere of Bobby Rush musical
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Three-time Grammy Award winner, 16-time Blues Music Awards winner, living blues legend and master showman Bobby Rush has entertained audiences worldwide in a career of more than seven decades, so safe to assume he is easy to spot, particularly at home in Jackson.
And yet, Rush managed to sneak into rehearsals at New Stage Theatre, as cast and crew careened toward opening night of a new musical about him, and hide. 
“I cheated a little bit, because I was here when they started, but I didn’t even want him to know,” Rush said, grinning as he pointed toward his co-writer on the musical and the show’s co-director and conceiver Stephen Helper. 
Rush scooched down in his seat to show how he hid about five rows back, lifting his head a bit for a peek at the action. He wanted to watch Helper’s reactions, see any changes in the show and judge whether actors liked the script (“You can always tell,” Rush said). But he didn’t want to make them nervous.
Then in rehearsal, the actor playing Rush walked down from the stage and into the aisle, playing to seats yet to be filled, when “Oh!” He found the man himself. “Mr. Rush is in the house, I see!”
Bobby Rush Credit: David McClister
Theater-goers will find Rush there, too — not ducking between rows, but in Rush’s life story up on the stage, from sharecropper to blues superstar with a big batch of his songs propelling the journey.  “Slippin’ Through the Cracks: The Bobby Rush Musical” has its world premiere this week at New Stage Theatre. 
A $49,000 National Endowment for the Arts grant supported the world premiere production. Visit Mississippi, Visit Jackson, Times Square Production and Hinds County Board of Supervisors are also sponsors.
The show’s title is a nod to the musician’s wits and persistence to slip through the cracks in obstacles such as prejudice, hardship and loss to pursue his dreams.
The show’s run through Nov. 1 is the culmination of a goal set years back.
The inspiration for it came through the car radio as playwright Helper, best-known for co-conceiving the Broadway smash hit “Smokey Joe’s Cafe,” drove down the road one day. Rush’s sly and saucy song “Sue” grabbed his ear, made him laugh and set up shop in his imagination.
Co-director/choreographer Matthew Johnson Harris (from left), show co-writer and blues legend Bobby Rush and co-writer/co-director/conceiver Stephen Helper gear up for the world premiere of “Slippin’ Through the Cracks: The Bobby Rush Musical” at New Stage Theatre. Credit: Sherry Lucas
“It was bluesy but really funny,” said Helper, who also recognized a bit of vaudeville timing in the tune. “Its timing is impeccable. I thought if I heard that song in a theater, I’d have a great, great time. That was the kernel.”
Research about Rush revealed a story ripe for telling on the theater stage, and Helper reached out about creating a musical. As he and Rush worked on the project, a partnership bloomed into friendship. New Stage Theatre has worked with the show’s creators since 2021.
“I wanted to grow it from its roots,” Helper said of the musical. New Stage Theatre helped shepherd it along.
New Stage’s summer 2022 workshop reading had actors in folding chairs with still photos projected overhead to set scenes. Even with that bare-bones setup, players’ skills, its powerful story and the score packed with Rush’s songs electrified the experience, for a show that guests lapped up and grooved to.
More than a half dozen actors from that workshop are back in the world premiere, including Mark Henderson as older Bobby Rush. Also returning for the premiere production are Hosea Griffith, Nicholas Patrick, Vershaune Stamps, Joy Brashears Amerson, Jayla M. Lomax and Chris Roebuck. They are joined by Actors’ Equity members Rajeer Alford and Melessie Clark, Jaden White, Grady Champion, Quintin Powell, Joe Tomberlin and Nancy Bigelow Cheney.
Money raised from the workshop helped fund a similar presentation in New York City, which raised money for a production. A one-night concert at Chicago’s Goodman Theatre kicked off that theater’s New Stages Festival in 2023.
“Then, it’s just been some perseverance on my part,” Helper said. Noting New Stage Artistic Director Francine Thomas Reynolds’ interest in helping further the show or do a production, “It’s just taken that amount of time to get a slot,” he said. In the meantime, he fleshed out some bits, and tucked others tighter.
Melessie Clark (from left), Jayla M. Lomax, Rajeer Alford, Mark G. Henderson, Jayden White and Joy Brashears Amerson perform in “Slippin’ Through the Cracks” in its world premiere run at New Stage Theatre. Credit: Destin Benford, courtesy of New Stage Theatre
Premiering it in the South was important, he said, “in the roots, from its culture, from a cast who really knows the blues, who knows Bobby Rush’s music. They are just born with a kind of knowledge that informs the show.” He and co-director/choreographer Matthew Johnson Harris can draw upon that to keep a real sense of authenticity.
“This is the chance to really try it all out, in front of an audience, not on folding chairs but with people who’ve paid money to come,” Helper said.
The setting is ripe, too, because it is Rush’s home. 
“He’s an international hero, but he’s also a local hero,” Helper added. “It’s important for a Jackson audience to celebrate its own.”
Choreographer Harris embraced his luck, working on this musical with Rush’s music and the sweep of time it covers. “The nearly 93 years that Bobby has been on this Earth allows me to really use African-American social dancing from the 1930s, ‘40s, ‘50s, ‘60s, ‘70s, ‘80s, ‘90s and 2000s, and tell a story of joy and resilience,” he said. It offers a glimpse, too, at the evolution of dance moves, from the Charleston in early juke joint sequences, to a more ‘90s-based Kid ‘n Play move in the second act.
“What I hope to bring through movement and also through, just, cultural dramaturgy, is a love letter to Bobby, to Mississippi, to Black culture, to Black dance,” Harris said, “and use that as another storytelling device to just track time.”
Amid all the song and dance in “Slippin’ Through the Cracks,” there runs a strong thread of resilience. 
“Any woman or man in life is doomed to fail,” Rush said. “It’s not if, it’s when. But when you fall and you can get up, that’s the important thing of life. If you can’t get up, have enough strength to turn over and look up.”
At 92, Rush is still learning, he said. “I still have hope. I’m still enthused about the things that I do. And I still would rather do it well enough to make sure that people like what I’m doing. 
“Even if they don’t like it, they can say, ‘Well, I don’t like Bobby Rush, but damn, he’s good.’” Rush chuckled, along with Helper and Harris. “That’s all that matters to me.”
Ditto for this musical about a lifelong entertainer. 
“It has to be good,” Rush said.
Inspiration is built into his tale of surviving and thriving, wrapped up in and swept along by the folk funk grooves, humor and heart that made Rush a blues superstar.
“If I can slip through the cracks and be where I’ve been, and who I am as a blues singer and a Black man at that — if I can make it, you can, too,” Rush said.
That is a message that has already hit home. Harris, though blessed to work in commercial theater in New York City for several years, still felt “othered” because of his humble beginnings, even in rooms with all-Black peers (some who’d gone to Yale or Juilliard) or in shows about Black lived experience, he said. 
Rush’s song “Just Be Yourself” became his mantra and a life goal, and seeing Rush live in concert was a liberation, he said.
“As he was up there, being so much himself, and he ended, saying, ‘If a dirt-poor country boy can make it, so can you,’” Harris said, his own perspective shifted. He told himself, “You are here, working on Broadway and you are thriving and you are a young Black man in 2026. Could you imagine being a young Black man in 1956, like Bobby had to be?”
That “you can, too” line has always been in this show, Helper said. 
“But when it’s represented and spoken by a man who can prove it and lived it and had to work around so many obstacles to achieve it … the content of those words is so much more profound.
“It’s a great thought and we all want to subscribe to it when it’s said by you,” Helper turned to Rush, “and hopefully by little Bobby Rush in our show, it will land in the same way.”
Performances of “Slippin’ Through the Cracks; The Bobby Rush Musical” continue at 7 nightly through Saturday, on Oct. 27 and Oct. 29-31, 2 p.m. Sunday and Nov. 1, and at a special 1 p.m. matinee on Oct. 28. Tickets — $50 with discounts for students, senior citizens, military and groups — are on sale at New Stage Theatre; call 601-948-3533 ext. 223 or visit newstagetheatre.com.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Lawmakers eye micro-hospitals as part of New Jersey’s healthcare future
text:
Lawmakers recently introduced a bill to enable licensed New Jersey hospitals to establish micro-hospitals, smaller facilities with lower costs that aim to expand access to care. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey could join a growing national trend under new legislation that would allow for micro-hospitals, small emergency care facilities with limited space for inpatients and lower operating costs than traditional hospitals. 
A handful of Democratic lawmakers recently introduced a bill to enable licensed New Jersey hospitals to establish micro-hospitals with up to 50 patient beds, as long as they are more than five miles from any competing acute care facility. The bill would also allow existing hospitals to convert or restructure an existing site as a micro-facility, with no restrictions on location. 
“We don’t want to lose hospitals in rural and underserved communities. That’s a big focus of the bill,” said bill sponsor Sen. Joe Vitale (D-Middlesex), chairman of the Senate health committee.
Under the proposal, micro-hospitals could offer primary and emergency care, lab, X-ray, and other hospital services, but would not be forced to support an operating room or surgical team, something that is required for acute care facilities in New Jersey. 
“It could be a way for hospitals to do what they do best, without worrying about services few patients use,” Vitale told the New Jersey Monitor.
The bill has not yet been scheduled for a hearing in the Legislature.
As proposed, the legislation calls for the state Department of Health to adopt necessary rules and regulations, but it would not create a new category of healthcare facilities under state law. Ambulatory surgery providers would not qualify to operate micro-hospitals unless they had a hospital license. 
The New Jersey Hospital Association, which represents hospitals, nursing homes and elder care programs, has yet to take a position on the bill. 
Micro-hospitals first emerged in the 1990s as a less-costly option to full acute-care facilities and are viewed as an effective way to reach rural patients and others who struggle to access medical services, according to a January 2026 article published by the National Institutes of Health. 
These facilities generally feature an emergency room with roughly ten beds, plus a similar number of inpatient beds, a lab, and limited imaging services. They are usually staffed by doctors, nurses, and emergency medical technicians, many of whom are cross-trained, but don’t have multiple specialists on-site. 
There is no nationwide tally of micro-hospitals, but the National Institutes of Health report said they tend to operate in states that don’t require a complex regulatory review for new hospital projects, like Texas, Colorado and, Arizona. Emerus, a nationwide for-profit hospital network, has teamed up with existing healthcare systems to open micro-hospitals in in Delaware and Pennsylvania.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska DED director defends grant management amid questions by state lawmakers
text:
Rendering of future Levi Carter Park Activity and Sports Complex at Levi Carter Park on the north shore of Carter Lake. That's in northeast Omaha near Eppley Airfield. The project is among recipients of a North and South Omaha Recovery Grant ($10 million). The grant program was the topic of a legislative special committee hearing Wednesday in Lincoln. Schemmer Architecture is the design team and Hausmann Construction is general contractor of this project site. (Courtesy of City of Omaha)LINCOLN — Amid concerns raised by a Nebraska legislative committee, the state’s director for economic development Wednesday defended her team’s handling of a roughly $235 million grant program aimed at lifting North and South Omaha.
The hearing before the Economic Recovery Special Committee featured a question-answer period between four lawmakers and invited managers of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development. DED oversees administration of pandemic-related grant programs.
State Sen. Terrell McKinney of North Omaha. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In the case of the “North and South Omaha Recovery Grant” program, funding originated from federal COVID-19 recovery dollars, but later was switched with state-funded projects to allow for more flexibility in meeting spending deadlines.
In January 2024, about 130 groups, ranging from Greater Omaha Chamber of Commerce leaders to lesser-known entrepreneurs, were awarded North-South grant funds for proposed projects intended to help transform some of the most distressed communities in the state.
State Sen. Terrell McKinney of North Omaha, the only original member of the special committee established in 2022, relayed concerns he said he’s heard from multiple grantees — that communication with DED staff has been “problematic and causing issues” in executing projects.
With an approaching December 2027 deadline for grantees to spend allotted awards, McKinney said, he was worried that some capital projects won’t be finished on time. 
 ‘Hard stop’ 

Projects include new or expanded youth-centric facilities, health clinics, a South Omaha park plaza makeover, a boost to a planned North Omaha global teleservices headquarters.
Maureen Larsen, director of the Nebraska Department of Economic Development, previously served as general counsel to the governor. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
McKinney said he’s fielded concerns about “everchanging reporting requirements” and alleged delays due to DED staff turnover. He wants “bottlenecks” to be cleared “sooner than later.”
Maureen Larsen, DED’s executive director, said she’d “be happy to look into” specific complaints if lawmakers provided names, and noted that grantees are held to contractual and statutory requirements. 
She said the department offers technical expertise to grantees yet one of the biggest complaints from her team is grantees that “ghost” the agency and ignore reporting and receipt requirements.
“We also have been, as a department, becoming compliant, hard stop,” said Larsen, who became the agency’s interim director in July 2025 and permanent director four months later. “We are working with past auditor findings. We are working with statutory requirements, rules, regulations and setting up best practices and policies for grant management.”
While some North-South projects are effectively finished, Larsen said none are officially “closed,” as funding was “front-loaded” and the agency awaits final documentation.
Among grantees whose project activities have been suspended, and who has criticized the process, is Randy J. Goodwin of Fallen Giant Films. His $5 million grant was to be used to build a Hollywood-esque industry that would help retain youth and grow the local economy. DED cited “significant noncompliance with respect to the financial management of its grant funds.”
Larsen acknowledged “high turnover rate” in the Omaha office working with North-South grantees and said the Pillen administration is hiring and also tapping temporary workers to add “bandwidth” to that team. Larsen said many Omaha-based DED workers have left for jobs offered by grantees they had worked with as state employees.
“Unfortunately, we can’t compete with some of the nonprofits and private sector, but we do try,” Larsen said.
She said DED wants the North and South Omaha economic development projects to succeed and encouraged grantees to wrap up work by the deadline. If the projects are not finished, she said, state lawmakers likely would decide next steps.
 ‘Huge concerns’

State Sen. Margo Juarez of South Omaha, a new member of the committee, said she was alarmed Wednesday by what she heard.
Omaha moviemaker says state-funded venture paralyzed as DED stretches suspension of $5M grant

“I have huge concerns, no doubt about it,” she said after the meeting. She said there appeared in some cases to be a communication gap on what is expected of grantees.
Other special committee members present at the hearing — where testimony was limited to the invited DED administrators — were state Sens. Christy Armendariz of Omaha and Jason Prokop of Lincoln.
After the meeting, McKinney — who was among the group of North and South Omaha lawmakers that pushed for the grant program years ago — said he was “still processing” Wednesday’s discussion. He said he had unanswered questions and was awaiting answers from DED staff.
“I’ll be concerned until the grant program is completed and everybody is done with their projects,” he said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: District 10 is up for grabs as new candidates Johnson, Rens fight for open seat in state Legislature
text:
The 2026 candidates for  Legislative District 10, from left: Cindy Johnson of Omaha and Rebecca Rens of Bennington. State Sen. Wendy DeBoer of Omaha is term-limited. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — In the politically split District 10, a seat in the Nebraska Legislature is up for grabs with its current representative ineligible for reelection.
State Sen. Wendy DeBoer of Bennington is term-limited after serving two consecutive terms representing the district, which encompasses a portion of northwestern Omaha and Douglas County. In her place, audiologist Cindy Johnson and small business owner Rebecca Rens are fighting for the seat.
The district is near equal in terms of the party registrations of its voter base. According to the latest voter registration statistics from the Nebraska Secretary of State, there are 9,920 registered Republicans, 9,260 Democrats along with 7,246 nonpartisan voters in the area.
The two candidates have taken different approaches in addressing party politics in their campaigns. Rens, a Republican, said she doesn’t hide her party affiliation when talking to voters, despite some saying her campaign is fighting an uphill battle because of it.
DeBoer is a Democrat, and has endorsed Johnson, but Johnson said she’s received support from across the political aisle. She said many voters she has encountered were once registered to a party, but have since absconded because they were frustrated by both sides.
“What I really think needs to happen is we’ve got to quit putting people in boxes,” Johnson said. “We’re not left and right. We’re not red and blue. We’re all Nebraskans.”
Neither Rens nor Johnson have been elected into office before, though Johnson currently serves in an appointed role as a representative on the Learning Community Coordinating Council for Douglas and Sarpy counties. Both candidates said they felt it was the right time and place for them to run.
Rens worked as the president and owner of a concrete construction company in northwest Iowa for more than three decades before moving to Omaha several years ago to be closer to her adult children. Since then, she started a small consulting firm, and said she’s found many similarities between running a business and campaigning.
“You are going out, you’re getting to know your people,” Rens said. “Rather than clients, I have voters.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Johnson started an audiology practice in Norfolk before moving to Omaha in 2010 to work for Children’s Nebraska. She currently works part-time providing hearing valuations to veterans. She said she is a former president of the Nebraska Speech-Language-Hearing Association, and has worked with the Nebraska Legislature in the past on hearing legislation.
From her perspective, Johnson said many of the voters in District 10 feel like their voices are not being heard in the Legislature, particularly after lawmakers slow-walked the implementation of several successful ballot measures in 2024. She said voters appear to be most frustrated by the response to the legalization of medical cannabis.
Johnson said voters are also concerned about taxes and the increasing cost of living in the state. She said working class residents have expressed that working multiple jobs sometimes isn’t enough to get by anymore, and they’re agitated watching others get ahead in front of them.
“If we’re going to be a pro-life state, then that means we take care of everybody,” Johnson said.
Rens said property taxes are at the top of District 10 concerns according to her conversations with voters. She said the instability of property valuations is making it harder for Nebraska to attract new businesses, residents and jobs, and said the state’s overall tax system may be in need of an overhaul.
“We can’t simply shift from one group to another and call it reform,” Rens said.
Both Rens and Johnson said they want to focus on affordability issues, if elected. Rens said she doesn’t support tax increases or tax shifts to make room for property tax cuts, but said she is interested in looking for new revenue streams.
Johnson said she is open with voters when asked that she does not have all the answers, but tells them that all options would be on the table.
“Any politician who says they have all the answers is probably lying to you,” Johnson said.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming family’s near-death experience inspires medical operas
text:
When Jeff and Nancy Lockwood arrived at their son’s hospital bed in Wenatchee, Washington, thousands of miles away from their home in Laramie, Ethan was on a ventilator and couldn’t speak. 
A head-on collision with a truck driven by a drowsy driver had left Ethan with 13 fractures, a brain injury and life-threatening damage to his heart. Doctors and nurses had gotten him through the night, including emergency surgery, before his parents arrived that morning in 2024.
“I don’t know the rules, so I ask the nurse, ‘Can I, you know, can I touch him?’” Jeff Lockwood told WyoFile. 
Wash your hands first, the nurse instructed.
“Not only can you touch him,” Lockwood recalls her saying, “But stand at his bedside, hold his hand as long as you can. Talk to him. Eat your meal in here. Smells, sounds, and touch are getting in. We don’t know exactly how this works with the comatose brain, but we know empirically that survival rates, recovery rates are much higher with this kind of contact.”
“So we did,” he said.  
Ethan’s accident and the grueling months of recovery that followed forced the family to confront not just their own mortality, but the power and limits of medical knowledge. They also realized, Jeff said, the challenges that healthcare providers face in integrating technical expertise with human compassion. Altogether, the experience inspired Jeff to write “Hurting, Healing, Hoping: A Trio of Medical Operas,” which premieres in Laramie this weekend. 
Baritone singer Dante Mireles, left, performs during a dress rehearsal of “Hurting, Healing, Hoping: A Trio of Medical Operas,” on Oct. 21, 2026, in Laramie. (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
Lockwood, a recently retired professor of philosophy and creative writing, said he hopes the operas will foster mutual understanding between patients, providers and caregivers. 
“One of things I want the opera to do is what I think a good professor does, or a good minister does,” he said. “And that is: I want to comfort the afflicted and afflict the comfortable. Those in the audience who are going through stuff, I want them to know they’re not alone. And those sometimes young people who assume that stuff happens to old people like me, or that bad stuff happens to other people, I want to discomfort people a little bit.” 
Each of the three 20-minute pieces shares a narrative thread, and together they’re designed to be accessible to a wide audience. The libretto, or lyrics, will also be projected over the stage. 
“This is a great starter opera,” Lockwood said, adding that an aficionado can also expect to appreciate it. 
Lockwood worked with composer Michael Udow, who will also conduct the performances. Udow spent 42 years as the principal percussionist with the Santa Fe Opera and 27 years teaching at the University of Michigan. 
The opera’s three singers will include tenor Thomas Bocchi, baritone Dante Mireles and mezzo-soprano Magdalena Wór. They will perform with an orchestra mainly featuring University of Wyoming Department of Music faculty members, including John Fadial, Jiwon Han, Ross McIntosh and Beth Vanderborgh. Sophia Oehlers Maeda, a Colorado oboist, will join them. 
Magdalena Wór and Thomas Bocchi, center, perform during a dress rehearsal of “Hurting, Healing, Hoping: A Trio of Medical Operas,” on Oct. 21, 2026 in Laramie. (Tennessee Watson/WyoFile)
While Lockwood has written a dozen fiction and nonfiction books, he said he chose opera in this instance because he believes it is the ideal art form for moving minds and touching hearts. This is his sixth opera. 
“Words tend to be something that we process rationally, analytically, cognitively. I mean, they can evoke feeling but not like music,” he said. “When you say, ‘God, I don’t have words for it,’ What you’re saying is, ‘I need music.’”
The opera’s two performances will take place at 7 p.m. on October 23 and 24 at the Gryphon Theatre in Laramie Plains Civic Center. Tickets can be purchased online. All proceeds will go to the Laramie Downtown Clinic.

name: WyoFile
title: Being an election judge
text:
Opinion

Along with many of my neighbors, I have felt a certain anxiety about our upcoming elections. Much of my worry derives from an array of false statements President Donald Trump has made suggesting that our elections are rigged. From his claim that Hillary Clinton didn’t actually receive more popular votes than he did in 2016 to his endless statements claiming that Joseph Biden did not win the 2020 presidential election, Mr. Trump has for years attempted to sow doubt and discord concerning the integrity of our elections. He accuses Democrats of going to great lengths to skew results in their favor while providing little evidence to back up his assertions.
On the face of it, the president’s claims seem baseless. The Republican Party holds the presidency and the majority of seats in both Congress and the Senate. Twenty-six states have Republican governors while 28 have Republican-controlled legislatures. If the Democrats are skewing results in their favor, they’re certainly not very good at it.
The president has also claimed that millions of people vote illegally and consequently, he has demanded a number of investigations into voter fraud, a notable recent example being in Nevada, where the White House claimed up to 16,000 people were illegally registered to vote. Pressed to provide evidence for this claim, the White House dropped the number of potentially illegally registered voters to 185. That’s about .00009% of Nevada’s 2,506,232 registered voters.
Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar noted that when state election officials received the list of the voter numbers flagged as possible noncitizens, it checked voter registration records, including the type of ID included in registration applications and found no evidence of anyone on the list being a noncitizen. Aguilar stated, “Our records do not support the Department of Homeland Security’s claims, and DHS has still not provided evidence to change that. Instead, DHS officials continue their attempts to intimidate election officials into compliance and deter voters with huge claims of fraud with no evidence. Repeating unsupported claims does not make them true.”
Recently the president has said he may send federal officers, including ICE agents, to monitor elections. That ought to give us all the willies not only because ICE officers have behaved violently and outside the law but because Article I, Section 4, Clause 1 of the U.S. Constitution reads, “The Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof;…” This clearly places the responsibility for elections in the hands of the states and state control of elections has been upheld in our courts throughout American history. One important result of keeping elections in the hands of the states is that it puts election administration closer to the voters.  
Here’s an example: I was for many years an election judge — a poll worker — in my community, walking over in the early morning to the Catholic Rec Hall on Election Day to welcome and assist voters. Our duties as judges included setting up the polling place and the voting equipment, directing voters to the correct precinct tables, distributing ballots and showing people how to vote, making sure every qualified voter was able to vote, closing the polling place at the end of the voting time and determining and certifying the results.
I knew a great many of the voters. They lived in my neighborhood. Many were friends or acquaintances. Those I didn’t know, I often recognized, having seen them in shops and businesses or at high school plays or sporting events or at the library auction. Voting day gave me a chance to say hello to a lot of people, to get to know the ones I hadn’t met before and to be of service in my community.
Because election judges and voters knew each other, we had faith in each other. I knew the voters weren’t illegally casting their votes, and the voters knew I wasn’t trying to illegally influence the election. 
Wyoming law requires that election judges “be divided between the participating political parties as equally as possible.” Because I’m a registered Democrat in a heavily Republican area, this meant that I was in demand as an election judge. So if you want to see what the job’s like, register Democratic. The county clerk will soon be calling and you’ll find yourself sitting at the polling station for very long days chatting with fellow poll workers from different political parties.
This is how we learn to trust in our elections, how we maintain faith in the integrity of those elections. It’s not by having agents of the federal government with masks and weapons suddenly arrive in town, but by recognizing that it is our friends and neighbors who help administer and verify the honesty of our elections, people with whom we share our communities and our democratic ideals.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Where are the debates? Idaho incumbents largely forgo debates and forums this year.
text:
From left to right: Coeur d'Alene attorney Arthur "Art" Macomber, former Idaho Congressman Raúl Labrador and incumbent Idaho Attorney General Lawrence Wasden debate on Idaho Public Television on April 19, 2022. (Photo by Aaron Kunz/Idaho Public Television)During the 2026 election cycle, Idaho voters have had very few opportunities to see Republican incumbents answer questions at live, public events. 
For years it was the norm for major candidates in statewide and federal races to appear live and debate each other.
Journalist Betsy Z. Russell asks a candidate question during an Idaho Public Television debate on May 6, 2016. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger)
“It was a tradition in Idaho,” said Betsy Russell, former longtime president of the Idaho Press Club and current president for Idahoans for Openness in Government. “That was how candidates, including incumbents seeking reelection, got out there and put their views and how they contrasted with those of their opponents, in front of all voters all across the state of Idaho.” 
Idaho Public Television, which for years has broadcast its Idaho Debates series statewide, did not have the staffing to put on the events this year, according to Melissa Davlin, IPTV producer and Idaho Press Club president. 
“I do think there are some incumbents who would have said yes to debates had that been a possibility,” Davlin said. 
Davlin also noted that there’s a national trend of candidates from both major parties declining debates. Of the 35 U.S. Senate seats up for election this year, 21 of them had no debate between the major candidates, ABC News reported. Similarly, of the 36 governors up for election, 21 of those races had no debate scheduled between two major-party candidates. 
“This is not Idaho-specific,” Davlin said. “… and you could say a big part of that is the siloing of social media. People who are running for office often have or feel like they have a direct line to voters.” 
The League of Women Voters of Idaho this year held forums for U.S. Senate candidates and gubernatorial candidates. The Republican incumbents in both of those races declined to participate. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s campaign spokesman previously told the Sun that he declined that forum because the individual who reached out to him to ask about participation had endorsed his opponent. The league’s president Jean Henscheid told the Sun that individual, former state Rep. Julie Yamamoto, had reached out in her own capacity and was not one of the event’s organizers. 
Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s campaign manager Joan Vargas did not directly answer a question about why the governor has not participated in debates this election cycle.  
“Governor Little has a proven track record of providing Idahoans historic tax relief, promoting a strong economy, cutting red tape, responsibly managing state government. On his watch, Idaho has made record investments in schools, roads, water, and other areas. Those historic accomplishments and facts are non-debatable,” Vargas wrote. 
“Governor Little has made it a priority to meet with Idaho families, businesses, and members of the press. Idahoans know what Governor Little stands for. They know he will continue to fight for them and make our state the place where our children and grandchildren choose to stay.”
Little was the only incumbent statewide elected official to not respond to the Idaho Capital Sun’s 2026 general election candidate survey. 
 Idaho candidates had a long history of debating until 2022 

Elinor Chehey has helped organize debates with the League of Women Voters of Idaho since the 1970s. 
“It seemed to go real well through the ’90s and since 2000 … and then suddenly in the last five or six years, it’s been different,” Chehey said. “With less participation.” 
The last election cycle that included races for federal office as well as all of Idaho’s statewide constitutional officers was in 2022. 
That year, Idaho Public Television hosted televised debates among Republican primary and general election candidates for secretary of state, attorney general, and superintendent of public instruction. It also hosted debates for general election contests for U.S. Senate and lieutenant governor. 
In this file photo, U.S. Congressman Mike Simpson, R-Idaho, speaks during the Salmon Orca Summit IV on the grounds of the U.S. Capitol on July 14, 2022, in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Jemal Countess/Getty Images)
Incumbents Little and U.S. Rep. Mike Simpson both announced at the time they would not participate in primary election debates, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher also joined Little and Simpson in declining to debate for the general election that year. 
Little became the first sitting governor seeking reelection to not debate his opponent, Russell said. 
“And that launched a cascade of other top officials, pretty much all Republican incumbents, who declined to debate their opponents,” Russell said. 
That year, there were also several general election debates that didn’t happen because the Democratic candidates declined, Davlin said, but the incumbents who refused were notable because they were “outliers.” 
“It used to make headlines when people weren’t willing to debate, because the expectation was that candidates would participate,” she said. 
Ahead of the 2022 debates, Simpson told the Idaho Press, “Republican voters don’t need to hear anything more from Bryan Smith,” referring to Simpson’s second-time primary opponent for Idaho’s 2nd Congressional District.
This year, Simpson campaign spokesperson Sarah Nelson told the Sun that the congressman only received one invitation for a forum hosted by the League of Women Voters of Idaho, “but unfortunately it didn’t work with the Congressman’s congressional schedule.” 
“The Congressman has always been willing to participate in debates as they work with his congressional schedule,” Nelson said. 
Fulcher’s campaign could not be reached for comment for this story.   
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Incumbent Idaho state superintendent bucks trend, participates in three debates

Incumbent Republican Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield participated in three out of four planned debates or forums ahead of her general election contest. 
Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield enters the House of Representative chambers to listen to Gov. Brad Little give his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“I saw it as an opportunity to highlight and showcase the work I had done, particularly being able to go back and say four years ago, I said this is what I was going to do if you elected me, and I delivered on the results,” Critchfield said.
She withdrew from the planned debate held by the news station KTVB, because the Constitution Party candidate Teresa Roundy in the race didn’t meet the organizer’s qualifications to participate and was not invited. 
Critchfield previously participated in a debate co-organized by Idaho Education News and the College of Idaho and a forum hosted by the Idaho Association of School Administrators. 
The school administrators association forum included all candidates in the race: Critchfield, Roundy and Democrat Becky Sundin Mitchell. The Idaho EdNews debate had a campaign-fundraising threshold for participation that Roundy’s campaign did not meet, because the Constitution Party candidate has not reported any campaign contributions this year, according to the Idaho Secretary of State’s database. 
Critchfield said after she participated in an event in which Roundy was excluded, she “felt that was wrong.” She chose not to participate in another debate in which one of the candidates would be excluded. 
“All three of us had to work to get our names on the final ballot, and people were already voting,” Critchfield said of her decision to opt out of the KTVB debate. 
On Oct. 12, all three state superintendent candidates participated in a debate hosted by Idaho News 6. 
She said she still felt criticized for dropping out of one, despite being the only statewide elected officer participating in any debates. 
“It was just nonstop commentary, and so I had to laugh a little bit at myself because I thought I was the one willing to do it, and not only did I do it once, but I did it three times,” she said. 
She said she doesn’t know why her colleagues have opted out, but can understand a hesitancy to participate. 
“I think there’s some trust issues,” she said. “And I can understand that and appreciate it because I just did three, and I get it.” 
 Idaho federal office challengers call on incumbents to debate 

Shortly after U.S. Sen. Jim Risch won his primary contest in May, independent challenger Todd Achilles publicly called for a debate.
Risch’s campaign couldn’t be reached for comment on this story. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, gives a speech at the service for former Gov. Phil Batt at the Idaho Capitol in Boise on March 9, 2023. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
Risch has participated in debates in the past, including the 2014 general election debate on KTVB, and the 2020 general election Idaho Public Television Idaho Debates event, which took place over Zoom. 
In his 2006 run for lieutenant governor, Risch declined to participate in the live public television debate after the station refused his request to appear separately from his opponent Democrat Larry LaRocco to answer questions, the Associated Press reported at the time. Risch said then that he was concerned about “disruptive behavior” from his opponent. 
In 2008, he again skipped the public TV debate for the May Republican primary and appeared in the taped KTVB debate, the Spokesman-Review reported. 
This year, the Achilles campaign recorded a video of the independent candidate approaching Risch to ask him to debate at the Boise Airport ahead of a ceremony to remember 9/11. Risch did not respond to Achilles in the video. 
The campaign for Democrat Kaylee Peterson, who is challenging 1st Congressional District U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher also posted a video of her approaching her opponent to ask for a debate. Peterson told the Sun the video was recorded at a Shoshone County GOP event. 
U.S. Rep. Russ Fulcher, R-Idaho, speaks with Republican supporters at the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove Hotel in Boise on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
In the video, Fulcher says, “First lesson in campaigning is don’t help your opponent.” 
“… In all fairness, I think this is the third time, whatever you’re selling, Idahoans aren’t buying,” Fulcher said in the video, addressing Peterson, who has run for federal office twice before. “I’m not going to help you.” 
Peterson told the Sun she thought, “how he behaved was pretty shocking.”
“I think his reaction wasn’t something you want to see from leadership,” she said.
The Idaho League of Women voters tried to schedule a forum with 1st Congressional District candidates, but the venue canceled the reservation. Zabel held a town hall herself on Oct. 20, but Peterson said her campaign had by then agreed to attend an event elsewhere. 
Peterson and independent candidate Sarah Zabel are slated to appear at a candidate forum Oct. 23 in Moscow, hosted by the local chapter of the progressive group Indivisible. Independent gubernatorial candidate John Stegner and Libertarian U.S. Senate candidate Matt Loesby are also expected to attend the Moscow forum. 
The Moscow-Pullman Daily News reported that Fulcher, Risch and Little declined to participate in this event.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee Republicans want electrocution or firing squads to replace lethal injection
text:
After two executions by lethal injection were botched in a matter of months, Tennessee lawmakers are considering alternative methods of execution, including the electric chair. (Photo: Getty Images)Tennessee Republican lawmakers are ready to change the state’s death penalty laws in the wake of two botched executions by lethal injection, including a renewed look at electrocution and firing squads.
Republican Rep. Jody Barrett of Dickson confirmed this week he is considering sponsoring legislation in 2027 to make firing squads a method for putting people to death, even though one Democratic lawmaker called the practice “depraved.”
Republican Sen. Tom Hatcher also said he is having a bill drafted that would either remove lethal injection from the execution process or reform it based on the results of a third-party investigation Gov. Bill Lee ordered after the failed execution of convicted murderer Christa Pike in September. Hatcher, a first-term senator from Maryville, acknowledged that eliminating lethal injection would leave electrocution as the only way allowed to put people to death.
“I think we’ve gotta do away with lethal injections,” Hatcher said. Short of that, he said the process needs to be changed and possibly have a standard third-party investigation for each execution, regardless of the outcome “to keep us and the public aware of what’s going on.”

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
He added he has spoken with other lawmakers who are looking at other options but said he’s not filing a bill for alternatives.
Tennessee allows death row inmates convicted before 1999 to choose the electric chair. Electrocution also is allowed if lethal injections drugs are unavailable or if lethal injection is found unconstitutional.
Asked what steps he would take if the governor’s third-party investigation comes back with a report saying lethal injections can be carried out effectively, Hatcher said it wouldn’t conflict with his plans and noted he could file legislation that could be amended based on the final report.
Barrett confirmed he’s exploring all options, including a firing squad. Other lawmakers, including Republican Rep. Paul Sherrell, broached the idea recently of public hangings to deter crime.
“After the trouble we’ve had with at least the last four years with the lethal injection, all alternatives need to be looked at,” Barrett said.
Such moves are likely to run into legal challenges that could last for years.
Democratic Rep. Aftyn Behn called the use of firing squads and hangings “depraved and ungodly.”
The governor put a last-minute hold on executions in May 2022 before the execution of Oscar Smith because the state failed to conduct required testing for the lethal injection drugs. 
Former U.S. Attorney Ed Stanton, who is handling the newest probe, conducted a previous third-party investigation of the state’s protocol, chemical testing and Department of Correction procedures. That study led to new protocol, yet two of the state’s last three executions failed this year. 
Tennessee GOP senators seek review of botched execution

A group of Republican senators urged Lee to conduct another investigation of the state’s death penalty procedures before the botched Pike execution, but he declined.
Barrett said Utah and South Carolina are using firing squads to carry out the death penalty and added that some experts are testifying that a firing squad is more humane than other alternatives, “a quicker, more painless death.” Other states allowing use of firing squads are Oklahoma, Mississippi and Idaho, the latter of which makes firing squads the principal means of execution. 
“If that’s truly the case, I think it’s something we should explore as a state, as a possible alternative to what we’re doing currently that doesn’t seem to be working very smoothly,” Barrett said.
Barrett said he’s been “adamant” for six to eight months that the state’s lethal injection protocol needs more “transparency.” If problems can’t be resolved by changing the protocol, lawmakers need to consider other methods as long as the state keeps the death penalty, he said.
Sen. Ken Yager also is among those saying the state needs to find other options, though he declined to say Wednesday whether he supports the use of firing squads.
“When a convicted murderer is sentenced to death, the state must be able to carry out the lawful sentence effectively. As we examine the best path forward to improve the process, I am open to considering other constitutionally sound methods of execution to ensure justice is delivered for victims and their families,” Yager, a Kingston Republican, said in a statement.
