name: Alabama Reflector
title: Campaigning around Alabama, Doug Jones tries to open a path for Democrats
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones speaking at a mock debate on Oct. 21, 2026, in Birmingham, Alabama. Jones faces an "uphill chug" to the governor's mansion, but he said the race is more about building infrastructure for the Democratic Party. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones, the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, faces an uphill battle to the governor’s mansion against his Republican opponent U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville, but he said his campaign is about building the Alabama Democratic Party.
Should Jones win, he will face a “hostile” Republican supermajority in the Legislature.
Alabama Democrats have the largest slate of candidates since 2018, leading to a stability within the party that the new chair attributes to Jones’ candidacy.




Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones pulled raffle tickets out of a campaign hat. In the audience, members teased the Democratic gubernatorial nominee about picking attendees in the front row to ask questions.  
“I did not set that up, folks. I promise you, I didn’t set it up,” he said after two people in a row came from the front row. The crowd of more than 300 at the September town hall in Anniston laughed. 
The next voter was also on the front row. The fourth voter was not on the front row, but he was close.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“I’m gonna go with 715,” he said as the voter raised his hand and the crowd laughed. “OK, moving back a little bit.”
Town halls like the one in Anniston have shaped Jones’ campaign. The candidate has used them to tout his proposals and draw contrasts with Republican gubernatorial nominee Tommy Tuberville. 
But Jones said in a recent interview that running for governor in Alabama as a Democrat remains an “uphill chug.”
“We’ve just got to grind it out, and we’ve got to stick to what we believe is the right thing in terms of what we want to do with state government,” Jones said. “We’ve also just got to stick with our process of not getting distracted with too much of the day-to-day stuff. Not get distracted with polls, not get distracted with all the money that Tuberville’s raised.”
Two polls released Tuesday showed the challenge the Democratic gubernatorial nominee faces. Both The Alabama Poll, run by Michael Lowry, a former aide to U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, and a poll conducted by the right-leaning Cygnal for Alabama Daily News and Gray Television found  51% of respondents said they would likely vote for Tuberville, and 39% for Jones, leaving about 9% undecided. 
Jones, who defeated former Alabama Supreme Court Chief Justice Roy Moore in a special election for the U.S. Senate in 2017, is the only Democrat to have won a statewide race in Alabama in the last 18 years.  
Tuberville has outraised Jones by nearly 2 to 1, bringing in almost $16.5 million since he launched his campaign in May 2025 to Jones’ roughly $6.4 million since his December launch. Messages seeking comment from the Tuberville campaign were left unanswered. 
But in a year where Democrats around the country appear to be on the offensive, other gaps appear to be narrower. Democrats saw increased turnout in May’s primary. In September, Jones raised $1.12 million to Tuberville’s $1.13 million. Jones outraised Tuberville by almost $6,000 in October’s first weekly report, reporting $258,500 in cash contributions to Tuberville’s $252,800. In October’s second weekly report, Tuberville outraised Jones by $130,000, though Jones outspent the Republican nominee.
Whether Jones can become the first Democrat to win an Alabama gubernatorial race since 1998 is uncertain. But for Jones, winning on Nov. 3 may be less a marker of success than rebuilding the Democratic Party.
“We haven’t invested in party infrastructure. We haven’t invested in candidates. We’re doing that now, and one of these days, I believe that one or both of the houses will flip majorities. But it’s not going to happen this year,” Jones said. “I think narrowing the gap in many places, which I think we can do, is success. Success is a building process.” 
David Hughes, a political science professor at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette who previously spent time at Auburn University at Montgomery, said in a phone interview Wednesday that if Tuesday’s polling is right, it would be a D+10 shift in Alabama’s R+20 environment. That would not be enough to win, but it could flip some Legislative seats.
“Flipping any seats is a win for the party,” he said. “They need to go after suburban districts with higher socioeconomic status voters, so folks with more education, more income. That’s where Democrats are rebuilding their brand right now.”
Travel around the state
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones’ “On the Road to Change” bus as seen on Oct. 13, 2026, in downtown Montgomery, Alabama. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)
Jones’ town halls and rallies, usually occurring on weeknights, take place across the state: in cities like Montgomery and Mobile, rural towns and safe Republican counties. Jones held his 20th town hall since July 1 in Tuscaloosa on Monday night. 
They draw crowds of varying sizes: 300 in Anniston, 300 in Shelby County, about 50 in Lowndes County, 400 in Baldwin County, 330 in Mobile, 130 in the Shoals and 2,000 at a rally in Huntsville. 
Jones said in a recent interview that no matter where he goes, he hears the same thing from voters. He said Alabamians are concerned about the rising cost of living, healthcare and a lottery.
“We’ll be doing more town halls, but the fact of the matter is, if you are going to be a governor for everybody, you’ve got to let folks know that you are there for them and you’re listening to them,” he said.
Voter concerns enhance Jones’ laundry list of policy priorities that he launched with in December. 
He wants to expand Medicaid, constitutionally protect IVF, independently audit the state’s prisons, end straight-ticket voting, push for early voting, “phase out” the state’s school voucher program, implement a lottery and enact a one-year moratorium on data centers. 
Doug Jones calls for affordability measures, government reforms in policy speech

If he wins, Jones will still need the support of the Alabama Legislature to fund most of his priorities. The Legislature has been controlled by a Republican supermajority since 2010, and GOP control of the chambers is almost guaranteed to persist after Nov. 3: nearly every Democratic nominee for the Legislature, many running in deep-red districts, would have to win to reverse that. 
The governor is also weak relative to the House and Senate, which can override gubernatorial vetoes by simple majority votes. But Jones says he can work with the Legislature. 
“Sit down on it, get a bourbon, talk about it, find out what they want, what it is they really are looking at and what they need. Let them hear what we really need, and we just talk and we find common ground,” he said. “I did that in the U.S. Senate.”
At the Anniston town hall in early September, he touted the 2019 elimination of the Widow’s Tax – a bill he co-sponsored with Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine. 
He markets the events as “unscripted” and often stays afterward to answer questions or greet voters. At the Anniston town hall, one voter asked Jones to pull his number to no avail.
Jones replied with a drawn-out “No, now let’s don’t get too anxious. I’ll see if I can find it in here, though. I’m sorry.” 
That voter’s raffle ticket was not picked, but Jones stays after for anybody that has questions or just wants to say hello.
Challenges ahead
Former U.S. Sen. Doug Jones waiting to go on stage at his gubernatorial campaign kickoff event in Birmingham, Alabama, on Dec. 12, 2025. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
The winner of next month’s election will likely face challenges from the get-go. Former Finance Director Bill Poole and Legislative Fiscal Officer Kirk Fulford have repeatedly warned state agencies that fiscal year 2028 will be “challenging” and budgets will need to be conservative. The state’s two public employee insurance boards are seeking more funding and increasing premiums or direct costs amid rising healthcare costs. 
Jones said in an interview that additional revenue from a lottery could help that. 
“I make no illusions about the challenges. I’ve said that in my town halls. This is not going to be, ‘These are the things that we want to do, and we’re going to do everything we can to try to find a way to do them,’” he said. “I think that there is potential revenue out there in other sources.”
Alabama is the last state east of the Mississippi to not have a lottery. According to a 2021 projection from the Legislative Fiscal Office, a lottery in Alabama would generate $272 million to $358 million. That additional revenue, Jones said, could also fund other priorities like Medicaid expansion. 
Jones said in an interview that there has always been an “appetite” for expanding the program, but never the will. He said he will do it with an executive order, leaving the Legislature to fund it.
“They hide under the guise of ‘oh the money.’ The fact is, 40 states have done this. They have found a way to do it,” Jones said. “That has clearly been a political issue.”
Hughes said Jones’ agenda would likely face many obstacles in the Legislature, especially after recent social media exchanges between the nominee and House Speaker Nathaniel Ledbetter, R-Rainsville.
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro (left) speaks with Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, on the floor of the Alabama Senate on April 8, 2026 at the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. (Brian Lyman/Alabama Reflector)
“They would almost certainly have a tempestuous relationship. In Alabama, the Legislature largely drives the bus, and so you know you’d see a situation in other southern states that have elected Democratic governors where the legislature just overrides their veto left and right,” Hughes said.
Outgoing state Sen. Greg Albritton, R-Atmore, said in a phone interview Monday that the political divisiveness in Montgomery has only gotten worse, and he sees no catalyst on the horizon that could change that.
“Unless they had some kind of meeting that they could agree on something,” he said. “But I just don’t know that that will happen politically. The right and left are just too far apart.” 
Senate Minority Leader Bobby Singleton, D-Greensboro, the chair of the Alabama Democratic Party, said in an interview Tuesday that he hopes Republicans could work towards “betterment of the state of Alabama” even with a Democratic governor. 
“It’s no different than with the Republicans being in power now. We don’t always agree with what we call their ‘Red Meat Agenda’ and the things that they want to get done,” he said. “There are also things that we are able to compromise on and make it work for both parties and for the state.”
Albritton said the only way Jones could get something done with a Republican supermajority would be through finding common ground, but said there is not much of it.
“He will be looking at a hostile legislative environment. It will be great fun for political observers, and no one else,” he said. 
Issue contrasts 
A mural outside the Doug Jones for Governor headquarters in Birmingham, Alabama, as seen on Sept. 30, 2026. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Data centers have become a major part of the race. Jones has said he will push for a one-year moratorium on construction of new facilities. That, he said, will give the Legislature time to pass guardrails and restrictions to ensure transparency. 
He said in an interview that he would enact the moratorium through an executive order, but would much rather the Legislature do it. 
“The best thing would be to work hard, get the people in place, and get those guardrails in place so that you can just lift it,” he said. 
Tuberville’s position has wavered. In July, he embraced the technology, saying “we’re going to do data centers,” and called community concerns “bullcrap.” In an opinion column in September, Tuberville said as governor he would work to give communities the power to reject data centers and put them in the state’s highest property tax bracket. 
Lowndes commission approves $1.15 billion tax break for a data center despite pushback

In a campaign ad earlier this month, Tuberville promised data center regulation and to remove tax breaks for the facilities. Speaking to the Birmingham Rotary Club last week, Tuberville affirmed his support for data centers, citing their economic impact. 
“We’re gonna start as he said, ‘We’ll take all your data centers,’” Jones said. “The next thing I know, we’re going to be a dumping ground for data centers and big tech, and a lot of our communities are going to be destroyed.” 
Hughes said the data center issue could help Jones with rural voters.
“They tend to poll the worst with rural voters, and so that could be grounds where Jones is able to pick up votes if he’s able to convince some rural voters to vote (Democratic) for data center stuff,” Hughes said.
Tuberville has called for the expansion of the CHOOSE Act, the state’s school voucher program. The program is currently limited to applicants whose household income is 300% above the poverty level, but is set to go universal next school year. 
Jones has called for a phase out of the program, keeping students who are currently enrolled in the program in it but closing it to future applicants. He said he fears the quality of public education in Alabama will “wither away and die” under a Tuberville administration. 
“That we will not just shirk, but we will abandon our duty to children in this state to get them educated in the best way, and we abandon it in favor of political pandering. And that money is going to leave public education,” Jones said. 
Building a party
The front window of the Doug Jones for Governor headquarters in Birmingham, Alabama, as seen on Sept. 30, 2026, featuring a cardboard cutout of the Democratic gubernatorial nominee and campaign signs for other Democratic nominees for Alabama’s constitutional offices. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Hughes said a 2026 winning map for Jones must look like that of his 2017 win.
“You need to have Black voters turn out at roughly 30% of the electorate, with the assumption that the Democrat’s going to win around 90% of those votes. Then to make it to the halfway mark, you then need to get about 30% of the white vote,” Hughes said. “That’s where most Democrats in the Deep South fail. You have quite a lot of racial polarization in partisanship in Deep South states like Alabama and Mississippi.”
But Jones, like many Alabama Democrats before him, must run for office while attempting to build a party that has struggled to be effective outside the cities since losing control of the Alabama Legislature in 2010. 
“I really believe that this election can change things in a different way, including a change in attitude,” he said. “Because I do believe that folks in this state, while you have partisans, most of the people in the state want to see change,” he said. 
Singleton was elected chair of the party in August amid broad frustration with the lack of resources candidates received. He said Jones’ candidacy has already yielded some results: The Democratic Party has its largest slate of candidates since 2018.
“Having someone with Doug’s experience has given us some stability at the top of the ticket, the ability to recruit other members along with that ticket on the constitutional offices,” Singleton said. “He’s given a lot of Democrats a sense of pride again to say that, ‘Hey, I’m proud to be a Democrat.’”
Jones said these signs of growth in the Democratic Party – candidates on the ballot, increased voter turnout, engaged conversations with voters – are what matters to him in his campaign.
“Everybody talks about blue waves and flipping things, and I don’t. I talk about just change,” he said. “My goal, one of my goals, has always been to just have a competitive two-party system in this state.”
Wednesday night, Jones held a mock debate in Birmingham where he used television and radio clips of Tuberville to demonstrate why his opponent is not qualified to be governor and his stances on many of the race’s top issues.
After the event, which drew roughly 300 people, Jones said his 20 town halls proved his theory that Alabamians agree on more than they don’t.
“That’s what’s important about this campaign. That’s what we’ve been talking about,” Jones said. “Tommy Tuberville has not. He has just been calling people socialists, communists, furries – you name it. It is the most bizarre campaign I’ve ever seen run. That’s what I believe. People in this state and these town halls have confirmed we’re really one Alabama.”

title: Arkansas Democrats look to make election gains in fast-changing Washington County
text:
Erick Soto (right) walks with a volunteer to put out signs in eastern Springdale, Arkansas on Sept. 19, 2026. (Photo by Phillip Powell/Arkansas Advocate).
Normally the biggest attractions at Parsons Stadium on the edge of Springdale are events held on the dirt arena like monster truck rallies, demolition derbies or the 82-year-old Rodeo of the Ozarks. 
But on a recent evening at the outdoor stadium, the focus for Washington County Democrats was corralling votes, not cattle.
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
“One of the reasons I’m here is to learn about who the candidates are,” Susan Marks, a retiree from Springdale, said as she watched a folk band play with her friend August White. “I’m registered as an independent but I lean left, and I wanted to find out more about Washington County Democratic candidates.” 
Northwest Arkansas is home to many new transplants like Marks, who says she usually votes for Democrats. White, who is also retired and a recent transplant to Fayetteville, said she got plugged into local Democratic politics from the “No Kings” protests.
Marks and White are the kind of voters Democrats are relying on as they try to defy recent history in a midterm election where President Donald Trump’s sagging approval numbers has given the party hope in solidly red states. Once the bastion of Republican support when Arkansas was a blue state, Washington County is key to Arkansas Democrats’ efforts in November.
“We aren’t ever going to ignore the Delta or central Arkansas, but if we are going to come back to power it flows through northwest Arkansas,” state Democratic Party Chair Marcus Jones told the Arkansas Advocate during the Democratic candidate event at the rodeo grounds.
Arkansas Democratic Party Chair Marcus Jones, who unsuccessfully ran for Congress in 2024, gives a speech at Parsons Stadium in Springdale touting Washington County Judge hopeful Dana Deree’s record on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Phillip Powell/Arkansas Advocate)
Between 2010 and 2020, Washington County’s population grew 21% according to the U.S. Census Bureau, driven in large part by people moving to the county. By 2050, regional planners estimate the county’s total population will grow to 420,000, a 58% increase.
Dana Deree, the Democrats’ nominee for Washington County judge and host of the rodeo event, is trying to build the coalition needed to flip Washington County. Deree speaks Spanish fluently and served in the Marine Corps, the Navy Reserves, as a diplomat in the U.S. Foreign Service, and as a former public school teacher at Little Rock Central High School. He often speaks about growing up poor in an unstable household and experiencing homelessness. 
Along with the county judge’s race, Democrats hope to flip three seats on the county’s quorum court to win a majority, and to win two statehouse districts in the party’s ongoing quest to break the huge Republican majority in the Legislature.
Democratic nominee for Washington County Judge Dana Deree speaks to voters at the rodeo event he hosted in Springdale, Arkansas on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Phillip Powell/Arkansas Advocate).
Deree might be a relatively new face in Washington County, but that may not be as big of a downside in a county rapidly welcoming new residents. While it’s not lost on him that Democrats are excited about him, he’s almost entirely running on finding solutions to the local infrastructure and population growth challenges the county faces, like a lack of affordable housing and an overcrowded jail.
“This county has only been Republican for ten years or so,” Deree said at the rodeo grounds. “And it is ripe for a comeback and my campaign is working hard to be welcoming to returners.”
The battleground
Washington County is a prime target for Democrats, anchored by the college town of Fayetteville and the University of Arkansas campus.


It’s also home to a growing and increasingly diverse population in neighboring Springdale — the home of Tyson Foods. The county also has small towns dotting rural areas, and suburbs and bedroom communities that trend Republican, like Lincoln, Goshen and Prairie Grove.
“Of course Fayetteville has long been a diverse, liberal town and that has not changed and if anything it is becoming more liberal,” political science professor Karen Sebold said about the elections. “So yeah, if there is going to be a battleground for the Democratic Party it is going to be Northwest Arkansas.”
In 2022, Democrats’ gubernatorial nominee Chris Jones eked out a victory in the county over Sarah Huckabee Sanders after Republican candidates won the county easily in every statewide contest between 2014 and the election that year. 
The last time a Democrat won the Washington County judge race was when the late Marilyn Edwards narrowly beat a Republican opponent in 2014. The Democratic nominees for county judge in 2018 and 2022 each lost by about 5 percentage points.
Despite that, in 2024 Democrat Vladimir Rivera Lopez narrowly beat an incumbent Republican for a spot on the county quorum court and Diana Gonzales Worthen flipped a seat in the Arkansas House when she won the race to represent the state’s first majority-Latino district. 
 


 
Along with the victories, the voting shifts between 2022 and 2024 hold other hopeful signs for Washington County Democrats.
Democrats still made larger inroads in many parts of Springdale. Now as candidates are heading into the final stretch, the questions of how rural areas turn out and how blue Fayetteville and Springdale can get may decide the results. Another place to watch is whether Farmington will trend toward Democrats or further toward Republicans as it did in 2024.


A race to the middle
Democrats are also getting a boost from local sentiment about the incumbent Republican county judge, Patrick Deakins, who was ousted in a primary runoff earlier this year. Deakins’ loss followed several high-profile fights on issues like open records and jail funding that spilled over into acrimonious county meetings.
Deree told the Arkansas Advocate he didn’t get in the race to run against Deakins and indicated that Tim Shepard’s defeat of the incumbent judge in the GOP runoff has made for a tougher race.
When Shepard and Deree met for a recent debate in Springdale, the two men had far more positive things to say about each other than negative. Both candidates spent most of the debate trying to persuade voters they were the least partisan and best at working with others. The two are running on similar platforms of bringing the county together across partisan and geographic lines.
Shepard’s main lines of attack on Deree are that he doesn’t have strong roots in the county and is too much of a partisan Democrat. Shepard says he is a conservative but has never been involved with either party in the county. Deree holds a position with the state Democratic Party and ran for a statehouse seat in central Arkansas as a Democrat in 2000. 
Deree talked up his outreach to rural parts of the county, including in his opposition to permitting new gravel and red dirt mines, while Shepard emphasized his rival’s support from Fayetteville liberals, such as former mayor Lioneld Jordan. 
Democratic nominee Dana Deree (left) and Republican Tim Shepard debate in the Washington County judge’s race in Springdale, Arkansas on Sept. 29, 2026. (Photo by Phillip Powell/Arkansas Advocate).
Deree has criticized Shepard as being a partisan Republican, pointing out that his rival has campaigned with figures like Republican state Sen. Clint Penzo, who unsuccessfully challenged U.S. Rep. Steve Womack from the right in the 2024 GOP primary.
Janet Oxford, who attended the debate with her husband Michael, said she supported Shepard but believed either candidate would be an improvement.
“There is a reason we have a democracy and that we talk,” Janet said. “Just because someone is one party or another doesn’t mean that you say ‘I’m right and everyone is wrong’ and you don’t get new ideas, and you never evaluate if you’re wrong on an issue and we need to have civil discussions.”
The couple has been in Washington County for decades. Michael said he will be supporting Shepard because of his work with volunteer fire departments like the one he runs in nearby Wheeler.
Shepard has outraised Deree by about $26,000, according to September campaign finance reports that were filed with the secretary of state Tuesday. 
Neither Deree nor Shepard said having their respective parties in the majority on the quorum court would matter to how they would govern. 



Deree has campaigned with some Democratic challengers and calls them friends. Shepard said that while he attends events with Republican officeholders, they don’t necessarily endorse each other. Some voters view the chance to oust three Republican incumbents in Farmington and Shady Grove as the referendum needed on the Deakins era.
“I wish I could say Dana’s got it in the bag, but I think it’s going to be a tough race. I believe both candidates are qualified and it will definitely be hands down better than what we’ve had either way,” Annie Langston, a Deree supporter, said after the debate.
Seeking a supermajority
Erick Soto, 25, organizes volunteers and canvasses the working-class, Latino and Marshallese neighborhoods of Springdale that will determine whether Gonzales Worthen keeps her seat in the statehouse as she faces a challenge from Republican Matt Goff, a retired Army veteran and longtime northwest Arkansas resident. 
(Photo by Phillip Powell/Arkansas Advocate)
Soto is a committed Democrat and the son of Mexican immigrants. He goes door to door in House District 9, usually talking with reluctant voters in fluent Spanish. Soto finds many voters are anxious to open their doors over concerns about Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and he thinks lower midterm turnout may be their biggest barrier to re-election. 
“People are tired of not seeing any change at all, and getting people to the polls is the major obstacle here,” Soto said. “If you brought a voting booth to people’s doors it would probably be a solid Democratic district, but I also think some people are feeling fed up so I think it will be a good year for Democrats.”
That race will be key in Democrats’ long-desired goal of breaking Republicans’ hold on the Arkansas House. Because Republicans hold more than three-fourths of the seats in the House and Senate, the party can pass most appropriations bills without any votes from Democrats. 
House District 9 is crucial to the strategy of breaking that supermajority, the state Democrats’ chair said. The party also sees an immediate pickup opportunity in neighboring House District 19 that covers northern Fayetteville, Johnson, and parts of southern and western Springdale.
Jamie Atkinson (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
That race features another newcomer to the region, Democrat Jamie Atkinson, who is trying to unseat Republican Rep. Steve Unger, a two-term incumbent. A retired Navy veteran and chaplain, Unger outperformed Trump in his district in 2024. 
Like Deree, Atkinson spent years in the U.S. Foreign Service and chose to invest and settle in northwest Arkansas after recently retiring. Unlike Deree, Atkinson hasn’t lived in Arkansas until recently — though he does point to generational connections to the state. 
Rep. Steve Unger (Photo courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
Unger has deeper roots in the district and touts himself as a more moderate conservative focused on local issues. He’s outraised Atkinson and has more cash on hand, according to campaign finance reports. Unger has complained his rival is portraying the Legislature as in control of gas, grocery and insurance prices.
“The cure for our toxic political climate begins with rejecting candidates who offer easy answers to complicated questions,” Unger wrote in a post on his Facebook page.
Volunteers gather at the county party’s headquarters in Springdale every Saturday, where Atkinson and his field coordinators send canvassers to different neighborhoods in the district.
One voter Atkinson encountered was Jodi VanBecelaere, a mom with two middle school-aged children who has voted for both parties in past elections. VanBecelaere hasn’t made up her mind on who to vote for in the House race, though she said she’s supporting Shepard’s bid for county judge.
VanBecelaere told Atkinson she’s worried about public schools and affordability. 
As he walked away, heading to the next door, Atkinson said, “This is the best use of my time, talking to voters. And as a matter of practice, I like to be conservative in my assessments of where I think people are.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Nashville judge temporarily blocks immigration status checks in HIV/AIDS program
text:
A Nashville judge on Wednesday temporarily blocked Tennessee health officials from imposing immigration and citizenship checks on people receiving services through the federally-funded Ryan White HIV/AIDS program. Pictured: Historic Metro Nashville Courthouse (Photo: Nashville.gov) (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A Nashville judge temporarily blocked Tennessee health officials from requiring immigration status checks of HIV-positive individuals enrolled in a healthcare safety-net program. 
Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles issued the temporary restraining order late Wednesday. The order prevents the Tennessee Department of Health from moving forward with a demand that organizations revise their contracts to include immigration status verification as a condition of serving patients in the Ryan White HIV/AIDS program.
The order extends to a companion program known as HOPWA, or Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS. Myles set a Nov. 4 hearing in the case.
The decades-old, federally-funded Ryan White program provides millions of dollars to every U.S. state to serve low-income individuals living with HIV/AIDS. States in turn distribute funding to healthcare and other providers who work directly with patients.
On Oct. 1, the Tennessee health department sent a memo to these providers citing new state law that requires verifying anyone seeking federal, state or local public benefits to be lawfully present in the United States. The law also comes with criminal penalties for employees who fail to verify patient status.
Nashville CARES, one of the Tennessee’s largest participants in the program, filed suit challenging the mandate earlier this week.  The federal government does not require immigration status checks as a condition of receiving services through Ryan White or HOPWA and federal law exempts such checks for programs targeting communicable diseases, it noted in legal filings. 
Lawsuit: Tennessee to impose immigration checks in HIV/AIDS safety-net program

Hundreds of its patients would be at risk of losing life-saving medical, prescription drug and support services — including financial assistance that pays the costs of private health insurance, Nashville CARES said in legal filings.
Represented by attorneys with the Tennessee Justice Center, the organization said the mandate violated state rule-making procedures and federal law. 
Attorneys representing the Tennessee Department of Health objected to a temporary injunction in a legal response to Nashville CARES’ initial petition. They argued that Nashville CARES was “essentially (asking) the Court to intervene in a contract dispute.” State attorneys also disputed the right of Nashville CARES to broadly challenge the state’s imposition of the new contract rules on all Tennessee organizations that participate in Ryan White program, arguing the case should focus only on Nashville CARES’ dispute. 
Myles’ temporary restraining order applies to all organizations that contract with the state to provide Ryan White services. 
The order blocks any effort to require immigration or citizenship status verification for any individual currently enrolled in the program, and any new applicant. Myles also blocked the state from restricting enrollment only to those able to provide proof of legal immigration or citizenship status.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Issue spotlight: North Dakota attorney general candidates cautious on AI use in law and order
text:
From the left, Democratic-NPL attorney general candidate Tim Lamb and Republican Attorney General Drew Wrigley. (Photos by Kyle Martin/For the North Dakota Monitor)Candidates for North Dakota’s top law enforcement position say artificial intelligence will be transformative for society but is not a replacement for humans in investigations or legal matters.
Republican Attorney General Drew Wrigley, a two-time former U.S. attorney and past lieutenant governor, is running for reelection in a rematch against Democrat Tim Lamb, a Grand Forks attorney, former school board member and retired Army major.
The 2025 Legislature passed laws banning possession of computer-generated child sexual abuse images and requiring a disclaimer for AI used in political ads. An interim legislative committee is studying AI and data center topics for potential 2027 legislation.
Data center legislation begins to take shape in North Dakota

Wrigley said he doesn’t “impulsively lurch for more regulation of things,” and prefers to have “candid, expert-driven, societally sensitive conversations about this emerging technology.”
He also pointed to his office’s participation in litigation against social media platforms related to age-appropriate accessibility, saying, “we’re going to try to always stay on the front edge of that.” Lamb has criticized Wrigley for not doing more to get a larger settlement amount for North Dakota in a 47-state Meta lawsuit.
Wrigley said he personally uses AI sometimes when researching or comparing consumer products, but has not integrated it into his work. He said he has encouraged his office’s division directors to look for ways AI can save time on tasks in a responsible, ethical way, not to foist their obligations onto a machine. Wrigley said he won’t ask the Legislature for more resources just because AI is a hot topic. 
If elected, Lamb said he would task an assistant attorney general to become an expert on AI topics. He also said he would work with other state attorneys general to develop oversight of AI and would prioritize consumer protection against AI fraud.
Lamb said he “would have to do some homework” and have discussions on what potential AI legislation might be necessary. He expressed concerns about AI models becoming too powerful and President Donald Trump and Congress not seriously considering regulations. Everything from transportation to commerce has government regulations, he said.
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

“What do we have that there isn’t government oversight? Nothing,” Lamb said.
Each candidate said the case of a Tennessee woman jailed for months last year in connection with a Fargo-area bank fraud because of her identification by an AI facial recognition software creates legitimate concerns. Her charges were eventually dismissed, and she is suing the city of Fargo for $10 million, according to court papers.
Lamb called it “a freak case” and said police officials “were all asleep at the wheel” throughout the chain of command. Wrigley said “there’s a little more to that story,” but called it “a cautionary for anybody” and a real concern. Investigators cannot take the human component out of their work or exclusively rely on AI, he said.
Similarly, Flock cameras have legitimate law enforcement uses, “but that doesn’t mean that that’s the end of the discussion,” Wrigley said. The cameras, which have been criticized as intrusive to privacy, have helped solve serious crimes nationally but need “a robust public discussion” about “where do we want the lines to be drawn,” he said. 
Lamb said Flock cameras need to be limited to specific purposes such as surveillance of a mass of people at football games or athletic areas, but not necessarily everyday activity on a street corner.
In the legal realm, AI will not replace human judgment, Lamb said. There might be some applications for AI in the legal profession, “but I don’t think it’s imminent,” he said.
Crimes across all categories in North Dakota down in 2025, report shows

Wrigley cited legal professionals he knows who use AI in initial legal research and to draft documents. AI shows great promise for advancements in the medical profession for treatment of diseases and other uses, he added.
“That’s why I say we’re foolish not to embrace new technology. We’re equally foolish if we don’t do it in a really thoughtful, thorough way, transparently understanding the upside and downside and then make societal judgments about where we want to draw those lines,” Wrigley said.
North Dakota’s attorney general oversees a two-year budget of nearly $63 million and 270 full-time employees. The annual salary is $197,841.
The AG also sits on North Dakota’s three-member Industrial Commission and five-member Board of University and School Lands, which oversee topics such as the state-owned Bank of North Dakota, various energy matters and state investments.
Lamb also ran unsuccessfully for state auditor in 2024.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado priest from Uganda released after 13 months in ICE detention in Aurora
text:
Two fellow detainees carried Rev. Edward Nalwamba, who will be 79 in November, out of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility in Aurora Tuesday because it did not provide him with a wheelchair when he left. (Photo courtesy of Joy Athanasiou)After 13 months in an Aurora immigrant detention center, where he became reliant on a wheelchair as his health deteriorated, a Ugandan priest who has lived in Colorado for more than 25 years was released by federal immigration officials Wednesday.
A judge ordered Rev. Edward Nalwamba’s release earlier this week. Two fellow detainees on Tuesday carried Nalwamba, who will be 79 in November, out of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement facility because it did not provide him with a wheelchair when he left. Private prison company The GEO Group operates the detention center.
“Everyone was so happy that he was being released, but … watching these other detainees, who are also being released, volunteer to carry him all that way and carry all of his possessions — it was heartbreaking, and it was infuriating,” Joy Athanasiou, one of his immigration attorneys, said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nalwamba told Newsline Wednesday that he’s sad for the other detainees he left behind in the detention center, who he said are all “good people.” But he is grateful for “kind people” who voluntarily carried him out of the facility, because he doesn’t know what he would have done without their help.
“They just hoisted me in their hands and began walking with me half a mile up to the vehicle that was going to pick me up,” he said. “That showed me they are good people by the way they went (out of their) way. They just did a good thing and they went away.”
Nalwamba said other countries treat their livestock better than he was treated while detained. The American immigration system is “calloused” toward human beings, and he said those working at the ICE facility are rude, rough and inhumane. 



Quotation







It is like you are an animal, like people are taking care of goats or cows. I have never imagined human beings treated like I saw in this place.


– Don't forget to add author


“It is as if they’ve gotten so used to treating people that way. It is like you are an animal, like people are taking care of goats or cows,” Nalwamba said. “I have never imagined human beings treated like I saw in this place.”
U.S. Sen. John Hickenlooper, a Colorado Democrat, said in a post on X that his staff visited the facility to ask GEO to provide Nalwamba a wheelchair and to allow him to call his caretakers.
“GEO staff assured us they would do both. They failed to deliver on either,” he said. “There is no excuse for this cruelty. None.”
Nalwamba’s lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition — a legal mechanism that challenges wrongful detention — earlier this year, but ICE told the judge it scheduled his deportation for June 30, so the judge denied the motion to release him. Cyrus Chung, a federal magistrate judge, ordered his release Monday after his lawyers filed a second petition since ICE continued to hold Nalwamba in its Aurora detention facility.
Nalwamba said he’s “in another world” after his release. He’s staying with a family who lent him an electric scooter to help him get around. He’s talked to his children, he had a good night’s sleep and he’s well fed.
“I am a happy man,” he said.
Athanasiou said that while she and his friends were “so happy and so relieved” ICE released him, they were nervous that it would not actually happen. ICE had said it would release him a couple times in the past, but since it never happened, his friends and supporters were skeptical. 
“I spent a lot of time … reassuring his friends and his community that they had to release him because the court ordered his release, that they couldn’t play games this time,” Athanasiou said. 
Worsening health
For months, Nalwamba presented respiratory symptoms that could be indications of tuberculosis. His symptoms include coughing, chest pain, a runny nose, a scratchy throat and voice, headaches, dizziness and general fatigue. 
The priest, who talked to Newsline while waiting to see a doctor at Denver Health’s TB clinic, joked that he’ll be “up and running” within a couple days. The family he is staying with took him to the doctor Wednesday to rule TB out since he was unable to get a clear diagnosis while in detention, Athanasiou said.
Colorado issues public health order over tuberculosis case at Aurora ICE facility

Getting other medical care, rehabilitation and physical therapy will come next, Athanasiou said, since Nalwamba had limited access to healthcare while in ICE custody. He was healthy and able to walk when ICE arrested him, but he received no physical therapy or support to help him regain strength, which Athanasiou said is partly why he is wheelchair-bound.
“You think about somebody being essentially imprisoned for a year, and then trying to come out and just resume their life, there’s a lot of pieces that have to get put into place,” Athanasiou said.
He’ll also return to his church community, which Athanasiou said has been very important to him. Reconnecting with the young men with developmental disabilities he previously cared for will be key to reestablishing himself, too.
Asylum case
A citizen of Uganda, Nalwamba first came to the U.S. for a religious conference in January 2002, but he stayed after his visa authorization expired. Colleagues in Uganda expressed fear that his life would be in danger, since government agents were looking for him. Nalwamba had previously testified in immigration hearings that he publicly condemned human rights abuses by the Ugandan government.
The priest wanted to file for political asylum after learning about threats to his life, but the attorney he hired at the time did not submit his application before the one-year deadline required by U.S. immigration law.
He retired two years ago after working as a priest at the Resurrection Anglican Fellowship in Greenwood Village for about 15 years. He worked full-time caring for a person with developmental disabilities before ICE arrested him in September 2025. 
Nalwamba had been under supervised release, without incident, since 2011, following a previous eight-month detention by ICE. He described his 13 months in the Aurora ICE facility this time around like a “maximum (security) prison” compared to last time. 
“You don’t want to go to the hospital, because they shackle you like you’re a bull,” he said.
Nalwamba’s attorneys in the spring filed a motion with the Board of Immigration Appeals to reopen his asylum case, and that motion is still pending. Political conditions in Uganda have “deteriorated significantly” since Nalwamba left, Athanasiou said, with widespread targeting of political opponents. 
The U.S. Department of State has a “do not travel” advisory for Uganda due to crime, health, terrorism and unrest. Athanasiou said Canada recently implemented a policy to allow anyone who receives a deportation order to Uganda to review whether Canada could grant asylum to the applicant given worsened political conditions.
‘Inhumanity and cruelty’
Athanasiou has worked with clients who have been in detention centers for upwards of two decades, and she said “this type of inhumanity and cruelty never existed” prior to last year. She said the White House and U.S. Department of Homeland Security leadership are intentionally ignoring federal standards that regulate immigration detention facilities.
“Previously, the government would enforce the private prison companies following those standards and would penalize them for violating the standards,” Athanasiou said. “Now, all of the oversight has been largely eliminated, and all of the government entities who used to hold the private prison companies accountable, those offices have really been hollowed out.”
Trump dramatically broadened the scope of ICE operations since he returned to office last year, seeking to carry out the “largest domestic deportation operation in American history.” ICE officers have arrested immigrants without permanent legal status across the U.S., regardless of how long they have been in the country, the legal status of their family members or whether they have criminal records.
Before Trump returned to office, Athanasiou said habeas corpus petitions were rare, with a few hundred or maybe a thousand filed annually. That’s because there’s never been “a mass-scale, unlawful detention by the government like we’re witnessing today,” she said. A ProPublica tracker identified almost 90,000 habeas petitions filed on behalf of detained immigrants since January 2025.
“Now, unfortunately, this is a daily scenario, and the demand is 100 times greater than what we can provide,” said Athanasiou. 
Nalwamba said he loves America and has always thought that African countries should aim to be like the U.S. But his time in ICE custody showed him that America has to change, too, he said.
“The American people (need to) insist that this immigration thing changes, because the way it is being done is not humane at all,” he said. “It is not what America is, the leader of the world.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Former congressman, military veteran make bids for Alabama’s 1st Congressional District
text:
Voters in Alabama's 1st Congressional District will choose between former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl, R-Mobile, and Clyde Jones, a U.S. military veteran to represent them in Congress. (Photos courtesy of candidate; graphic by Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)South Alabama voters will send a former congressman or a retired DuPoint worker to Congress next month in the state’s only open U.S. House contest. 
Former U.S. Rep. Jerry Carl, R-Mobile, and Clyde Jones, a military veteran, are making their pitches to voters in the 1st Congressional District. 
The district previously covered a portion of the Wiregrass and Mobile County and all of Baldwin County. It  was redrawn earlier this year during a special session of the Alabama Legislature. The district now covers Mobile, Baldwin and Escambia Counties and a large part of Covington County. The Cook Political Report rates the district as R+17, solidly Republican.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Carl, the Republican nominee who represented the district from 2021 to 2025, said he decided to run again because of his past experience in Congress.
“I like the pace of Washington, I enjoy the challenges of Washington. I think I did a great job, and I think I will continue to do a great job,” Carl said. “I’ll work with the president. I’ll work with leadership in the Senate and in Congress, and I don’t think you’re going to find anybody else down in this system than that.”
Jones, the Democratic nominee, said in an interview Wednesday morning that he “felt like we need a change.”
“We needed representation, someone who wanted to represent everyone-not one particular party, but everyone that’s in congressional district one,” he said.
Carl said he wants to focus on improving the business environment in Mobile and Baldwin Counties and affordability.
“The cost of living is outrageous. We’re all experiencing the pressure from that,” he said. “Diesel fuel and gas prices, you know, are a little different. We’re having to pay more for that, which is hurting all of us.”
Carl did not specify how he would address affordability. His campaign website connects Carl’s support for a balanced budget amendment and support for spending cuts with inflation. A message seeking comment was left with Carl Wednesday.
Jones is also prioritizing affordability, but also wants to focus on accountability and access to healthcare by putting money back into the Affordable Care Act.
“The supplements that were taken away for the ACA (Affordable Care Act) caused premiums to go up. This year alone, 95,000 people have lost healthcare in Alabama because they can’t afford their premium. So, if we can get those back into the budget and get those supplements back out to people to help cover their healthcare costs, it will be something that can be done pretty much right away,” Jones said.
Tax credits for the ACA expired last year, leading to a 23% (95,000) drop in enrollment for the program.
The state’s redistricting efforts have also come up on the campaign trails for both candidates.
“A lot of people in the city of Mobile, they just didn’t understand what happened, or they didn’t know about what happened,” Jones said. “So, I would always have to start my speeches into groups in Mobile with ‘I am not running against Congressman (Shomari) Figures,’ which again adds another level of confusion, but also gives an opportunity to educate people on the actual change.”
Carl said while redistricting has played a role in his campaign, he has shifted to encouraging Republican voters to the polls.
“The key is, how many can you get out? Can you get out more Republicans than you can Democrats? And that’s a fear that we all have,” Carl said. “If they (Republicans) take that same comfort level in this race, we could easily lose. So we’re really trying to motivate our Republicans to get out.”
According to federal campaign finances, Carl has raised $277,500 and spent $298,900 through Oct. 1. Jones has raised $97,500 and spent $105,200 through Oct. 1. 
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: West Virginia can’t invest its way out of losing coverage
text:
A hospital “H” sign. (Photo by Sarah Ladd/Kentucky Lantern)West Virginia has been given an extraordinary opportunity to invest in the future of rural health care.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is providing our state nearly $200 million in federal funding for 2026, with additional funding available through 2030. The program promises to expand access, strengthen the healthcare workforce, improve technology and modernize how rural health care is delivered.
Those are worthwhile goals. We should put these dollars to work. We should use them wisely. And we should hold ourselves accountable for making sure they improve the lives of people in every corner of our state.
But there is a fundamental problem with presenting this investment as though it answers West Virginia’s rural health crisis. It doesn’t. West Virginia cannot invest its way out of losing health coverage. The distinction matters.
The Rural Health Transformation Program is a five-year investment designed to change how healthcare is delivered. Medicaid is an ongoing source of health coverage and healthcare financing for hundreds of thousands of West Virginians.
One cannot simply replace the other. The numbers tell the story.
West Virginia received nearly $200 million for the first year of the Rural Health Transformation Program. Over the full five-year program, the federal government will distribute $50 billion nationally.
At the same time, analyses of the federal law’s Medicaid cuts estimate that West Virginia stands to lose more than $5.3 billion in Medicaid funding over the coming decade.
That is not a solution to a funding crisis. It is a fraction of what is being taken away. And we need to be honest about what these new dollars can — and cannot — do.
The Rural Health Transformation Program can support telehealth. It can support remote monitoring, artificial intelligence and other technology-enabled care. It can help recruit and retain healthcare workers and develop new models of delivering care.
All those things have a place in the future of rural healthcare. But AI cannot replace a doctor, telehealth cannot replace a hospital and technology cannot replace health insurance.
A person does not become insured because a new digital platform connects them to a provider. A rural hospital does not become financially stable simply because it has new technology. A community does not maintain access to healthcare when the people who live there can no longer afford to use it.
This is particularly troubling because West Virginia’s rural hospitals were already vulnerable before these Medicaid cuts.
There are hospitals in our state operating on razor-thin margins, some with negative revenue. We have declining patient volumes and persistent workforce shortages. Our hospitals serve an older, sicker and poorer population, and many rely heavily on Medicaid and Medicare, which reimburse providers at rates that can fall below the cost of providing care.
A national analysis published last year identified eight West Virginia hospitals at heightened risk of closure.  The analysis does not predict that these hospitals will close. It demonstrates where the financial pressure could be greatest. West Virginians  deserve to understand the vulnerabilities within their own communities and how policy decisions directly affect them. 
That is the part of this conversation that cannot be solved with a ribbon cutting for a new program.
When a hospital loses Medicaid revenue, it does not simply lose money for innovation. It often means fewer services, fewer providers, more uncompensated care, longer travel distances and, ultimately, the possibility that a hospital that has served a community for generations may no longer be able to keep its doors open.
And not only will there be a massive spike in uncompensated care, but we will see aggressive patient collection efforts that will increase West Virginians’ medical debt and undoubtedly more personal bankruptcies.    
Moreover, beginning Jan. 1, 2027, certain adults ages 19 through 64 enrolled in Medicaid expansion will generally have to complete 80 hours each month of qualifying work, education, training or community service — or meet another exemption — to maintain coverage.
For the people affected, this is not an abstract policy debate. It is another requirement they will have to understand, document and navigate to remain connected to healthcare.
West Virginia has already experienced what happens when administrative requirements become barriers to coverage. During the Medicaid unwinding, people lost coverage because they missed notices, did not understand what information was being requested or could not complete the renewal process on time.
Now we are asking many of the same people to navigate another set of requirements. And when people lose Medicaid, the consequences do not stop with them. They show up in doctors’ offices. They show up in hospitals’ uncompensated-care costs. They show up in pharmacies. They show up when someone delays treatment until a health problem becomes an emergency. And they show up in the financial stability of the very rural health care system we are now being told this new funding will transform.
That is the contradiction we need to confront. You cannot make a healthcare system more sustainable by simultaneously making it harder for people to pay for the care they need.
If we want people to work, they need to be healthy enough to work. If we want people to manage chronic conditions, they need access to a doctor and the medications they need. If we want rural hospitals to remain open, they need patients who have coverage and can pay for the care they receive. If we want mothers and babies to have healthy outcomes, women need access to prenatal and maternity care before a crisis occurs. And if we want West Virginians to live healthier lives, they need health coverage they can count on.
This is not an argument against the Rural Health Transformation Program. It is an argument against pretending that it solves a problem it was never large enough to solve.
West Virginia should take advantage of every dollar available to strengthen rural healthcare. We should invest in our workforce. We should improve transportation. We should use technology where it genuinely improves care. We should expand access to specialists. We should find new ways to bring care closer to people’s homes.
But we also must protect the foundation underneath all those efforts. People need coverage. Providers need patients who can pay. Hospitals need predictable revenue. Those things are connected.
We cannot celebrate an investment in rural health care while ignoring the much larger loss of Medicaid dollars that threatens the stability of that same system.
West Virginia has spent years bringing down our uninsured rate. The Affordable Care Act and Medicaid expansion changed what healthcare access looks like for hundreds of thousands of West Virginians.
That progress matters. And it can disappear much faster than we built it.
So, as we move forward with rural health transformation, let’s measure success by more than dollars awarded, programs launched or technology deployed.
Let’s ask the questions that matter to the people we are trying to serve.
Can they get an appointment? Can they afford to go? Can they get there? Is there a provider close to home? Will their local hospital still be open? Can they afford their prescriptions? And when they need care, will they still have health insurance?
West Virginia has an opportunity to build a stronger rural healthcare system. Let’s seize it. But let’s not confuse an investment with a replacement.
We cannot build a stronger healthcare system by making it harder for West Virginians to remain insured. We need to invest in our hospitals, our providers and our communities. And we need to protect the coverage that allows West Virginians to use them.
We need both.

name: VTDigger
title: Gov. Scott put property taxes and school consolidation center stage. Now Amanda Janoo is rallying opposition.
text:
A sign questioning the property tax rate seen in Jericho on Friday, October 16, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

JERICHO — Henry Listenik Jr. says he’s paying double what he did last year in property taxes. 
The 69-year-old voted for Gov. Phil Scott in 2024, but Listenik said he doesn’t think Scott has followed through on his promises. Now Listenik doesn’t know who to vote for.
The Jericho resident said that his kids, who are parents themselves, are considering moving out of state because they can’t find jobs or keep up with the cost of living. 
“Does our governor hear that?” he said in an interview. 
Vermont’s property taxes are among the highest in the country and have risen more than 40% on average over the past five years. Scott, the five-term Republican, has campaigned on affordability since his first run for governor. And he’s persuaded legislators to use state revenue to buy down property taxes for the past two years. 
Property tax rates are tied directly to education spending under the state’s current school funding system, which allows for little state control over how much local school districts spend. 
Vermont’s system is totally unique because it generally allows local school districts to spend however much they want to educate students, as long as voters approve. Then, they subsequently calculate property tax rates for the average homeowner based on how much the district plans to spend per student. Because districts have this discretion over their own spending, there’s wide variation across the state in how much districts pay to educate each student. 
Scott has pushed for a funding model that would allow the state to dictate school spending, rather than leaving it up to local districts. He reasons that a state-directed model could reign in costs and subsequently lower property taxes. Under his proposed model, districts would receive money from the state based on how many kids are enrolled and how expensive they are to educate. 
A consolidated education system with larger, regional schools would reduce building maintenance and staffing costs, Scott has said. A consolidated model would also improve student outcomes, Scott has argued, because it would help close gaps in resources between schools. 
To his Democratic challenger Amanda Janoo — a political newcomer stoking a competitive race for governor — Scott’s vision for reform is a “a thinly veiled attack on public education,” she said in an interview. 
Janoo offers a platform that challenges Scott’s vision — and she’s rallying Scott’s opposition. Janoo is opposed to school consolidation and said she wants to make small schools sustainable by turning them into community centers of sorts, offering services such as healthcare, afterschool programs and adult school. She wants to lower property taxes for the average homeowner by levying higher taxes on second homes and short term-rentals. 
In a September poll from Vermont Public, 41% of respondents said it was more important to them to keep property taxes as low as possible than it was to keep their local public school. Only 28% said it was more important to keep their local school. 
It was equally important to 29% of respondents to keep property taxes low and preserve their local school. 
An outsized number of polled Republicans — about two-thirds — said it was more important to keep property taxes low, while only a quarter of Democrats in the poll agreed. 
Scott said during a press conference last month that he believes his position on education has made him less popular among voters, responding to two recent polls that showed a decline in his favorability. 
“But I don’t regret anything that we’ve done. I think it’s necessary that we fix the system that we have,” Scott said. 
Vermont spends among the most per-student nationwide, yet most students aren’t meeting grade-level standards, and graduation rates are declining. Its schools see troubling rates of declining enrollment. 
Funding the system
Scott envisions education reform as the key to lowering property tax rates and has called the issue Vermont’s “most critical challenge.” 
Meanwhile, Janoo’s platform vows to address some of the root causes of rising education costs, namely behavioral care for students and staff health insurance. She said she plans to lower healthcare costs in part by creating a system for universal primary care. 
She envisions a tax system in which education funds are less solely dependent on taxing primary residences and include taxing second homes or Airbnbs.
Levying taxes on other forms of property would “discourage the use of housing for that purpose and also generate revenue that can reduce the property tax burden for residential Vermonters,” Janoo said. 
Key to Scott’s vision is transitioning to a state-directed funding model, called a foundation formula, in tandem with school consolidation. 
Most states use a foundation formula model, which allows the state to decide how much it spends to educate each student, with certain added adjustments for kids who are more expensive to educate, such as those from low-income families or English language learners. Scott has said that a foundation formula would help offer more resources to rural schools, and his education secretary has blamed test score disparities on the state’s current funding system. 
“For what we’re paying, we should be number one,” said Scott in a recent campaign video. 
Under current state law, Vermont will transition to a foundation formula model in 2029 so long as districts have the opportunity to consider mergers, and legislators pass laws to decide the specifics of the formula, among other contingencies. 
Sheldon Foley, 42, of Waitsfield, said that he’s now paying $4,000 more in annual taxes than he did five years ago. After growing up in the Warren and Waitsfield area, he said it’s possible he might get priced out of his hometown and be forced to move. 
“I’d be silly not to consider it,” Foley said.
Foley doesn’t have kids, and said he doesn’t know “the nuts and bolts” of the state’s education system. But he thinks the state needs reform to deal with its declining enrollment, he said. 
“I’d hate to see schools close, but this isn’t sustainable,” Foley said. He said he plans to vote for Scott.
As lawmakers continue to debate reform, Scott has gotten them to follow his lead on using state revenue to buy down property taxes. This year, legislators agreed to spend $105 million in state revenue to soften the blow of what was a 12% average projected increase in property taxes. 
Consolidation or keeping schools 
While Scott has supported using property tax buydowns for short-term relief, his push for a consolidated model as a long-term fix has taken center stage in state politics, garnering both fans and skeptics. 
After pushing for forced school district merger legislation this year, Scott ultimately joined lawmakers in backing a process that incentivized voluntary mergers. That process is getting underway this fall. Merger committees are required to submit a final report to the state in September 2027, and any mergers are expected to appear on the ballot on Town Meeting Day in 2028. 
David Schoales of Brattleboro will be voting for Janoo because they disagree with Scott’s vision for consolidated school districts, they said. The retired educator sits on the steering committee for the Rural School Community Alliance, a coalition of educators and parents that want to preserve rural schools. Schoales said they aren’t convinced a consolidated model would save money or lead to better outcomes for students. 
“It doesn’t look at the effect on students, it doesn’t look at the effect on education, and again, it doesn’t save any money,” they said. 
Any costs saved by efficiencies in a consolidated model will be offset by other cost increases such as transportation, Schoales said. When schools in Arkansas consolidated, a 20 year study found the state saw little cost savings, according to The Hechinger Report.
Janoo, who grew up in Strafford attending classes of about a dozen students, said she wants to preserve rural schools because she sees them as pillars of rural communities. 
The state has already witnessed a steady economic decline and a “hollowing out of a lot of our communities,” Janoo said. To close a community’s school is to basically give up on it as a whole, she said. 
Janoo said she supports the community schools model, which focuses on providing resources to meet kids’ basic needs. A handful of schools across Vermont received federal grant funds in 2021 to pilot the model. In some schools, the program involved creating a food shelf for students, and in others it involved driving students to doctors appointments. Although federal funds dried up in 2024, some schools have kept the practice going on their own dime.  
“I just know how important small schools and rural schools are in particular as the center and hub of our communities,” she said.
