name: WyoFile
title: The mountain elite: A Wyoming skier worked three jobs to be on the first U.S. women’s biathlon team
text:
In the early 1980s, cross country ski racers staged a novel event — a 50K (31-mile) marathon — that drew regional athletes to a Nordic course just west of Yellowstone National Park.
A University of Vermont racer, Pam Weiss was living in Jackson Hole and decided to test herself at the race in West Yellowstone, Montana, even though she had not skied that distance before. A former collegiate competitor told Weiss of the competition while the two were training at Trail Creek Ranch at the base of Teton Pass.
“I’d never skied, I don’t think, more than 20Ks in a day,” Weiss said. Nevertheless, when she heard of the marathon she said, “that sounds like fun.”
Things can get bitter in winter up at 6,666 feet next to the Yellowstone supervolcano. On marathon day, the elements delivered “a really bad snowstorm,” Weiss said.
She strode out along the undulating course and eventually found herself setting a pace. “I remember turning around and seeing there were about 30 guys in the line behind me.”
A bicycle racer too, Weiss figured she’d share wind-breaking and pace-setting chores the way cyclists do in a peloton. So she moved aside briefly, ready to get back into the train behind a new leader.
“Nobody would let me back in until the end of it, and then I had to fight my way in,” she said. “None of them wanted a woman ahead of them.”
Weiss won the woman’s marathon that day, unseating the reigning queen, who was, Weiss said, “most upset.”
Efforts like that marked Weiss’ path from a New Jersey home to Vermont ski slopes, Wyoming cross country tracks and international biathlon venues where she skied and shot for the red, white and blue. She carried the colors at world championships in 1985, ’86 and ’87 and to the cusp of Olympic competition.
But just to the cusp. When it came time to add a new event to the 1988 Winter Games, women ski-shooters came up short. Instead of adding women’s biathlon to the schedule, the ultimate deciders of what constitutes athleticism chose … curling.
For a finely honed skier, being upstaged by un-sculpted players pushing 44-pound Scottish granite shuffleboard pucks across ice was “majorly disappointing.”
Be one with the bullet
Despite the Olympic snub, Weiss found herself at the top of the world during her time racing and shooting for the first U.S. women’s biathlon team. In one world championship relay, she was among the four leaders going into the second shooting test at the standing, offhand 50-meter range.
A Russian was just ahead of her, a Fennoscandian racer next to Weiss as they plinked away at their five grapefruit-size targets. Weiss was one shot better than her neighboring competitor.
“So I got to leave the range and ski out ahead of her, and she never caught up with me.”
“I was coming into the range with my pulse at 170 and while I was shooting, my pulse would drop, for say 30 seconds, down to 90.”Pam Weiss
With Weiss, American women who were used to obscurity found themselves at the front of a huge European stage. “I would finish a race and there would be lines of people wanting your autograph,” she said. “Nobody in our country even knows what the sport is about,” she thought, “and over here I’m a hero.”
Weiss explained the discipline needed to wed the vigor on the track to an unwavering shooting stance. “I was coming into the range with my pulse at 170 and while I was shooting, my pulse would drop, for say 30 seconds, down to 90.
“You don’t hold your breath,” she said, “because then your muscles will start trembling. You try to get in sort of a zone or [create] a Zen-type feeling. My approach would be to just brush aside everything but me and the bullet going through the target.
“Be one with the bullet” was her mantra.
Nobody races
Weiss’ father, a volunteer ski patrolman, started her shuffling around a golf course on wooden skis when she was about 6 years old. Once on the slopes, “I was bored just skiing,” she said. “I wanted to race.”
Her parents were unmoved. “Nobody in our family races,” was the dictum.
So, as she did for the rest of her life, Weiss found her own way, babysitting to raise enough cash to go to a training camp.
At the University of Vermont, Marilyn Cochran, an Olympian whose sister won a gold medal, coached her and made Weiss part of her Thanksgiving family. At school, while majoring in botany and environmental studies, Weiss switched from alpine to Nordic racing.
Her first job after school was in Wyoming with the Bridger-Teton National Forest where she ranged over the hills in a male-dominated profession. “I was always trying to prove myself as equal,” she said. “As a 22-year-old, I was quite fit.”
She wasn’t fit for her first year of graduate studies in Vermont, however. Weiss met Jackson Hole ski coach Peter Ashley who was tapped to become the first women’s national cross-country coach.
He told her to shuck her studies and race. “I hated the program,” she said of her graduate work. So she quit school, “much to my parents’ horror.”
Again, she had to finance her way “doing odd jobs, waitressing — you name it — whatever I could do to make ends meet.”
When the first national women’s biathlon team was being formed out of the field of cross-country racers, “I wrote my best letter I could,” she said, and earned a berth. “A lot of us had never really done any shooting before. I was lucky enough to pick up a rifle and have some instant good results.”
Aside from the Cochran sisters, almost all of her coaches have been men and, save for a female shooting coach, that was the situation when the military ran the first women’s biathlon team.
“They had no clue what to do differently for the women.”
Soldiers had the idea that you got fit by exercising until you dropped, she said. That’s not good. “You have to be very smart about quitting before you’re overtrained.”
While racing for a startup biathlon program, Weiss skied onto the world stage packed with professionals. “Their countries supported them,” she said. “It was a job for them. I was doing three jobs at a time, just trying to make ends meet and trying to train.”
A car crash kept her out of the tryouts for the 1992 Olympics. By the end of her career, she had been a national biathlon champion and was inducted into the U.S. Biathlon Hall of Fame.
Weiss, now 72, went back to school after her competitive ski career to become an accountant. The profession was “something that was a lot easier as a woman to get into.”
“I was doing three jobs at a time, just trying to make ends meet and trying to train.”Pam Weiss
She also was a partner with her husband at the New Zealand Kayak School in Murchison, New Zealand, which they operated for decades. Their son, Liam, became an Arctic and Antarctic sea kayak guide, a photographer and lecturer after graduating from college.
In New Zealand, where Weiss lives for about half the year, she tells friends she is uncertain what young women in Wyoming face today.
“I was explaining to them what’s going on in many parts of the U.S. and especially Wyoming where women trying to have children have all sorts of obstacles thrown at them,” she said. “If they want a family, they’re not well-supported in a state like Wyoming.
“In certain jobs, women are still climbing a ladder to prove themselves,” she said of the Equality State. “But it has gotten a lot better.”
In female athletes, Weiss sees “a younger version of me,” she said. “It’s just so cool to watch the opportunities and the goals that these women are setting for themselves. I just hope that there’s some inspiration from people before them.
“There’s always the element of having to work through some of the obstacles, but sometimes that just makes you stronger.”
The post The mountain elite: A Wyoming skier worked three jobs to be on the first U.S. women’s biathlon team appeared first on WyoFile .

name: WyoFile
title: Our strengths lie in our communities
text:
Opinion

WyoFile’s recent piece, “Amid Wyoming’s mental health struggles, governor hopes successor prioritizes the issue,” cites mental health access as a contributing factor to Wyoming’s high suicide rates. Integrating behavioral health into primary care is one best-practice that has improved mental health access in other states. Wyoming funded a few integration initiatives through its Rural Health Transformation Program. Yet, suicide risk reduction requires more resources for communities, not just healthcare systems. 
Social factors drive suicide risk. When families start addressing these at home, the suicide rates will further decline. Do our Wyoming families know their vital role as part of the solution?
According to the Centers for Disease Control, Wyoming children have higher rates of Adverse Childhood Events than the national average, ranking in the highest cohort with Montana and the top state, Oregon. Examples of these events include: not having enough food to eat, losing a parent to divorce or death (including suicide), living with someone who misuses alcohol or other substances, and suffering physical or verbal abuse by a parent. Research concludes four or more adverse childhood events render individuals 12-30 times more likely to attempt suicide compared to those with zero events. Addressing these events in Wyoming remains critical to reducing suicide risk, possibly alleviating the mental health access problem in the long-term.
This is why First Lady Jenny Gordon tirelessly targeted food insecurity. When she began her initiative, 20% of Wyoming children had insufficient food to eat. It explains why Gov. MarkGordon has framed suicide as a social issue — not just a mental health one. His successor must propagate this message too. Unless suicide is discussed at home during the sensitive time period in which parents teach their children about other safety issues like avoiding drugs, not talking to strangers and “safe touches,” it’s doubtful that lasting risk reduction will occur. Suicide isn’t his problem or their problem, it is our problem. It is happening in our families, towns, schools and churches. 
To be clear, Wyoming culture isn’t the problem; it is the solution. 
If we teach our children how to cope with strong negative emotions, they may not drink as much alcohol when encountering hardships as teens and adults. We should normalize self-help instead of criticizing this as “weak.” Stop relying on “cowboy up” sentiments, which may have worked in years past but evidently fail among members of the younger generations. Let’s help cultivate a resilient generation by teaching them how to manage adversity. This means adults must set positive examples while shifting their life philosophies as they teach their children about overcoming adversity without resorting to substance misuse and suicide. Are Wyoming parents equipped, resourced and ready for this? 
Leveraging Wyoming’s cultural values of independence and self-reliance, along with the appreciation of helping someone who is in a dangerous situation, helps reduce suicide risk across communities — the Wyoming way. But culture change takes time, and persistence.  
There are signs that culture change has begun under Gov. Gordon. The rise in help-seeking demand signals cited in WyoFile’s recent article substantiate that culture is shifting. Help-seeking is on the rise, which is part of the solution. Increased referrals to behavioral health and rising calls to 988, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, are indicators of progress — not signals of things getting worse. 
Can Wyoming parents, schools and faith communities increasingly help young people better cope with adversity early in life? Is the next governor willing to target adverse childhood events through parent education programs in schools? Will our faith communities help by partnering with nonfaith organizations? 
Can we please provide support for bereaved families and friends  after every single Wyoming suicide so that communities stop experiencing these deaths as trauma and we dissuade onlookers from believing suicide is a viable option to life’s worst days?
These are the upstream programs and initiatives that will reduce further suicide risk in Wyoming. Our strengths lie in our communities. I hope and pray the next governor will help the culture evolve by empowering and resourcing people locally.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Tobacco manufacturers donate $27K to Idaho AG Labrador’s campaign, years after settlement tweaks
text:
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 National Police Week roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., alongside Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and other officials. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General's Office)Republican Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador and Gov. Brad Little’s re-election campaigns received more than $20,000 each in donations from tobacco and nicotine manufacturers.
In race for Idaho attorney general, a Democrat is trying to unseat a long-time Republican official

The donations come in the first election cycle for the statewide offices after Labrador struck a complex deal in 2024 with tobacco manufacturers to essentially not fight in court about a pool of settlement payments that tobacco manufacturers tend to dispute. At the time of the agreement, Labrador’s office said the deal essentially guaranteed the state a big chunk of money up front, but the deal also left millions of dollars on the table that could have come to the state over a longer period of time.
In an interview last week, Labrador said he didn’t communicate with the tobacco manufacturers about their contributions to his campaign, and he defended the deal over the settlement funds. His campaign received $27,000 in donations from tobacco manufacturers. 
“They donated after the litigation was done. … Probably for them, it’s also a good thing to get out of the litigation and not having to spend years and years of litigation,” Labrador said. “So, they support the work that I do. They support other things that I’m doing, and I don’t really question; I receive donations from a lot of different people.”
Idaho tobacco settlement secures millions in funds, rather than spending years to litigate payments

Labrador, the state’s top attorney and a former congressman, said many other states reached a similar deal. The agreement was over disputed funds from a massive 1998 settlement with tobacco manufacturers that set up decades of multi-million dollar payments to states to reduce smoking.
“It was costing the states millions of dollars to litigate these cases, so in the end, it ended up just being better for the state. And we received a substantial amount of money for the state, and we didn’t have to worry about: Would we lose in some future case … then, you lose the entire amount?” Labrador said. 
Little’s re-election campaign received $25,000 in donations from tobacco and nicotine manufacturers. His campaign could not immediately be reached for comment. 
The online prediction market platform Kalshi donated $5,000 to Labrador’s campaign last week, months after Labrador pushed for the state’s authority to regulate sports betting, Idaho Education News reported.
 Companies linked to Marlboro, Zyn makers donated the most to Labrador’s campaigns

The tobacco manufacturers also donated to other state officials, including to several state lawmakers, along with political action committees, or PACs. On the whole, Labrador received the most donations, with Little behind in a close second.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Companies linked to Philip Morris, the manufacturer of the cigarette brand Marlboro and Zyn nicotine pouches, were among the biggest donors to re-election campaigns for Labrador and Little. The companies donated $22,000 to Labrador through three affiliated companies, and $20,000 to Little through the same string of companies, along with making donations to Idaho PACs and other statewide and legislative candidates.

PMI U.S. Corporate Services, a domestic arm that focuses on smokeless alternatives such as Zyns, gave Labrador $5,000 in the primary, and $5,000 in the general election. Those are both the maximum donations allowed per election cycle in Idaho. This corporation also gave the same donations to Little in the primary and general, along with donations to several incumbent Republican legislators and statewide officials. The company donated $15,000 between this year and last year to the Idaho Prosperity Fund, a PAC run by Alex LaBeau, the head of the Idaho Association of Industry and Commerce, a powerful lobbying group in the state. 
PMI Global Services gave Labrador $1,000 in the primary and in the general. The first donation came through on Sept. 25, 2024, about five months after Labrador had reached the new deal on tobacco settlement funds. The company donated $1,000 to 2026 campaigns for Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf and Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, along with smaller donations to dozens of state legislators, Republicans and Democrats alike. The company also gave $15,000 in 2025 to the Idaho Victory Fund, a PAC, which is run in part by Chad Hennggeler, who works as a fruit grower, Ysabel Bilbao, an Idaho lobbyist.
Altria Client Services, which is owned by the tobacco company’s parent company, gave Labrador $5,000 donations in the primary and general elections. The company also gave Little, the state’s governor, $5,000 in the primary election. (The company’s lobbying arm, based in Washington, D.C., gave Little a separate $5,000 primary donation.) The company gave maximum $1,000 primary and general election donations to several members of Republican legislative leadership’s re-election campaigns, including House Speaker Mike Moyle, Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon and House Majority Leader Jason Monks. Smaller donations went to other incumbent Republican legislators in Idaho, along with Democratic state Rep. Steve Berch, who has raised the most of any legislative candidate in Idaho. 

Reynolds American, a North Carolina-based tobacco manufacturer behind cigarette brands such as Newport, Camel and Lucky Strike, contributed $5,000 to Labrador’s primary election campaign. The company gave the same amount to Little’s primary campaign, along with:

$1,500 to the Senate Republicans PAC of Idaho
$1,000 to either primary or general campaigns for: state Rep. Tanya Burgoyne, who lost her primary election; state Sen. Jim Guthrie; state Rep. Chris Bruce; and state Rep. Elaine Price, who are all Republican incumbents. Republican state Rep. Rob Beiswenger received a $500 donation from the company, along with Idaho House Minority Leader Ilana Rubel, a Democrat.

Companies linked to the tobacco manufacturers could not be immediately reached for comment. In a statement, Philip Morris’s domestic company said its donations are part of a bigger effort. 
“Philip Morris International’s U.S. businesses (PMI U.S.) participate transparently in the political process, including by supporting candidates and organizations that understand the issues affecting our business, adult consumers, and trade partners,” the spokesperson for PMI U.S. Corporate Services said. “We make these contributions as part of a comprehensive government affairs engagement.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Millions from Musk, pro-Trump group and party super PACs flood Colorado’s 8th District race
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans, left, a Fort Lupton Republican finishing his first term in Congress, and Manny Rutinel, a Commerce City Democrat and former state legislator, debated on Oct. 7, 2026, in Berthoud ahead of their race to represent Colorado's 8th Congressional District. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)All four of Colorado’s Republican congressional incumbents are receiving help from deep-pocketed super PACs in the run-up to the Nov. 3 midterm election — but one race in particular is drawing double the amount of outside spending as all the other races combined.

As of Oct. 20, $18.9 million in super PAC spending has flowed into Colorado’s 8th District race during the general election between incumbent Republican U.S. Rep. Gabe Evans and his challenger, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel, according to Federal Election Commission disclosures. Outside groups have reported independent expenditures totaling $9.4 million across Colorado’s three other competitive congressional races this year.
Only two other House contests in the country — in North Carolina’s 1st District and Florida’s 25th District — have attracted more total spending by campaigns and PACs than the race between Evans and Rutinel this election cycle.
It’s the third election cycle in a row that the battleground 8th District — Colorado’s newest and most diverse congressional district, drawn by an independent commission in 2021 to include parts of Denver’s northern suburbs along with southern Weld County — has attracted tens of millions of dollars in campaign spending, much of it by partisan super PACs associated with Republican and Democratic leaders in Washington.
Unlike candidate campaign committees, which are subject to individual contribution limits and can’t accept money from certain kinds of contributors, super PACs can accept unlimited donations from individuals, corporations and other groups, including so-called “dark money” nonprofits that don’t disclose their donors.



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



While Evans had raised and spent $4.2 million in direct campaign cash as of Sept. 30, his reelection bid’s financial firepower is coming largely from pro-Republican super PACs, which have spent another $10.4 million to support his candidacy. That total includes more than $6 million from the Congressional Leadership Fund, a group associated with GOP House leadership and Speaker Mike Johnson; $1.5 million from No Going Back PAC, linked to President Donald Trump; and $843,000 from Americans for Prosperity, the advocacy network of conservative billionaire Charles Koch.
Evans has also received $344,000 in support from America PAC, founded by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man and a close Trump ally. Musk is also a top donor to the Congressional Leadership Fund, having given the group $20 million this year. Other major funders of the PAC include conservative megadonor Miriam Adelson and the dark-money group American Action Network.
Similarly, Rutinel, whose campaign reported spending a little over $3 million between his June Democratic primary victory and Sept. 30, has received more than $8.6 million in Democratic super PAC assistance during the general election. Like Evans, the bulk of that help has come from the group associated with his party’s House leadership, the House Majority PAC, which has aided Rutinel’s campaign to the tune of $4.3 million. That group’s top donor is a dark-money nonprofit, House Majority Forward.
Other groups backing Rutinel include the Mainstream Colorado Fund, a new super PAC that has reported contributions from several other PACs and the dark-money Sixteen Thirty Fund; and the LCV Victory Fund, a PAC associated with the League of Conservation Voters.
Other races
With control of the House of Representatives at stake in the midterms, Democrats say they’re targeting all four GOP-held congressional seats in Colorado, eyeing an unprecedented 8-0 sweep of its House delegation. The state’s four Democratic House incumbents face only token opposition this year, and none of the four races has attracted super PAC spending or significant fundraising by GOP challengers.
In the race in Colorado’s 5th District, where Democratic challenger Jessica Killin’s campaign has substantially outraised incumbent GOP Rep. Jeff Crank, spending from Republican super PACs is helping to offset Crank’s financial disadvantage. The 5th District, long considered a safe Republican seat, is centered on Colorado Springs, where Democrats have grown increasingly competitive in recent elections.
Crank’s top super PAC backer is Trump’s No Going Back PAC, which has spent $2.4 million on his behalf. Americans for Prosperity, Crank’s longtime employer, has also spent $680,000 supporting his candidacy. Killin, meanwhile, has received a total of about $1.5 million in support from the House Majority PAC and an array of other pro-Democratic groups.
Incumbent GOP Rep. Jeff Hurd has benefited from more than $1.6 million in spending from No Going Back and another Trump-affiliated group, the Safety and Affordability PAC, as he looks to hold on to his seat in the 3rd District, which spans much of Colorado’s Western Slope. His Democratic opponent, Aspen businessman Dwayne Romero, has lagged far behind Hurd in campaign fundraising, and also hasn’t received any significant super PAC support to date.
In the 4th District, which includes Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher has spent nearly $10 million in campaign cash so far during the 2026 election cycle, and has received a late boost of $1.5 million in super PAC spending opposing Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition, a clean-energy group.
As she looks to pull off an upset in Colorado’s most Republican-leaning congressional district, Laubacher is benefiting from a 6-to-1 financial advantage over incumbent Boebert, whose campaign has spent just $1.1 million in the 2026 cycle, while receiving about $760,000 in help from a PAC associated with the far-right House Freedom Caucus.

Friday, Oct. 23 is also the deadline to register to vote in advance of the Nov. 3 general election. However, if eligible voters miss the Oct. 23 deadline to register to vote in advance, they can still register to vote at their polling place on Election Day. 
To request a free absentee ballot, Idaho voters can visit www.voteidaho.gov, the official election website of the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office. Otherwise, voters can request an absentee ballot at their local county clerk’s office or mail an absentee ballot request form to their county clerk. 
Idahoans must already be registered to vote to request an absentee ballot. 
If Idahoans don’t vote by absentee ballot, they can participate in early voting, which began in most counties recently, or vote in person at their polling place on Election Day, Nov. 3.

In this year’s general election, all of Idaho’s statewide constitutional officers, like governor and attorney general, are up for election. In addition, all 105 seats in the Idaho Legislature, three of Idaho’s four seats in Congress and county positions all across the state are being voted on. 
On top of that, all Idaho voters will vote on a ballot initiative, Proposition 1, that seeks to restore the right to an abortion in the state.
There are also two proposed amendments to the Idaho Constitution that all Idaho voters will weigh in on. 
One proposed amendment, House Joint Resolution 6, would make English the official language of Idaho. The other proposed amendment, House Joint Resolution 4, would make it so that only the Idaho Legislature would be able to legalize marijuana and other drugs. If a majority of voters vote for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would give up their right to ever run a ballot initiative to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis or any other drug.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Congressional candidates for Shelby County districts raise combined $4.6M in 90 days
text:
U.S. Congressional District 9 candidates Justin J. Pearson (D) and Brent Taylor (R); District 5 candidates Charlie Hatcher (R) and Chaz Molder (D); and District 8 candidates Heidi Kuhn (D) and David Kustoff (R). (Pearson, Taylor, Hatcher and Molder photos by John Partipilo for Tennessee Lookout; Kuhn photo courtesy of kuhnforcongress.com; Kustoff photo courtesy of kustoff.house.gov)Candidates for Tennessee’s three newly drawn congressional seats that represent parts of Shelby County raised a combined $4.6 million in the 90 days leading up to October, campaign finance records show.
Tennessee’s Republican supermajority redrew the state’s congressional district map in May, splitting Democratic stronghold Shelby County into three districts in an attempt to create another Republican-held seat in the 2026 midterms.
The 5th and 9th districts now stretch from Memphis to Middle Tennessee, and the hundreds of thousands of dollars flowing into those races show both parties are treating them as competitive. Both seats are open, meaning there are no incumbents to contend with. 


The District 9 race has the narrowest projected Republican advantage with a lean of five to nine points. The district also drew the most contributions during the third quarter. State Rep. Justin J. Pearson, a Memphis Democrat, raised nearly $1.3 million between July 1 and Sept. 30, reports show. The majority of that funding came from individuals, with about $62,000 coming from political party committees and political action committees, or PACs, according to Pearson’s October 2026 filing with the Federal Election Commission.
Pearson faces Sen. Brent Taylor, a Memphis Republican, who reported the second-highest contributions in quarter three. Taylor’s roughly $1.1 million in contributions includes about $543,000 in loans, followed by $432,000 in individual contributions and around $169,500 in contributions from political party committees and PACs.
Candidates for District 5 — which now stretches from Memphis through Northwest Tennessee and part of Williamson County — brought in nearly $1.8 million combined since July 1. The district has a Republican lean of between six and 10 points.
Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, a Republican, reported just over $1 million in contributions, including $849,000 from individuals and about $141,000 from PACs or party committees. He also personally kicked in more than $10,000.
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, Hatcher’s Democratic opponent, raised nearly $781,000 in quarter three. Molder’s receipts include $629,000 from individuals, $102,000 from PACs or party committees, and about $48,000 in transfers from other committees. 
In the 8th Congressional District, incumbent Republican Rep. David Kustoff faces Democratic candidate Heidi Kuhn. This race’s cash infusion didn’t come close to the amounts given in the other Shelby County seats. Kustoff, who was first elected to the seat in 2016, raised just under $286,000 to add to his expansive existing war chest. Of that, $123,000 came from party committees or PACs. 
Kuhn, the former Shelby County Criminal Court Clerk, reported raising nearly $55,500 from individuals.


Kustoff has the most cash on hand with nearly $3 million. He reported spending $305,000 since July 1 to defend his seat against Kuhn, who reported $20,500 on hand and spent around $50,000 in that 90-day period.
In the non-incumbent races, Democratic candidates have the most cash on hand leading up to the election, reports show. 
Pearson reported nearly $1.2 million remaining in his campaign account, and Molder reported about $1 million.
Taylor is not far behind with about $822,000, and Hatcher has $753,000.
Molder’s campaign spent the most in the third quarter at nearly $1.2 million, followed by Pearson with $973,000 in expenses.
Taylor spent $740,000 and Hatcher spent $352,000.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Lowndes County Commission sued over approval of hyperscale data center
text:
Residents gather in the Charles Smith Annex for a special meeting of the Lowndes County Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, in Hayneville, Alabama. The commission was sued for violating the Alabama Open Meetings Act for the body's last meeting, and residents and advocates alledge Tuesday's meeting was a violation of another state law. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector) 


Key points

Two residents have sued the Lowndes County Commission over the approval of a 2,200-acre hyperscale data center last week, alleging its approval of the project and tax breaks violated the state Open Meetings Act.
The commission held a meeting Tuesday morning attended by 125 people in which commissioners disputed whether to approve the minutes of the previous meeting.
Residents have expressed concerns about noise and water use for the proposed facility, which would use enough electricity to power 1 million homes.




HAYNEVILLE — A lawsuit filed Sunday alleges that the Lowndes County Commission’s approval of a 2,200-acre hyperscale data center — which would be Alabama’s largest — violated the Alabama Open Meetings Act. 
The commission last week approved Project Red Clay and a $1.15 billion tax break for the facility, surprising residents, advocates and two commissioners who voted against the proposals. 
The lawsuit came days before a standing-room only special meeting of the commission Tuesday morning, in which at least 125 county residents crowded into the commission’s regular meeting place. The commission has been forced to a larger space for previous meetings to accommodate crowd sizes.
According to the proposal, the project will operate 24/7. It requested 1,500 megawatts of energy capacity from Alabama Power, enough to power roughly 1 million homes. The entire state of Alabama has about 2 million households and about 2.4 million housing units.
The center’s planned location is along U.S. Hwy 80 and Alabama Hwy 21 in unincorporated Lowndes County, which runs along the historic Selma to Montgomery trail.
Rep. Prince Chestnut, D-Selma, the commission’s attorney, told the governing body that the only options for the commission Tuesday morning were to approve the minutes of the prior meeting, or table them for a future meeting. The commission meets on Monday for its next regular meeting. The lawsuit was not addressed. 
“The only thing that you could take up is possibly considering the minutes, to adopt the actions taken at the Oct. 13 meeting, because that would be consistent with authorizing related actions,” Chestnut said. “It would be the will of the commission.”
In quick succession, Commissioner Robert Harris motioned to approve the minutes of the prior meeting and Commissioner Dickson Farrior, the vice chair, moved for a point of order.
“This matter has already been decided. The Lowndes County Commission has a special meeting, and it wasn’t posted on the door right there for the minutes to be dealt with,” Farrior said.
Under Alabama law, county commissions can only address or act on what is on the agenda for a special called meeting. The notice posted on the entrance to the commission’s meeting room said the body would “consider adoption of resolution and order authorizing execution and delivery of  a project development agreement and a tax abatement agreement for Project Red Clay and Authorizing Related Actions.”
Lowndes commission approves $1.15 billion tax break for a data center despite pushback

Commissioner Charlie King, Jr., the chair, moved to approve the minutes until Farrior objected. 
“I don’t have to rule on what you just brought up. You need to make a motion on what you just brought up. You just made a statement, and you’re entitled to your statement,” King said to Farrior.
Farrior then moved to table the minutes, which failed 2-3. The minutes were approved 3-2. King then adjourned the meeting. As the commissioners left, the crowd called out praises for Farrior and Commissioner Joseph Barganier, who voted with Farrior each time, and heckled the other commissioners.
“We’re proud of you,” one called to Farrior and Barganier.
“We’ll visit you in jail,” another called to the other commissioners.
The commissioners, except for Farrior and Barganier, signed the minutes immediately after the meeting adjourned. Farrior said that has never happened before. 
King, Harris, Chestnut and Commissioner Fletcher Hayes declined to comment on their way out of the room. 
The public notice for a special meeting of the Lowndes County Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, posted on the entrance to the meeting room’s door in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
Ryan Anderson, an attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, questioned the legality of the commission’s actions in an interview after the meeting.
“The (commission) attorney’s position, from what I can tell, is that approving last week’s minutes was a related action authorizing the tax abatements, but I think that there could be a legal question there of if it really falls into the meaning of ‘authorizing related actions,’ as Commissioner Farrior pointed out,” she said.
She said approval of the minutes would have been legal at Monday’s meeting, and approval of the project proposal and tax break were legal since the meetings are regular. 
Lowndes County residents demand transparency in hyperscale data center development

Farrior said in an interview after the meeting that he looked up the section of Alabama’s law applicable to special meetings of county commissions in preparation for the meeting. He represents the northeastern portion of the county, where the data center’s proposed location is. 
“In fact, I looked it up last night,” he said. “It was on the agenda, but it was not on the notice. This is the notice right here that was put on the door.”
Barganier, who represents the southern portion of the county, said in an interview after the meeting that he voted against approving the minutes to try to stall the data center.
“It being in the middle of the county, that’s the fastest growing area in Lowndes County, or the only growing area in Lowndes County, and now it’s gonna kill that,” he said. “I guess they should have put it in a different place.”
Lowndes County Commissioner Dickson Farrior pointing out the section of the Alabama Code that requires special meetings of county commissions to only address what is posted on public notices after a contentious meeting of the commission on Oct. 20, 2026, in Hayneville, Alabama. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)
The lawsuit was filed on behalf of two residents, who seek relief through halted commission votes and civil penalties, according to the complaint. 
On Monday, presiding Circuit Judge Cleveland Poole recused himself from the case. As of Tuesday afternoon, another judge has not been assigned.
Barganier said that many of his constituents, who do not live near the proposed site, have asked him to oppose the development because of its location. In addition to its historic significance, it is also the most populous area of the county. 
Lowndes County, like many counties in the Black Belt, has seen a population decrease between 2010 and 2020. But the census tract at the proposed location of Project Red Clay via the U.S. Census Bureau is the most densely populated part of the county, 21.7 people per square mile. Other tracts in the county are 14.8, 12.3 and 9.7 people per square mile. 
“If they got out somewhere where nobody was around or something, I would probably go for it,” Barganier said. “But 254 houses. They’re gonna disturb those families for the rest of their lives.”
Farrior said he wished the commission would have debated the project proposal and tax breaks before they voted on them, but that opportunity was not given.
“There’s issues about the water, there’s issues about the power, there’s issues about the environment, there’s issues about the property values and the health of the people that live around there, and none of that’s been dealt with,” he said. “It was just thrown in our face for us to vote on, and it’s something that should have been talked about before it was voted on, but it was just pushed through.”
John Urquhart, a Lowndes County resident who lives next to the proposed data center site, said in an interview that he “didn’t expect any less” from the commissioners on Tuesday, but he is very proud to be represented by Farrior. 
“So, so proud of our commissioners, Farrior and Barganier, and how they stood up for us. To see them refuse to sign those documents at the end of that meeting. That’s the gentleman we need sitting on those seats,” Urquhart said. 
Urquhart is part of a resident coalition called Protect Lowndes County that has been pushing back on Project Red Clay for months. He said that while there are likely no more commission votes left, Protect Lowndes County’s work is not done.
“It’s probably going to only help our cause,” he said. “Protect Lowndes County is so much more than this … Going forward, we got a lot more we want to do. We want to see these offices cleared up. We want to see the commission be like it should, representing the county.”
Key points box written by Editor Brian Lyman.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Trump announces $8B fuel relief program for farmers, but timeline and payment details are hazy
text:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture will spend $8 billion in temporary aid to farmers, President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)President Donald Trump announced Monday that the U.S. Department of Agriculture will make $8 billion in one-time payments to American farmers to help offset “temporary market disruptions” and high fuel costs.
The announcement comes after repeated requests for relief amid high diesel fuel prices that economists attribute mostly to the war in Iran. Trump previously issued an executive order offering to make untaxed off-road dyed diesel available for on-road use to alleviate a small portion of diesel costs. Farmers and truckers have been hesitant to embrace this option, as it remains unclear whether the federal tax owed for on-road diesel will merely be deferred until a later date.
The Harvest Fuel Relief program will use a formula to determine how much farmers can receive based on the crops they grow and loss modeling, according to the USDA. Payment rates for Title I commodities — major row crops including wheat, soybeans, corn, oats, peanuts and more — are expected to be released in November. It’s not clear if they will come before or after the Nov. 3 midterm election. Payment rates for other commodities “will be announced at a later date,” and specialty crop producers and fishermen are “encouraged to provide data related to increased fuel costs” to the USDA via email for consideration.
The department has not released a payment timeline. And Congressional approval may be needed to shuffle funds to cover the $8 billion expense, Politico reported Tuesday.
More guidance issued on suspended enforcement of off-road diesel rules
Trump’s executive order instructing the U.S. Treasury Department to defer federal taxes on dyed off-road diesel and allow the slightly cheaper fuel to be used on highways runs through the end of the year.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said the state would suspend enforcement of its rules limiting the use of the red-dyed diesel fuel to off-road vehicles through the end of October.
President Donald Trump holds up an executive order he just signed waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State and federal fuel taxes are typically used to pay for road maintenance, so fuel used solely in off-road vehicles is usually exempt from these taxes. The tax-free fuel is dyed red to differentiate it from regularly taxed diesel.
The Internal Revenue Service, IRS, said it would not “impose a penalty when dyed diesel fuel is sold for use or used on highways nationwide” through Dec. 31, according to guidance issued on Oct. 14. The relief is retroactive to Oct. 1. 
The IRS will pause fuel inspections for on-road dyed diesel for that time period. 
While the IRS stated that “taxpayers need not maintain records necessary to substantiate their eligibility for relief,” national federation of energy trade associations Energy Marketers of America is encouraging its members to track gallons of dyed diesel sold to highway vehicles anyway. The organization emphasizes that the IRS has not yet indicated that the federal diesel tax will be forgiven, and that money may be difficult for fuel retailers to recover from customers later.
“If the deferred tax ultimately comes due, those records will be the best defense against an IRS estimate of liability,” Energy Marketers of America stated in an Oct. 15 regulatory alert.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Commentary: Idaho helped start the nuclear age. We should help write what comes next.
text:
Researchers work in the Idaho National Laboratory's Hot Fuel Examination Facility. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory)In July, the U.S. Department of Energy named Idaho as a finalist to host one of three Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses.
As former legal counsel for Idaho Gov. Butch Otter and administrator of the Idaho Governor’s Office of Species, Minerals, and Energy Coordination, I’ve spent years working on nuclear policy. I think Idaho is the logical location to host one of these campuses. I also think we can do so without surrendering the protections two governors fought hard to win.
In nuclear campus talks, Idaho Gov. Brad Little says protecting Snake aquifer is ‘nonnegotiable’ 

As proposed by DOE, winning campuses would accept approximately 33,000 tons of the country’s used nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states where some would remain for final disposition. Understandably, that might set off some alarms— perhaps images of the green goo from “The Simpsons” come to mind.
And given the federal government’s proclivity prior to 1995 to dump nuclear waste here without a clean-up plan, our state leaders were right to fight for the health and safety of Idaho’s people and environment.
 Idaho is in the lead when it comes to nuclear technology

For the past 30 years, the 1995 Settlement Agreement has served as Idaho’s strongest and one-of-a-kind negotiating tool with the DOE to protect public health and the environment while addressing nuclear waste. But technology has advanced rapidly, and we’ve discovered that what was previously deemed “waste” or “spent fuel” has a lot more life left and can be recycled and reused.
In 1995, the signers of that agreement could not have contemplated a thriving nuclear industry where fuel is not merely used once in a reactor and then prepared for permanent disposal. Today, new reactors can run on used fuel, and there’s a growing interest in recycling and repurposing its components.
Much of what we know about the opportunities for used fuel is the result of the work done at Idaho National Laboratory. INL leads the pack nationally in used-fuel research. Next year, it will evaluate how used high-burnup fuel holds up in long-term storage. Being named host of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus recognizes what is already happening in Eastern Idaho and expands on it.
The opportunities for recycling fuel at or near INL are significant. And recycling what’s onsite now and what may come from other parts of the country ultimately means less material that is truly “waste.” That is a win for the industry and a win for Idaho.
 Questions remain on what a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus would mean for Idaho

There are still many unknowns and unanswered questions about what becoming a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus might mean for Idaho. The Nuclear Waste Policy Act must be amended by Congress before any new campus can be designated. That law names Yucca Mountain in Nevada as the location for the used fuel and waste contemplated by the DOE.
The Nuclear Waste Policy Act is also not clear about if or when DOE must take title of commercial used fuel.
All used fuel at INL is owned by DOE. But as commercial reactors continue to be developed, questions remain over whether DOE is ever obligated to take ownership of the fuel used by these reactors or whether there is opportunity for those companies to recycle and reuse it.
DOE must also pay significant sums to whoever is storing this used fuel and waste. So far it has remained silent on that point.
 We should build upon Idaho’s foundation with the 1995 Settlement Agreement

The Settlement Agreement is Idaho’s strongest negotiating tool, and we should continue to use it that way as we look closely at the opportunity to be a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus host.
Idaho’s current practice is to allow, through waivers to the Settlement Agreement, limited “research quantities” of used fuel to enter the state for INL to study. (The Navy’s fuel, which differs from this research fuel, is handled under its own addendum and negotiated separately.)
The innovation campus deal should be contemplated the same way. What is DOE trying to build, and what does it aim to deliver by the end of 2027, 2028 and beyond? Much of what it hopes to accomplish is already in progress in Idaho.
A comprehensive overhaul of the Settlement Agreement is likely not necessary for all parties to win. Keep the agreement intact, and write Idaho’s terms into whatever comes next.
How, for instance, can the nuclear sector take advantage of reprocessing and recycling opportunities to minimize the overall volume of genuine “nuclear waste” requiring secure disposal? It would be a shame not to leverage the existing Settlement Agreement, but even more disappointing to let this opportunity that bolsters our economy and puts Idaho front and center of the burgeoning nuclear energy surge fall away.
Idaho is uniquely positioned to be the place that figures out how to study, recycle and reuse that fuel, a contribution that could shape national and global energy for generations.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Data center legislation begins to take shape in North Dakota
text:
Rep. Anna Novak, R-Hazen, speaks during a meeting of the Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee on July 15, 2026. Novak tuned in remotely on Oct. 20, 2026, to present the framework of her proposed data center regulations. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)A lawmaker from North Dakota’s coal country is working on proposed legislation to regulate some of the more controversial aspects of data centers in the state. 
Rep. Anna Novak, R-Hazen, briefed some of her legislative colleagues Tuesday on the framework of her bill. It focuses on three aspects: the cost of electricity, water use and requirements for when a facility is decommissioned. 
“Those are the major concerns of the North Dakota citizens,” Novak said. “The locals certainly have their responsibility on things. But when it comes to those three things, they’re looking for help from the state, and that’s very reasonable.”
The state government does not directly regulate data center development, though there have been increasing calls for the state to take action. 
Data center concerns dominate public comment for new legislative committee

The first focus of Novak’s bill is enshrining the principle of “bring your own power” into state law. The bill would formally prohibit any costs associated with data centers from being transferred to ratepayers. 
Novak said it is important for North Dakota citizens to know their electricity bills are not going up because of data centers. The legislator noted there are examples of large data centers creating a benefit for electricity consumers in North Dakota, but that ratepayers should be protected in instances where that is not the case. 
“We need to codify that rate shifting to residential customers cannot occur because of large loads or data centers,” Novak said.
She’s also looking for a way to ensure ratepayers have access to clear information on why the cost of electricity is going up when a utility proposes a rate increase. 
“The price of milk, bread and eggs are going to go up because that’s just what happens over time. Electricity rates will also go up, but they should stay in line with those things,” Novak said. “It’s reasonable for people to want to understand why their electricity rates are increasing.”
The bill would also require all data centers to use closed-loop water cooling systems, because those facilities use less water. 
“We’re just getting through a drought right now, and so this is a valid concern of citizens,” she said.
Novak is also working on a section that would require a plan for repurposing the structure when it is ready to be decommissioned. The proposal will likely include a bonding requirement for the developer. But the lawmaker said a requirement to tear down the building and fully reclaim the site is unnecessary and unreasonable. 
“It seems wasteful to me,” Novak said.
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, said he is uncomfortable requiring a specific industry to have a plan for decommissioning when other facilities, like an Amazon distribution facility, do not have to do so. 
“I understand the reasons for it. But you’re picking out one industry to make sure they do reclamation. Meanwhile, we have ethanol plants, we have a soybean crushing plant, we have a battery manufacturing plant in Fargo,” Nathe said. “They’re not required to have reclamation plans.”
Rep. Mike Nathe, R-Bismarck, speaks during a meeting of the Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Committee on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Capitol. (Photo by Jacob Orledge/North Dakota Monitor)
Rep. Jonathan Warrey, the Casselton Republican chairing the interim Artificial Intelligence and Data Centers Committee, said the long-term decommissioning is a valid concern because the industry’s economics are changing so quickly and most data centers are signing 15-year lease agreements. 
“These other industries that you reference have been around for decades, or centuries in some cases. And so I do wonder, as a state, what do we do in year 16?” Warrey said. “That is what we have learned is these are 15-year agreements from well-resourced companies, but year 16 and beyond becomes a question mark.”
Novak noted the potential long-term problem of decommissioning is what county commissioners are “asking for the most help on,” based on her conversations with local officials. She warned inaction from the state could lead to more stringent requirements at the local level.
Other lawmakers are developing ideas for policy changes surrounding data centers as well. Sen. Dean Rummel, R-Dickinson, suggested narrowing the sales tax exemption used by data centers to only apply to computing equipment. 
“Get rid of the exemptions on fiber optic, on the racking, on the cooling systems, everything else that should not have an exemption,” Rummel said. “We could still say we have a sales tax exemption, but it’s extremely narrow.”
Rummel said doing so would reduce the value of the sales tax exemption from tens of millions of dollars to a few million. 
Casselton-area residents question data center location on prime farmland

Sen. Jose Castaneda, R-Minot, said the Legislature should consider requiring every county to draft a local data center ordinance that addresses certain topics, such as setbacks or noise limitations, so the public and developers both know where they stand ahead of time. 
“We would still allow local control at the county level to allow them to decide what they want, how they want it,” Castaneda said. “You have to come up with an ordinance that, at a minimum, covers these items.”
He said the requirement would allow everyone to operate on the “same sheet of music.” Sen. Janne Myrdal, R-Edinburg, agreed and said the state’s rules should help make local control possible, but not outshine those local ordinances. 
“How they do those ordinances is up to them, as long as it doesn’t violate state law,” Myrdal said. “I think the more the Legislature does, the more we trample the local authority.”
Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot, said in an interview after the meeting that he thinks all data center zoning decisions should be made at the county level, rather than the city or township level. 
“We can’t have this multi-tiered structure of different political subdivisions trying to compete with one another for what’s the most local form of control,” Hogue said. “We do need some local decision-making authority, but it shouldn’t be multi-tiered.”
Data centers can’t be stopped, but good policy is needed, NDSU researcher says

Some lawmakers are worried that Novak’s protections for electric ratepayers could have unintended consequences for other industries that also use large amounts of electricity, like oil refineries or ethanol plants. 
But others are cautioning against legislation that targets data centers specifically. They warned against trying to pick winners and losers among different industries.
“We maybe need to look big picture at where we want to regulate industry as a whole, instead of pigeonholing, you know, this factory or that factory,” Castaneda said. “These are all industries that have an effect on our power grid.”
Novak’s bill is still a work in progress and the final language has not been determined. She said she is working with various agencies and stakeholders to find the right approach prior to the legislative session that begins in January.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: What we leave our children in the Monongahela National Forest
text:
Bickle Knob is part of the Monongahela National Forest in Eklins, West Virginia. (Photo courtesy of the Forest Service)I want my ashes scattered at Bickle Knob.
That may seem an unusual place to begin discussing forest policy. But it explains why the Monongahela Forest matters to me.
I taught my sons at Bickle Knob in Elkins, West Virginia. Soon, my son will take my granddaughters there.
The trails, streams and panoramas have enriched and continue to enrich my family’s life. Our family’s story is one among many in “our home among the hills.” Preserved public lands hold those connections across generations.
Families whose stories there have not yet begun deserve that chance too. That is moral geography.
Existing regulatory protections for West Virginia’s natural resources should remain in place. That is why I oppose the Trump administration’s proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule. Mountain State Spotlight reports that more than 180,000 acres across West Virginia’s national forests could lose the rule’s protections against roadbuilding and logging. The Monongahela is among the forests affected.
Years ago, while completing postdoctoral training in the Chicago area, my oldest son announced that he wanted to go fishing. He was 3.
Having little experience, I bought books, sought expert advice and purchased equipment considerably more sophisticated than our fishing skills.
Eventually, his younger brother joined us. As we prepared for visits home to West Virginia, fishing became an opportunity to teach both boys how to walk safely in the woods and leave no trace.
One evening at an Illinois forest preserve, darkness was approaching. I asked how they would find their way back to the car.
“With our flashlights, Dad!” my oldest replied.
He helped his younger brother turn on his flashlight and took his hand. Neither knew that I had placed reflective markers along the trail. Their flashlight beams caught the markers, and the way back lit up.
I was right behind them.
At the car, I reminded them that other trails would not have our markers. I told them how proud I was that they had been careful and had cared for each other.
I think of that evening as I watch my son now teach my granddaughters. Learning to walk in the woods means paying attention to where you place your feet and where the people you love are walking. It means enjoying a place while accepting responsibility for how you move through it.
Adults making decisions about our forests might consider that lesson.
I am not a forester. My training as a pediatric psychologist has taught me to examine evidence carefully. When the subject is a forest where my son is passing along our respect for the beauty of West Virginia to my granddaughters, I have a responsibility to do so.
The Roadless Rule generally restricts road construction and timber harvesting in inventoried roadless areas. It includes exceptions, including limited cutting of generally small trees to reduce uncharacteristic wildfire effects when specified ecological conditions are met.
The administration argues that rescission would give local forest managers more flexibility to address wildfire and forest health. Forest Service research describes long intervals between fires across much of the Monongahela landscape, alongside areas with more frequent historical fire in its drier eastern areas near the Virginia border. That varied history calls for continued scientific judgment. It does not by itself justify removing roadless protections.
Our own history also warrants care. The 1930 fire at Dolly Sods offers a caution: logging debris and removal of forest cover contributed to a devastating fire that consumed deep organic soil layers, in places down to bedrock.
That does not prove that modern timber harvesting always increases fire risk. It challenges the assumption that more logging necessarily makes a forest safer. Rescission would not itself authorize logging. Future projects would still have to comply with forest plans and applicable law. Calling the change “flexibility” does not tell us whether it is wise.
Responsible forestry has a place in West Virginia. So does protecting places where quiet woods and the chance to pass them on are themselves public benefits.
West Virginia’s history of extraction should make us especially vigilant against weakening existing protections for our natural resources.
Federal officials must demonstrate why existing exceptions within the Roadless Rule are insufficient. West Virginia’s congressional delegation should defend existing protections for our natural resources, including this rule.
My granddaughters and other children will inherit the consequences. Perhaps they will have children of their own to take into these woods and say, “This is where my father brought me. This is where his father brought him.”
And then take a small hand and gently and respectfully keep walking.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Early voting in Colorado outpaces 2022 midterm election
text:
A voter drops off their ballot at a ballot drop box outside of the La Familia Recreation Center in Denver Tuesday, Nov. 5, 2024. (Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)More than half a million Coloradans have already voted in the 2026 midterm election, according to the first turnout report from the secretary of state’s office. 

As of late Monday, 509,364 voters already submitted their ballots — good for about 12.6% of all active voters in Colorado. Most ballots returned have been mail ballots. 
Democrats outpace Republican voters with 33.4% of ballots returned so far compared to 24.2%. Unaffiliated voters, who represent just over half or all registered voters in Colorado, make up 41.3% of ballots returned. 
Early turnout from all parties so far is outpacing the 2022 midterm elections, while unaffiliated and Democratic turnout also outpaces 2024. 
Early voting in the 2026 midterm election in Colorado outpaces the 2022 midterm election. (Graph from Colorado secretary of state’s office)
Voters 55 and older cast about 68.5% of ballots so far. 
El Paso County, the county with the largest population in the state, has the highest turnout so far, representing 12.5% of ballots returned.
Voters who register to vote through Oct. 26 can expect to receive a ballot in the mail.
Coloradans can update their voter registration through Election Day. 
Voters have until 7 p.m., Nov. 3, to return their ballot at a drop box or polling center or vote in person. A valid ID is required to vote in person.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Newcomer challenges 30-year incumbent in Alabama’s most Republican U.S. House district
text:
In Alabama’s 4th Congressional District, U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville (left), who has held the seat since 1997, faces Democratic nominee Amanda Pusczek (right), a first-time candidate. (Photos courtesy of candidates; photo illustration by Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)Candidates for Alabama’s 4th Congressional District both said residents are facing ongoing hardships but the two focused on different issues as part of their campaigns.
Democratic nominee Amanda Pusczek, a first-time political candidate, is challenging U.S. Rep. Robert Aderholt, R-Haleyville, who has represented the district since 1997. The district comprises parts of the northern part of Alabama. It includes Blount, Cullman, DeKalb, Fayette, Franklin, Lamar, Marion and Marshall counties, and parts of Colbert, Lauderdale and Tuscaloosa counties.
The area is one of the most conservative in the country. In 2024 more than 82% of voters in the district chose Donald Trump for president, according  to an analysis from The DownBallot. The Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that analyzes elections, rated the district as “Solid Republican.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Pusczek moved to the district from Missouri when she was 6 years old. She works as a nurse.
“I learned something from an early age, which is to be of service,” she said in an interview on Monday. “Your life only has value as to what you can give out into the world. That has been my guiding star for a very long time.”
Aderholt said Monday that he was “learning everyday how to better serve the district I represent.”
“Seniority matters in Washington, and I feel I am in a position where I can continue to help the people of the 4th District,” he said.
Both candidates cited the pressures of inflation and high gas prices. Pusczek blamed tariffs imposed by Trump as well as the conflict with Iran.
“People are burning through their savings right now, and people might lose their entire savings. Those who have worked for their entire lives are now almost gone,” she said. “Younger folks like me, we can’t even begin to contemplate saving when we are living paycheck to paycheck. I would say we are living in an affordability crisis.”
Aderholt cited the war in Iran, and said he was hopeful “that the President will move on this war and end it in a very short period of time, if nothing else, because of gas prices.”
But Aderholt added that he does not second-guess the president’s decision to initiate the conflict because “I know Iran wants to destroy the United States. I know they would love nothing more.”
Pusczek also criticized Aderholt for voting for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act touted by Trump in 2025. The legislation did not extend enhanced tax credits for the Affordable Care Act to reduce insurance premiums for households who buy insurance in the marketplace. In Alabama, ACA enrollment dropped 23% after the tax credits expired last year.
The legislation also shifted some of the cost of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to the states. Alabama could pay an additional $174 million if the state does not reduce the error rate, which is affected by changing household circumstances.
“With the cuts, I have thousands of constituents who are in a greater threat of food insecurity than they were before,” Pusczek said.
Aderholt pointed to tax cuts in the legislation, such as reducing the taxes on tips earned by workers.
“At the end of the day, it is going to lower prices,” he said. “I think, for the average person, it will help. This is bringing more money back to the average person, even the low-income person.”
Each candidate focused on a different set of priorities for the campaign. Pusczek highlighted healthcare, protecting people’s rights and affordability. Her campaign website said she wants to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 and enhance collective bargaining for unions. She also wants to increase resources for rural healthcare. She proposed forgiving some of the student loan debt for physicians who choose to practice in rural areas and reclassify emergency medical service as a public utility.
Aderholt focused on economic development on his campaign website. One of his goals is to secure funding for the district to expand the economy. The U.S. Navy invested $900 million in a manufacturing project involving Hadrian, a defense contractor developing a facility in Cherokee, through funding provided by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
“I have had the opportunity to work with a lot of counties and cities that are not highly populated, or a lot of income because of their tax base, and trying to help them with sewer connections, and trying to get some highways in there to connect to certain areas so that they can do economic development on their own,” Aderholt said.
