name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Commentary: Welcome to silly season: Kentucky politics and the circus we help create
text:
It's been 34 years since Kentuckians sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate. This year, when they elect a successor to Republican Mitch McConnell, it will be a referendum on President Trump and also a conservative state's choice for the nation's direction. (Getty Images)Every October, Kentucky politics undergoes a peculiar transformation. Campaign advertisements become nastier, accusations grow louder, and rumors that spent months buried suddenly find their way into mailboxes, television commercials, and social media feeds. Candidates who spent the summer shaking hands and kissing babies begin searching for skeletons in their opponents’ closets.
Welcome to what politicos affectionately call “silly season.” It’s that wonderful time when politicians aren’t frightened by things that go bump in the night or monsters beneath their beds. Their greatest fear is what might come crawling out of their closets: secrets long buried, skeletons carefully concealed, and past indiscretions resurrected for public consumption.
Depending on the campaign’s toxicity, particularly in federal elections, these revelations can test marriages, destroy relationships, jeopardize careers, and threaten reputations. Nothing is sacred, and almost everything becomes fair game. Naturally, every election brings familiar complaints: “Politics has gotten so negative!” “I’m tired of the attacks!” “Why can’t candidates discuss the issues?”
Bless your hearts. There’s a reason your mailbox receives 14 negative campaign mailers for every wholesome family portrait featuring a candidate, spouse, two children, and a golden retriever staring lifelessly toward some imaginary Kentucky horizon.
Political science offers some explanation. A 2007 meta-analysis published in The Journal of Politics, The Effects of Negative Political Campaigns, found that negative campaigning tends to be more memorable and can increase voters’ knowledge, although researchers found no reliable evidence that it wins more votes.
Another study, Do Negative Messages Work?, published in American Politics Research, found that credible, relevant attacks can damage voters’ evaluations of opposing candidates, while excessively harsh attacks can backfire.
Negativity captures attention, shapes perceptions, and fuels conversation. Whether it changes your vote is another question. As my Mamaw Cel would say, “People just love to bitch.” And Lord knows, Kentucky politics provides plenty of opportunities.
We complain about negative advertisements while consuming, sharing, and debating them. We eagerly anticipate the next scandal, then express remarkable indignation when another appears.
Yet politicians perform on a stage the public helped build. You are not merely the audience; you are the conductor. Your attention sets the tempo, your reactions determine the volume, and your appetite for spectacle encourages another performance. The more you feed it, the more you receive.
But we can change the performance by demanding something better than recycled slogans, partisan talking points, and political theatrics. Instead of asking whether someone is sufficiently conservative, liberal, Republican, or Democratic, ask questions that actually matter.
Do you support the First Amendment, including the rights of people whose speech you despise? Will you hold our research universities accountable for increased direct payments that increase Medicaid costs and burdens taxpayers? What specific policies will put more money in Kentuckians’ pockets and make it easier for families to put food on their tables?
As October surprises emerge and accusations circulate faster than gossip at a church potluck, remember that political culture reflects more than candidates’ conduct. Of course, this does not absolve politicians of responsibility. The distinction between a politician and a statesman emerges when someone possesses the character to say, “Enough,” even when the audience demands an encore. You cannot spend eleven months rewarding the spectacle, eagerly awaiting scandal, and then pretend to be appalled by the performance.
If you’re going to complain about the circus, acknowledge your role in buying the tickets. And politicians, put on your big-boy or big-girl pants. Neither side should forget who helped build the damn stage.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: For some Kentuckians, data centers are top of mind. Will the issue sway voters this fall?
text:
Dana Hanson, center, an organizer for We Are Mercer County, sits in the crowd listening to the Mercer County Fiscal Court during a Sept. 28 meeting. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)Dana Hanson has seen plenty of political divisiveness on the news and social media in recent years. And up until about a year ago, the Mercer County resident who had voted for Republicans “her entire life” had viewed politics as two-sided — the left versus the right. 
But over the past several months, as she and other residents have organized in opposition to a proposed hyperscale data center in her rural Central Kentucky county, she hasn’t noticed that partisan division among her neighbors. 
“I don’t see it anymore. I don’t see it. I don’t see it from the people I surround myself with,” Hanson said. “I definitely think that there’s been like a little bit of a kumbaya moment here, and not just in Mercer County — I think throughout the country.” 
Hanson is one of the organizers with the nonprofit group We Are Mercer County, whose members have pushed back with strong concerns — over the use of farmland, environmental and utility bill impacts — about a proposed hyperscale data center near the small Mercer County city of Burgin. The group of residents began to coalesce after the county planning and zoning commission began crafting regulations seeking to regulate where the power-intensive operations could locate; county leaders rejected those regulations earlier this month. 
But before she helped form the group, she didn’t care or tune into Burgin city council meetings, let alone care that much about local politics. The data center issue has since had people packing into the Burgin’s firehouse and Mercer County fiscal court meetings, holding homemade signs and wearing blue “We Are Mercer County” shirts. 
Kentucky does not yet have hyperscale data centers operating in the state; unlike the massive scale seen in other states such as Ohio and Virginia, technology companies have poured billions of dollars into building infrastructure, in part to support artificial intelligence services. But at least one hyperscale data center is under construction in West Louisville, and other proposals are progressing — with litigation in some instances trying to stop the projects. 
For some Kentuckians, particularly those dealing with active data center proposals, the issue has been galvanizing. Whether it will sway voters at the ballot box this fall, in Mercer County and beyond, remains to be seen for Hanson. 
She said a lot of people in her county, where she’s lived since 2018, don’t like to talk about politics and won’t put out yard signs. 
Hanson, who changed her registration from Republican to Independent in 2022, also said a lot of people won’t cross party lines this fall, in a county where the majority of the registered voters and the incumbents in county government are Republicans. 
“This started with a data center, and it’s turned into something way bigger than just a data center. It’s about transparency and accountability, and how elected officials treat the people they’re supposed to represent,” Hanson said. 
Campaigns and politicians weigh in
At a data center “listening session” hosted earlier this month by Lexington Democrat Rep. Adam Moore in Frankfort earlier this month, it wasn’t just Kentuckians from Mercer County who came to a committee room to levy their data center concerns. 
More than 60 Kentuckians from at least 15 counties, from Daviess County to Pike County, came to the meeting. A common theme of their comments: accountability of elected officials. 
Christy Collins of Breckinridge County told the handful of Democratic state lawmakers and one Republican that her fears extended to the potential of artificial intelligence, saying that “they want us to sacrifice our way of life so they can train AI to replace human workers and collect our data.” 
Many of the attendees at the Mercer County Fiscal Court meeting brought signs expressing opposition to data centers. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
“We are here today to protect our future and ready to vote any elected leader out of office if they refuse to protect our lands,” Collins said. “I say our land is worth more than their data, and we, the people of this commonwealth, have the right to vote no on data centers.” 
Politicians running for office at all levels of government are paying attention, particularly as polling has shown public approval of data centers has plummeted — one poll showing that more than six in ten Americans strongly oppose a new data center being built where they live. 
In the closely watched race in Central Kentucky’s 6th Congressional District, which includes Mercer County, Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado have used the issue as fodder for attacks. Dembo has accused Alvarado of having investments in data center stocks, and Alvarado has suggested Dembo is collecting “campaign checks” from a contractor involved in data center construction. 
In a recent television debate, Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Charles Booker charged Republican candidate Andy Barr of “getting paid by the telecom companies” that want data centers  “in your backyard.” Barr said he didn’t believe Kentuckians should pay higher utility bills because of data centers and that he believed in “local control”. But he also said the country needed to win the “AI race”, echoing rhetoric from President Donald Trump in support of data centers. 
One social media post from Trump, warning that data center critics would end up “backwards and poor” if they rejected data centers, saw bipartisan backlash in Kentucky including from state Rep. Savannah Maddox, R-Dry Ridge. 
Maddox told the Lantern that the Trump administration’s advocacy for data centers has caused Kentuckians to be “somewhat skeptical, if not concerned outright, for the impact that data centers could have on their communities.” 
“We do not need a top-heavy approach, a propaganda arm, if you will, pushing data centers on people and saying that you’re not patriotic if you don’t support them,” Maddox said. “What I am seeing here on the ground, not just in my district but across the Commonwealth, is that data centers have mobilized voters. And I think that they have gotten them paying attention in a way that they maybe previously would not have.” 
What will voters do? 
Stephen Voss, an associate professor within the University of Kentucky’s Department of Political Science, compared the “nuisance” of data centers to political science research that shows the closer wind energy farms are to people, the more “backlash against elected leaders” there would be. 
“Voters do punish these nuisances that come with these developments, and that, to me, is something similar,” Voss said. 
But Voss said he believed the impact of data centers to push broader political movements remains limited outside of communities actively dealing with data center proposals. He said that is until people “really started getting hammered” in their pocketbooks, like through high utility bills. 
In Mercer County, the local focus on data centers has become apparent in some races.
Mary DeLima, 65, and her dog Bo wait for the Burgin city council meeting to start on Tuesday. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Liam Niemeyer)
Republican state Rep. Kim King, who represents Mercer County, in a 30-second reelection advertisement began with the statement that she was “holding big tech and data centers” accountable. King had voted for a Republican-sponsored bill that sought to ratepayer protections against data centers, but the bill died on the last day of this year’s legislative session. 
She’s facing a rematch against Democratic opponent Katrina Sexton, a Mercer County school teacher who King defeated by more than 40 percentage points in 2024. Earlier this year, a member of We Are Mercer County also accused King of dismissing local data center concerns; King did not respond to emailed interview requests from the Lantern. 
Hanson, one of the group’s organizers, said she is “cautiously optimistic” about election day. The group itself doesn’t make endorsements as a nonprofit.
“I’m hopeful that the people of Mercer County have seen enough, and had enough, and taken enough,” Hanson said. “A lot of people will not cross party lines, and I get that. But there’s going to be a lot of people who are, and if that’s what it takes to get better leadership, that’s what we’re going to do.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Joe Courtney, George Austin square off in Eastern CT’s 2nd District
text:
This is the second in a series of stories profiling candidates in each congressional district race.

Connecticut’s 2nd Congressional District is one of the more competitive seats in the state, on paper. 
When Joe Courtney first ran for office in 2006, he was part of the blue wave that swept Democrats back into the majority — but in his own race, he flipped a Republican-held seat by eking out a victory with an 83-vote margin.
In the 20 years since, the Democratic congressman has easily won reelection to a seat that covers all of eastern Connecticut through a coalition of voters that cuts through party lines. But Courtney says the district — the most rural in the state — still resembles the one he’s represented for the past 10 terms.
“I don’t think it’s changed that much, honestly,” Courtney said. “I think if you look at the composition of who’s in town halls in terms of mayors and councils and state legislature, it’s still definitely purple. The one lesson I learned by winning by 83 votes is that you just don’t take it for granted, and we’ve been very aggressive out there.”
Courtney, 73, faces Republican George Austin, who hopes to improve his party’s chances despite a tough political environment for Republicans nationally. Touching on a common theme this year among both Democrats and Republicans, Austin, 38, said he wants to see new faces in Congress in the hopes of getting more done and breaking up the partisan gridlock.

George Austin, Republican nominee in the 2nd Congressional District, talks with customers as he campaigns at Sarapes Mexican Restaurant in Enfield on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Austin supports terms limits in Congress and wants to keep the door open to considering an age limit for candidates since there’s already a minimum in place. He argues that “entrenched career politicians” in Congress have contributed to the malaise of the body and the attitude of kicking the can down the road on many issues. That frustration led him to become a first-time candidate.
“Too many of our members of Congress, of our elected leaders — they’re out of touch,” Austin said. “It’s 100% a byproduct of being in office for too long, with seemingly bulletproof incumbency.”
“Your priorities shift,” he continued. “I don’t want to throw the age question out there just to be trendy. But for those reasons, I think age is definitely a factor.”
Austin is a business owner and works in construction. He noted local Republicans haven’t “put up a blue-collar candidate in a long time.”
He has a similar assessment of the 2nd Congressional District, noting there is a “large contingent of Republicans voting for [Courtney].” He’s seen houses with yard signs for both Republican gubernatorial nominee Ryan Fazio and Courtney. Austin’s approach to the campaign is reaching out to low-propensity and swing voters.

Congressman Joe Courtney, left, talks with New London Mayor Michael Passero before a roundtable discussion to discuss the  21st Century ROAD to Housing Act at the New London Community Recreation Center on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Democrats are hoping for a repeat of the 2006 midterm elections when they rode a blue wave back into both the House and Senate majority. One of those candidates was Courtney, who earned the nickname “Landslide Joe” for his nail-biter race that year, defeating three-term Republican incumbent Rob Simmons by just 83 votes.
Courtney sees some similarities between 2006 and 2026. In both years, Republicans held political trifectas — majorities in both chambers of Congress and control of the White House — and were clouded by unpopular wars in the Middle East. Courtney also pointed to the wave election in 2018, when Democrats took back the House amid voter frustration over healthcare and GOP efforts to repeal the Affordable Care Act.
But he recalled then-Congressman Rahm Emanuel, who oversaw the committee working to take back the House majority, not being convinced until late in the 2006 campaign that prospects were looking good for Democrats.
“This could be another 2006,” Courtney said when he reflected on the midterms a month ago. “Having said that, I still think it really wasn’t until mid-October before I think people really felt like this is really going to happen.”
That hasn’t changed how Courtney campaigns across the district, whether it’s up in the Quiet Corner or down along the shoreline. He said he’s held more than a dozen town halls, some via telephone, over the past two years.
“People actually notice if you’re not around,” Courtney said. “That’s why I make a point of it, in terms of accepting invitations for various events and meetings and get out there. We have a very strong message to talk about in terms of the work on Seapower [subcommittee] and how directly connected it is to the economy right now.”
Austin said he doesn’t fit neatly into a box when it comes to the Republican Party. 
“I don’t like to consider myself a 401k conservative,” he said. “My family being Hispanic, our family values are very traditional, and they lean very conservative, which I am bringing to my brand of politics,” Austin said, describing economic policies meant to preserve and boost families, especially the next generation, who are more skeptical to have children for a variety of reasons including economic anxieties.
But he’s made some distinctions between himself and the GOP on issues like President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax bill, artificial intelligence and the tactics of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Austin said he would have had difficulty voting for the “big beautiful bill” because it added to the federal deficit. He said he ultimately would have backed it and wants permanent tax cuts for small businesses.
Another area where Austin diverges a bit from party is on ICE. He argued that stronger security along the border to stop illegal immigration is a net positive. But ICE’s approach, including raids at Home Depot where federal agents camped out in parking lots, “really leave a sour taste in my mouth.” He said he wants ICE to fix the problems and focus on more standard law enforcement, though he called abolishing the agency a “nonstarter.”
Austin’s family has its own immigration story. His father illegally crossed the southern border from Mexico multiple times and eventually made his way to Connecticut, where he met Austin’s mother. He got legal status through marriage, and his mother gave birth to Austin. When he was 17, he met his wife in Mexico and went through legal channels to bring her and his stepson to the U.S.
Courtney has opposed ICE’s actions throughout the country and supported congressional Democrats’ push to enact guardrails, like a ban on masks for federal agents and changes to arrest warrant policies. But negotiations fell apart earlier this year during a shutdown of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and Republicans passed a party-line bill to fund DHS without implementing the sought-after reforms.
Courtney, meanwhile, has touted his committee work in Congress as beneficial to Connecticut and particularly the 2nd District. 

Speakers including, from left, Joe Toner, executive director of the Connecticut State Building Trades Council, Rep. Joe Courtney, Mark Rayha, president of General Dynamics Electric Boat, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Rob Brule, Waterford first selectman, and Matt Pugliese, deputy commissioner of the Department of Economic and Community Development, toss dirt during a groundbreaking ceremony at Electric Boat’s Waterford Campus, the former Crystal Mall on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

He sits on the House Armed Services Committee and currently serves as the top Democrat on the Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee. He also serves on the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. If he wins reelection and Democrats take back the House, Courtney could become the chairman of the Seapower subcommittee.
His assignment on Seapower puts him in a prominent position to work on issues that dovetail with the defense needs of the 2nd District, given Naval Submarine Base New London and General Dynamics Electric Boat, which are both based in Groton. He got another nickname, “Two Sub Joe,” during his first term by increasing the production cadence from one to two submarines per year.
Courtney highlighted the boost for Electric Boat with the late July announcement of the $76.6 billion contract from the U.S. Navy that’ll go toward the construction of nine Virginia-class submarines and five Columbia-class submarines. He believes it provides confirmation that the work won’t disappear and could extend well into the 2040s.
Along with affordability more broadly, Courtney said housing has been one of the most pressing issues in his district and around the country. He’s been campaigning on his support for bipartisan legislation known as the “21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.” The bill seeks to boost housing construction, authorize a pilot program to convert vacant and abandoned properties into housing and expand access to other types of housing such as factory-built manufactured homes.
Noting the housing shortage around the country, Austin said he would want to change the tax code to incentivize married couples who are empty nesters to move out and provide younger families with more options. 
There are some areas of agreement between the two candidates, particularly around artificial intelligence.
Courtney co-sponsored legislation that would rein in some of the tax incentives for data centers that were in Republican tax bills from 2017 and 2025.
He said the issue started to pop up in the district a few years ago amid plans for a proposed data center at Millstone Nuclear Power Station. The project fell through.
“When it first started, I think people’s understanding of the issue was pretty limited,” Courtney said. “But then, when they realized the fact that this was going to end up making utility costs go up and causing disruption in terms of the town settings and whatnot, it hit the tipping point there. … You got a pretty good taste of the power of this issue politically.”

George Austin, Republican nominee in the 2nd Congressional District, talks with customers as he campaigns at Sarapes Mexican Restaurant in Enfield on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

For Austin, he’s made AI guardrails a centerpiece of his campaign. He supports a “kill switch”  and wants to keep the technology out of the classroom.
The Connecticut Republican’s views on AI come into stark contrast with many in his own party, including the president, who has touted the technology and the data centers that power it.
Austin said the issue is causing anxiety among Americans over things like job security and learning in schools, and he sees it as a national security issue. And he views it as something that could become a national emergency “if left unchecked.”
“It’s such a powerful technology that if we get ahead of it as best as we can, we can dampen the blow, if you will, when it comes to protecting American industry, when it comes to having data centers in places we don’t want, and having them be net positives for their communities as opposed to being eye sores or just sucking down oodles and oodles of ever-increasing energy,” Austin said.
Austin said Trump has been “very nonchalant” about the growing debate over AI. Austin voted for Trump for president but said he’s willing to take different positions.
“Just because of that doesn’t mean he’s right about everything,” Austin said. “I’m not in favor of the war in Iran, and I’m not in favor of this nonchalant attitude that he and most of Congress evidently have towards AI.”
In the final weeks of the race, Courtney continues to hold a cash advantage, but he and Austin spent similar amounts over the past three months.
Austin has spent money on radio, magazine and Facebook advertising as well as text messages and campaign merchandise like banners, signs, magnets and shirts. He gave his campaign a $240,000 loan.
Austin is on two ballot lines and was cross-endorsed by the Independent Party of Connecticut.
Courtney and Austin are participating in at least two forums, including a meet the candidates event in Storrs that took place on Monday night. Courtney has described the campaign and interactions between the two candidates as “very amicable.”
In-person early voting began Monday, Oct. 19 and runs through Sunday, Nov. 1. The last day to request an absentee ballot is Nov. 2.

name: VTDigger
title: Advocates for homeless Vermonters say new rules put ‘process over people’
text:
Motel 6 in Colchester on Oct. 20, 2026. Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

Carly Berlin covers housing and infrastructure for Vermont Public, in partnership with VTDigger. 
At a series of heated meetings, advocates for unhoused Vermonters called on Gov. Phil Scott’s administration to reverse course on its implementation of a sweeping homelessness law passed earlier this year.
The architects of the legislation and others have argued that the Department for Children and Families’ new rules governing access to motel rooms are overly restrictive and delay or block unhoused people from entering shelter. Advocates say applicants calling for a motel voucher have routinely sat on hold with the state for hours only for calls to drop, or to learn that there are no rooms that suit their needs available near them, leaving them to sleep outdoors. 
Some are calling on a legislative oversight committee to reject officials’ rules. 
“This is process over people, and it is not comporting with the intent of the statute to be flexible – to bring people in instead of keep them out,” said Leah Burdick, a staff attorney for Vermont Legal Aid, at a hearing last week. 
DCF officials have defended their work, arguing that they had little time to draft the new guidelines after the law went into effect in June. They say they have cut down on wait times in recent weeks, and that they need to prioritize people with the highest needs for a limited number of available motel rooms.
“We want to fix the problem of homelessness. We have the task of putting people into 700 rooms,” DCF Commissioner Sandi Hoffman told lawmakers, following an hour and a half of testimony from advocates imploring officials to effectively scrap their rules and start over. 
The law, Act 143, was an attempt to better organize the fragmented system serving the over 4,800 people experiencing homelessness in Vermont. It set up a “continuum” of shelter options for unhoused people, from rental aid to prevent homelessness to highly structured shelters to low-barrier settings with looser rules around sobriety. 
Private hotels and motels, which have been the single largest provider of shelter in recent years via Vermont’s motel voucher program, remain a part of the continuum as a kind of last resort. Under the law, their use is more limited, with lower caps on the number of rooms the state can use and how long individuals can stay in them.

Motel 6 in Colchester on Oct. 20, 2026. Carly Berlin/Vermont Public

Act 143 was designed to go into effect in phases over the course of several years. DCF’s first round of new rules, which took effect Sept. 1, focused on changes to the state’s use of motels as shelter.
Officials ended the use of the 211 helpline for motel intake on nights and weekends, effectively requiring that people seek vouchers from DCF during regular business hours. Meanwhile, DCF has enacted a new screening process, asking people a list of detailed questions to determine whether they should get priority access to a motel room.
That screening process has become a main point of contention for advocates and legislators. Act 143 required “a brief, standardized initial assessment” for people seeking aid. The new system put in place by DCF, critics say, is lengthy and confusing, sometimes requiring multiple phone calls over the course of several days. 
The questionnaire itself asks people to describe their current housing situation, medical conditions, and community supports. Their answers guide a DCF worker to assign them a score based on their risk. That score has immediate stakes for whether or not someone gets a motel voucher.
The highest scoring households — which include all families with minor children, along with  people experiencing acute medical or domestic violence emergencies — get a motel placement when any space is available. But lower scoring households only get referred to a room when there are 50 to 100 rooms available, depending on their level of need, according to DCF guidelines. 
Jessica Radbord, an attorney with the ACLU of Vermont, obtained public records showing how DCF has trained staff on the new assessment. In one hypothetical exercise, an applicant is staying with a partner who has a history of physically harming them. The applicant reports escalating tension to DCF, including verbal threats, along with the fact that the home has hazards like a lack of heat. DCF workers are instructed to code the risk as a three out of four, because violence is not actively occurring.
“That lower score … makes placement, especially when rooms are scarce, less likely, even if rooms are immediately available,” Radbord told lawmakers last week.
Despite the hurdles described by advocates, the number of motel rooms in use by the state has actually increased markedly since the new rules went into effect: from 390 rooms in late August to 668 on Oct. 19. That’s still under the 700 rooms allowed by law. 
DCF officials say fewer people were seeking motel vouchers over the summer because they’d likely run out of their allotted days for the year, or had found other accommodations during warmer weather, and are now seeking shelter again.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Advocates for homeless Vermonters say new rules put ‘process over people’.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Shillings brings homegrown biz experience to electoral bid
text:
Libertarian candidate Lauri Shillings responds to a question during the Indiana Secretary of State Debate hosted by the Indiana Debate Commission, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026, at WFYI Public Television Studios in Indianapolis. (Photo by Doug McSchooler for Indiana Debate Commission)This is the final of four profiles in Indiana’s secretary of state race.
Lauri Shillings presents herself as a homegrown everywoman aspiring to statewide office.
“I’m very much a working-class person. I’ve never held less than two jobs,” said Shillings, who works as a creative director for the University of Indianapolis when she’s not campaigning. She gave up a third gig as an adjunct professor at Ivy Tech Community College to run for office, and has put her design firm and video-game streaming channel on hold.
“I’m always working. I understand the hustle, and I think people of Indiana respect that because I don’t think they have somebody (in the race) besides me that truly represents the working class of Indiana,” she added.
Where other secretary of state candidates have been hounded by criticism of time spent outside Indiana, Shillings hasn’t strayed far from her hometown in Montgomery County — where her family has lived since 1824.
Both of her parents have worked as first responders, with Shillings’ father serving about three decades as chief of Coal Creek Fire and Rescue across more than 50 years in the field.
“That was my experience with how leadership should work, where you step in and do the work that you need to do in your community,” said Shillings, who now resides in Hamilton County.
Volunteer to ‘face of the party’
Shillings’ journey to the Libertarian Party began a decade ago, amid Donald Trump’s audacious entry into national Republican politics, when she “became really invested in how leadership in our government is supposed to be, and felt real concern about that.”
“I’d never been a straight-ticket voter,” she said. “I’d always voted for the best person for the job, which lent me to the Libertarian side of things, where … you have to align with the person doing the work.”
Shillings stepped from simply casting a ballot to volunteering her time and talent after her partner — Danny Lundy, who is also now her campaign manager — invited her to join him at Libertarian events.
Indiana Libertarians nominate Lauri Shillings for secretary of state

“Once I became involved, I saw there was nothing but work that needed to be done,” she said.
Shillings, who holds an associate degree in visual communications from Ivy Tech and a bachelor’s degree in community and nonprofit leadership from the University of Indianapolis, has lent her graphic design skills to the Libertarian cause.
She was the “primary source” for two-time Libertarian gubernatorial nominee Donald Rainwater’s social media designs and branding, said Libertarian Party of Indiana Chair Stephanie Dasbach, who met Shillings while working on that campaign.
Shillings said she still does pro bono work for political campaigns and nonprofits “because everybody deserves good branding,” even as she has taken on party leadership positions.
She has chaired the Libertarian Party of Hamilton County since 2020 and has served as the state central committee’s 5th congressional district representative since 2023.
This is her second campaign. Shillings in 2024 made an unsuccessful bid for Congress.
“I’ve seen her go from just being a volunteer, helping with artwork, helping with whatever needed to be done, to becoming the county chair, to now being the face of the party, and she’s doing a very good job with that,” said Mark Rutherford, a longtime Libertarian who served twice as vice chair of the national party, ran for secretary of state in 2018, and who has known Shillings for more than a decade.
Entrepreneur support
The secretary of state’s office oversees elections, securities, auto dealer and business services.
Departing officeholder Diego Morales, a Republican, has worked with the GOP-led Legislature to increase scrutiny of citizenship in voting in pursuit of election security.
Last year, he revealed the office had provided detailed voter information to federal authorities. He and Attorney General Todd Rokita later announced that a federal review found 165 noncitizens have registered to vote in Indiana and 21 have cast ballots in elections here.
It is illegal under both Indiana and federal law for noncitizens to vote in elections. No state charges have been brought.
Libertarian Lauri Shillings talks with a Hoosier at ArcFest on Oct. 3, 2026, in Indianapolis. (Photo from campaign)
Shillings said there are “checks and balances in place currently.”
“There’s been very little voter fraud in the last 10 years,” she continued. “… It is a false narrative to slam in an immigration policy that I don’t think we need, especially in Indiana. We already have a voter ID (law) that says you have to prove who you are to vote in in this state, and it’s effective, and it works. So I don’t think that’s necessary to expand upon.”
Instead, Shillings has drawn on her design and entrepreneurship experience to propose an overhaul of the secretary of state’s website, including campaign finance functions and business services.
She recounted navigating the website herself and encountering “not found” errors or outdated forms. She posits that modernizing the website — so Hoosiers can more easily find candidates for office, their donors, post-election audits and more — could improve the public’s perception of election security.
“I think if people felt that the office was doing the work and knew about it, they might be more secure in their own feelings about how our elections are run,” she said.
She also wants to make IN BIZ, the state’s portal for businesses, easier to navigate for small owners confused about how to file paperwork or fix errors — and use AI for basic help outside business hours.
“When I’m running a business, it’s usually at 11 o’clock at night, after my day job, after I’ve taken care of my household duties … like 9 p.m. till midnight,” Shillings said. “… And if I can’t reach somebody during business hours because I’m already obligated to do something else, it’s real frustrating for me to work on a business of my own — my own dreams — without having that support.”
Ballot access bid
Shillings’ run will fulfill another purpose that neither Republican nominee Max Engling nor Democratic nominee Beau Bayh must consider — and which independent candidate Greg Ballard hopes to achieve for the nascent Lincoln Party.
The secretary of state contest is the ballot access race for Indiana political parties. The winner and runner-up earn major party status for their groups. Minor party candidates must earn 2% of the vote to secure their party’s right to select candidates at convention for automatic listing on the general election ballot.
The Libertarian Party has maintained that since clearing the 2% mark in the 1994 election, but hasn’t yet cracked the 10% threshold required to trigger state-funded primary elections.
“We don’t take lightly that we’ve had our ballot access 30-plus years,” Dasbach said. “… And knowing that you know there’s a flooded field does say, ‘Hey, we need to work harder to make sure that we can maintain that.’ … I am confident that we will reach that threshold.”
She believed Shillings will beat out Ballard for the protest votes cast by Hoosiers dissatisfied with the Republican and Democratic parties, pointing to the party’s decades of history.
The only independent poll released in the race so far, commissioned by Free Press Indiana, showed Shillings with 6% support and Ballard at 5%.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Guns, drugs, AI, budget cuts join traditional maladies at public health forum
text:
Gov. Wes Moore speaks at the ninth annual Bloomberg American Health Initiative forum in Baltimore, to highlight recent state healthcare policies like the Vax Act. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)A daylong public health forum in Baltimore on Tuesday touched on health challenges that likely aren’t found in any medical textbook: gun violence, artificial intelligence, social media and “the ravages of Washington” under the Trump administration.
Those were just some of the wide-ranging topics at the 2026 Bloomberg American Health Summit, the ninth annual gathering of more than 500 fellows with Bloomberg American Health Initiative and local and national leaders in public health research and policies.
Topics in the Baltimore Marriott Waterfront event also included more typical, and persistent, public health concerns like combating drug overdoses and diverting patients from emergency rooms as a first resort.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott (D) were featured speakers at the event, where elected officials and health officials discuss where city and state policies can help combat emerging public health challenges.
Moore told the room full of Bloomberg fellows he was grateful for their work as “the ones to tackle the problems that are difficult…. You’ve been the ones who have made the impossible, possible.” He said that those efforts are needed “now as much as ever before,” as recent changes to Medicaid and federal funding cuts threaten to strain health systems in Maryland and across the nation.
“We have a federal administration that is willing to take away healthcare for more than 10 million Americans … and in Maryland we are protecting our people from the ravages of Washington,” Moore said.
Gov. Wes Moore discusses statewide public health efforts, like increased access to vaccines and help for families facing insurance loss due to changes to Medicaid eligibility. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
He highlighted $25 million in new funding to help offset an anticipated rise in uninsured Marylanders seeking medical care at the emergency department, due to changes under the 2025 budget reconciliation bill, H.R. 1.
“That money will help members of our community who have lost healthcare coverage because of H.R. 1 to be able to get healthcare at a local community health center and at our health departments,” Moore said. “And it will help to keep them out of costly emergency rooms.
“I do not understand a philosophy where simply thinking that putting people into emergency room care is somehow either good medicine or, frankly, good economically,” he said.
The funds were approved in July by the Health Services Cost Review Commission, and the Maryland Health Care Commission has opened applications for federally qualified health centers and certain local health departments to apply for that grant funding.  Those funds will help boost access to preventive care so that individuals are less likely to seek out care at Maryland’s already struggling emergency departments.
Moore also highlighted the new Vax Act, which grants the state health secretary authority to recommend vaccine policies different from those set by the federal government, due to the Trump administration sowing doubt on the effectiveness or safety of certain vaccines.
Gun violence as a public health issue
At several points throughout Tueday’s summit, Scott was praised for the rapid decline in Baltimore homicides from gun violence in recent years, including from Michael R. Bloomberg of Bloomberg Philanthropies.
Scott urges local leaders to develop response plans following last year’s mass overdose events

“Baltimore has been leading the way under Brandon Scott, he deserves a round of applause,” Bloomberg said. “Over the past three years, the city murder rate has fallen by 60%, further and faster than any other major American city … He’s the real thing and he’s doing a real good job.”
But for Scott, the job is not done, as more than 100 people still died by gun violence last year.
“Gun violence is the reason that I, at the ripe old age of 7, decided I wanted to be the mayor of Baltimore,” he said. “When you grow up in a neighborhood where I’ve been a victim of gun violence, I was robbed … had a gun to my head, it hits differently for you.”
While other cities have also seen gun violence decrease, Scott has framed gun violence prevention efforts as a public health problem. That was initially an unpopular approach, but it has grown in recognition over time.
“We have to think about public safety through a lens of public health, and how it impacts everyone and everything,” Scott said. “You do the right thing no matter how unpopular it is and no matter that it means that you might not keep your job…. Your job is to save as many people as possible.”
Struggles with AI
The effects of digital technologies, social media and AI has gained more attention in recent years, due in part to a recent $17.1 billion settlement involving social media company Meta. Washington, D.C., 47 states and three U.S. territories alleged that Meta-owned platforms like Facebook and Instagram were harmful to kids and designed to be addictive.
Maryland is set to receive up to $327 million from the settlement, and policymakers are already discussing how those funds should be used to help the state’s youth navigate digital platforms and new technologies.
One of the emerging challenges that public health researchers, providers and officials are concerned over is the effect of artificial intelligence on the mental health of children and teens.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Emily Haroz, deputy director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, said that almost 20% of 12- to 18-year-olds have used AI chatbots for mental health reasons. She said that AI programs may be helpful as a screening tool to identify which kids are facing severe mental health challenges to connect them with other resources.
But some fear that AI chatbots can worsen mental health challenges for kids. Laura Reiley, a journalist with the Cornell Chronicle, said her daughter died by suicide last year after having lengthy conversations on her mental health with an AI chatbot.
“Her chatbot functioned as her doctor, said it was her therapist,” Reiley said. “And when she said, ‘I have decided to kill myself after Thanksgiving,’ it said, ‘You are so brave to tell me that.’”
Reiley said that there need to be more safety measures in place.
“Chatbots need to say upfront what they are and what they aren’t … They are not clinicians, they are not people,” she said. “I also think every iteration of these chatbots need to be tested with clinicians … these conversations, the safeguards around them are pretty good in the short conversation but things go off the rails the longer that conversation goes.”
Joshua Sharfstein speaks on a panel at the Bloomberg American Health Initiative meeting. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)
Haroz said that some states are trying to limit the negative effects of AI, with limitations of its use in schools and other policies, but data on what works is very limited right now.
“Thinking about regulatory approaches is really important, and states have been carrying a lot of this work on their own, but it’s also been in the absence of a lot of evidence,” Haroz said. “Ultimately we’re doing this without really knowing how they are helping or hurting people.”
Dr. Joshua Sharfstein, director of the Bloomberg American Health Initiative and former chair of Maryland’s hospital rate regulating board, announced that the initiative was going to start a program designed to tackle youth mental health in digital environments.
“It’s going to be part of our adolescent health work, more details will be forthcoming, but we’re really excited to be engaging a bunch of fellows and organizations in that work,” Sharfstein said. “We’ll be involved in research to understand what’s been happening and develop ideas for policy, including policy on how to spend some of the money that’s coming in through these settlements.”

name: National
title: In 6 states, ballots include bans on noncitizen voting
text:
Voters cast their ballots on the first day of early voting at the Hillary Rodham Clinton Children’s Library in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday. In Arkansas and five other states, voters are considering ballot measures that would make it clear that only U.S. citizens may vote.  (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)Voters in six states are considering ballot measures in the midterm elections that would make it clear that only U.S. citizens may vote — and block local governments from expanding that right to others.
Proposed constitutional amendments in Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia would explicitly bar noncitizens from voting. Federal law already does this for federal elections, and no state allows noncitizens to vote in statewide elections.
So why the need for constitutional amendments?
Sponsors of the amendments — primarily Republicans — say they want to preemptively bar cities or other local governments from allowing noncitizens to vote in local elections, as municipalities in California, Maryland and Vermont have done.
“I know it looks like we’re just doing right-wing nutty stuff for the sake of doing it, but no,” said Jack Tomczak, vice president of outreach for Americans for Citizen Voting. The group has worked to pass citizen-only amendments around the country.
“If you want to vote, we believe — philosophically, ideologically — that you should be a citizen before you get a say in how a city, state or country runs things.”
Arkansas state Rep. David Ray, a Republican, called Arkansas’ ballot measure “preventative” in a news conference last month.
“We know that bad ideas, whether they’re in California or Illinois or Maryland or some other state, there’s nothing that magically stops those bad ideas at that state’s borders,” he said.
Some election watchdogs say the ballot measures are a political stunt, an effort to turn out conservative voters in midterm elections that look daunting for Republicans. In swing states such as Arizona, and in states including Alaska where Republican candidates are facing surprisingly tough elections, it could motivate conservative voters to show up at the polls rather than tune out the election.
“I think it’s in large part tied to the current political environment and the Trump focus on noncitizen voting,” said Joshua Douglas, associate dean for research and a professor at the University of Kentucky Rosenberg College of Law.
“There’s also a political aspect to it that some legislators think this is a good way to energize their base to come out to vote, which can have an effect in other elections.”
Data center backlash set to sway midterm elections

This year’s ballot measures are the latest in a flurry of similar initiatives in recent years: Between 2018 and last year, states put 15 citizenship requirement measures on their ballots. Eight of those were in 2024.
Voters approved all 15 measures by healthy margins, with an average of 73% voting in favor, according to Ballotpedia, which tracks election results. Though Republican legislators have been responsible for getting most of those on the ballot, Democratic legislators in some states, such as Iowa, also have voted for them.
But some experts caution that constitutional amendments that limit voting to U.S. citizens curb local autonomy.
“A one-word change can actually make a big difference,” Douglas said. “This is really about, ‘Do we want to give localities the power to decide who their electorate is?’”
Local control
In recent years, 21 local governments in California, Maryland and Vermont, as well as Washington, D.C., have allowed noncitizens to vote in certain local elections, such as for school boards. Some of these jurisdictions, such as Takoma Park, Maryland, also allow people as young as 16 to vote in local elections.
They can do this because the language in many state constitutions says “every citizen” or “all citizens” have the right  to vote. That language usually is interpreted to mean that states must allow all citizens to vote, not that the franchise has to be limited to citizens, Douglas said.
“The concept is (that) the locality can define who their community is, who their electorate is, and that they shouldn’t be excluding people who are within that community as they’ve chosen to define it,” said Douglas, who specializes in election law and voting rights.
“There’s also an aspect of local control. I think that’s what these communities that have chosen to do it have had in the background.”
Democrats could win majority of governor’s offices for first time in 16 years

The only citizenship voting measure put on this year’s ballot by citizen initiative, rather than the state legislature, is in Alaska.
The effort was spearheaded by Alaskans for Citizen Voting, a campaign backed by former Republican state lawmakers.
“The law should be clear and easy to understand,” said Grant Robinson, spokesperson for Alaskans for Citizen Voting. Robinson said he’s unaware of any cities in Alaska that have tried to allow noncitizen voting, but calls it an opportunity for Alaskans to be proactive.
“We want to make sure the people of Alaska have the opportunity now to affirm their position that voting is reserved as a privilege of being a U.S. citizen,” he said.
A complex history
For significant portions of the nation’s history, noncitizens have had the right to vote.
“The citizen voting rights issue is an interesting one because we often think of voting rights as expanding through American history, but resident voting rights for people who aren’t citizens have actually contracted,” said Sam Novey, chief strategist at the University of Maryland Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement.
Throughout the 1800s, many states and territories allowed foreign-born noncitizens to vote. But beginning in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, state ballot measures passed that repealed or restricted noncitizen voting.
Efforts to extend noncitizen voting rights in certain local elections, Novey said, is the latest iteration of a “long legacy of suffrage movements in the United States building power and momentum by winning that right in sub-national and sub-state elections.”
In Wyoming, for example, women successfully pushed for the right to vote in 1869, five decades before they won national suffrage in 1920.
Many of the cities that allow noncitizen voting have done so for school board elections.
“Even if you believe voting should be restricted to U.S. citizens, as many Americans do, that brings up an interesting question in the case of U.S. citizen children of noncitizen residents,” Novey said.
Allowing noncitizens to vote for school boards ensures all citizen children have a voice — through their parents and guardians — in the election of school officials who have significant control over their lives, he said.
Trump’s focus on noncitizen voting 
The Trump administration has been focused for more than a year on pressuring states to root out election fraud, which he has said, without evidence, is rampant.
The citizen voter ballot measures feel like “part of this broader trend of exploring and implementing additional restrictions on voter participation or involvement in the voting process,” said Wren Orey, managing director of the Bipartisan Policy Center’s Elections Project.
States that have audited their voter rolls have found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare.
A 2024 Georgia state audit discovered 20 noncitizens registered to vote, representing 0.000002% of the 8.2 million registered voters in that state. In Iowa in 2025, a state investigation confirmed 277 noncitizens had registered to vote, about 0.00013% of 2.1 million registered voters. And a yearlong review of Utah’s voter rolls completed earlier this year found just 27 confirmed noncitizens out of more than 2 million registered voters, or 0.000014%.
Voters to decide fate of state taxes this fall

Elsewhere, states in recent years have enacted proof-of-citizenship laws that will make it more difficult for some voters to cast their ballots.
Many of the laws — including those in Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota and Utah — require documentary proof of citizenship before a person can register to vote in state and local elections.
Around 12% of registered voters lack the kinds of documents that proof-of-citizenship laws typically require, Orey said.
