title: AFT president backs Lawrence, criticizes Trump administration education cuts
text:
American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten stumps for Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence at the AFL-CIO in Lansing on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Standing outside the Michigan AFL-CIO building in Lansing, Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, threw her support behind William Lawrence, the Democratic candidate for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District.
Lawrence, a Lansing-area political organizer, is challenging the incumbent Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) for control of Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, one of the nation’s most closely contested House races.
“This congressional district could be the difference between a working person’s majority in the House of Representatives or not,” Weingarten said during her speech, where she criticized the growing wealth divide between America’s wealthiest and working people.
“All eyes are on Michigan to make sure that Democrats are elected and that we have an opportunity to really make change and make lives better for all of us,” said Terrence Martin, the president of AFT Michigan, who praised Lawrence as a strong supporter of labor and social justice movements. 
Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence campaigns alongside Terrence Martin, the president of the American Federation of Teachers Michigan and AFT President Randi Weingarten on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten and Democratic Congressional Candidate William Lawrence at the Michigan AFL-CIO, Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)American Federation of Teachers Michigan President Terrence Martin with AFT President Randi Weingarten and Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
Lawrence said he and Weingarten would be a “dangerous duo” in Washington, because he is an organizer. 
“I understand that power concedes nothing without a demand, and we will not win a New Deal, a social compact for the 21st century without a serious struggle of organized people insisting on what we deserve together,” Lawrence said.
He spoke out against the job losses and cuts to research funding at Michigan State University prompted by cuts in federal funding, and slammed efforts to push AI into classrooms at the expense of teachers.
“If you think we suffered learning loss during the pandemic – and we did – we’re about to see something that much worse if we allow unregulated AI in the classroom – especially at the primary and elementary school level – to go unchecked for another year or two years,” Lawrence said.
Speaking with reporters at the end of the event, Weingarten said the Trump Administration had made public education into a Jenga board.
“They have been pulling out in public education and in higher education to pay for tax cuts for the rich,” Weingarten said, later stating that “This administration prefers billionaires to those who are going to college.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: All you need to know about Louisiana’s property tax constitutional amendments
text:
Five of the 10 constitutional amendments on Louisiana's Nov. 3 election ballot would change property tax laws. (Photo by Wes Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)Louisiana voters will consider 10 constitutional amendments on the Nov. 3 ballot, half of which would change the amount of property tax collected that fund police, parks and public schools.
If approved, the proposals could provide enhanced tax breaks for certain military veterans’ families, senior citizens, people with disabilities and those who fix up blighted properties. One would also give new flexibility to local taxing authorities. 

Elected officials have limited options when they want to make property tax policy changes because all such laws are embedded into the Louisiana Constitution and require a statewide vote to change them. For example, if legislators or the governor want to create a new property tax exemption or enhance an existing one, even for only one parish, they typically have to get a constitutional amendment approved.

Jan Moller who leads Invest in Louisiana, a progressive think tank, said the constitution’s grip on property tax laws means voters are frequently asked to make decisions that impact very few citizens.

For example, Amendment 1 allows surviving spouses of deceased disabled veterans to transfer a property tax exemption to a new house. It is expected to affect a small group of people, as only 229 people claimed the exemption last year, according to a legislative fiscal analysis.  

“This isn’t going to break the bank for any local government because it only applies to maybe a dozen people at most,” Moller said last week at an online forum the Public Affairs Research Council of Louisiana hosted.
There are arguments for making it difficult to change property tax policy, said Steven Procopio, PAR’s president, in an interview this week. If property taxes laws weren’t in the constitution and didn’t require a statewide vote, legislators might be tempted to lower them to unsustainable levels, he said. 

Property tax cuts are popular, but state lawmakers don’t have to deal with the consequences because they affect local government and school system revenue, Procopio added.

The number of property tax amendments on this year’s ballot could be the result of bottled-up demand, said Sen. Franklin Foil, R-Baton Rouge, chairman of the Senate Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Committee that vetted all the proposals.

There has been a push over the past few years to expand Louisiana’s popular homestead exemption, which waives homeowners from paying taxes on the first $75,000 value of their primary residence. As those efforts stalled, legislators came back with proposals offering more narrow tax relief, said Foil, who sponsored Amendment 1.  
Opposition to the property tax amendments has created strange political bedfellows. Conservative and liberal policy groups have come out against many of the proposals, though for different reasons. 

The Power Coalition for Equality and Justice, an organization that promotes progressive policies on matters such as criminal justice and voting rights, is against all five property tax amendments. 

“Expanding property tax breaks means less money for schools and local services,” the group stated on its website about a few of the amendments. 

Meanwhile, the Pelican Institute for Public Policy, a conservative group that generally pushes for tax reductions, is opposed to four of the property tax amendments. The organization has come out against amendments 1, 6, 9 and 10 because they single out special groups of people — like spouses of deceased veterans, senior citizens and blighted property developers — for tax breaks. It creates an unequal system overall, where people are paying different tax rates for similar properties, said Daniel Erspamer, the institute’s chief executive officer. 

“If you have a certain amount of money to raise to meet a budget, and you give one group or several sets of groups special treatment, you lower rates or lower assessment for one group of people … You have to raise it on someone else,” Erspamer said during the PAR forum last week.
The following summaries cover the property tax-related proposals on the statewide Nov. 3 ballot: 
Amendment 1
The surviving spouse of a military veteran who had a disability related to their service could continue claiming a property tax exemption even if they move out of the home they purchased with their late partner.


Enabling legislation: Act 39 
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027
Supporters: Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs, Leaders for a Better Louisiana
Opponents: Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 2
Local governments could remove existing deadlines, tied to property reassessment cycles, to raise property tax rates to the maximum amount allowed. It’s aimed at allowing local governments to keep property tax rates lower for a longer period of time. Under the current system, local officials have said they feel pressure to sometimes raise rates prematurely because if they don’t, they lose the ability to do so in the future. Opponents argue the proposal would create more uncertainty for taxpayers about when their property tax bills would be raised and by how much. 

Voters rejected a similar amendment in November 2022. Supporters say the ballot language is clearer now and expect a better outcome.


Enabling legislation: Act 273 
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, Pelican Institute, Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Louisiana Chemical Association, Police Jury Association of Louisiana, Louisiana Municipal Association 
Opponents: Power Coalition

Amendment 6
Local governments could increase the homestead exemption for many people 65 and older if their parish or municipality’s voters approved a tax break for seniors through a separate, local ballot initiative. Only households with income of $100,000 or less — or a higher threshold when that income cap is adjusted for inflation — would qualify. The surviving spouse of a deceased person who received this more generous tax break could also claim it as long as they are only five years younger than their partner who died.
This proposal has the ability to affect tens of thousands of Louisiana households, as 184,000 people claimed the underlying exemption for seniors in 2025, according to a legislative fiscal analysis. 

Enabling legislation: Act 274
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2028 
Supporters: No prominent organizations have come forward to endorse this amendment. 
Opponents: Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 9
Under current law, people 65 or older, disabled veterans, other residents who are totally and permanently disabled, and the spouses of military members killed or missing in action qualify for a special property tax freeze. This proposal would raise the existing income threshold for people to qualify for those enhanced tax breaks from $100,000 to $150,000 per household. The threshold would be adjusted to match inflation rates in future years. Around 422,000 properties were subject to the existing special exemption in 2024, according to a legislative fiscal analysis. 

Enabling legislation: Act 220 of 2025

Enabling legislation: Act 220 of 2025
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: No prominent organizations have come forward to endorse this amendment. 
Opponents: Leaders for a Better Louisiana, Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

Amendment 10
Local governments could adopt property tax breaks for blighted properties once they are rehabilitated. For derelict residential property, up to 75% of its renovated assessed value could qualify for exemption for 20 years. For vacant, unimproved land next to a residence or commercial building, up to 25% of its assessed value could qualify for 10 years. 


Enabling legislation: Act 272
Effective date: Jan. 1, 2027 
Supporters: Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, Leaders for a Better Louisiana 
Opponents: Power Coalition, Pelican Institute

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Commentary: Do we really need to see mugshots in television newscasts?
text:
Mugshots can be problematic because they infer guilt whether or not there's a conviction. Newsrooms must decide the conditions under which they use them in newscasts. (Illustration courtesy of Poynter)
In the wake of George Floyd’s murder in 2020, some local newsrooms across the country started to make changes in how they cover people of color. Many promised to use fewer mugshots in their reporting. Journalists acknowledged that they were part of the problem. By publishing mugshots, which were disproportionately of Black and brown people, local news reports were amplifying harmful and inaccurate stereotypes. 
In 2026, newsroom practices vary across the industry. Indianapolis TV stations have revised their mugshot policies in recent years in an effort to minimize unnecessary harm. I spent a couple of weeks watching the local 6 a.m. news broadcasts of WTHR and FOX59 to get a sense of their overall practices. 
Neither station uses an excessive number of mugshots in individual stories or mugshot galleries, which are large groups of mugshots. I found both stations used mugshots occasionally, in line with their stated policies.
When should news outlets use mugshots in the reporting?
There was one recent story though, that presented a stark contrast.

On Sept. 29, both stations reported that 11 men were arrested for soliciting children for sex. The police ran a three-day online sting operation, and the men went to a Westfield location where they believed they would meet a 15-year-old girl, possibly to engage in sex. The Hamilton County Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force made the arrests. All but one of the men were from Central Indiana; one was from Texas.

WTHR chose not to include any of the 11 mugshots in its broadcast story. Reporter Ashton Hackman’s story included the age and hometown of each man arrested. His report also contained descriptions of the sting operation, including fragments of the conversations between the decoy and those arrested.
(Courtesy banner)
WTHR news director Cyndee Hebert told me the station has two rules for determining when to use a mugshot. First, the prosecutor needs to formally charge the suspect. In this case, officers had made the arrests, but the station did not have access to the prosecutor’s statement of probable cause or charging documents. 

Second, Hebert said, the newsroom needs to be committed to following the case through until its legal conclusion. That’s important because charges often get reduced or dropped. 

“This was a case where there were 11 or 12 people and it was not one that we were committed to following through to find out the outcomes of every single case,” she said. “So we did not use the mugshots.”

FOX59’s story included all 11 mugshots in its coverage. Reporter Claire Curry, included press conference statements from Hamilton County Lt. Doug Baker and other officers. FOX59 reported the names, ages and locations of each of the men arrested in Westfield. The story did not include details about the sting operation. 

I asked FOX59 and CBS4 news director CJ Hoyt why his station aired the mugshots.

“Crimes against children are a category where we are more likely to use mugshots,” he said. 

“Sex crimes against children often have unknown victims,” Hoyt said. “That is the primary motivation. But there is also the seriousness of these kinds of crimes, where we believe there is a public interest.”

For Nexstar Media Group stations, including FOX59 and CBS4 in Indy, mugshot policies are decided at the station level by regional news directors. The policy for these local stations was adopted in October 2022 based on newsroom discussions about crime coverage.

Hoyt noted that the station has scrutinized its use of mugshots in the past and made changes to better cover crime locally. 

“We also know that the broadcast of lots of mugshots is pretty bad television; people don’t want to see it,” Hoyt said. “It gives the viewer an impression of the market that’s probably not accurate when you’re listing a lot of small crimes. It creates the impression that maybe there’s more crime happening than there is.” 

The station also learned about viewers’ preferences from its own focus groups. Viewers who participated in this research said that seeing lots of mugshots felt repetitive. The focus groups also showed that viewers can’t distinguish between stories, Hoyt added. 

How local TV news portrays crime coverage, down to how often and in what circumstances they use mugshots, has broader implications for building trust with different communities and how accurately news organizations are documenting crime.
Mugshot decisions begin with law enforcement and newsrooms’ discretion
The Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Department issues mugshots only upon request, an agency spokesperson told me. They will only share photos of adults, not juveniles, and only adults who have been arrested as part of an IMPD case.

The Marion County Sheriff’s Office has a similar policy and makes mugshots available to the press and general public through public records requests. Special circumstances, such as active criminal investigations and federal detainee holds are exceptions to the rule. 

Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office uses an automated system to post the mugshots of those who are booked into their system. In the case of 11 men arrested for child solicitation, FOX59 searched the automated system to find the mugshots and use them in their story.
 


Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



For newsrooms, mugshot policies are mostly rooted in public safety concerns, said Kerwin Speight, Poynter Institute faculty member, who has more than 20 years experience in TV news. “It’s okay to use a mugshot in an emergency or breaking news situation, where there is imminent concern or danger,” he said. “Does a mugshot need to be used for the person arrested for stealing from a store? Probably not.”

Speight is one of several Poynter faculty members who lead programs for journalists from newsrooms across the country on covering crime. The course, “Transforming Crime Reporting into Public Safety Journalism,” encourages reporters to ask law enforcement additional questions before they decide to use a mugshot on TV.

Is a dangerous suspect at large and are police asking for help in making an arrest?

Do police believe more victims will come forward if they see an image of a suspect? 

When it comes to mugshot policies, local TV news is all over the place, Speight said.

“Some stations are taking a more methodical approach to using mugshots–only using them in a breaking news situation or if a person has been convicted of a crime,” he said. “Others use them all the time. I watch stories and newscasts and there are news organizations that will use a mugshot when reporting any crime. I’ve seen newscasts where it’s story after story using mugshot after mugshot. I’ve seen stories where the mugshot is used as the primary source of video or graphic for a story.”

Journalists have to ask deeper questions, Speight said. Questions like: could I tell the story without the mugshot? What does the mugshot do? What purpose does it serve? 

“In part, because the majority of the mugshots are Black and brown people and they do nothing to enhance the coverage beyond putting somebody’s picture out there that they did this crime,” he said.

This practice, over time, distorts the public’s perception of crime, perpetuating the myth that Black and brown people are more likely to be criminals. 

It also erodes trust. A 2023 Pew Research Center Study found that 42% of African Americans say “the news only covers certain segments of Black communities” and 43% say “the coverage significantly stereotypes Black people.”

Even though an arrest doesn’t automatically mean a conviction, when people see a mugshot they infer guilt, said Sarah Lageson. She is an associate professor of criminology and criminal justice at Northeastern University in Boston, who has researched and written about data privacy and the U.S. criminal legal system.

“There are due process problems here, as people may be exonerated, been wrongly arrested, or have yet to have their day in court,” she said. 
Balancing the public’s need to know with crime trends adds context to coverage
It’s a good sign that Indy’s top two newsrooms are paying attention to how they use mugshots. 

As news consumers, we need local coverage of crime stories to accurately reflect danger in our city so we are aware of public safety concerns. IndyStar has called out politicians for overstating the city’s crime trends. Using mugshots in newscasts can also distort what’s happening in the city. As newsrooms work to gain the trust of the communities they serve, having a firm mugshot policy that accounts for potential harm may help build that trust.

I think it’s good that our local news stations have become more thoughtful about how they use mugshots. And I think they could go even further and be more transparent. I would be in favor of seeing stations restrict their use of mugshots to cases where a dangerous person is on the loose, presenting a clear public safety threat. 

And if every time a station ran a mugshot, a reporter or an anchor told the audience why, it would help us understand the newsroom’s intentions. (“We’re running this mugshot so you can help police find the person responsible.” “We’re running this mugshot because we knew you’d want to know about this celebrity.”) 

Next time you see a mugshot in a news story, ask yourself: is there a reason for me to see this image? And does that reason outweigh the permanent record that will follow that person, before their case has been adjudicated and long after their sentence has been served? 

 


Please write to me at indypubliceditor@poynter.org.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Commentary: Think capping ticket prices will save you money? Think again.
text:
Boygenius, an indie rock supergroup, performs at the MGM Music Hall at Fenway in Boston on Sept. 26, 2023. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)This article first appeared on CommonWealth Beacon and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
Massachusetts fans are paying steeper and steeper prices to go to concerts and see their favorite bands.
It’s a frustratingly common experience: sitting at the computer for hours continually refreshing the window just to get the opportunity to buy a ticket, if they aren’t sold out yet. The lucky few who actually break through have to hand over a small fortune for a ticket – and pay for not just the price of admission, but also service fees and add-ons that drive the cost even higher.
For too many families, attending a concert has become prohibitively expensive, pricing out entire communities from the experiences that bring people together.
Gov. Healey is right to look at this issue. Unfortunately, the proposal included in her supplemental budget bill, called “The Great Divide Act,” will likely only make the problem worse. That’s because the policy strengthens the very monopoly that has made ticket buying so expensive: Ticketmaster.
The Great Divide Act has some smart policies, including a ban on deceptive websites and “speculative” tickets, which are listed for sale before the reseller even owns the ticket. Such policies hold bad actors accountable and should be enacted.
But consumer concerns stem from the bill’s price cap, which only applies when fans resell tickets. At first glance, capping prices on websites like SeatGeek and StubHub to 10% above a ticket’s original cost might sound like it benefits everyone. In reality, it’s really a giveaway to Ticketmaster and its parent company Live Nation. While the monopoly makes more money, fans will be left with the unintended consequences.
The National Consumer League doesn’t oppose price caps as a matter of principle. But to have any chance of working, they must be backed by robust enforcement and a serious strategy to fight fraud. Sadly, Gov. Healey’s proposal includes neither.
The Great Divide Act’s price caps will almost certainly result in far fewer tickets being listed on regulated resale marketplaces. While no one likes paying above face value for a ticket, these marketplaces do provide a safe, regulated place for consumers to buy tickets to sold-out events and even find below-face value bargains when events don’t sell out.
What won’t change if the bill becomes law is that fans’ demand to see their favorite artists and teams will inevitably exceed the supply of tickets. With far fewer tickets available on secondary marketplaces, desperate fans will seek out unregulated marketplaces like Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, TikTok and other platforms. There will be a huge incentive for scammers to flood these unregulated marketplaces with fraudulent tickets, ripping off an untold number of Massachusetts fans.
We’ve already seen this play out in Australia and Ireland, where ticket resale price caps are in effect and fraud rates are 400 percent higher than the United Kingdom, which doesn’t have a cap.
Just north of the border, the same pattern is emerging after Ontario enacted a price cap earlier this year. In Massachusetts, experts ranging from the president of the Boston chapter of the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners to a former State Police sergeant have warned about the wave of fraud this law could unlock.
Someone who pays a premium for a ticket on a regulated resale platform may be frustrated by the price, but a paper trail exists. There’s a customer service team and a path to a refund if something goes wrong. A fan who sends cash to a stranger on social media through Venmo risks both their money and their ticket, with no recourse.
Capping resale prices doesn’t just hurt fans through a higher chance of being scammed. It could also lead to higher ticket prices, overall.
Today, Ticketmaster controls an estimated 86 percent of concert ticket sales, while its parent company Live Nation owns or operates some of the largest concert venues and manages some of the biggest musical acts. That’s why a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general, including Massachusetts AG Andrea Campbell, took the company to court for illegal monopolization — and won.
If this price cap passes, that 86 percent monopoly then inches closer to 100 percent.
Fans will have no alternatives to Ticketmaster. A company whose CEO says tickets are “underpriced” and that uses dynamic pricing to increase the cost fans pay in real time can’t be trusted to bring ticket costs down.
Eliminating the only competitors preventing Ticketmaster from controlling every ticket transaction in Massachusetts—and setting whatever price they want—is not consumer protection. It’s regulatory malpractice.
During a recent Boston Public Radio segment, Ken Casey of the Dropkick Murphys told Gov. Healey that Live Nation is “the real enemy in the room.” She should take that message to heart, abandon this misguided resale price cap, and pursue legislation that addresses the monopoly’s predatory pricing practices.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
text:
"The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion." (Getty Images)
The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability, but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment.
A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans — including 4 in 10 Republicans — believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.
This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs.
I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices — including taxation and public spending — enabled this 40-year rise in inequality.
Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%.
Inequality by the numbers
Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 — and from 27.4% in 1999.
These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class — the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% — who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data.
But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth — almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.
Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices — especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.
How taxes play a role
Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats.
The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research — including international studies — doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.
Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940.
It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.
Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways — including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares.
By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%.
The new drivers of inequality
Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.
One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs.
The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy — while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil.
Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%.
This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “A Brief History of Equality,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Commentary: How Maine Morning Star covers elections
text:
Voting at Freeport High School during Maine's Nov. 4, 2025 election. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: How to register, key dates, who’s on the ballot and where the candidates stand on the top issues facing Maine.]Maine Morning Star’s election coverage is aimed at informing the state’s electorate with timely, nonpartisan news and information that they need to cast their vote. We think our work connecting Mainers to their government is key to a healthy democracy.
Readers often have questions about how we do that work, and the decision-making process that undergirds our coverage. You can find the answers to some common questions below, and on our elections page, which has all of our elections stories and resources.
We approach our elections coverage by focusing on what voters want to hear from candidates, rather than trying to determine who’s ahead before the votes have been cast or counted. 
Because all our work is centered on state government and politics, we get a lot of new readers during elections. If you’re new here, Maine Morning Star is an independent, nonpartisan news organization. All of our reporting is produced by a four-person team based in Portland and Augusta.  
Our newsroom is part of States Newsroom, the nation’s largest nonprofit news organization, whose aim is to support newsrooms in each state capital. Our funding comes from States Newsroom — you can see all national supporters and financial disclosures here — and local donations from readers like you.
In addition to reported stories about candidates, we produce a voter guide. This year, the Morning Star team asked every Maine candidate for U.S. House, U.S. Senate, and governor their positions on several issues most relevant to readers. Most candidates responded to the questionnaire. 
Along with their answers, the guide includes some basic biographical information, their party affiliation, whether they are incumbents and links to their campaign sites. The guide also includes information about each district, as well as the term length and salary for each position.
How we explain voting
We have an election page devoted to the information voters need to successfully cast their ballots, including relevant dates, a how-to guide and an interactive map that shows who is running in each legislative district.
How we hold politicians accountable
We ask politicians the questions we know our readers are asking, and we don’t just report their responses — we dive into their backgrounds to produce stories highlighting the rhetoric as well as the records of those running for U.S. Congress and governor. 
Also, the candidate responses to the questions in our voter guide are useful for helping voters make their pick, and also for keeping candidates accountable to the promises they made on the campaign trail once they’re elected. 
How we choose which races to cover
We prioritize our coverage where we can be most useful. Our four-person team isn’t able to closely cover all 186 seats in the Maine Legislature on the ballot, so we use our best judgement to decide which races to focus on. We strive to cover races that are the most competitive, or whose outcomes may have a significant effect on politics and policy in Maine. We also factor in what interests our readers.  
How we cover misinformation
In our reporting, we seek the documented, verifiable facts on issues. In elections, candidates make claims that do not always match what we can verify. In cases where political claims may mislead Mainers, we will use documentation and context to bring the full picture. While we strive to verify facts through multiple sources, we sometimes get it wrong, and we commit to transparency by noting factual corrections in our stories. We do not use AI as a source and you can find our full ethics policy on our website.
Does this align with what you see in our coverage? Can you think of something we missed? Please let us know at info@mainemorningstar.com.

title: ICE looks to boost staffing at intelligence hubs in Vermont
text:
A Department of Homeland Security office off Industrial Avenue in Williston, Vermont on Tuesday, October 7, 2025. (Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger)U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could hire more workers at its offices in Vermont as part of a $100 million plan to boost intelligence-gatheringfor the branch of the agency that carries out arrests and deportations, federal records show.
The plan, which is not final, calls for 24 positions evenly split between ICE’s Law Enforcement Support Center and its National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, both of which are in Williston. They’re among 142 total positions proposed for ICE offices around the country, all of which would be staffed by a government contractor.
The workers would provide “intelligence research and analytical support” for ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, often abbreviated ERO, according to a contracting document published online last month. That includes “understanding emerging trends, identifying potential threats, recognizing intelligence gaps, assessing relationships and patterns” and a number of other duties.
The contractors would work with a mix of classified and unclassified information, and at least some of them would need “top secret” government security clearance, according to the document. ICE estimates the total cost of the nationwide plan, called ERO Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, would be more than $100 million, according to another federal record published last month.
The government has been “conducting market research” for the plan and issued a request for information to potential contractors, which was due late last month, according to the published records. A final contract could be awarded around February, the magazine The American Prospect reported last week, citing intelligence contracting experts.

One of the Williston centers, the Law Enforcement Support Center, is located on Harvest Lane. It operates a round-the-clock service for police nationwide to get information on a person’s immigration status, as well as a tip line for the public. Workers there also generate leads for immigration enforcement agents and process biometric data for other federal law enforcement agencies including the U.S. Secret Service, according to ICE’s website.
Less than a 10-minute drive away on Industrial Avenue, the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center also develops leads for ICE operations, using an array of digital tools to provide “critical investigative support for daily arrest efforts” according to an agency webpage.
Together, the centers are a major node in ERO’s national intelligence-gathering network. Another key facility, the Pacific Enforcement Response Center, is located in Southern California. That center would get nine contract workers under the plan outlined last month.
The plan marks at least the third time ICE has considered increasing its staffing at Vermont’s facilities since President Donald Trump took office a second time last year, but the agency has disclosed little information publicly about those earlier efforts.

Both Vermont centers have been regular sites for protests in Trump’s second term. Some of those demonstrators have been arrested and are now facing trespassing charges.
The demonstrations in Vermont have been a far cry from the violent clashes that have erupted between protesters and federal agents in other parts of the country. Earlier this month, protesters wrote anti-ICE messages with chalk on the facade of the Law Enforcement Support Center and blocked the road in front of the building using garden beds.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request for more information Monday about its plans for the facilities in Vermont.



This story was originally published by VTDigger, a sharing partner of Maine Morning Star and its parent organization, States Newsroom.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Steil, Berman face off in debate for 1st Congressional District seat
text:
1st Congressional District Democratic candidate Mitchell Berman, left, and Republican incumbent Bryan Steil, center, debate Tuesday at radio station WCLO in Janesville, responding to questions posed by WCLO's Tim Bremel, right. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District incumbent U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil (R-Janesville) and his Democratic party challenger, Mitchell Berman, parried for an hour Tuesday in their only face-to-face encounter scheduled before the Nov. 3 election.
The debate took place in the studio of Janesville radio station WCLO and was moderated by Tim Bremel, who hosts the station’s daily morning talk program.
Steil is a corporate lawyer who has represented the 1st District since 2019. Berman is an emergency room nurse who won the Democratic nomination in August. The two took contrasting approaches during the hourlong exchange.
Berman has focused his campaign on rising costs, including for healthcare, and Tuesday he returned several times to the 2025 massive tax and spending bill — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — that Steil voted for. The Republican-authored legislation cut taxes for the wealthy while cutting funding for Medicaid and other safety-net programs over the next decade.
“Our healthcare has been gutted and has become unaffordable, and we’re seeing politicians in Washington enriching themselves and working at the behest of their corporate donors and special interests,” Berman said in his opening remarks. “That’s why I got into this race, and we need to change and make Washington work for working people again.”
Steil defended his vote and said he has been working “to clean up Washington.” He accused Berman, and Democrats in general, of lying about the 2025 bill’s impact and also appeared to accuse Berman of positions that the challenger never took.
Bremel’s first question cited a poll that put inflation and the cost of living at the top of voters’ concerns. He asked the candidates to identify “one specific federal policy you would prioritize to improve household finances for the residents of the First District.”
Berman called for repealing “blanket tariffs” levied by the Trump administration. “We know that tariffs are a tax on the American people, and everyone knows we’re paying more for everything at the store right now because of that,” Berman said. Steil “has voted to continue these blanket tariffs eight times, and that, to me, I think is unconscionable.”
When it was his turn, Steil praised the Trump administration’s embrace of fossil fuels to “unleash American energy.”
Steil highlighted provisions in the 2025 tax law that cut taxes on overtime pay and tips, a new $6,000 tax deduction for people 65 or older, and another measure that makes changes to the federal child tax credit, expanding it for some families.
“My opponent opposes that tax relief,” Steil said of Berman in a follow-up comment. Berman took exception to that charge.
“Those components of tax relief that my opponent just talked about, I don’t oppose,” Berman said. He asked Steil, however, why those four provisions “for regular working class people” are set to expire after 2028 while the bill’s “tax relief for billionaires was made permanent.”
Steil ignored the direct question. “We just have a firm disagreement,” he told Bremel. “I’m working to reduce taxes for people here in South Central and Southeastern Wisconsin,” he added, and reiterated Berman’s opposition to the 2025 bill without answering the question Berman had posed.
Healthcare costs
Bremel’s next question, focusing on public concerns about healthcare costs, asked the two for their first priority in making “changes to the federal healthcare system,” including how it would be paid for.
Steil again defended his vote on the 2025 bill, accusing Berman of putting out “false information” about the Medicaid provisions. The Republican congressman said the bill “results in an increase in $1 billion in federal money coming to the state of Wisconsin for Medicaid.”
The $1 billion refers to additional Medicaid matching funds to the state under a provision in the 2025-27 Wisconsin budget. That boost resulted from a deal reached between Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and Republican leaders in the state Legislature. State lawmakers and the governor rushed the budget to be signed before the federal provision took effect, which would have cut Wisconsin off from the additional money without the state budget change.
Berman didn’t address that issue, but countered that in contrast to the $1 billion Steil touted, the federal bill cut “a trillion dollars from Medicaid over the next 10 years.” He also cited projections that 270,000 Wisconsinites could lose insurance coverage after the expiration of enhanced subsidies to lower the cost of Affordable Care Act marketplace health policies.
“I know what that looks like when people are showing up to the hospital underinsured and uninsured, and that cost gets shifted to folks who have insurance,” Berman said.
Steil said the bill’s Medicaid work requirements on “able-bodied, childless adults of working age” would strengthen the program. He also credited the federal bill for “removing illegal immigrants from receiving free taxpayer-funded healthcare.
According to the Center for Children and Families at Georgetown University, undocumented immigrants and many immigrants with legal status were already prevented from getting Medicaid coverage.
“This legislation creates red tape, which makes it more difficult for people who qualify for those benefits to obtain them, and so they lose their benefits,” Berman responded.
Berman said nothing about Medicaid and immigrants, but Steil replied, “My opponent is arguing to use your taxpayer dollars for illegal aliens. That was very clear right there.”
Replied Berman, “I don’t believe that’s what I said.”
Campaign finance
In response to another question, about campaign finance and congressional ethics, Berman cited his endorsement by the campaign finance reform group End Citizens United.
“We are a grassroots-funded campaign, and we don’t take any corporate PAC money,” Berman said.
Steil contended that Berman’s claim was a lie because an ad in which the Democrat said he doesn’t take corporate PAC money was paid for by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “What do they take? Corporate PAC money,” Steil charged.
“If you look at my FEC reports, there is no corporate PAC money,” Berman said, referring to his campaign’s filings with the Federal Election Commission.
Steil’s most recent filings show his campaign has $1.6 million in corporate PAC donations, 31% of the $5.3 million he raised in 2025-26, according to Open Secrets, an independent group that tracks money in politics analyzing FEC data.
On Social Security and Medicare, Steil said the programs should be protected by “rooting out wasteful spending.”
Berman responded by observing that Steil had voted against 2022 legislation authorizing Medicare to negotiate prices on select drugs with pharmaceutical companies, and that the Trump administration had cut jobs from the Social Security Administration, making it more difficult for people to navigate the system.
“Our current administration pardoned multiple people who committed egregious Medicaid and Medicare fraud,” Berman added, “and I was wondering if my opponent would denounce that.”
In response, Steil referred to “significant, record-breaking arrests and convictions in Milwaukee County” relating to Medicaid fraud, but added that “there’s a lot more work to do to root out the waste, fraud, abuse in these federal programs.”
On immigration, Berman called for “transparency and accountability” in the federal agencies responsible for immigration enforcement, “making sure these organizations are following the law and getting the most heinous criminals off of our streets and focused on those folks.”
Steil said immigration policies should be linked to “workforce needs” in the U.S. “I don’t support amnesty,” said Steil. “It sounds like my opponent does.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Straight from Trump’s lips: Support for Roger Marshall of Kansas and digressions aplenty
text:
President Donald Trump looks for the news media while speaking at an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)Kansas was honored with the presence of the president of the United States on Monday night.
Donald Trump traveled to Park City, just outside Wichita, to voice his support for Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall in his unexpectedly tight race against Democrat Adam Hamilton. I’ve written about that contest at length. You’ve heard my takes.
You might not have heard Trump’s opinions. As an epoch-defining leader, Trump carried unique importance that October evening as he urged Kansas voters to vote for Marshall as through they were voting for him.
Trump’s unique approach to political rhetoric has been a longstanding fascination of mine, from the time that I first saw him in person in Nashua, New Hampshire, more than a decade ago. In 2015, I wrote: “The actual content of his short stump speech was a series of digressions, touching on his proposal to build a White House ballroom, China’s currency valuation and reheated GOP talking points. In one brief passage, he managed to mash together Benghazi, the IRS investigation of conservative groups, the president’s golf game and executive orders.”
Trump’s speeches have only lengthened and deepened since then, offering the kind of profundity only achievable by those with uncommon wisdom or catastrophic head injuries.
Here are five curious passages from Trump’s Monday night free-for-all.
 
‘He couldn’t figure out the stairs’
“You know, I have the all-time in history Christian vote. I have the evangelical vote, the Christian vote. I have by — I know more. I know more than anybody.
“As somebody said about me — I shouldn’t say this. This is terrible. They said a certain pastor from a place in Dallas, Texas. He said — you know, I shouldn’t say this. Should I say this, Roger?
“He said, ‘You know, he might not read the Bible as much as us. He might not know every passage and he might have some other little weaknesses. But one thing about him — he’s the greatest leader, and he’s going to lead us to a period of time in Christianity, in Christianity, that nobody else can do. That nobody else can do.’
“And he turned out to be right. Turned out to be right. I’ll never forget it. I said, ‘I don’t know. Am I insulted by that, or is that a compliment?’
“But he was a — he’s a great guy. Dallas, Dallas, Texas.
“All of us here tonight represent the greatest nation in the world, and frankly, our nation was not so great two years ago. It was an embarrassment. We had a president that couldn’t find his way off a stage. He couldn’t. He couldn’t figure out the stairs. You got more stairs on these stages. You know, I think the federal government puts them up, Roger.’ ”
 
‘His views aren’t of a pastor’
“In fact, when she (Kamala Harris) ran, you know, we had a debate. Biden didn’t do great. It was not one of the greatest debate performances. He was slightly off that night, and they decided, ‘Let’s get rid of him.’ This is like a prize fighter goes in — Dana White, UFC — and you’re beating the hell out of the guy. And now they say, ‘Let’s remove him and put a new guy in.’ That’s no good.
“But fortunately, the new one was Kamala, and she was no better. But she’s leading. She’s leading. I don’t know if she knows that.
“Let’s call her up and tell her. I can’t believe it.
“But very importantly, Adam Hamilton. So he donated a lot of money to all these people. He didn’t give me anything. He didn’t give me, and he should have. That would have been a wise thing to do, but he didn’t because he’s not for us. He’s not. He doesn’t have our views. He doesn’t have our values. And he happens to be other than being a pastor. He’s a pastor, I guess. But he doesn’t act like a pastor because his views aren’t of a pastor.
“Adam Hamilton wants to take away your guns, and, and by the way, one of the most important issues. There has been nobody better on the Second Amendment than me.”
 
‘Request strongly money owed’
“I’d rather have you have all paper ballots, by the way. It’s a lot better. Save a lot of money. You save a lot of money.
“And I have to say this. Somebody said, ‘Oh, don’t say it. Nobody believes it.’ But I have to say it because I think it’s appropriate. Roger was given a real. I know the guy. He’s one of the — he’s a tough guy and all, but he’s also high quality, and he’s a fine person. And he was given a bum rap because he was mandated by law to request strongly money owed from patients.
“You’re not allowed not to do it. You have to, by law, go after those people.
“And they made it like, ‘Oh, he was some kind of a Shylock type guy.’ And if he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the law. He would have been breaking a very strong criminal law, and he would be subject to criminal arrest and liability.
“And he didn’t do it. It was the law firm that did it. I don’t know what they did. They’re probably tough, but they were mandated to be tough by the law, and they gave him a bum rap. So I don’t know if I should be saying it, but that’s the way it is, Roger. I have to tell it like it is.
“You got screwed with that stuff. And the other thing, he had somebody again, he had to collect. A judge ordering a patient’s arrest. A judge ordered a patient’s arrest for not showing up to court many, many times. A patient just refused on a routine court case to settle it up, and the judge was very tough.
“And that’s the way it is. It’s just, he didn’t make, he didn’t do it. The judge was very tough because the judge, and it wasn’t really even the judge’s fault. The judge was mandated to be this way, and it has to do with the federal government, and it has to do with the collection of money for the federal government. And that man did nothing wrong. So I just want to set the record straight.
“That should not happen to a good person, and fake ads like that shouldn’t be allowed. Oh, I’d love to sue the media. I would love to sue.
“Sullivan. We — Sullivan v. Sullivan. Oh, I’d like to have them change that. They would have — then they’d really be finished.”
 
‘If you don’t love them, just forget’
“They gave us the worst inflation in American history, the highest energy prices in American history. They gave us the worst inflation. It was really 48 years, but I think it was history. And sometimes they’ll call me out. ‘It wasn’t history. It was 48 years.’ Oh, OK. I actually think 48 years sounds worse.
“I don’t know why, but they gave us the worst inflation in American history, the worst trade deficit in American history, and they allowed 25 million people to pour across our borders from all over the world. And if they win the midterms, they will do it again. They’ll get rid of the border. They’ll get rid of all the tax cuts. We have no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security from our seniors.
“No estate tax. So you leave your children your farm. You love your children. Your children love the farm. They want to take your farm under the previous administration, and they want to end this, by the way.
“If that happened, they go after your farm. They go after your children. They have a big tax. Your children go to the bank, the local friendly bank that turns out to be not so friendly, and they go after your children. And bad things happen. Often bad things happen. I got rid of the death tax, or the estate tax as it’s more commonly known.
“But all small farms, businesses — so you can leave your small farm or business to your children if you love your children. Now, if you don’t love them, just forget. I just wasted about two minutes. You don’t love your — is there anybody in this room who does not love their children? Because you know Kansas is, I think, known for a lot of love.”

 
‘I don’t even talk about myself’
“But less than two years ago, radical left Democrats handed us the dark age. It was the dark age. It was a dark, dirty period, weaponization like nobody’s ever seen. Hey, I was the ultimate. I mean, I don’t even talk about myself.
“What they did with me, but now I look. And I say, ‘Oh, gee, I’m in the Oval Office.’ I say sometimes, I’ll say, ‘Nobody appreciates what I’ve done.’
“I’ve created the greatest, you know. We have 22 trillion coming in. No, I do it. You know, we just we just did favored nations in medicine, like as an example, and all these things. And I did so much, and did so much. And you know, we’re in the golden age of America. We were the dark ages.
“But I say oftentimes, nobody appreciates what I did. I feel very sad.
“No, no, no. I took drug prices from the highest price in history to the lowest, and the press doesn’t write. No, that’s OK. Don’t worry. You’re killing my final line here. That’s OK. I never will turn down applause.
“But now I say to myself, sadly, as I sit in the most magnificent office in the world, the most powerful 3,000 feet, 3,000 square feet, most powerful by hundreds and hundreds of times, I’d say nobody appreciates how great a president I am.”
 
Listen to the man
As the leader of our nation and the free world, Trump wields unimaginable power, coupled with incredible influence.
Yet the national news media often prefers to process his rhetoric through random spokesmen and spokeswomen, quotes from anonymous aides, or handcrafted press releases.
This seems curious, given that Trump regularly speaks to the public at great length. He posts daily to his Truth Social platform, also at great length. The least those who support him or oppose him can do is pay attention to the actual words he uses and the actual stances he takes. What does he mean to convey to the people of Kansas and the greater nation?
This is the mind, and these are the words, of our duly elected president. Drink it in.
Clay Wirestone is Kansas Reflector opinion editor. His first book, “Opinionated: Kansas Journalists Who Proved Why Commentary Matters — Then and Now,” was published in September 2026 by the University Press of Kansas. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Georgia Recorder
title: Ballot amendment would pave the way for dedicated funding to upgrade Georgia’s 911 system
text:
A proposed constitutional amendment would create a designated fund where lawmakers can earmark state money to modernize and standardize Georgia’s 911 system statewide. Photo credit: Pikusisi-Studio via Getty Images Georgia is currently in the midst of transforming its 911 system to incorporate new technology in a world where most calls to emergency services are made from cell phones rather than landlines.
But how quickly the state finishes that upgrade may depend on the outcome of one of this year’s three ballot questions. A proposed constitutional amendment would create a designated fund where lawmakers can earmark state money to modernize and standardize Georgia’s 911 system statewide.
Rep. Chuck Martin. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Notably, the measure would not actually allocate any state or local money to the fund. State Rep. Chuck Martin, an Alpharetta Republican who sponsored the resolution creating the ballot question, said that if the constitutional amendment is approved by voters, state lawmakers will need to pass enabling legislation next year to determine how funds will be allocated across the state.
“The idea is that this is the first step toward creating an infrastructure where we can create a sustainable funding mechanism, so that Georgia has a ubiquitous, first-class 911 system moving forward,” he said.
As part of the process, lawmakers will need to pass legislation to change the existing local 911 fee to a state one. Martin said the question of how those state funds will be allocated to municipalities will be determined with input from city and county governments, as well as 911 directors. Without that enabling legislation, Martin said, the fund will still exist, but it will sit empty.
“If we can’t come to a conclusion that our cities and counties agree with, that our [911] directors agree with that would be the best way to move forward, we will have a fund that money won’t be deposited in it, money won’t be distributed from,” he said.
But Martin added that smaller counties in particular would greatly benefit from an increase in funds and more modern technology to address emergencies.
‘The same level of service in any county you go to’
[Voter Guide: 2026 General Election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
According to the Georgia Emergency Communications Authority, more than 80% of 911 calls are made from wireless devices, such as cell phones. However, the technology used throughout the state’s emergency infrastructure has not changed much since the system was first established in 1968, when most calls were placed on landlines. 
State lawmakers are currently hoping to implement a network called Next Generation 911, which would allow first responders to more precisely identify a caller’s location and allow the public to send photos, videos and text messages to 911 centers in addition to placing calls.
Thomas Cisco, the Forsyth County emergency management director and president of the Georgia 911 Directors Association, said that some counties in Georgia are already using the updated technology, but many counties still rely on the older technology.
“Right now, we have 156 different public safety entry points that have all different varieties and varying degrees of technology when it comes to answering telephone calls and dispatching,” Cisco said. Under a Next Generation 911 system, he added, “you’ll get the same level of service in any county you go to, from the smallest county to the largest county.”
Only 17 of Georgia’s 159 counties are currently Next Generation 911-compliant, according to Clint Mueller, the deputy director of the Association County Commissioners of Georgia.
Georgians currently pay a $1.50 monthly fee on their cell phone bills that is intended to go toward funding their local 911 systems. But Cisco said that storing the money in a designated fund would allow any unused funds to roll over to the next fiscal year and prevent lawmakers from diverting the money elsewhere.
But could the money be diverted to non-911 purposes? 
Warnock urges greater federal oversight of automatic license plate readers

The resolution creating the ballot question passed through both chambers of the Legislature early this year with unanimous support and appeared to be relatively uncontroversial. But earlier this month, a grassroots organization called Galvanize Georgia voiced opposition to the measure, warning that the funds could be used to purchase automated license plate readers like Flock cameras, which have come under fire after numerous instances of misuse by law enforcement officials.
A spokesperson for the state House Speaker said the funds would not be used for automatic license plate readers, citing state law that defines the specific technology used in Georgia’s 911 system.
“The proposed constitutional amendment is clear that this funding is only for upgrades to 911 systems, which do not include Flock cameras,” said Kayla Green, a spokesperson for House Speaker Jon Burns of Newington. “These funds may only be used to upgrade emergency communication systems that strengthen direct communication between Georgians and first responders.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio groups take measures to protect voting during November midterm election
text:
Early voting in Ohio at the Franklin County Board of Elections. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal) Ohioans are voting in the midterm election, and as they are, an array of groups is working to ensure that it’s free and fair. 
Absentee and early in-person voting started last week in the Nov. 3 election last week. As they have, a consortium of pro-democracy groups has positioned monitors at polling places, set up an election hotline and has lawyers and others waiting to be dispatched if problems arise.
At the same time, the NAACP announced plans to open a legal war room of its own on Oct. 24.
Many of the measures are routine, but fears are elevated this year.
President Donald Trump already tried to overturn an election he lost in 2020. 
Behind in the polls, he’s again making false claims about election security. In May he would not rule out the possibility of sending federal agents to polling places — which many legal experts say is illegal.
In the face of that, volunteers are working to ensure normalcy in this year’s election.
“There’s a very robust election-protection effort,” said Mia Lewis of Common Cause Ohio.
She said her group, the Ohio Voter Rights Coalition, the League of Women Voters, the American Civil Liberties Union and other groups are training and have deployed poll monitors. 
The political parties have observers inside polling places where they observe what’s happening, but aren’t allowed to talk to voters. Nonpartisan monitors are outside polling places, where they answer nonpolitical questions and watch for problems.
“We answer people’s questions and make sure everything is going smoothly,” Lewis said. “Poll monitors are the eyes and ears on the ground of the Ohio election-protection system.”
The groups also have lawyers available if legal issues arise, and “peacekeepers” such as ministers and social workers to dispatch if things get tense, Lewis said.
And there’s a national election protection hotline — 866-OUR-VOTE (687-8683) operated by the Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights Under the Law. Anyone with questions or who sees potential problems can call.
“We have access to that on the back end, so if problems are reported we can try to solve them in real time,” Lewis said. “We try to spread the word about the hotline as much as we can before the election because the more people know about it, the more voters we can help, the more problems we can solve.”
The group operating the protection hotline can accommodate languages other than English.
So far, most of the problems the Ohio groups are hearing have to do with confusion about deadlines and absentee voting, Lewis said. She added that recent changes in the state haven’t helped.
The rights groups want all Ohio citizens to know that hundreds of volunteers have fanned out across the state and they should feel safe voting. Lewis said that’s especially true for citizens who were born outside the country or have foreign-sounding names.
“We definitely hope they aren’t discouraged from voting because they feel things are strange this year,” she said. “We really, really hope that doesn’t happen. We want folks to go out and vote and exercise their rights.”
Meanwhile, Ohio is among the 16 states the NAACP is including in its midterm war room, which will provide “a dedicated phone line, email addresses, and digital forms for voters to submit any cases of alleged voter intimidation, suppression, or issues while voting,” the group said in a written statement.
 “The NAACP will respond to credible cases as they emerge to help ensure eligible voters can cast their ballots and have those ballots counted.”
The state-level hubs will launch by Oct. 24. They come after conservatives on the U.S. Supreme Court have dramatically weakened the 1965 Voting Rights Act, which was intended to ensure all citizens have equal access to the ballot — and to representation in government.
“We cannot buy into the fear,” NAACP President Derrick Johnson said in a written statement. 
“Donald Trump wants us to be afraid, because he is a deeply unpopular president. He’s afraid of losing his grip on Congress, so he wants us to stay home and make it harder to vote. Real power belongs to the people, and the NAACP is ready to protect all voters when they go and cast their ballots.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Will 2026 renew Ohio’s battleground status?
authors: Robert Alexander, Ph.D., David B. Cohen, Ph.D.
text:
Photo by Hill Street Studios/Getty Images.Ohio enjoyed the benefit of being on the national stage in politics for well over 100 years. Indeed, the state voted for the winner of the presidency in 30 out of 31 elections from 1896 to 2016. That number grows to 37 out of 40 if you go back to the Civil War. 
In three consecutive elections beginning in 2016, Donald Trump’s dominance in the Buckeye State has led most to question whether Ohio should be written off as a purple state and categorized as reliably red. 
After all, the state voted to the right of the nation by 5.4 points in 2016, 6.4 points in 2020, and 5.3 points in 2024. 
Republicans have controlled the Ohio House of Representatives since 2011, and many voters weren’t even alive the last time Democrats controlled the Ohio Senate in 1984 (though some of this dominance can be explained by Republican-led gerrymandering of Ohio’s General Assembly districts).
Yet, you don’t have to squint your eyes too much to see Ohio is in play in 2026.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
October visits from President Trump, Vice President JD Vance, former President Barack Obama, and an expected $750 million in campaign dollars being spent in the state strongly suggest competitive statewide contests. 
A recent BGSU/YouGov poll gives an edge to Democrats by 6 points in both the gubernatorial and U.S. Senate races. The Cook Political Report now rates both races as “toss-up” despite both having started in February 2025 as “likely Republican.” 
So what’s going on here? Is Ohio suddenly a swing state again or is this a typical rebuke of a president’s party in a midterm election? The answer likely lies somewhere in between and has major consequences for the competitiveness of Ohio beyond 2026. 
While it is true that Republicans have been dominant in the state as of late, a strong streak of independence also moves many Ohio voters. 
They are often less ideological than political observers believe and more motivated by kitchen table topics. 
Polling tells us that Ohioans value economic security, fairness, and whether candidates understand their concerns. They also have a deep distrust of political and economic elites. Successful statewide campaigns have typically resonated with voters along these dimensions. 
The October 2026 BGSU/YouGov Poll shows deep economic anxiety. Sixty-five percent of Ohioans say the national economy has gotten worse over the past year, while only 17% believe it has improved. 
The economy remains the top concern of voters, followed by inflation, government corruption, and health care. 
Like the rest of the country, Ohioans are frustrated by the status quo and that only serves to hurt Republicans–the party in unified control of both the national and state government. 
President Trump remains the dominant figure in Ohio politics, but his coalition is showing signs of strain. His approval rating in the BGSU poll stands at 39%, with 58% disapproving, nineteen points under water. 
Among voters who supported Trump in 2024, 24% now say they regret their vote to some degree. Among independents who voted for Trump, that number rises to nearly one-third. 
This voting bloc has always been critical in Ohio elections and we are seeing a surge of early voting by those who are non-affiliated. 
The BGSU poll finds that independents support Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy (54%-22%) and Democratic Senatorial candidate Sherrod Brown over Republican Jon Husted (49%-21%). 
A sizable number of independents currently say they are voting for a third party or someone else (24% in the gubernatorial race and 30% in the Senate race). Of course, we won’t know whether these preferences translate to actual votes until after the November election. 
Notably, we are not seeing some emphatic embrace of Democrats in this cycle.
A majority of independents think neither party stands up for working people (53%), fights for working families (59%), puts Ohio workers first (56%), understands everyday Ohioans (64%), keeps promises (77%), or cares about people like themselves (69%). This presents a future opportunity for Democrats to regain some lost ground with these voters.
Indeed, when party labels have been less obvious, Ohio voters have supported Democrat-aligned policies. 
For instance, in 2023, voters protected abortion access through the state’s Constitution (57%-43%) and legalized recreational marijuana (57%-43%). 
Given that Republican leaders in the state urged voters to reject both policies, the results are telling. Absent party identification, voters in the state prefer self-determination and limited government, over simple culture war binaries. 
Parties matter but candidates and context matter too. In addition to concerns over the economy, Buckeye voters want candidates they can trust and who they believe best understands their concerns. And this is where Acton and Brown do particularly well among independents. 
Acton leads Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy on every single trait among independents. Her biggest strengths are caring about ordinary people (+34), sharing my values (+32), honesty (+27), and keeping promises (+25). 
Likewise, Brown leads U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, the Republican candidate, on every single trait among independents. We see wide margins when it comes to caring about ordinary people (+43), honesty (+41), sharing my values (+31), and good judgment (+26). 
If these poll results end up being accurate, they will go a long way in explaining how Democrats were able to overcome the partisan advantage Republicans have had in the state. 
If Democrats are victorious they will need to continue to focus on economic concerns, reject political extremes, and speak to the frustrations of everyday Ohioans. 
Ohio remains one of the best tests of where American politics is headed. 
The results of this election will not only determine control of the governor’s office and a U.S. Senate seat, but will reveal whether Ohio is once again a battleground or will continue to be a reliably red state. 
If it’s the former, then be prepared for a barrage of campaigning in the Buckeye state for the 2028 presidential election. 
If it’s the latter, expect a respite from political advertising by the presidential campaigns for the foreseeable future.
