name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: What a new fight over chemical safety reveals about our changing politics
text:
Drinking water photo from the Ohio Governor's Office.For years, the politics of chemical safety seemed trapped in the same old argument. Environmental advocates called for stronger regulations. Industry warned about costs and government overreach. Democrats and Republicans returned to familiar corners, while families continued to wonder what was in the food they ate, the water they drank, and the products they brought into their homes.
That old pattern is changing.
Across the country, a new and increasingly cross-partisan coalition is forming around a simple idea: Americans shouldn’t have to choose between a strong economy and healthy people. Parents, workers, farmers, doctors, veterans, small-business owners, environmental advocates, and consumers are finding common ground in the demand for cleaner food and water, safer products, and greater accountability from the companies that put chemicals into our lives.
This isn’t just a theoretical alliance. It’s already exerting power.
Earlier this year, 73 Republicans joined Democrats in the House to vote for consumer safeguards involving agricultural chemicals in the farm bill, going against their party’s leadership. That vote reflected something larger than a single legislative dispute. It showed that elected officials are beginning to recognize what their constituents already know: defending people from harmful exposure is not a left-wing or right-wing concern. It matters for everybody.
We know this movement because we represent different parts of it. One of us served in Congress for 20 years as a Democrat from Northeast Ohio. The other has worked across public health, environmental, and consumer-safety efforts as the leader of MAHA Ohio. We don’t come from identical political traditions, but we share a conviction that has become increasingly difficult to ignore. That defending human health can unite Americans across the political spectrum.
That is the heart of the emerging left-right convergence.
The debate now before Congress over the Toxic Substances Control Act, or TSCA, is one place where this new politics is taking shape. TSCA governs many chemicals used in manufacturing and everyday products. The law gives the Environmental Protection Agency authority to gather information, require testing, evaluate risks, and restrict or prohibit certain uses. Food, drugs, cosmetics, and pesticides are generally regulated under other federal laws. 
The law is complex, but the question at its center is not: Who bears the burden when a chemical may harm people?
In 2016, Republicans and Democrats came together to strengthen TSCA. Their changes required the EPA to evaluate chemicals already on the market, established deadlines, and increased transparency.
Today, lawmakers are again considering changes that could weaken toxic chemical regulation. Supporters of changes say the EPA needs a more predictable process so manufacturers can plan ahead. But, as health advocates on the left and right warn, weakening requirements could make it harder to identify dangerous exposures and defend Americans. 
While it’s increasingly clear that the EPA needs staff, information, and the money to do its job, the larger story is about whether our political system can respond to what families are experiencing in their everyday lives.
People are tired of being told that concern about toxins in food or products is partisan. People are tired of learning that a substance was widely used before anyone fully understood its effects. People are done with discovering that the products marketed as convenient, modern, or profitable may carry risks that fall most heavily on children, workers, pregnant women, farmers, and communities already facing pollution.
A parent who wants safer products for a child may not use the same political vocabulary as an environmental lawyer. A farmer concerned about soil and water may not describe the problem in the same terms as a public health researcher. A conservative voter who wants less crony capitalism may not frame the issue like a progressive advocate. But they can still arrive at the same conclusion: companies should not be allowed to put people at unnecessary risk, and government should not be blocked from action when evidence demands it.
A new movement for human health is giving people from different backgrounds a reason to stand together.

text:
The Ohio burgee. (Getty images file photo.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• Pollution. Ideastream’s Jeff St. Clair reports, “Judge preserves Ohio provision allowing citizens to sue polluters.”
A Franklin County court ruled Ohio lawmakers acted illegally when they added a provision to last year’s state budget that would have taken away citizens’ right to sue polluters.
The Oct. 14 ruling by Common Pleas Judge Julie Lynch preserves the state’s Air Nuisance Rule, a 50-year-old provision that allows communities and citizens to sue polluters for violating the federal Clean Air Act.
Last summer, Republican lawmakers added language to the state budget directing the Ohio EPA to repeal the rule and a provision that allows citizens to use air quality monitoring data as evidence.
• Republicans for socialism? Politico reports, “GOP-linked PAC spends over $1M to boost third-party socialist in Ohio Senate race.”
A GOP-aligned super PAC has more than tripled its investment in the Ohio Senate race over the last week as it seeks to boost a socialist candidate — an apparent attempt to sink former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown’s chances.
• Whiskey. Cleveland.com’s Anna Staver reports, “Ohio man’s fight to make whiskey at home reaches U.S. Supreme Court.”
An Ohio man who wanted to distill whiskey at home may help decide whether millions of Americans can legally do the same.
On Monday, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to hear a separate challenge to the 160-year-old federal ban on home distilling.
• Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reports, “Musk Ordered Starlink Slowdown That Blindsided Ukraine.”
Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of Starlink relied on by Ukraine, a decision that sparked panic in Kyiv and confusion inside the Trump administration, U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter said.
Both Musk and President Trump have expressed anger at Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries in recent weeks, which the president blames for high energy prices. Last week, Musk capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network, the people said, rendering some offensive drones and interceptor drones virtually useless.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The CSCU consolidation — a mismanaged disaster
text:
Over the years I have been an outspoken critic of the consolidation of the 12 independently accredited community colleges into one CT State Community College with a single accreditation. It has saved no money, and in fact, has cost much more, and has meant the end of each college’s ability to meet the needs of its unique student body and its unique community.
The independent colleges were transformational, as one college, the campuses can be nothing more than transactional.
To be clear, my alternative plan is to return us to independently accredited community colleges that will again be able to support and serve our local students and communities, and then ask the state of Connecticut to fund us at a level that will allow us to properly do that job.
We create a better future for Connecticut and for the country when we are structured to support our distinct community and student needs and we are funded properly. In an AACC (American Association of Community Colleges) 2022 report that analyzed FY2019-20 data, it noted that for every tax dollar spent on community colleges there is a $6.80 return on investment. According to that report, in FY2019-20 alumni of U.S. community colleges generated $898.5 billion in added income for the national economy. To give context, the report notes that is equal to about 4.1% of the total U.S. gross domestic product.
Who knew when Jane Gates, then the CSCU Provost; Merle Harris, then a member of the Board of Regents; and David Levinson, then the Interim CT State CC President, wrote the op-ed in the CT Mirror July 07, 2020, and ended it with the below statement they would be so prophetic. Unsurprisingly, it shows in everything being done to create a third-rate college. “This is our promise to Black and Latinx students. Connecticut State Community College is being built for you. A college designed for your success. A college that will serve to change Connecticut generation by generation.”
And, in the creation of CT State, it has been made clear that the Black, Latinx, and all students from the wrong side of the socio-economic spectrum are not worthy of the kind of education offered to their counterparts at other colleges and universities.
Unfortunately, the continuous drip, drip, drip of CSCU scandals involving money, sex, fear, bullying, and humiliation are shiny objects that overshadow issues concerning the education of our students. The CSCU system’s deeply entrenched mismanagement has been a disaster in the educational arena, its reason for being in the first place. And the community college consolidation has only made the educational journey for our students more complicated and less productive.
As an illustration of how our legislators cherry-pick what they want to believe, instead of asking questions and listening to those of us who are directly affected by this disaster, here is a quote from State Sen. Derek Slap who is the co-chair of the legislative Higher Education and Employment Advancement Committee. This quote comes from a WFSB Sept.  22 article entitled “Lawmakers Call for Reforms After Scandals at Top of Connecticut State College System:”
“Well, what’s ironic is that the outcomes for students have been improving, and so the system, in terms of delivering a high-quality and affordable education for thousands and thousands of students in Connecticut, that has been a success, and it’s being marred right now by scandals at the very top.”
For our legislators to believe everything is going very well on the academic side while the system is mired in sexual, monetary, and other ongoing scandals takes a true stretch of the imagination. Asking questions to determine how deep the dysfunction is within the CSCU and CT State systems should not be optional at this point.
Being offended by the John Maduko report, and, apparently, never bothering to read the Ferrilli report, the AASC&U (American Association of State Colleges & Universities) HR Assessment, and others, that addressed systemic educational issues that negate the above statement should also not be optional. However, sensational scandals will always attract more attention than the mundane issues of whether the CSCU and CT State systems are truly benefiting our students’ education.
How can anyone take the Board of Regents and the CSCU and CT State administration at their word on educational statements while, at the same time (belatedly) questioning their actions, or lack thereof, regarding the money, sex, and bullying scandals? It is time-consuming, and boring, to learn what is really happening in the education area. And learning the truth might require action, and that would require work.
Our students, our communities, and our future are the pawns in this chess game. And right now it looks like the game is rigged against an ending that will benefit this state or this country.
Lois Aime is Director of Educational Technology at CT State Norwalk (aka Norwalk Community College).

name: Mississippi Today
title: New video shows chaotic moments before Senatobia police shot toddler
authors: Joseph Cranney, Mukta Joshi, Eduardo Medina, and Devon Lum
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Joseph Cranney is a reporter at Verite News. Mukta Joshi is a reporter at Mississippi Today. She is spending a year as a New York Times Local Investigations fellow. Eduardo Medina is a reporter covering the South for The New York Times. Devon Lum is a reporter on the Visual Investigations team at The New York Times.
Moments before a Mississippi police officer fired at a car in June, killing a toddler inside, five officers rushed out to a Walmart parking lot in pursuit of two women who were accused of stealing diapers and baby clothes.
Newly released videos show a gray sedan, carrying 1-year-old Kohen Wiley, his mother and another woman, reversing and slamming into a parked vehicle as police officers run toward the car and order the driver to stop.
As the car stops, the officers approach and surround the vehicle before the driver accelerates and lurches left, appearing to travel toward at least one of the officers before passing between two of them. At least one officer shoots into the vehicle.
The chaotic scene in Senatobia, captured on body cameras worn by two of the five officers and by surveillance cameras, provides the first glimpse of a shooting that has rocked the tiny city and raised questions about whether the officer was justified in opening fire at the vehicle.
This undated photo shows Kohen Wiley. The Mississippi Department of Public Safety says a police officer responding to a shoplifting call on Sunday, June 14, 2026, shot at a car that allegedly drove in the officer’s direction, 1-year-old Kohen. Credit: Courtesy of Carlos Haynes and Veronica Robinson
The Mississippi attorney general’s office, which declined to comment on the video, announced on Monday that it would not bring criminal charges against the officer who fatally shot Kohen.
The compilation of several body-cam and surveillance clips was first published by a Mississippi news outlet, Darkhorse Press. A law enforcement official confirmed its authenticity on the condition of anonymity because the official was not authorized to provide information about sensitive matters. A video analysis by The New York Times, Mississippi Today and Verite News showed the footage matched portions of video of the shooting captured by a bystander.
The body-cam footage released Tuesday is from the perspective of two of the law enforcement officers who responded to the scene in June, but not from the officer who fired. It does not show the entirety of the police response, nor does it clearly show Kohen, his mother and the other woman driving the vehicle..
The body-cam footage begins from the perspective of one of the officers, whose identity is unknown. It shows him rushing toward the gray sedan.
The footage then shows the vehicle move in reverse and hit a parked S.U.V. as officers approach, yelling at the driver to stop. When the sedan moves forward, at least one officer appears to be in front of it on the passenger’s side; a second officer also stands near the vehicle, closer to the driver’s side. Both have their guns drawn. As the vehicle approaches them, at least one of the officers opens fire. The officer appears to fire three more times while standing to the side of the vehicle.
Grainy surveillance footage included in the compilation published by Darkhorse Press also captures the moments from more of a bird’s-eye view. In that footage, two women — one holding a child — are seen running toward a vehicle and reversing in it as law enforcement officers chase them.
More video of the incident has yet to be seen by the public. Kohen’s family is scheduled to view it Thursday morning. Veronica Roberson, the toddler’s grandmother, said state officials had informed the family that the footage included surveillance videos from Walmart, along with five body-worn cameras.
The Senatobia Police Department on Wednesday, July 15, 2026.  Credit: Mukta Joshi/Mississippi Today
Hunter Foster, an officer with the Senatobia Police Department, was placed on leave while state authorities investigated his actions at the Walmart. Although he has not been named as the one who opened fire, Officer Foster is the only officer among those present that day who was placed on leave.
The shooting death touched off weeks of protests and calls for transparency in Senatobia, a city of roughly 8,400 located roughly 40 miles south of Memphis. Activists and Kohen’s family had been calling on the authorities to release police body-camera or dashcam footage.
Kohen’s mother, Vellesiya Wiley, said she had been holding her son in her arms in the front passenger seat when the driver, Latoya Ferrell, tried to back out of a space and then drive forward. Ms. Ferrell was seriously injured. 
In the hours after the shooting, the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation issued a statement saying the police had fired at a vehicle when it drove toward an officer, “almost striking” one.
Attorney General Lynn Fitch, a Republican who is running for governor next year, has been Mississippi’s top prosecutor since 2020 and a vocal supporter of law enforcement, even as the Legislature has delegated her office the duty of reviewing investigations of police shootings and deciding whether to seek criminal charges. In late September, Fitch said she had cleared police in 82 of 86 officer-involved shootings during her time in office.
In a 2024 statement, she said, “The good men and women who wear the uniform to keep us safe and maintain law and order in our communities need to know that their Attorney General will always have their back. We are their partners and whether we call it Back the Blue or Back the Badge or Blue Lives Matter, it all comes down to this: Supporting law enforcement is the right thing to do.”
Jerry Mitchell and Julie Lee of Mississippi Today and Aric Toler and  Alexander Cardia of The New York Times contributed reporting.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Miller-Meeks, Bohannan spar on Iran war, rising costs in 1st District debate
text:
Democrat Christina Bohannan is having a rematch against U.S. Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks for Iowa's 1st Congressional District seat in the Nov. 5, 2024 election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Republican Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Democrat Christina Bohannan emphasized their willingness to break from party lines during the 1st Congressional District debate Tuesday — while also trading barbs on issues like rising costs and immigration.
The two candidates met for a debate hosted by KWQC and KCRG at St. Ambrose University in Davenport, the only live debate scheduled in the highly competitive U.S. House district ahead of Election Day. The seat is held by Miller-Meeks, who has served in the House since 2021 — a seat she has defended against Bohannan, a University of Iowa law professor who she defeated in the last two general elections.
Polls and political forecasters believe this year may be different — the Cook Political Report rates the race as “leans Democrat,” signaling a potential shift in the upcoming election. There has also been signals that Republicans may be viewing the district differently in the final weeks before the election, as the Congressional Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, withdrew funding from the race earlier in October.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Though Miller-Meeks has won in recent election cycles, the district which includes Iowa City, Davenport and Burlington has regularly seen close election results. The Republican won her 2024 election by a margin of just under 800 votes following a recount, and won her first election to the House in 2020 by a margin of six votes. In the debate, Miller-Meeks argued she was “an independent thinker, a doctor, and veteran who has put Iowans first” through her service and in Congress — and said her voting record reflects this.
As Iowans struggle with high costs of living and surging fuel prices, Miller-Meeks said she supports pausing U.S. exports of diesel as well as pausing the gas tax. She also said her vote in favor of the 2025 “One, Big Beautiful Bill” helped Iowans by lowering taxes on tips, overtime and Social Security.
“And I brought the largest steel mill in America’s history to Lee County,” Miller-Meeks said, referencing the $15 billion steel mill by Mesabi Metallics planned in southeast Iowa announced by President Donald Trump in late September. “Good paying jobs. It’s not just where prices are, it’s also having the ability to have a job and to be able to afford to pay to have a standard of living. So bringing that steel mill here, with 1,700 permanent jobs at $49 an hour, will be transformational. I’m going to continue to work. It’s not enough, we’ve got more to do. But, you know, we haven’t worked fast enough to overturn the disastrous policies and the high inflation of the last administration, but we’re gonna keep working to do just that.”
Bohannan said Miller-Meeks’ comment shows “she’s still blaming (other) people for her policy decisions.” The Democrat argued her opponent has supported measures that will raise costs for Iowa families during her time in Washington, D.C., pointing to her vote for the OBBB Act — which included cuts to Medicaid — as well as previous votes against measures to restrict Trump’s tariff policies and on war resolutions regarding the U.S. war with Iran.
“She has voted eight times for the tariffs that are driving up costs across the board, she voted five times for the Iran war that’s driving up the cost of fuel and fertilizer — including twice casting the deciding vote to prolong that war,” Bohannan said. “If she had chosen to vote a different way, either one of those times, that war would have ended months ago.”
Bohannan emphasized that the tax component on tips and overtime included in the 2025 Republican tax and spending act is set to expire in two years, but said, “the massive tax breaks that she gave to billionaires and data centers, those don’t have an expiration date.”
“Those have been her priorities while in Congress,” Bohannan said. “So it’s ironic for her to talk about trying to lower costs now. There is a lot that we can do to lower costs — end those tariffs, end the war, let Medicare negotiate for lower drug prices — but we’re not gonna do it as long as the people who are in office, who caused this problem, are still there.”
Miller-Meeks broke party lines in September to vote in favor of the Iran War Powers Resolution, a measure to require congressional approval for Trump to continue the war in Iran. She was joined by six other Republicans — including U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, representing Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, who also faces a challenging reelection race. The previous two times the U.S. House voted on Iran war powers resolutions, Miller-Meeks opposed the measure.
In the debate, Miller-Meeks said she had opposed war resolutions prior to September because of the time limit put in place by the 1973 War Powers Act — the measure passed in the aftermath of Vietnam to require congressional approval for continued military operations after 90 days.
“Presidents have 90 days. I gave the president that,” Miller-Meeks said. “We had a ceasefire. When the ceasefire collapsed, the Iranian regime had (been) decapitated, and their nuclear program was severely hampered, I voted to end the Iran war. … As a veteran, I can tell you that needs to be done. It’s heart wrenching to take care of veterans who have been injured in war or to attend the funerals. The president needs to bring a plan to us, and we need to bring diesel prices and gas prices down.”
Miller-Meeks also pointed to her support for Ukraine as it faces a war against Russia — though she criticized the administrations of former Democratic presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden for the conflicts, saying Russia’s invasions into Ukrainian territory “seems to happen whenever there is a Democrat president.”
“We funded, and I voted to fund, and to assist Ukraine, as they bought weapons from the United States,” Miller-Meeks said. “… But the Biden administration … They didn’t conduct a war. Rather, they funded a war and asked us to help fund a war without any evidence of how they were gonna conduct that. They didn’t allow Ukraine to fire missiles into Russia. And so, this is a war that I think could have ended much earlier with much less loss of life, much less refugee status, and it’s unfortunate that there was not a plan by the Biden administration for how to conduct this and what was expected of the Ukrainians to be able to protect themselves and their sovereignty.”
Bohannan said she also supported Ukraine — but said blaming Democrats, who are out of power, does not address the current U.S. lack of support for the country, or explain actions like Trump’s move to allow import of Russian diesel.
“Look, we should be supporting Ukraine in this war,” Bohannan said. “This was unprovoked aggression by Russia, and … I agree, President Biden did not do enough to end this war earlier. But by the same token, President Trump is not doing enough. And, in fact, now, he is just completely surrendered to Vladimir Putin on these economic sanctions. That makes America look desperate and weak throughout the world, and it is not going to do anything to bring down fuel prices — because we all know that the problem with fuel prices is the war in Iran, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.”
Bohannan also highlighted her willingness to oppose the Biden administration as proof that she would not be beholden to the Democratic Party if elected. Bohannan said she believed “President Biden was way too slow to secure the border,” and brought up her decision to call for Biden to withdraw from the 2024 presidential election after his “disastrous debate,” she said.
“We are way too divided among parties, and I think we need an independent voice who will stand up to her own party, not be a rubber stamp, and who will work across the aisle,” Bohannan said.
But Miller-Meeks argued her opponent was “extreme” and did not support law enforcement or immigration enforcement policies — a claim Bohannan denied. The Republican also said her track record in Congress shows she will work across the aisle to advance Iowans’ interests.
“When I break with my party, I have voted to cap insulin at $35. I voted to end the Iran war. I voted to protect women,” Miller-Meeks said. “Mainstream policies. When you vote and break with your party, you don’t vote with the Republicans … you vote with the far-left extreme. I’m mainstream, you’re extreme.”
Both candidates agreed that U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley was an inspirational figure for them in Iowa politics, and both affirmed they will accept the results of the Nov. 3 election.
The major-party candidates in three of Iowa’s four congressional districts have participated in at least one televised debate. The 2nd District candidates have debated twice, including an “Iowa Press” debate Oct. 8.  The 4th District candidates debated Oct. 14. The 3rd District candidates are scheduled to debate Oct. 27.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘I wanted him to be the guy’: Trump stumps for Whatley, GOP slate as voting in NC gets underway
text:
GREENVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 20: North Carolina U.S. Senate candidate, former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley (R) shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump after speaking during an election rally at Pitt-Greenville Airport on October 20, 2026 in Greenville, North Carolina. President Trump is rallying support for local Republican candidates including North Carolina U.S. Senate candidate, former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley. (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)GREENVILLE, N.C. — Terry Holyfield, a retired factory worker from Burlington, once drove over four hours to see President Donald Trump speak. She said she’s seen him at least 10 times, and would drive even further to see him if she could. 
On Tuesday, she drove over two hours to see him in Greenville, and said she’s pleased with the Trump administration’s handling of immigration and border security. 
Like many other North Carolinians, she’s not happy with the cost of living as food and fuel costs continue to rise. But when voters cast their ballots on Nov. 3, Holyfield said she still plans to vote for Republicans. 
“Things cost too much, but I’m voting straight red down the ticket to lower them,” she said. 
In a recent poll from Elon University, economic issues and the cost of living were the top issues voters across the board identified as most important on their minds as they head to the polls on Nov. 3. 
But this rally wasn’t about winning over undecided voters. It was about making sure reliable GOP voters like Holyfield actually turn out in this election. 
To do that, GOP candidates focused on the issues that have motivated their base for years — crime, COVID, immigration, transgender people and election security – as well as Trump’s repeated promise of a $5000 check for every adult if Republicans win. 
In front of a crowd of around 1,000 GOP loyalists, Trump joined Republican candidates at the Pitt-Greenville Airport for a rally to encourage supporters to support the Republican slate Nov. 3. 
Trump said his administration plans to give every American $5,000 if Republicans take the U.S. House and Senate, a claim he’s made at other rallies across the country despite skepticism, even from his supporters.  
“If the Democrats win, you will have a 1929-style economic depression without question,” he said. “If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket, an economic success for our country like we have never ever seen before.”
“If we lose, you get nothing,” Trump added.
Outside experts have said the proposal would cost the country $1.2 trillion on top of the current $40 trillion federal debt. But the president insisted his tariffs — which are largely paid for by American consumers – would pay for it, although experts say tariff revenue would fall far short.
Trump also touted the economy, but downplayed high fuel costs in his speech amid a highly unpopular war. 
“This is a very small price to pay for keeping a nuclear weapon away from the world’s number-one state sponsor,” he said. 
During the rally, Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley repeated similar points he’s made on the campaign trail. He said he will work with President Trump, while advocating for tax cuts and lower healthcare costs. 
But Whatley did not mention the cost of living, other than to blame opponent Roy Cooper’s record as governor during the COVID-19 pandemic for contributing to the state’s affordability crisis. 
“Roy Cooper has stood in your way by raising costs,” he said. 
Whatley currently trails Cooper by 14 percentage points according to a WRAL/WSOC poll, a margin that’s changed little since the primary election in March. 
Democrats see opening in NC as Whatley campaign pauses ads

Whatley’s campaign’s failure to move the polls led two GOP PACs to pull their ad buys in NC at the beginning of October. However, CNN reported Tuesday that a Trump-associated PAC, Securing American Greatness, contributed $2.2 million to Whatley’s cause in the past week. 
Ahead of the rally, Sen. Kandie Smith, D-Pitt, held a press conference and pushed back on Whatley’s views on affordability. 
“[Whatley] has repeatedly said we need to ‘stay the course’ in Iran…He even downplayed record gas prices and said ‘we’re not getting gouged’ at the pump,” she said. “I don’t know who believes that.”
Whatley and Trump also warned that a vote for Democrats would lead to a socialist or communist takeover of American government. That argument resonated with Jessie Gotti, who drove about 75 miles from Jacksonville, North Carolina, to attend his first Trump rally.
Gotti, who works for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, said his vote is shaped by his concerns about the direction of the Democratic Party.
“I’m concerned that the DSA movement is progressing so steadily,” he said, referring to Democratic Socialists of America. He said he was worried about the movement’s agenda and the policies its supporters want to advance.
Gotti said those concerns make it important for people to pay attention to elections and participate in the political process.
“If we don’t stand up now, the landscape will be completely different,” he said. “But what are we leaving if we do nothing?”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Alaska voters’ privacy could be at risk from state’s handling of voter rolls, judge says
text:
A banner showing President Donald Trump hangs on the Department of Justice on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)An Alaska Superior Court judge said last week that the Alaska Division of Elections may have violated the Alaska Constitution’s right to privacy when it handed an uncensored version of the state’s voter list to the U.S. Department of Justice last year.
On Friday, Judge Adolf Zeman turned down the division’s request to dismiss a lawsuit filed this spring by the League of Women Voters, Alaska Black Caucus and the Alaska chapter of the American Civil Liberties Union.
The three groups are arguing that the Division of Elections and Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom violated the state constitution when they provided an unredacted state voter list — including driver’s license numbers, home addresses and partial Social Security Numbers — at the request of the U.S. Department of Justice.
As part of the handover, the division’s director, Carol Beecher, signed a memo stating that the division will remove voters from the list within 45 days if the DOJ determined they were ineligible to vote. The memo also says the DOJ may share the data with a private contractor and store it out of DOJ control.
Writing last week, Zeman said that the Alaska Division of Elections failed to negotiate restrictions on the DOJ’s influence over Alaska’s voter list.
“Instead, the state has given DOJ carte blanche to submit whenever it pleases, a list of whosoever names it decides, for whatever reason DOJ determines, for any number of eligible voters,” he wrote.
He said that while the state may point to a clause in the memo that says any removal request must be legal, “the court remains unconvinced that such a clause on its own can shield this matter from judicial consideration.”
The plaintiffs had argued that the Department of Justice is creating an unauthorized national voter database and intends to conduct criminal and immigration investigations not otherwise permitted by law. 
The state disputed that claim, and attorneys representing the state argued in September that the three plaintiffs lacked the standing to bring a case, that the case wasn’t ripe because the DOJ hasn’t yet requested the removal of any Alaska voters and that sharing the information would not cause “embarrassment, anxiety, humiliation, harassment, or economic and physical reprisals” among Alaskans.
Zeman wrote that the state may claim that plaintiffs are wrong about the potential abuse of Alaskans’ data, “however, on a motion to dismiss, this court is obligated to accept plaintiffs’ claims as true. Therefore, the court finds that the privacy claims survive dismissal.”
He went on to conclude that “given the fundamental nature of the rights at stake, the seriousness of the allegations and the existence of similar litigation in other states, this court shall allow this case to proceed to discovery and fact-finding that will determine whether plaintiffs’ claims have merit.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland to open new waterfront park overlooking the Bay Bridge
text:
A view Tuesday of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge from the soon-to-open Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Maryland will start accepting online reservations Nov. 6 for a new park overlooking the Chesapeake Bay, less than 10 miles from downtown Annapolis and a stone’s throw from Sandy Point State Park.
The sprawling, 293-acre property, known as Holly Beach Farm, boasts wooded hiking trails, small bayfront beaches, farm fields and a 9-acre freshwater pond — along with scenic views of cars and trucks humming along the Chesapeake Bay Bridge, and sailboats and ships passing beneath it.
For now, the state plans to allow about 20 individuals per day to access the site by reservation only, for activities including hiking and birding, said Paul Peditto​, an assistant secretary at the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.
The agency will manage Holly Beach as a natural resources management area, a wilder alternative to state parks, which tend to feature more amenities, larger parking areas and more manicured trails.
From left, Maryland Secretary of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz, Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman and DNR Assistant Secretary Paul Peditto at an event showcasing the new Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
But the property, donated to the state by the Chesapeake Bay Foundation in 2023, still needs lots of work. Agency officials say they’ve set aside $3 million for repairs and enhancements.
That to-do list includes a lengthened 450-foot fishing pier, with a new 6-foot berth to accommodate larger vessels. The vision, officials say, is to one day attract ferries hosting Annapolis tourists, Sandy Point visitors or groups of local schoolchildren on field trips. But the department is also looking to open the property to a broader swath of boaters, said Maryland Secretary of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz.
“We’re really looking forward to welcoming boaters to come over and anchor and enjoy these little bits of magic right outside of downtown Annapolis,” Kurtz said.
Holly Beach is the sixth new public land the Maryland Park Service has opened or dedicated this year, including Savage Highlands State Park in Garrett County and Freedman’s State Park in Montgomery County.
“This is the sixth and final celebration that the Maryland Park Service will host this year. That is truly a phenomenal accomplishment, and I could not be prouder of my team,” said Maryland Park Service Director Angela Crenshaw.
The idea of turning Holly Beach Farm into a park was met with trepidation from the neighbors who live along the single-lane winding road leading to the new natural resources management area, said Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman (D). In 2021, Pittman publicly backed a bid by the National Park Trust to obtain the land and open it to public use.
“There was a lot of concern that what the trust was talking about doing, or what the National Park Service might do, would be really turning it into what you think of as a national park, with a highway with a lot of cars coming in and out, and a lot of pavement — and destroy the natural area,” Pittman said.
Maryland officials hope that a lower-key natural resources management area — with limited public access to start — will strike the right balance.
Future plans include the addition of five hunting blinds along the water’s edge, and completion of a host of projects to stabilize several of the park’s eroding shorelines, which have been battered by the windswept waters of the Chesapeake Bay.
The new Holly Beach Farms Natural Resources Management Area includes a nine-acre freshwater pond close to the Chesapeake Bay, pictured on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A nine-person construction crew at the Maryland Department of Natural Resources has been restoring a farmhouse at Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area, pictured on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A view from the soon-to-open Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area in Anne Arundel County on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A sailboat sweeps past the new Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area during a showcase event for the new park on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)The Maryland Department of Natural Resources plans to refurbish and lengthen an existing pier at the new Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area, pictured on Oct. 20, 2026. The agency also plans to deepen its berth to six-feet, allowing larger vessels such as ferries to moor at the new park. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A view of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge from the soon-to-open Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland Secretary of Natural Resources Josh Kurtz speaks during an opening event for Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland Park Service Director Angela Crenshaw speaks during an opening event for Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Maryland Department of Natural Resources capital planning director Eric Luedtke speaks during an opening event for Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)Anne Arundel County Executive Steuart Pittman (D) speaks during an opening event for Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A view of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge from the soon-to-open Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A sculpture sits on a farmhouse lawn at the Holly Beach Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)A view of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge from the soon-to-open Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area on Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/ Maryland Matters)
Meanwhile, a small in-house construction crew has already been hard at work restoring a waterfront farmhouse on the property that faces that 4.3-mile bridge connecting Annapolis and Kent Island. The hope is to transform the two-story home, which fell into disrepair after it was vacated in 2001, into a rentable meeting space for local organizations.
But when the crew first entered the home, they weren’t sure it was salvageable, said Maynard Woodworth, an engineer and architect who leads the agency’s construction team. Abandoned to the elements, the home had become infested by racoons, and it featured sodden carpets, termite-infested wood, rotting floorboards and a weather-beaten and partially collapsing exterior.
“It took a while, but we feel great that we fixed it up and saved it,” Woodworth said.
Still, the home needs new siding, along with electrical, HVAC and plumbing work. It also needs fresh drywall, painting and other interior improvements. Thus far, the state has spent about $150,000 restoring the house.
When it came to deciding whether to demolish or refurbish the dilapidated house, it was a “toss-up” for DNR officials, Peditto said during a showcase event Tuesday at Holly Beach Farm. But the agency ultimately decided to move forward with the renovation effort, given that erecting an entirely new structure would be more costly.
The Department of Natural Resources plans to refurbish and lengthen an existing pier at the nes Holly Beach Farm Natural Resources Management Area, and deepen its berth to 6 feet, allowing larger vessels such as ferries to moor at the new park. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
Holly Beach Farm traces its origins back to 1907, when Sylvester W. Labrot Sr., a businessman from Louisiana began acquiring tracts of land along the Chesapeake in Anne Arundel County.
Initially, the property operated as a dairy farm, but by 1930, it was regarded as one of the largest thoroughbred horse breeding and training operations in the United States, complete with housing for nearly 100 horses and a private one-mile training track.
Upon his death in 1935, Labrot passed the property down to his son William Henderson Labrot, who would negotiate the sale of 725 nearby acres of his family’s land to the state, which became Sandy Point State Park.
And in 2001, Leonie Labrot Gately sold the 326-acre heart of the family’s estate to the Conservation Fund. It would be transferred to the Chesapeake Bay Foundation the next year.
Hilary Harp Falk, who became president and CEO of the foundation in 2022, arrived with “fresh eyes,” she said Tuesday. After a year of careful study, she and the foundation’s board of trustees decided to begin a search for a new steward for the property.
“It was time to allow the property to become something more than CBF had been able to do,” Harp Falk said.
The foundation, which maintains a headquarters in nearby Bay Ridge, had mainly been using the property to host school groups for outdoor education programming. But the foundation recognized the property had more potential for expanded public access, Harp Falk said.
“That is not something that the Chesapeake Bay Foundation has a lot of experience doing. So we’re really excited about that potential,” she said. “Also, it needs a lot of restoration. There are invasive species out here. There is coastal erosion. Those things need attention, and the Maryland Department of Natural Resources is really best-positioned to take those challenges on.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Attorney general’s office failed to track, monitor millions in outside legal contracts
text:
Maryland Attorney General Anthony G. Brown (D) told auditors his agency is working to implement better systems for tracking and monitoring contracts for outside law firms, but that effort may not be completed before the end of 2027. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)State auditors are calling for tighter controls and monitoring of outside law firms hired by state agencies, after finding a lack of procedures in the attorney general’s office make it difficult to track millions paid to nearly 100 firms.
The 26-page review of the Office of the Attorney General by the Office of Legislative Audits also found the agency paid nearly $2 million for a case management system that has yet to be fully implemented as required by the now-expired contract.
“OAG did not have adequate procedures and controls for the procurement and use of outside counsel by State agencies, resulting in the inability to properly budget, track, and monitor related payments,” auditors noted in their report.
In a letter to auditors, Attorney General Anthony Brown agreed with the findings and said his office was committed to “corrective actions.” But in more detailed responses to the report, the agency noted hurdles remain an impediment to resolving the findings.
The audit, released Tuesday, reviewed contracts with outside firms between June 2022 and May 2026. Auditors identified 120 contracts awarded to 97 outside law firms totaling nearly $63 million, an amount equal to roughly 70% of the $86 million fiscal 2025 budget for the attorney general’s office.
Nearly $40 million in fees to outside legal counsel was paid by five state agencies, according to a recent audit, that found the attorney general’s office failed at tracking and monitoring those expenses. (Source: Office of Legislative Audits)
The costs of those contracts run in the tens of millions of dollars. Auditors said $63 million was paid to 54 of the 97 outside firms hired. Five agencies combined for more than 60% of the legal fees auditors tracked.
Auditors, in the report, cautioned that the full extent of legal payments is unknown.
Some agencies paid for services provided to a different government entity. Other payments were not recorded in the state’s accounting system. Those payments are not reflected in some of the auditor’s calculations.
“As a result of these conditions, we could not determine the total fees paid to outside counsel for the services used by each agency or identify the total claims/settlements paid,” auditors note in the report.
Brown’s office, in a detailed response, said efforts to improve management and tracking of outside law firms are “ongoing.” Part of that effort includes the creation of “repository of all” outside contracts. That effort, started roughly three years ago, is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.
But the office said it lacks “the necessary authority or tools to oversee, track, or monitor the payment processing of invoices for outside counsel services by our client agencies.” It said it would issue guidance to state agencies on tracking and monitoring contracts and recording payments by the end of next year.
In another finding, auditors noted that the agency spent $1.8 million for a case management system that was not fully implemented before the contract expired in June 2025.
Auditors faulted the agency for “failing to obtain critical information required by the contract (such as weekly status reports) to monitor the vendor’s progress.”
The report noted that the attorney general’s office did not disclose “ongoing vendor issues” to the Board of Public Works when it sought approval of a renewal option. The board approved the extension at a cost of $475,000. Auditors said the amount should have been withheld until the system was fully implemented.
“This is significant because as of April 2026, approximately one year after the contract ended (and 7 years after the original estimated implementation date), the system has not been implemented in one division and was only partially implemented in another,” auditors wrote.
The finding was noted in an earlier audit in which the agency vowed to resolve the issues by June 2023.

name: California
title: ‘Borders on the absurd.’ California fights Trump lawsuit to set aside 20,000 ballots
text:
California’s top attorney called on a federal judge to block the Trump administration’s efforts to force the state to set aside up to 20,000 ballots that prosecutors claim could have been mailed to noncitizens.
In a court filing Tuesday in federal court in Los Angeles, Attorney General Rob Bonta said the lawsuit the Trump administration filed last week “borders on the absurd.” 
“At best, this litigation is a reckless political stunt,” Bonta’s filing reads. “At worst, it threatens to disenfranchise thousands of Californians this election.”
Bonta’s filing came a day after federal prosecutors announced they’d charged 28 California green card holders for allegedly voting or registering to vote in violation of laws prohibiting noncitizens from participating in elections. In his filing, Bonta noted the arrests represent just .0001 percent of the 23 million registered voters in California.
In announcing those charges Monday, federal authorities said they also asked a judge to issue a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction that would force the state to segregate the 20,000 ballots. Bonta is urging the court not to issue the order.The case has profound implications across the country with the midterm elections two weeks away. The U.S. Constitution gives states primary authority to independently conduct their elections. The Trump administration is testing whether it has the legal right to pause a state’s vote counts based on a list of possible noncitizen voters that federal officials acknowledge may be inaccurate.
In his filing Tuesday, Bonta said the Trump administration has lost 26 different lawsuits as it sought unredacted voter rolls from states in its hunt for evidence to support President Donald Trump’s unfounded voter fraud claims.
“The government has lobbed allegations of widespread voter fraud at the states, only for those allegations to crumble under scrutiny,” Bonta wrote. “As one court recently noted, the federal government’s citizenship records are ‘known to be unreliable.’”
The Department of Homeland Security recently claimed that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. DHS sent the state the names of only 185 voters. Nevada officials confirmed they were all U.S. citizens. Similarly, in Pennsylvania, DHS alleged the state had more than 14,000 noncitizen voters on its rolls, but prosecutors have only charged nine with illegally voting. 
Acting Deputy U.S. Attorney General Trent McCotter said Monday that the 20,000 possible noncitizen voters in California were enough “to fill a small stadium,” but he acknowledged that number could be an overcount. 
“There may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens,” McCotter said. “We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us.”
McCotter said its list of possible noncitizens was based on public voter rolls the federal government obtained from California, which it then cross-referenced with “other government databases, other public information.”McCotter said all 28 defendants charged Monday are on the list of 20,000 names, a number that he said was “just the floor” and likely to grow.
Officials skeptical of federal methodology
State officials and independent election experts have been skeptical of the Trump team’s methodology after federal authorities notified state officials in July that there could be as many as 190,000 noncitizen voters in California. 
In Bonta’s filing, he noted that the California secretary of state had asked for a detailed accounting of how the federal government came up with that figure, but the Trump administration would not put it in writing. Instead, federal authorities proposed a virtual meeting, which state officials declined. 
“To date, DHS has not provided evidence, documentation, or any other information to the Secretary’s Office in support of its assertions that there ‘may be’ noncitizens registered to vote in California,” Bonta wrote. 
“If they wanted to cooperate, they have our number,” McCotter told reporters Monday. “They know who to contact. … There’s clearly just no motivation on their part.”
Bonta noted in his filing that state officials have been complying with federal grand jury subpoenas seeking information on about 300 people that federal prosecutors are investigating.
On Oct. 13, the U.S. Department of Justice sent a letter to Secretary of State Shirley Weber informing her it had sent a thumb drive to Los Angeles County election officials containing “a list of names the federal government believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a … ballot,” according to Bonta’s filing.“DOJ demanded that Secretary Weber ‘review the list within 48 hours to determine whether any citizens are listed,’” and, for anyone whose citizenship the state couldn’t confirm, to set aside their ballots or stop ballots from being mailed to them.
Weber refused, telling the federal government that voting was well underway, Bonta wrote.
The federal government sued California two days later. 
In its lawsuit filed last week, the justice department said it is “not practicable or feasible” for the federal government to dig deeper into the thousands of names it had flagged as possible noncitizens before the 2026 election concludes, despite wanting California to do that in the middle of an election.
In declarations filed with the court Tuesday, Los Angeles County election officials said they’ve done a preliminary analysis of a sampling of 200 of voters from the federal government’s thumb drive. They said that many of the names on the list appear to be citizens, and that most had not voted and were not sent ballots.
David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research, a nonprofit whose mission is to restore trust in the American election system, told reporters last week he expects California will prevail in the suit.
“I expect the courts are not going to respond favorably to the DOJ acting with such a lack of diligence in this case, and apparently almost seeming to try to set California up,” said Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department attorney. “If they had been honest with California back in July, and had an honest belief that the number of citizens/noncitizens on the voter list were as they claim, they could have been transparent and shared that data. But they didn’t.”
Did immigrants know they committed a crime?
Meanwhile, some of the 28 green card holders who were arrested Monday in the voter fraud sting told reporters that they didn’t know they had done anything illegal; others said they had no idea they had registered to vote. 
Prosecutors alleged that 22 suspects voted in at least one election including as recently as the June primary; five only registered to vote and one submitted a provisional ballot in 2020.
Kamlesh Shah, a 68-year-old immigrant from India, told The Sacramento Bee in an interview that he voted in 2024 for Vice President Kamala Harris, but he thought he was allowed to since he had applied for citizenship after living in the country for three decades.
He visited a Sacramento County polling place and handed over his identification. An election worker gave him the OK and a ballot, Shah told the Bee.
“I can hardly walk and talk,” Shah told the Bee Monday at his Sacramento senior living facility. “Now I have to face these charges.”
Ana Domínguez, 60, a native of El Salvador living in Long Beach, said she didn’t remember registering to vote, The Los Angeles Times reported Monday. She’s accused of registering to vote in 2006 and then lying about it 20 years later on her immigration paperwork. 
Election experts say that such stories are common in voter fraud cases.
“We know from past experience that sometimes people register to vote accidentally, as when there is a mistake at the DMV,” Rick Hasen, a UCLA School of Law professor, said Monday in a blog post. “There is only a crime if the government can prove willful violations of federal law.”
Hasen wrote that it was telling how few were charged on Monday, despite Trump and his allies spending years aggressively hunting for evidence of a massive election fraud conspiracy that they have not proved exists.
“If DOJ could prove many more cases, we would have heard about it,” he wrote. “They’ve been on an aggressive hunt nationally for such fraud. It’s not surprising they’ve found little because it is a small problem.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom on Tuesday said on social media that “any credible allegation of voter fraud should be taken seriously and investigated,” but he questioned the timing.“If the feds were serious about this, they would have done this long ago — not in the middle of people voting, which inherently and needlessly sows distrust and doubt in our democracy,” he wrote.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC Republicans and Democrats tout their fundraising hauls as proof of ‘momentum’
text:
Flags provide a backdrop for a news conference held on the first floor of the Statehouse in Columbia, South Carolina, on Monday, Jan. 13, 2025. (File photo by Travis Bell/STATEHOUSE CAROLINA/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — With early voting underway in South Carolina, campaigns are boasting their latest fundraising reports as get-out-the-vote efforts continue.
GOP gubernatorial nominee Alan Wilson, the state’s attorney general since 2010, raised $2.5 million from July 1 through Oct. 14, according to the last pre-election filing. It showed he entered the last three weeks of the campaign with nearly $1.7 million cash available to spend.
Wilson’s latest filing shows the best fundraising haul in the pre-election span that includes the third quarter for any statewide candidate in South Carolina ever, outside of campaigns for federal office.
“The momentum behind this campaign is unbelievable,” said Woods Wooten, spokesman for the Wilson campaign. “As early voting gets underway, we are entering the final stretch with historic fundraising, strong grassroots support, and tremendous enthusiasm for Alan Wilson’s plan to make South Carolina more affordable for families.”

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

The candidate is on a statewide bus tour for the two weeks leading up to Election Day. Republicans on the bus will include Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp.
His Democratic opponent, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, posted by far his best fundraising report of the campaign, with more than $867,000 collected. He had about $136,000 cash on hand as of Oct. 14, his filing showed.
While that leaves him far less to spend on his message in a reliably red state, Johnson touts receiving more individual donations than prior Democratic campaigns for governor, suggesting broad support from voters.
“The momentum this campaign has built is unprecedented,” Johnson’s campaign said in a statement to the SC Daily Gazette. The funds “will keep us communicating with voters through Election Day. Our team continues to fuel that fire, and we need every citizen who believes what we know is possible to jump in with us.”
Senate race
In the U.S. Senate race, Democrat Annie Andrews blew past Sen. Darline Graham in fundraising, with third-quarter totals of $9.4 million to $2.4 million, according to Federal Elections Commission filings. But both campaigns are touting their numbers as successful team efforts.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Polls and political analysts show the contest narrowing. The Cook Political Report shifted the race again Tuesday, this time from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”
On Wednesday, President Donald Trump is set to visit the Upstate to rally support for Graham, as he did in Myrtle Beach ahead of the special GOP primary runoff she won Aug. 25 to replace her late brother on the ballot.
Her completely unexpected campaign didn’t begin until late July. Her path to the ballot included a 10-way special GOP primary exactly one month after her brother’s death. Andrews’ fundraising started in May 2025, when she launched her campaign against Sen. Lindsey Graham.
Darline Graham’s team raised $2.4 million for the quarter ending Sept. 30 when including the $1.1 million raised directly for her campaign account and $1.3 million collected by a campaign-tied political action committee. Her campaign headed into October with $610,000 cash.
The campaign’s “bruising primary, runoff, and now a general election” span less than four months, Graham said in a news release. “I am proud of our team’s efforts to raise the funds necessary to win in November during this most challenging time.”
Andrews’ third-quarter haul brought her total for the campaign to $19.7 million. She raced into October with $2.3 million cash available.
“Annie’s strong fundraising numbers show the growing enthusiasm and excitement behind this campaign. … South Carolinians are rallying behind a mom and pediatrician,” the campaign said in a statement. “We’re taking this momentum all the way to Election Day.”
Outside spending from PACs working to help or harm the candidates are also spending significantly in the race, and Graham’s campaign gets a boost there.
According to filings of independent expenditures, PACs have spent $6.9 million to oppose Andrews and $3.4 million to oppose Graham. PACs reported spending $8.4 million to support Graham and $1.8 million to support Andrews.
Big fundraising totals don’t always translate to electoral results.
In 2020, Democrat Jaime Harrison raised $57 million in the third quarter as polls showed he could defeat Lindsey Graham. But he ultimately lost by 10 percentage points. His total raised for the campaign was $132 million, compared to Graham’s $109 million, which at the time was the nation’s most expensive U.S. Senate race.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis: Tough fentanyl laws have led to 60% dip in drug deaths in three years
text:
Florida Department of Law Enforcement photo taken during 2025. (Photo via FDLE X account)More than 600 pounds of fentanyl, 800 pounds of cocaine, and nearly 1,000 firearms have been seized and nearly 3,000 drug arrests made in Florida since 2023, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Tuesday during an Orlando press conference.
DeSantis — appearing along with Sara Carter, director of the Office of National Drug Policy, and Larry Keefe, director of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement — attributed those accomplishments to a 2023 law establishing the State Assistance for Fentanyl Eradication (SAFE) grant program.
DeSantis said the law, and his administration’s vigilant efforts on border control, have helped put Florida in the national forefront in the fight against fentanyl.
“I think we’ve sent the the appropriate deterrence message, that you shouldn’t be doing this in the United States but, if you are going to do it, you do not want to do it in the state of Florida. You will regret having done that, and we will make sure that we hold you accountable,” the governor said.
The Legislature appropriated  more than $22.5 million for the SAFE grant program in state fiscal year 2026-27 budget, which runs from July 1 through June 30, 2027. All law enforcement agencies in the state can apply for the grants and, according to the FDLE homepage, grants are still available for the current year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.This grants can be used by law enforcement for:

Overtime
Travel
Investigative supplies
Approved equipment
Contractual services
Approved training

Money’s also available for “other costs associated with cases focusing on fentanyl eradication.”
The governor credited First Lady Casey DeSantis for her work “curtailing the demand” through programs in Florida schools that aim to educate children about the “devastating consequences of drug abuse, but particularly when you’re talking about things like fentanyl.”
“Deaths due to fentanyl have declined by almost 60% since this program went into effect in 2023,” the governor said.
He added: “We have reason to believe that it’s falling even more since then.”
DeSantis cited annual reports by Florida Medical Examiners Commission as the source for his information.
The reports track drugs medical examiners detect during autopsies, including benzodiazepines, amphetamines, hallucinogenics, inhalants, and opioids.
It flags opioid-related deaths, those in which opioids are identified as either the cause of death or present in the decedent’s system. The reports track opioid-caused deaths or deaths in which, after examining all evidence, the autopsy, and toxicology results, the medical examiner determines the drug played a causal role.
The 2025 report shows 4,094 opioid-related deaths that year, a 24% decrease over the previous year.
There were 2,494 opioid-caused deaths reported for the year, a 33 % decrease from the previous year.
“We have reason to believe that it’s falling even more since then,” DeSantis said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Hospitals: Federal changes will worsen Minnesota healthcare crisis
text:
Rahul Koranne, the president of the Minnesota Hospital Association, speaks at a Capitol press conference alongside rural hospital executives Tuesday Oct. 20, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)Minnesota hospitals had a record high of over 2 million emergency department visits in 2024. That year, more than a quarter of hospitals lost money on operations.
The Minnesota Hospital Association painted a bleak picture of Minnesota healthcare Tuesday in a new report titled “A Statewide Crisis of Care.” The hospitals are gearing up for what could be a bruising budget year at the Legislature in 2027, as efforts to counteract federal Medicaid cuts will run into the state’s own long-term fiscal challenges.
At a Capitol press conference, executives of rural hospitals spoke of the federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act’s impact on what they described as already weakened hospital financials.
“Instead of ‘HR1,’ I’m gonna call it ‘H1R1’ because it’s gonna be like a pandemic when it hits,” said Rick Ash, the CEO of United Hospital District in Blue Earth, referring to the bill’s other moniker, for House Resolution 1.
The law, passed in July 2025, is the signature domestic initiative of the second Trump administration, cutting both taxes and social services — primarily Medicaid — and increasing spending on immigration enforcement. The report warns that the Medicaid provisions on state provider taxes will remove “the machinery that held hospital finance together.”
State governments tax healthcare providers — such as hospitals — and use the revenue to fund Medicaid, which pays providers. It seems circular, but the federal government matches state spending on Medicaid, so state provider taxes are a way to funnel federal Medicaid dollars into the state. The Minnesota Department of Human Services estimated that reductions on state provider taxes in the OBBBA may leave hospitals with $1 billion less per year, a figure cited in the hospital association’s report.
The OBBBA is also projected to decrease Minnesota’s Medicaid population by 140,000 people due to new work requirements, which will increase uncompensated care costs by hospitals, which are required to accept uninsured patients in their emergency departments.
“We’re still going to care for them. Those costs have to be covered somewhere. And we’re not sure how that’s going to work right now,” Ash said.
Ash said that over half of United Hospital District’s patients are insured through Medicare and Medicaid, public insurance programs on which hospitals have a negative margin, which executives said helps lead to operating losses.
Rachelle Schultz, the CEO of Winona Health and a board member of the hospital association, said that Medicare and Medicaid “reimburse less than the cost of care.”
“The result is a hospital in distress,” Schultz said.
Private insurers pay hospitals significantly more compared to Medicare and Medicaid because rates are set in contracts negotiated between insurers and providers, instead of through government formulas. Commercial hospitals prices have gone up as hospitals have consolidated and grown, which many health economists say is a key driver of America’s lack of healthcare affordability.
Hospitals say those high prices pay for their high expenses, and that they are not to blame. At the press conference, Rahul Koranne, the president of the hospital association, pointed instead to the insurance and pharmaceutical industries for rising healthcare costs, previewing the lobbying fights between the three industries in the next legislative session.
“The money is being taken away by for-profit big pharma companies, large for-profit insurers,” Koranne said. “Follow the money.”
Koranne advocated for protecting 340B, an obscure drug discount program that lets hospitals that treat low-income patients buy drugs at a discount and keep the savings. A bipartisan bill strengthening and extending 340B failed to pass in the 2026 Legislature amid an expensive lobbying battle between hospitals and drug companies.
