name: Nebraska Examiner
title: 18 changes suggested for state funding, local property taxes for K-12 schools
text:
Former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, center, speaks at a meeting of Nebraska's School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. At left is Tom Briese, a former state treasurer and former state senator from Albion. At right is Grant Latimer, a policy adviser to Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Among recommendations to increase state funding for Nebraska’s 244 school districts was one adopted Tuesday to increase per-student aid by at least 4% annually.
A draft of the 16-page report from Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission offers 18 recommendations, most of which would tweak the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act, known as TEEOSA. The formula distributes state aid to school districts statewide. This includes the annual bump of at least 4% in foundation aid per student, from $1,500 to $1,560 for the 2027-28 school year.
Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission meets on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In addition to the recommendations, a portion of Tuesday’s discussion featured a guideline to policymakers that state support for K-12 schools be maintained at 51% alongside local property taxes.
“I applaud the work of the commission and what’s being presented here, but we have to be much more ambitious in what we propose here somewhere,” said Commissioner Tom Briese, Nebraska’s former state treasurer (2023-25) and a former state senator from Albion (2017-23).
The recommendations head to the 49-member Legislature. Lawmakers will have final say on whether to adopt any of the suggestions.
‘Not in the cards’
Briese and others suggested that the 51% state contribution was the bare minimum. In Briese’s view, that number should be “substantially higher,” as high as the state taking on 100% of K-12 operational expenses to offset the largest source of local property taxes.
“That’s not in the cards at this date, but I’m pretty confident there’s several folks in here that’d like to see something far above 51%,” Briese said.
Associate Superintendent Liz Standish of Lincoln Public Schools speaks at a meeting of Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Dave Murman of Glenvil, chair of the Legislature’s Education Committee, said he, too, was thankful for but not satisfied with the recommendations. He is one of three non-voting lawmakers serving on the commission.
Associate Superintendent Liz Standish of Lincoln Public Schools said the commission had not discussed the state-local mix in a year. She said she felt uncomfortable stating in the report that the number should be increased until the commission deliberated further.
What’s the right state-local mix?
Standish said “huge progress has been made” with state funding support, which districts appreciate. But she encouraged commissioners to utilize new data that Nebraska Department of Education staff helped compile and consider the state-local percentage next year.
“All I’m asking for is let’s reflect on where we are with this new data set that we’ve studied over the course of the last year and then, as a commission, have time for deliberative conversation about, OK, what do we think the right mix in Nebraska might be?” Standish said.
The new Nebraska School Financing Review Commission receives a briefing on the various components that make up the state’s mainline school funding formula under the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunity Support Act, better known as TEEOSA. Sept. 22, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, who chaired the Legislature’s Revenue Committee for six years, said it was OK for the commission to say commissioners disagreed.
“I think to turn in a report of this diverse of a group and say we all agree on everything … if I were a senator, I would find that doubtful,” Linehan said. “I’d be calling each of you and saying, ‘Did you agree with this?’”
Reaching consensus
Superintendent John Schwartz of Millard Public Schools, the commission vice chair, suggested that instead of saying “no consensus,” the commission could phrase it more positively. He suggested adding that “additional processing is needed to see if a consensus on what the state funding level target should be.”
Linehan said it was pretty clear the commission is divided and that the lack of consensus isn’t a secret, “nor should it be a secret.” She said money appropriated to public schools should keep going to public schools.
Superintendent John Schwartz of Millard Public Schools, vice chair of the School Financing Review Commission. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The commission ultimately amended the report to state: “While the commission agrees that the state’s contribution should be maintained at a minimum of 51%, there is currently no consensus regarding the appropriate level of state funding beyond that threshold.”
One notable school district, Omaha Public Schools, has opposed increased reliance on state funding, a point of contention in Nebraska’s 2024 special session focused on property taxes. 
Shavonna Holman, who sits on the OPS board and the commission, was not present Tuesday.
Increased aid to school districts
Lawmakers, with Gov. Jim Pillen’s backing, created the commission in 2025 to improve Nebraska state funding for K-12 schools with the goal of also mitigating property tax increases.
Eight of the commission’s proposed adjustments would amend caps for local spending, such as providing three-year averages for enrollment calculations and changing factors for limited English proficiency and poverty considerations.
Other recommendations would tweak factors in TEEOSA, such as calculating poverty, limited English proficiency, technological needs and basic year-over-year funding.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, center, addresses the new School Financing Review Commission during its first meeting. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
If adopted, schools would be allowed to carry forward unused property tax authority under their base cap, such as if they increased spending by less than 3% when the base cap was 3%. But the recommendations call for wiping out built-up taxing authority over the past three years if it came from an override vote and was not used in that same year.
“Collectively, these changes reflect measured changes to the existing revenue cap which better align with the intent of the legislation while preserving local control. These changes also make adjustments to reflect the impact data on the operation of the cap since its inception,” the report states.
If all of the recommendations had been adopted before the 2026-27 school year, the commission estimated nearly $55.5 million more aid to local school districts.
In total, 232 school districts would have seen an increase in aid, up to 43.32%, while 12 would have received a slight decrease, between 0.42% and 14.11%.
TEEOSA would have risen to $1.15 billion in state aid being distributed to school districts.
For 2026-27, TEEOSA consists of calculating a school district’s “resources” — six different sources, including an estimated property tax calculation based on district valuations — minus a district’s “needs” — 18 categories, including poverty, transportation, summer school, limited English proficiency and student growth. 
All school districts receive foundation aid, but districts only receive additional “equalization aid” if their needs are greater than their resources. Only 44 of 244 districts were equalized this year.
Property taxes and the state budget
As of current state budget projections, lawmakers will need to close a $209 million deficit through mid-2027 by May of next year. At the same time, lawmakers must address that hole and the $847 million that would grow if left unchecked by mid-2029.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward speaks at a meeting of Nebraska’s School Financing Review Commission on Oct. 20, 2026, at the Nebraska Department of Education in Lincoln. At left is state Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln. Both are non-voting members of the commission. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln, who will introduce the revenue side of changes that the commission has recommended, said the commission has been focused on determining what would serve schools but also Nebraska taxpayers.
“While we do have an upcoming session that will have budgetary challenges, I think it’s important that we do everything we can not to compromise on what would be the best possible policy that we can create,” Bostar said.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, whose 2025 legislation created the commission, said she plans to introduce the suggested TEEOSA changes if she’s reelected in two weeks. She said cleaning up part of the formula will be a “slam dunk.” The other, more challenging part is the increased foundation aid. 
Hughes said the commission and lawmakers alike don’t want the 51% state support to backslide, and lawmakers will see if they can reach the suggested 4% minimum increase. She said it needs to be a priority in 2027.
“It’s going to be some hard conversations of where do we want to spend,” Hughes said. “All I keep hearing about, in addition to affordability, is the property tax issue.”
How big of a budget hole the Legislature will need to fill will be finalized at an economic forecasting meeting next week. Linehan and Briese are new members of that board, too.
‘Work is just beginning’
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher, who chairs the commission, said he was thankful the commission has twice unanimously approved an annual report, which he joked will prevent some sleepless nights, at least for him.
Nebraska Education Commissioner Brian Maher. Aug. 8, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“It’s also not reflective that our work is done,” Maher said of the 2026 report. “I think, as it’s been stated many times today, in some ways, our work is just beginning.”
The commission’s approval authorized an internal executive committee to polish up the report, up to non-substantive changes, and submit it to the Legislature by the Nov. 1 deadline.
The commission will next meet in the first quarter of 2027. The legislative session begins Jan. 6.

title: Chuck Schumer PAC spends $1.2 million for Scott Colom as pundits say Hyde-Smith lead is waning
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A top Democratic super PAC focused on U.S. Senate races announced Tuesday that it will spend $1.2 million on an ad campaign in Mississippi for Scott Colom.   
The ad, paid for by the Senate Majority PAC aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, marks the group’s first entry into Mississippi’s heated Senate race this cycle. Colom is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, whom the ad calls a “‘do nothing’ senator who voted to kick people off Medicaid while pocketing thousands from special interests.”
The ad buy from Schumer in the election’s homestretch is a notable development since Schumer had earlier been criticized by figures such as U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, Mississippi’s only Democrat in Washington, and some other congressional Democrats for failing to spend more on Colom’s campaign.

“Scott Colom is the senator Mississippi deserves – and he can win,” Schumer said on social media after the ad campaign announcement. 
Thompson had said Democrats were “missing a golden opportunity” by overlooking Mississippi. Those comments came after the official campaign arm of Senate Democrats excluded Mississippi and Colom’s campaign from a $40-million investment in 10 battleground states. 
But multiple Democratic senators have visited Mississippi to campaign with Colom, and Schumer attended a fundraiser for him this summer. Mississippi’s Senate race has since gained national attention and attracted a steady stream of Democratic power players. 
Former Vice President Kamala Harris will campaign with Colom in Columbus on Thursday, and former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg will visit cities along the Gulf Coast on Oct. 27.
The ad highlights Colom’s record as a district attorney and highlights his Christian faith. It also criticizes Hyde-Smith, saying she has failed to pass any meaningful legislation and that she voted for Medicaid cuts.
Candidates for Mississippi’s U.S. Senate seat in the 2026 midterms are, from left, Ty Pinkins, Cindy Hyde-Smith and Scott Colom.
In a statement, Hyde-Smith’s campaign said the late investment from Schumer was evidence Colom was “too liberal” to win, pointing to issues such as immigration and transgender rights. 
“It took Chuck Schumer and his Super PACs thirteen months to run a single ad for Scott Colom,” said Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s Campaign Manager. “Team Cindy is confident that voters will reject this radical agenda at the ballot box on November 3rd.” 
News of the ad campaign broke on the same day the Cook Political Report, a reputable election handicapper, moved the Senate race in Mississippi from solid Republican to likely Republican. Other national pundits and prognosticators say races in deep-red states including Mississippi are becoming more in play as the Trump administration’s approval ratings tank and consumer prices continue to rise.
In a statement, Gerard Henderson, Colom’s campaign manager, said Mississippi is in play “because thousands of Mississippians volunteered and chipped in.”
“We clearly have the momentum and resources to win on November 3rd and prove to the nation that Mississippi Matters,” Henderson said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Wicker urges US-Ukraine deal as Trump strains ties with Zelenskyy and eases up on Russia
authors: By Ben Finley, Matthew Lee and Konstantin Toropin, Associated Press
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S.-Ukraine alliance is careening toward a possible breaking point, with Moscow strengthened by President Donald Trump’s recent rejection of new Russia sanctions and Kyiv undermined by disruptions in satellite support for its drones during the war.
Trump’s relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has always been a moving target, while the Republican president has frequently boasted of his rapport with Russian leader Vladimir Putin. But relations between the U.S. and Ukraine appear to be at a new low, threatening to tip the balance of the war to Russia’s favor and imperil America’s security interests across the globe.
“At this moment in time, things look blacker than they ever had regarding this administration’s policy towards Russia and Ukraine,” said John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under President George W. Bush and now a scholar with the Atlantic Council.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a media conference at the EU summit in Brussels, Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. (AP Photo/Omar Havana)
Trump has been lobbing insults at Zelenskyy for over a week and turning to policies that benefit Putin, while Ukraine’s president has said he feels betrayed and worries for his country’s future. But the American president can still shift on Zelenskyy — especially as he faces bipartisan outrage from lawmakers — which Trump has done before.
Trump famously thrashed Ukraine’s leader in the Oval Office last year, warning him to “make a deal or we are out.” Washington briefly suspended intelligence sharing. But Trump was praising Zelenskyy by that July and said they “actually developed a good relationship.”
“Trump is a mercurial guy,” Herbst said. “He can wake up tomorrow morning, decide he’s done enough on this, and he might start to lean back in the other direction.”
No one has taken responsibility for satellite restrictions on Ukraine
Trump’s recent decisions have baffled experts and infuriated Democrats and some Republicans ahead of pivotal midterm elections in two weeks.
After The Wall Street Journal reported that Putin raised the prospect of a meeting with Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, Trump told reporters Monday that he was open to it but expected it to focus on denuclearization efforts. Asked whether he would be willing to negotiate the end of the war without Zelenskyy, Trump appeared to indicate yes.
“I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” Trump said.
Trump decided Friday to waive sanctions on Russia in a bill that Congress overwhelmingly passed to support Ukraine. Named after late South Carolina Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation targeted the flow of financial resources fueling Russia’s war.
President Donald Trump speaks to the media on the South Lawn of the White House before walking to board Marine One, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)
That rebuke followed Trump’s announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel fuel in a long-shot effort to curb high gas prices. The agreement was pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia without making a difference in global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war against Iran.
Then there were changes in SpaceX’s satellite support to Ukraine’s military, for which no one has taken responsibility.
Starshield is a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service and the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communication. Zelenskyy says his country is facing major speed restrictions, so Ukrainian drones have been unable to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk, a Trump ally, has said Starshield is controlled by the U.S. and any limits are decided by the military and ultimately Trump. But Trump told reporters Friday that he did not order restrictions and doubted that Musk did either.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that Ukraine wants access to Starshield but doesn’t have it. On Monday, he said the Pentagon controls Starshield, and “Ukraine has benefited from it” and wants to expand its use to conduct attacks beyond its territory.
The U.S. military has not responded to questions about its involvement.
And while Russia has launched new attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy said Monday that Kyiv once again received no early warning of the latest attacks from partners such as the U.S.
“Russia killed six people, including a mother and her child, who was just over a year old,” Zelenskyy said on X, adding that this “is how Russia responds to sanctions waivers and reduced pressure.”
Trump and Rubio say Washington hasn’t stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv that has helped Ukraine counter Russian attacks.
Experts say Trump is trying to appease Putin
Dan Fried, a former U.S. ambassador to Poland and assistant secretary of state for European affairs under Bush, said he was mystified by the Trump administration’s shifting positions on Ukraine.
Fried said he first thought Trump’s diesel fuel announcement was aimed at trying to influence the midterms with cheaper fuel prices. But what followed has changed his opinion.
“It all seems designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy and curry favor with Putin,” said Fried, now a scholar with the Atlantic Council.
Fiona Hill, who was Trump’s Russia adviser on the National Security Council during his first term, said Trump could be trying to appease Putin over worries that Russia could do more to support Iran.
Since Trump launched the Iran war in February, Russia has sent drone technology to Tehran and information that could help it strike American warships, aircraft and other assets in the region.
“So maybe this is it — Putin’s just calling in a chit for not devastating Trump through Iran as he could do by helping the Iranians,” said Hill, now a senior fellow with the Brookings Institution.
Trump revealed his worries on social media Sunday, saying, “Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way.”
Criticism grows in Congress
One factor that could nudge Trump toward a detente with Zelenskyy is the cascading criticism from Republicans. They are facing a surge of Democratic momentum in the final stretch of the midterms, which will determine control of Congress.
Pennsylvania Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, a moderate Republican in a competitive race, is calling for congressional hearings into the Starshield disruptions and “immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.”
Democratic Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal said on X that he and retiring Republican North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis organized a call with Zelenskyy and a bipartisan group of lawmakers Monday, including about disruptions to U.S. intelligence sharing.
Zelenskyy, in a video of the briefing posted online, also noted that Ukraine has “almost no Patriot interceptors left from the United States” and claimed “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partners have already paid for.”
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, center, is joined by from left: Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Sen. James Risch, R-Idaho, and Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., as he arrives at the U.S. Capitol for a meeting of bipartisan leaders of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, Tuesday, July 28, 2026, in Washington. Credit: AP Photo/Rod Lamkey
Mississippi Republican Sen. Roger Wicker, who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, urged Trump to take up Zelenskyy’s pledge to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in exchange for U.S. targeting assistance to stop Russia’s missiles. 
“President Trump can lower prices at the pump today by simply agreeing to this deal!” Wicker posted on X.
Regardless of which political party controls Congress next year, lawmakers will likely revolt if Trump enters into a deal with Russia and China over Ukraine, said Fried, the former ambassador to Poland.
“It is clear that we are sitting on considerable leverage over Putin,” he said, “but also clear that we are not using it. It’s a mess.”
Associated Press writers Lynn Berry and Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Judge: Teacher put on blast by state officials should be reprimanded, not suspended
text:
Gainesville High School via Alachua County School Board.An Alachua County teacher should be issued a written letter of reprimand for allowing classmates to label a student the “most likely to become a dictator” during the 2022-2023 school year, an administrative judge ruled.
This recommendation came more than a year after former Education Commissioner Anastasios Kamoutsas vowed to “take every necessary action to ensure this teacher never teaches again.”
Lauren Watts, a world history teacher at Gainesville High School, was cast into the public spotlight last year by Kamoutsas and a mom who told the State Board of Education the teacher had given her son that label in history class years before. 
The administrative judge did not find that Watts intentionally embarrassed the student. She did find that Watts violated the Principles of Professional Conduct for the Education Profession by not making a “reasonable effort to protect the student from conditions harmful to learning and/or to the student’s mental and/or physical health and/or safety.”

A teacher chose to designate a student as the “most likely to become a dictator.” A parent brought this issue to my attention. I immediately took action to investigate the issue. I found probable cause and will take every necessary action to ensure this teacher never teaches again.
— Anastasios Kamoutsas (@StasiKamoutsas) August 21, 2025

Despite Kamoutsas’ vow to keep Watts from teaching ever again, the state ultimately tried for a one-year suspension of her teaching certificate followed by two years of probation, but was unsuccessful. Additionally, the state tried for a $1,000 fine and a written reprimand in her certification file.
Judge Yolanda Green recommended a written reprimand be issued against Watts and that a suspension was not necessary.
Due process
The Florida Education Association said the ruling “strongly upholds Florida educators’ fundamental right to due process.”
Kamoutsas, according to the FEA, “filed an administrative complaint without conducting the statutorily required investigation or giving Ms. Watts her statutorily required opportunity to respond.”
The student’s mother brought the incidents to Kamoutsas’ attention during an August 2025 Board of Education meeting in which board members questioned Alachua County School Board members about unrelated matters.
The mother identified herself as a “proud conservative” during the meeting, calling the district “toxic for conservative families.”
The alleged treatment of her son was “all because of his conservative values and our perspectives,” she said. 
According to Kamoutsas’ formal complaint, Watts “allowed students to disparage” the son, a ninth grader at the time, “when students suggested that [the student] was a Hitler sympathizer.”
Kamoutsas posted to social media last year that he’d complained to the Education Practices Commission one day after the parent brought the matter to his attention. 
The student’s mother did not testify during the formal administrative hearing. 
According to statements in the record of the investigation, a student “testified that at the beginning of the lesson about Hitler, Ms. Watts remarked that every year a student ‘falls in love with Hitler.’” 
According to statements on the record, a student “recalled no one saying [the student] was a Hitler sympathizer in that moment.”
A classmate testified that “another student said [the student in question and one other] looked like they would sympathize with Hitler. [The other student] distinctly recalled that Ms. Watts ‘shut it down’ by telling students to ‘stop because it was inappropriate and we weren’t allowed to say that type of stuff,’” according to the ruling.
“This ruling sends a clear message: Florida’s educators have a right to due process,” Spar said in a news release. “But what happened to Ms. Watts goes beyond due process. The Commissioner made an unsubstantiated claim that Ms. Watts intentionally targeted a student for their political views, rallying the public against her before the facts were established.”
The investigation was launched as State Board of Education grilled Alachua County School Board members during a series of hearings over allegedly politically charged remarks.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Rather than targeting educators online or subjecting them to the court of public opinion, state leaders should focus on strengthening public schools and fostering environments where every student can pursue their dreams,” Spar said. 
The court record references comments from the student in question that Watts “displayed a Black Lives Matter and Pride flags in her classroom, but did not display other flags.”
Superlative
As for the “dictator” superlative, the investigation found the awards were peer-nominated.
“[The student] took a photo of the whiteboard and sent it to his family group chat, stating, ‘so the only negative thing on the board, I was voted for,’” the ruling states, adding that Watts later encouraged the class to nominate other students for the dictator superlative. 
The student felt “embarrassed” and did not say anything privately to Watts, according to the ruling. He did not walk to the front of the class to receive the award. 
“[The student] stated that based on his personal family experience he did not want to be associated with dictators and felt the superlative was a gross misrepresentation of his character,” the ruling states. 
The student identified himself as “a big history aficionado.”
“[The student] was questioned about screenshots of a public YouTube channel that he created and managed called ‘The Student T.M. Manifesto’ (a play on the Communist Manifesto); a photo of him wearing a Soviet-style hat; as well as a social media post in which he stated he wanted to be a ‘Central African dictator.’ [The student] authenticated the screenshots but explained these were jokes or were related to his interest in history, not indications that he wanted to be a dictator,” the ruling states.
The student said he could not say that Watts intended to embarrass him and acknowledged the superlatives activity was voluntary.
Watts has no other negative notices on her record.
Watts testified she would have stopped the activity had she known a student was upset. Afterward, when she learned the student was unhappy, she sent an apology to the student’s mother.
Now president of Polk State College, Kamoutsas’ tenure as education commissioner was marked by him putting local education officials on blast via social media for various perceived grievances, including the appropriateness of library materials in schools.
In the specific post in which Kamoutsas called for the teacher to lose her livelihood, state Rep. Taylor Yarkosky, a Republican from Montverde, replied that Kamoutsas was displaying “excellent work and leadership.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Democrats underscore benefits of red flag laws as attorney general candidates split on their use
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9 mm ammunition at a gun range. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Lawmakers and gun violence prevention advocates defended Michigan’s red flag laws on Tuesday, joining the Democratic nominee for attorney general, Eli Savit, in advocating for additional education and other measures to prevent gun violence in the state.
During the virtual press conference, the speakers detailed the differences between Savit, who testified in favor of red flag laws when they were under consideration by the state Legislature, and Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd, the Republican AG nominee, who has raised due process concerns about the laws, which allow courts to issue an order temporarily barring individuals from buying or possessing guns if they are at risk of harming themselves or others.
The bills passed in 2023 alongside other measures aimed at preventing gun violence. While the red flag laws create a legal structure for courts to issue Extreme Risk Protection Orders, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer also signed off on legislation demanding universal background checks for firearm sales and setting safe storage requirements for guns and ammunition.
In 2025, 514 Extreme Risk Protection Orders to confiscate guns were requested under the state’s red flag law and 407 were issued. State Rep. Kelly Breen (D-Novi), who sponsored one of the bills in the package, said the way these laws are being utilized is largely in line with what the sponsors expected.
“Officers are using this as a tool to resolve crises, and we are even seeing certain law enforcement officers who have said they’d like to see this law repealed initially, they are now using this law to save lives,” Breen said. 
Rep. Kelly Breen (D-Novi), chair of the Michigan House Judiciary Committee, listens during the committee’s March 1, 2023 hearing on gun reform legislation. | Photo by Anna Gustafson
She explained that the people whose weapons are confiscated have a right to a hearing to ask the court to end the order, and officials have not seen anyone charged with filing a false petition.
While Breen noted how red flag laws can be used to prevent suicide by removing a weapon in the midst of a crisis, state Sen. Stephanie Chang (D-Detroit) noted how they can be used to protect victims of domestic violence, as access to a firearm makes it five times more likely that an abusive partner will kill their female victim.
They are also an important tool supplementing personal protection orders, and can be key for ensuring the safety of someone looking to leave their abuser, Chang said. 
However, Extreme Risk Protection Orders are only useful if someone knows about the law and seeks help to file the petition, Chang said.
Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit accepts the Michigan Democratic Party’s nomination for attorney general at the party’s nominating convention in Lansing on Aug. 29, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
If elected as attorney general, Savit said he would defend the state’s red flag laws. He also pledged to work with lawmakers to pass additional measures to prevent violence before it occurs and to ensure everyone in the state knows about them.
On his candidate page on the Michigan Republican Party website, Lloyd states that he would “work with the Governor and the Legislature to repeal Michigan’s red flag laws and replace them with approaches that respect due process while addressing legitimate public safety concerns.”
Savit said he didn’t understand Lloyd’s concerns, noting that Michigan’s law was modeled after legislation that was upheld in other parts of the country.
“We have not seen any real documented abuse of these laws,” Savit said. “But what we have seen is a fair judicial process: guns temporarily removed from the hands of those who might be reasonably expected to cause harm with them, and judges denying them when the evidence simply isn’t there. That’s process.”
Michigan Republican attorney general nominee Doug Lloyd (right) speaks with U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers (left) during the Straits Area Lincoln Day dinner in Mackinaw City, Mich. May 1, 2026 | Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance
In a statement to Michigan Advance, Lloyd spokesman Keith Schipper reiterated Lloyd’s belief that the way Michigan’s red flag laws are written infringes upon Michigander’s constitutional rights.
“As Attorney General, he will work with stakeholders, advocates, and lawmakers from both sides of the aisle to pass a law that protects victims and constitutional rights,” Schipper said. “But let’s be clear: Doug will enforce laws, like this red flag law, that he personally disagrees with, and he has signed warrants as Eaton County Prosecutor to enforce red flag laws. This is in stark contrast to his opponent who legalized hallucinogenic drugs, ended cash bail, and ignored the pleas of human trafficking victims when he decriminalized prostitution.”
Savit previously told Bridge Michigan he did not intend to bring the policies he adopted to the local level to the rest of the state, saying those decisions should be made by local prosecutors.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico lacks clear standards for how state agencies should conduct internal audits, report finds
text:
New Mexico Legislative Finance Committee Program Evaluator Guillermo Caraveo, left, and LFC Deputy Director Rachel Mercer Garcia, right, deliver a report to state lawmakers on Oct. 20, 2026, about New Mexico's lack of clear standards for how state agencies should conduct internal audits. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico currently lacks uniform requirements for how state agencies should conduct internal audits, according to a new state analysis.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A Legislative Finance Committee report, presented to state lawmakers at Tuesday morning hearing in Santa Fe, followed up on a 2022 report that found internal audits’ scope, structure and effectiveness varied greatly across state agencies. Currently, LFC officials told state makers, those issues persist and positions dedicated to oversight have decreased since 2022.
“There’s nothing in statute right now that specifies which agencies should have these types of functions,” LFC Deputy Director Rachel Mercer Garcia said during Tuesday’s hearing
She added that unlike New Mexico, many states across the nation have laws that either establish statewide inspector general offices or specify which types of state agencies should have their own internal auditors. Some mandate that state departments have an internal auditor only when their annual budget is above a certain threshold.
The report came as lawmakers this year have intensely focused on the error rate in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, which is among the highest in the nation.
Some lawmakers on the interim Legislative Finance Committee committee Tuesday said that adopting statewide internal auditing standards would be a step toward remedying high error rates.
“All we’re doing is inviting waste, fraud and abuse if we don’t have internal audits in every department,” Rep. Mark Duncan (R-Farmington) said.
The report recommends the Legislature consider creating requirements for internal audits at state agencies and departments. Specifically, the report recommends requiring that audit reports be released to the public when appropriate and allowing internal auditors to operate independently and objectively. 
Rep. Joy Garratt (D-Albuquerque) recommended the requirements specify the qualifications to become an internal auditor.
Lawmakers discussed how any legislation they craft in the upcoming 2027 session will take place under a new governor. Rep. Nathan Small (D-Las Cruces), who chairs the interim Legislative Finance Committee, said he didn’t think a one-size-fits-all approach would work, but acknowledged a need to develop stronger standards.
“We wouldn’t want in a three-person agency an inspector general, but I think the sentiment is very clear that more internal auditing is a good thing,” Small said. “I think a stronger approach as we go into a new administration makes a lot of sense.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Gov. Kay Ivey commutes death sentence of Toforest Johnson
text:
Toforest Johnson is seen in this undated photo. Gov. Kay Ivey Tuesday commuted Johnson's death sentence to life without parole. Major questions have been raised about the credibility of a witness whose testimony led to Johnson's conviction for the 1995 murder of off-duty Jefferson County Sheriff's Deputy William Hardy. (Alabama Department of Corrections)Gov. Kay Ivey Tuesday commuted the death sentence of Toforest Johnson, whose conviction for the murder of an off-duty Jefferson County sheriff’s deputy in 1995 has faced years of questions over the conduct of prosecutors and the reliability of a key witness.
Ivey said in a statement Tuesday that she had concerns that “there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment, death.”
“My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole,” the statement said.
Ty Alper, an attorney for Johnson, who has always maintained his innocence, said in a statement Tuesday that the commutation “was made possible by Alabamians from all sectors of society united in their belief that Toforest does not belong on death row. That list now includes Governor Ivey.”
“Toforest Johnson is innocent,” the statement said. “Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family.”
Johnson was convicted in 1998 for the July 19, 1995 murder of William Hardy, a Jefferson County sheriff’s deputy who was working as a security guard at a hotel, in a hotel parking lot. No physical evidence tied Johnson to the crime, and a jury deadlocked at his first trial.
At his second, a witness claimed to have heard a “Toforest” confess to the crime on a three-way prison phone call. The witness, Violet Ellison, was later paid a $5,000 reward, a fact prosecutors did not share with Johnson’s defense team.
Jefferson County District Attorney Danny Carr in 2020 issued a report that cast significant doubts on the investigation and prosecution. Several Alabama political figures, including former Lt. Gov. Bill Baxley and former Alabama Chief Justice Drayton Nabers, have called for a new trial or for Johnson’s conviction to be overturned.
Ivey has presided over the most executions of any Alabama governor since the death penalty was reintroduced in 1983. In 2025, Ivey commuted the death sentence of Rocky Myers over questions of his guilt. In March, Ivey commuted the death sentence of Charles “Sonny” Burton, who was sentenced to death for the 1991 murder of Doug Battle in a Talladega AutoZone during a robbery. Burton did not kill Battle and was not present in the store when Battle was killed.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee judicial panel dismisses private-school voucher lawsuit
text:
A crowd in a Cordell Hull Legislative Building committee room expresses displeasure with Gov. Bill Lee's 2024 school voucher plan. A three-judge panel ruled in October 2026 the voucher plan doesn't violate Tennessee's constitution. (Photo: John Partipilo)A Tennessee judicial panel dismissed a legal challenge of the state’s private-school vouchers, finding that the constitution doesn’t prohibit creation of the $260 million-plus program.
The three-judge panel dismissed the entire case filed in 2025 by a group of parents who said Tennessee’s Education Freedom Scholarship Act violates the constitution by shifting funds to unaccountable private schools that discriminate against students. The decision also dismissed claims against Gov. Bill Lee based largely on the finding that he is not responsible for enforcing the act.
The program provides vouchers worth about $7,500 to 35,000 students in its second year and can be expanded annually by 5,000 children, depending on funding by the legislature. It provides funds for three categories of students, including those at 300% of the federal subsidized lunch program, up to $180,000 for a family of four, students with no family income requirement and children who qualify for the state’s Education Savings Account program for low-income children.
Tennesseans challenge state’s private-school voucher program

The panel, made up of Chancellor John Rambo of upper East Tennessee, Judge Joseph Howell of Madison County and Chancellor Anne Martin of Davidson County, found that Tennessee’s Constitution doesn’t prohibit creation of a private-school voucher program, even though it requires a system of free public schools. The ruling found that the constitution’s “silence” about private-school funding gives the General assembly broad power to set up the program.
The group of parents who sued the state claim it diverts hundreds of millions of dollars in state funding away from public schools, exacerbating “an already deficient educational system” that lacks staff, services and programs to enable children to learn successfully.
Defendants argued that the constitution “merely mandates” the legislature keep a free public school system “in existence and does not address any requisite level of funding.”
The panel found that the plaintiffs’ constitutional challenge should be made against a statute such as TISA, which funds the public school system, not the private-school voucher program.
EdChoice Legal Advocates, a pro-voucher group that represented two families who intervened in the lawsuit, called the decision “an important victory” for Tennessee parents who want to keep their children in schools where “they’re happy, learning and thriving.”
Critics of the private-school voucher program say it creates a new entitlement that serves students who were attending private schools already, placing a burden on the state budget and shifting money from public schools.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ hits Geico with hefty fine for billing $10M too much for car insurance
text:
Investigators say Geico and its affiliates had to repay $10.5 million they overbilled New Jersey motorists for car insurance in 2023 and 2024. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey officials accused Geico of overcharging motorists $10.5 million for car insurance and slapped the Maryland-based company and its affiliates with a $1.2 million fine for a “systematic pattern” of improper business practices.
Officials in the state Department of Banking and Insurance’s consumer protection office began investigating Geico in September 2024 after customers complained about the company’s underwriting and rating, claims, and policy terminations. The department released its findings Tuesday.
Investigators examined the company’s activity between June 2023 and May 2024 and found problems impacting more than 15,000 policyholders. They say Geico charged higher rates than the department approved, canceled policies for improper reasons, did not include required language on notices that could lead to policy nonrenewal, and failed to inform policyholders of their rights for those who kept vehicles declared a total loss.
The penalty comes as car insurance rates soar in New Jersey, a trend that has prompted advocates to criticize the department for approving most rate hike requests and urge officials to do more to protect consumers, especially as inflation rises and affordability worsens.
Susan Ochs, the department’s acting commissioner, said her agency works to end bad business practices that harm New Jersey residents. The department also investigates life, health, managed care, and property and casualty companies to ensure they comply with state insurance laws and treat the public fairly.
“This penalty settlement and the corresponding refunds to policyholders demonstrate our commitment to fostering the trusted, accountable, healthy marketplace that will best serve New Jerseyans,” Ochs said in a statement.

Besides Geico, investigators also examined its affiliates Geico Secure Insurance Company, Geico Choice Insurance Company, Geico Indemnity Company, and Geico Casualty Company.
As part of its enforcement action against Geico, investigators made recommendations for the companies to correct their procedures.
Geico began refunding customers the premiums they were wrongfully charged while the investigation was still ongoing, according to the department.
The year investigators began their probe, Geico and its affiliates sought rate hikes ranging from 6.8% up to 26.3%, with the department approving increases of 6.8% to 19.1%, according to data the New Jersey Monitor obtained earlier this year through public records requests.
New Jersey consistently ranks among the top 10 costliest states for car insurance.
Consumer protection advocates have long complained about how car insurance companies decide rates, demanding lawmakers ban insurers from assessing risk using factors advocates deem discriminatory, such as a motorist’s education, marital status, occupation, zip code, credit history, and other things that have nothing to do with driving. The insurance industry has fought such efforts, and lawmakers have not acted.
The department advises that residents who have insurance problems can file a formal complaint against any insurance company online or by calling its hotline at 800-446-7467 or 609-292-7272.

title: Gov. Little, state officials to travel to Arco for Idaho ‘Capital for a Day’ on Oct. 22
text:
Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. Little and other top take officials will travel to Arco on Oct. 22 for "Capital for a Day" events. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Arco, also known as “The Atomic City,” will serve as Idaho’s “Capital for a Day” on Thursday. 
Gov. Brad Little and other top state officials will travel to Arco for events taking place 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Oct. 22 at the Lost Rivers Community and Senior Center, located at 555 S. Water St. in Arco.
Little, other statewide elected officials and agency directors regularly travel to smaller Idaho communities for Capital for a Day events.

I am eager to listen to the voices of Butte County and collaborate on the issues that impact this community, helping us build a state government that truly delivers for Idahoans.” 
The small Butte County city was the first in the world to be lit by electricity generated solely by nuclear power — this occurred for about an hour in 1955.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Hundreds of pregnancy-related prosecutions in Oklahoma, report finds
text:
A report found hundreds of pregnancy-related prosecutions in Oklahoma since the constitutional right to abortion was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court. (Getty Images)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma has had at least 222 criminal cases related to women’s pregnancies or births since the 2022 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that allowed the state to end abortion access, according to new data released Tuesday by a nonprofit that advocates for pregnant women.
Nationwide, there have been over 900 such cases but this number is likely an underrepresentation of pregnancy-related prosecutions, according to the report released by Pregnancy Justice, which works to “defend the rights of pregnant people.” 
Of the 23 states reviewed in the report, Oklahoma had the second highest number of pregnancy-related prosecutions, trailing only South Carolina. That state had 381 cases filed. 
The organization attributes Oklahoma’s high number of cases to a 2020 Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals ruling that found an unborn fetus was protected as a child under the state’s child neglect statute. 
Wendy Bach, a professor of law and one of the co-principal investigators for the report, said Oklahoma is 1 of 3 states where a court has set this precedent. The other states are South Carolina and Alabama, she said. 
“No other states have those appellate opinions,” she said. “So those courts signed off and said, ‘This is a viable legal prosecution that makes a difference.’ … Because of that opinion and because of Pregnancy Justice’s extensive experience in working on this issue, we knew Oklahoma was likely to be a hot spot. So frankly, we devoted a lot of resources to finding those cases.”
While the U.S. Supreme Court’s Roe v. Wade decision upheld the right to abortion in the U.S. for decades, the nation’s high court overturned it in 2022, ruling that the U.S. Constitution does not guarantee a right to abortion. Since then, abortion access has varied by state.
Oklahoma lawmakers have banned all abortions except to save the life of the mother. 
Bach said it’s difficult to compare the number of pregnancy-related prosecutions before and after the fall of Roe v. Wade because the methodology used to study the cases has changed. 
Since 2022, there have been many legal changes to scrutinize pregnancy, she said, including the codification of fetal personhood and use of criminal statutes for child endangerment prosecution. 
A vast majority of the criminal charges reviewed by researchers were related to child neglect, endangerment or abuse statutes, according to the report. 
“Oklahoma isn’t vastly different from the rest of our dataset,” Bach said. “They are charging on a theory of child endangerment based sometimes solely and sometimes in addition to other allegations based on drug use during pregnancy.”
Researchers found 13 cases nationwide where pregnant women faced allegations related to “obtaining, attempting or researching an abortion,” according to the report. While the charging documents noted those allegations, the women were charged with other offenses, the report found. 
Three of those were in Oklahoma, Bach said. 
“Criminalization does not create care,” she said. “It does not create health. It does not create safe families. In fact, we strongly believe that it deters women from precisely the care they desperately need.”
Most of the cases studied in the report stemmed from a medical setting where a pregnant woman’s health information was shared with the criminal legal system, according to the report. 
When women feel at risk seeking healthcare because it could put them or their pregnancy at risk, it deters them from going to the doctor for the care they need, Bach said. 
“People want to be moms and if they think they’re going to lose their children and be prosecuted, they’re not going to seek healthcare,” she said.
Policy needs to change so that healthcare providers can carry out necessary medical testing and patients can trust they won’t be reported and prosecuted, Bach said.

name: National
title: Birth centers are linked to better health outcomes, research shows, but 10 states have none
text:
Sarah Simmons, a midwife and co-owner of Maple Street Birth Center in rural Okanogan County, Wash., holds a newborn. Washington state has among the highest number of birth centers in the country, but a new report identifies 10 states that have none amid a spate of closures over the past three years and reported difficulties with state regulations and costs. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Simmons)Birth centers are an option for those with low-risk pregnancies and are correlated with more positive health outcomes, but 10 states do not have any birth centers at all, and more could be built with certain state policy solutions and different models of care, a new report suggests.
Birth centers can be an attractive option for pregnant patients seeking fewer medical interventions and a more “home-like” childbirth experience that is still attended by professionals. Centers are often chosen by Black, Indigenous and Hispanic patients, who experience negative maternal and infant health outcomes at disproportionately higher rates than white patients, research shows.
The Commonwealth Fund, a nonpartisan, private foundation that supports independent research on healthcare issues, released the report Tuesday. Using data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Association of Birth Centers and other state-level data, the report found 10 states — Arkansas, Hawaii, Iowa, Kentucky, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Rhode Island and Vermont — have zero birth centers.
Eight other states have only one birth center. Conversely, the states with the highest number of centers are California, Florida, Texas, Virginia and Washington.  
Black midwives are suing Southern states, claiming regulations make it harder to help patients

Birth centers are usually staffed by midwives, and are sometimes subject to tight state regulations such as certain staff requirements and referral relationships with local hospitals. The report shows the number of people choosing birth centers for delivery is still quite small, at about 1%, but the popularity of home births and birth centers surged during the COVID-19 pandemic. About 75% of those using birth centers were non-Hispanic white women, the study data showed, while about 12% were Hispanic and 6.6% were Black.   
Gene Declercq, professor of community health sciences at Boston University School of Public Health and lead author of the study, told Stateline the number of home births has remained steady in recent years, but that birth center rates have declined slightly as more centers close nationwide. Stateline reported earlier this year that two dozen centers closed between 2023 and 2026, with some publicly blaming onerous regulations and steep increases in malpractice insurance.
“The problem is not that there’s been closures, the problem is the closures are random, they have to do with other things, not what the state needs at that time,” Declercq said. There is no plan to replace that care, he added, which sometimes forces people to seek care even further from home.
Regardless of regulations, Declercq said the financial side can still be difficult to navigate if the center is solely reliant on births, especially if it wants to take patients using Medicaid. Low reimbursement rates in addition to high costs of renting or purchasing a building can make it challenging or impossible with a low number of births per year. According to the study, about 40% of patients at birth centers did not use insurance and paid out of pocket.  
Declercq, who has studied maternal health policy for nearly 20 years, said more birth centers could be possible under different health models, including as part of a community health center or women’s health center that would provide a steadier source of revenue in addition to births.  
“That provides an infrastructure that can be really helpful to the provision of care, because now … the birth center can go under the umbrella of the health center’s malpractice,” he said. “They have a billing system already in place and the population is right there.”
One of those models identified in the study is in Washington, D.C., at the Community of Hope Family Health and Birth Center. That center combined midwives, doulas and home-based postpartum support with primary care, behavioral health, dental care, transportation and food assistance services, and served more than 700 pregnant patients in the span of a year and a half. 
Close to 90% of those patients were Black, and 71% were insured by Medicaid. The study said the center’s patients had better perinatal outcomes compared with others in the surrounding D.C. area, with a lower proportion of low birthweight babies, especially among Black patients.
“Tying together community care with enhanced maternity care when women need it can be really effective, because then they have a place to go back to after they have their babies that knows them,” Declercq said.
Editor’s Note: Five Stateline reporters are 2026 fellows for the Association of Health Care Journalists’ U.S. Health System Reporting Fellowship, a program that is financially supported by The Commonwealth Fund.
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: West Virginia Public Service Commission makes power rule a goal, not a mandate
text:
John E. Amos Power Plant, seen in June 2013, is a coal-fired plant owned and operated by Appalachian Power, a subsidiary of American Electric Power in Winfield, West Virginia. (Getty Images)Just in time for the winter, West Virginia regulators have tweaked a rule tucked away in the state’s controversial data center law, possibly avoiding hikes in electricity bills. 
The West Virginia Public Service Commission, which oversees water, gas, sewer and electricity utilities, determined a clause in the law that called for power plants to run at 69% capacity is aspirational, rather than mandatory. 
In a decision issued Oct. 15, the Public Service Commission recommended that power plants in the state should strive to achieve a 69% capacity factor — meaning, the actual amount of electricity produced by a plant over time compared to the maximum amount of juice it can produce. But power plants don’t have to “if doing so will cause an increase in the charges for electric energy.” 
West Virginia electricity rates are among the highest in the country, partly due to the fact that nearly 90% of the power comes from coal fired plants. Coal is one of the costliest forms of electricity generation in the country as of 2024, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, a federal agency that tracks fuel costs. 
Environmental and consumer advocacy groups, alongside power companies, argued in favor of making the rule a goal, on the basis that energy demand fluctuates. For instance, power use might be down at 2 a.m., when most people are in bed. But the demand goes up at 7 a.m., as they get ready for work. 
Emmett Pepper, policy director at Energy Efficient West Virginia, said running plants wide open would make electricity costlier for everyday West Virginians. 
“We found there were some problems, but generally they’re not running them unless they’re going to be cost effective,” he said. “I think they’re running them a little more than they should have, but nowhere near 69% of the time.” 
However, the West Virginia Coal Association and the United Mine Workers asked the commission to make the rule mandatory. The association argued that if West Virginia burned its coal at its own plants, it would be cheaper for ratepayers than buying the electricity from the grid and more in line with the intent of the law. 
“With HB 2014, the Legislature and the Governor said plainly that the state’s coal-fired power plants are to be upgraded and operated at the highest achievable capacity factors,” wrote Chris Hamilton, president of the West Virginia Coal Association, in an Aug. 20 comment. 
However, the PSC determined that a mandatory rule would exceed the scope of what the Legislature intended. 
Del. Bob Fehrenbacher, R-Wood, was one of the co-sponsors of the state data center law, House Bill 2014. He said he believes the PSC got it right. 
“The intent (of the rule) is to be able to run at those higher capacity utilizations, but also the intent in the legislation was to protect the ratepayer, and that appears to be in this latest version of the rule,” Fehrebacher said. 
The proposed rule will now go before the Legislative Rule-Making Review Committee, which consists of both state senators and delegates who look over the rule and offer amendments. 
Del. Jonathan Kyle, R-Randolph, is a co-chair on the committee. He said the committee will be taking the rule up in either November or December.
“The most important thing is we make sure nothing inside that rule will increase the cost on ratepayers,” Kyle said. 
Once it passes that committee, it will be introduced as legislation during the regular session in January 2027.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa Board of Regents selects new Center for Intellectual Freedom director
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents on Oct. 20 2026, selected a permanent director for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa. From left: Regents JC Risewick, Robert Cramer and Christine Hensley attend a regents meeting on April 24, 2025. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Board of Regents has selected Carson Holloway as the new director of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, opening a new chapter for the center amid conflict over its development.
Board of Regents President Robert Cramer said he appreciated the “time and energy” center interim director Luciano de Castro put into the center in its first year of operation, but disagreed with the narrative de Castro presented in his annual report to the General Assembly.
“We have a very different view of what has happened in the last year, and a different view of how we should move forward,” Cramer said. “So our new director is ready to make that shift, and will very soon have a very different story to tell.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Holloway currently serves as chair of the University of Nebraska at Omaha’s department of political science and interim chair of the philosophy department, according to his curriculum vitae. He also launched a constitutional studies forum at the university in 2022.
Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa Director Carson Holloway (Photo courtesy of the Iowa Board of Regents)
In the report, de Castro lists instances of what he called potential illegal actions taken by board of regents staff and University of Iowa officials that limited the center’s development and progress in setting up courses and other programming.
Whoever would succeed de Castro in the director position would be “operating under close control by a Board that has consistently followed the University administration’s preferences,” he said in the report. Operating in this way, de Castro wrote, would lead the center’s future required course offerings to becoming a “staged pretense of reform, rather than the real change that could have been truly valuable to the students of the University of Iowa.”
Cramer, who has described himself as a conservative during past board of regents meetings, said Tuesday that de Castro “should have understood that the board takes an active role in the institutions it governs.” He noted de Castro was an open supporter of the legislation that places the center director as reporting to the regents board.
The board also has a responsibility to Iowa taxpayers, whose money has gone through state appropriations to the center through the UI, Cramer said. The center tried working within the UI policies before they realized that “we need to have some separation,” he said.
“Then the board office, under the direction of the board, attempted to assist the center in its creation and use of those tax dollars,” Cramer said. “However, it became readily clear that there was a small subset of the advisory council on the center, and the interim director, that appeared that they did not want any oversight of the center and its use of taxpayer dollars by following the university policies or board advice and counsel.”
At that point, Cramer said the board office worked with the UI “to make the center an independent unit,” with a board committee created to oversee it and placing the university in a vendor role so the center can access its services. Hiring a permanent director was the next step in ensuring the center’s success, Cramer said the board felt, leading to resignations on the advisory council.
In his report, de Castro said he was told by UI Provost Kevin Kregel that the center “cannot function as an academic unit within the University of Iowa.”
Regent Christine Hensley, chair of the board’s Center for Intellectual Freedom committee, said she had many learning opportunities during the “long, drawn-out” director search process, including learning that the center’s model is unique in the U.S. and that other civics centers want to see this one succeed.
As there was no “playbook to go by” in creating this center, Hensley acknowledged they operated on a trial-and-error basis.
“I would be the first to admit that we probably made some mistakes along the way,” Hensley said. “But I’m feeling confident that in the next 18 months, we’ve got just a great opportunity to move forward, and the center is going to be in a really good place.”
De Castro will end his tenure with the center this week, but Iowa Board of Regents Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman said in an email Holloway’s start date, as well as his compensation package, have not been negotiated yet. De Castro said in the report he doesn’t wish to continue in the director role beyond his interim duties under the current conditions, despite having applied for the job, as he doesn’t believe the director’s duties can currently be completed as the General Assembly wanted.
Two of his recommendations in the report would have the board suspend its search for a permanent director and hire a new interim director in the meantime.

title: Acton’s brother condemns attack ad featuring her estranged mom in Ohio governor race
text:
Vivek Ramaswamy, left, and Dr. Amy Acton, right. (Photo by Morgan Trau & WEWS.)The campaign of Ohio Democratic governor candidate Dr. Amy Acton released a statement from her brother Tuesday morning condemning an attack ad against her spread by right-wing online influencers featuring her estranged mother.
In the attack ad spread by supporters of Acton’s opponent, Ohio Republican candidate for governor Vivek Ramaswamy, Donna Arthur speaks directly to the camera and repeatedly calls her daughter a liar. There is no disclaimer on the video explaining who paid for it.
Arthur is estranged from Acton and her brother Philip Stearns. As a child, Acton claimed Arthur’s husband sexually abused her, and when the case went to court Arthur sided with her husband.
In a 2019 interview with Youngstown Vindicator, Acton explained there were “accusations of molestation events” even before the man met Arthur, but after he abused Acton there was enough evidence to go to trial.
“In the courthouse after they were charged,” Acton told the Vindicator, “I went to give her a kiss, and she just turned her cheek away. That was the last time I ever saw her.”
Acton said Arthur and her husband skipped bail and left town.
[Voter Guide: 2026 Ohio General Election Voter Guide: Races, deadlines, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
In a 2020 interview with the anti-abortion group Operation Rescue, Arthur disputed Acton’s version of events, but the story acknowledges Arthur borrowed $10,000 for her husband’s defense and that their attorney suggested they move away until the charges were dropped.
Shortly after the ad began circulating on social media, the Acton campaign shared a statement from her brother.
“It’s not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother’s husband into a political talking point,” Stearns said.
“After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants.”
The Ohio Capital Journal reached out to Ramaswamy’s campaign for comment. In an email, Ramaswamy spokesperson Connie Luck didn’t address questions about who paid for the ad but didn’t reject it either.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We don’t know what happened between Amy and her mother, who first spoke out about Amy in 2020,” Luck said, “but we know that Amy Acton is a serial fabulist who has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of before deciding who to entrust as governor.”
She echoed Ramaswamy’s repeated criticism of Acton for refusing to debate and insisted it’s Acton who has “resorted to lying” about Ramaswamy and her own record.
“If Amy disagrees with these criticisms, she should stand before the people of Ohio, answer the questions, and let voters decide for themselves,” Luck said. “The fact that she won’t, and Vivek will, should tell you everything about who’s really lying.”
Ohio law requires political ads to carry a disclaimer explaining who paid for them. It is unclear how that statute applies to videos on social media, but any alleged violation would have to be investigated by the Ohio Election Integrity Unit in the Ohio Secretary of State’s office before any potential prosecution.
