name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas congressional candidates lean on prominent supporters in 2nd District race
text:
U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt, R-Kansas, speaks ahead of President Donald Trump at an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City. Schmidt is seeking reelection against Democratic nominee Don Coover. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Democrat Don Coover and Republican Derek Schmidt stood with partisan allies as their congressional race in Kansas’ 2nd District entered the stretch run.
Coover, a southeast Kansas veterinarian and former U.S. Army pilot, on Monday welcomed to Leavenworth former U.S. Sen. Jon Tester of Montana. Schmidt, the incumbent U.S. House member and a three-term state attorney general, was on stage Monday night in Park City for the Republican Party’s barnstorming rally hosted by President Donald Trump.
“This is going to be one of the elections we’ll talk about for 50 years because, hopefully, we are going to change the direction … and get back to the middle of the road,” Coover said. “We need a Congress that assumes their responsibilities.”
Coover said Jan. 6, 2021, rioting at the U.S. Capitol was a “very disappointing” moment for him. He said it offered a glimpse of what transpired once Trump was elected to a second term in 2024.
“I don’t see anybody in Congress putting a brake on this,” Coover said. “I find that enormously alarming.”
Sabot’s Crystal Ball, a campaign prediction organization, shifted Tuesday the Coover-Schmidt race from “safe Republican” to “likely Republican.” On Friday, Cook Political Report shifted the 2nd District of Kansas from “solid Republican” to “likely Republican” given voter frustration with economic conditions and evidence of Trump’s shrinking favorability.
Schmidt was elected in 2024 to the eastern Kansas district of the U.S. House. He said the election of Trump two years ago enabled the federal government to pivot away from Democratic President Joe Biden. Trump’s victory led to sealing of the southern border, adoption of federal tax cuts, reduction in crime and strengthening of the military, Schmidt said.
“My friends, we have made a lot of progress,” Schmidt said. “Don’t be distracted by the noise. There are problems left to solve. We are not going to solve what troubles America by turning around and putting in charge the people who caused many of the problems.”
He urged Kansans to take part in the Nov. 3 election because the alternative could be Democratic Party leadership of the U.S. House or U.S. Senate.
“We can say we meant it two years ago when America and this state said we are going in a new direction and solve problems rather than wring our hands about them,” Schmidt said.
Schmidt was recently endorsed by the National Federation of Independent Business’ PAC in recognition of his voting record on behalf of small businesses.
Tester, a Montana farmer and Democrat who served in the U.S. Senate from 2007 to 2025, said the upcoming election was an opportunity for a course correction. He said Coover’s defeat of Schmidt would help reshape policy in Washington, D.C.
“You guys have an incredible opportunity,” Tester said. “This is somebody that, when he goes back there, he’ll change the way people think. Why? Because he’s a man of the soil. We need folks to understand rural America.”
On Tuesday, Coover was endorsed by the End Citizens United organization working to reverse the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2010 decision blocking federal restraint of dark money expenditures in politics.
“Corporate money in politics is stopping Congress from making any progress on lowering prices,” Coover said. “Our government needs to be accountable to working people, not wealthiest donors at the top.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: High schoolers host only debate for this SC congressional seat
text:
Democrat Zyon Khalifa (left) and Republican U.S. Rep. Joe Wilson (right) debate at River Bluff High School on Monday, October. 19, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)LEXINGTON — South Carolina’s longest-serving Republican in Congress and the Democrat trying to unseat him met Monday for their only debate — not before a ticketed primetime TV audience but in a high school auditorium, answering questions written and asked by students.
The mid-day debate between Rep. Joe Wilson, who’s represented the 2nd District for almost 25 years, and Democrat Zyon Khalifa was organized by students in Lexington One school district’s Center for Law and Global Policy Development.
“It’s important for them to be a part of the political process, to engage in civil discourse, and to learn to value multiple perspectives,” Michael Burgess, one of the program’s three teachers, told the SC Daily Gazette. “They are a part of this election, and they can take that and show people that, hey, you can have disagreements without being disagreeable.”
It was Wilson’s fifth election cycle participating in a student-led debate at River Bluff High, the largest high school in his home county. Since 2016, it’s also hosted the only 2nd District debate.
While located at River Bluff High, the program is open to all juniors and seniors throughout the school district. The audience also included students in other high school government classes, as well as supporters of each candidate. Other pre-election political events hosted at the center include a U.S. Senate candidate forum ahead of the GOP special primary in August, and a forum for local school board candidates last month.

For more on our 2026 election coverage and information on voting in South Carolina, check out our Voter Guide.

As for students’ questions for Wilson and Khalifa, topics included the war with Iran and federal funding.
The audience heard some clear policy differences between the 79-year-old congressman and 25-year-old first-time candidate.
Asked about the death penalty, Wilson said he supports existing laws on capital punishment, and they should continue to be enforced.
In South Carolina, there have been seven executions since September 2024, when they resumed following an unintended 13-year hiatus. The last federal execution was in January 2021. The question seemed to reference the U.S. military’s announced-then-canceled livestreaming of a firing squad execution Dec. 3, though the student didn’t specify.
Khalifa, a recent law school graduate, said he opposes the death penalty. Mistakes in the judicial system can and have been made, he said, adding that “death is something you cannot turn back.”
A question on immigration saw some agreement. Both candidates said the border should be secure.
But they disagreed on Trump’s deportation initiatives. Wilson praised them. Khalifa said Congress should fund more immigration judges and ensure there’s due process for people living in the U.S. illegally who the government is trying to deport.
The candidates also sparred over political polarization.
Wilson blamed today’s extreme political divide on “Trump derangement syndrome,” a phrase coined during President Donald Trump’s first term to describe people consumed by their hatred of him.
Khalifa said Wilson contributed to the divide 17 years ago when he yelled “You lie!” during President Barack Obama’s September 2009 healthcare address to a joint session of Congress. Kahlifa called the then-unprecedented outburst one of the “biggest moments in our political history which created polarization.” Wilson apologized to Obama immediately after the speech.
The debate Monday coincided with the first day of early voting in South Carolina, which continues through Oct. 31. Election Day is Nov. 3.
For some students in the audience, the midterms mark the first general election they’re eligible to vote.
“I’m 18 and I’m going to be a voter,” said Bianca Moncrieffe, a student in Lexington One’s Law and Global Policy program. “It’s really nice to be able to hear the candidates that are going up for election and understanding their perspectives and hearing how they’re responding to the questions.”
An hour after the debate, Democrats in other statewide races in South Carolina held a news conference at the state Democratic Party headquarters in Columbia complaining about the lack of debates this election cycle.
Khalifa, who lives in Aiken County, said his team offered Wilson about a dozen potential dates for debates, but Wilson’s team agreed only to the one at River Bluff High.
“I feel like they don’t want people to see it,” Khalifa said.
In response, Wilson said he’s not avoiding debate. “I am in a debate every election because it’s the people’s office,” he said about the 2nd District, which covers all of Lexington, Aiken and Barnwell counties and parts of Richland and Orangeburg counties. “I don’t use the term ‘my’ office.”
He said the location is special to him partly because when he was in high school, the young Republicans club he was a member of wasn’t allowed to meet in school. “Now you can have political discussion,” he said.
Khalifa said he hopes the takeaway for students in the audience is that the contest is “bigger than party.”
It meant a lot to hear from students telling him they appreciate that he’s running, he said: “It’s time for change.”
A Democrat last represented the 2nd District in 1965, when Rep. Albert Watson resigned, then ran successfully as a Republican to fulfill the rest of his term.
Voters first sent Wilson to Congress in a 2001 special election following the death of U.S. Rep. Floyd Spence. He won re-election in 2024 by 19 percentage points.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: In a redrawn congressional district, Kathy Castor faces her toughest battle
text:
Kathy Castor and Mike Beltran at WMNF radio in Tampa on Oct. 2, 2026. (Photo by Valerie Smith)When the Republican-controlled Florida Legislature approved Gov. Ron DeSantis’ congressional redistricting map earlier this year, members intended to remove some of Florida’s longest-standing Democrats from the 28-member delegation.
People like Debbie Wasserman Schultz and Kathy Castor.
Wasserman Schultz swiftly (and controversially) shifted to a seat designed to remain blue in South Florida. Castor didn’t have that luxury in the Tampa Bay area, where her Congressional District 14 had historically been solidly Democratic while the rest of the region has predominantly been red (with a six-year interregnum between 2016 and 2022 when Democrat Charlie Crist represented the congressional seat in Pinellas County).
The reconfigured map removed a portion of St. Petersburg and other parts of eastern Pinellas County and included more conservative parts of Hillsborough County, changing it from a district that went for Kamala Harris by more than 7 points in 2024 to one that supported Donald Trump by more than 10 points.
Now, nearly 20 years into her tenure, Castor, 60, faces the biggest challenge of her career as she runs against Republican Mike Beltran, who served in the Florida House for six years and won a contested eight-person primary in August.
Yet even with that strong GOP bent, several national nonpartisan election raters have moved the race from “leans Republican” to “toss-up.”
With a substantially new electorate to introduce herself to (her campaign has said she maintains 35% of her original district), Castor has run television ads proclaiming her ability to work with Republicans and how she has “broken” from her fellow Democrats in supporting legislation such as a full ban on congressional stock trading.
She was one of eight Democrats to vote for a resolution “denouncing all forms of socialism” earlier this year (along with Central Florida Democratic Rep. Darren Soto, also now running in a more GOP-leaning district).
Speaking in Lakeland last month on a bill that featured Vice President JD Vance, Beltran, a trial lawyer, claimed the new district lines had Castor “masquerading as a moderate” in a desperate attempt to maintain her presence in Washington.
Both candidates have attempted to portray the opponent as too extreme and out of the mainstream.
Beltran, 42, is a New York City native and Harvard Law School grad who moved to the Sunshine State in 2010. An attorney, he served in the Florida House representing southeast Hillsborough from 2018 to 2024.
He has boasted about his independence from his party, such as opposing Gov. Ron DeSantis’ budgets on several occasions. “I’ve worked across the aisle in Tallahassee,” he said during a Tampa Tiger Bay forum Oct. 16, adding that he had opposed “all sorts of special interests: Big Pharma. Big Tech. Landlords. Developers. Trial lawyers. Insurance companies. And the list goes on.”
On some issues, though, he’s leaned more to the right than the majority of his fellow Republicans in the Legislature.
A Second Amendment advocate, he challenged GOP leadership during the 2023 session by filing an amendment to allow the open carry of firearms. The GOP House speaker and Senate president said at the time that the permitless-carry bill Beltran tried to amend was just fine how it was crafted, without an open-carry provision. (Florida’s ban on open-carry was ruled unconstitutional by a state appeals court in 2025).
Abortion rights differences
He is strongly against abortion rights. In the immediate aftermath of the reversal of Roe v. Wade by the U.S. Supreme Court in 2022, he promised to support banning all abortions in the state, with certain exceptions.
He sponsored legislation to make performing or attempting to perform an abortion a third-degree felony, subject to 10 years in prison.
That prompted Castor to declare Beltran “the most extreme candidate that has been up for election in the Tampa Bay area when it comes to abortion.”
“Did you not sponsor a bill that would criminalize the behavior of doctors and nurses, their ability to provide reproductive care? Because I was doing some research on your record and I was appalled that you would target doctors, nurses, providers for the care they need,” she said in a debate held on WMNF 88.5 FM in Tampa (which this reporter co-moderated).
Beltran didn’t deny the legislation but went on offense in his response.
“You what I’m appalled at? That you voted against the Born Alive Protection Act,” he said. “That law says that if a baby is born in a botched abortion and the baby is alive on the operating table, that medical providers don’t need to provide care to that baby. That’s infanticide that you voted for. You voted against the bill that would have protected them. You said that you wanted to protect mothers. You said that you wanted to protect children in the first year of their lives — what about those children? “
A factor that could help Beltran is voters’ exhaustion with incumbents.
Serving in Congress for two decades has left Castor vulnerable to charges she was part of a body that failed to deliver for voters.
Mike Beltran and Kathy Castor at Tampa Tiger Bay forum on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)
Immigration
Regarding comprehensive immigration reform efforts, which have gone nowhere for years, Beltran says he supports more “legitimate” immigration measures that include support for H1-B and guest worker visas. He argues Democrats had a chance to change immigration policy when they controlled all levers of the federal government during a period of the Obama administration.
“Where was the immigration reform then? It’s hasn’t been done in 20 years that my opponent was in office,” he said.
The closest a comprehensive immigration reform bill came to passage was in 2013, led at that time by then Republican U.S. Sen. Marco Rubio (now Secretary of State), which passed 68-32 in the Senate. However, then-GOP House Speaker John Boehner refused to bring the bill up for a vote in Congress’ lower chamber.
For her part, Castor says she has voted for millions of dollars to enforce the southern border, but adds, “We also need laws for a pathway … to citizenship for people who play by the rules and pay taxes and learn English.”
Regarding Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Trump 2.0 era, Castor says the agency is “out of control” and needs to be “reigned in.” She specifically argues ICE agents must use body cameras like local enforcement does.
Beltran insists Congress needs to give U.S. Customs and Border Protection and ICE “the tools they need to do the job correctly,” and says it was important for the Trump administration to prioritize removing gang members, violent criminals, and national security threats. “And we’ve done that.”
As far as alleged incidents of ICE attacking U.S. citizens and running amok on city streets, he acknowledges that “when you’re dealing with tens of thousands of people, there are going to be a few mistakes.”
Castor has brought home the bacon for her Tampa Bay area district over the decades, including improvements to senior housing, Tampa International Airport, and MacDill Air Force Base. Her public profile probably received the most attention when she served for eight years as chair of the Select Committee on Climate Change from 2018 to 2022 (she’d been an environmental attorney).
Beltran has pointed out that he’ll hardly be a stooge for the Trump administration if he goes to Washington, emphasizing that he has voted against the GOP line.
“I’ve had the courage to vote against special interests when my own party had lost its way,” he has said. “I’ve voted against insurance companies, home builders, trial lawyers.” He’s also boasted that he resisted pressure to endorse Ron DeSantis when he ran for president in the 2023-2024 cycle, one of seven Republicans in the Legislature not to do so.
Property insurance
One of the biggest points of contention between Democrats and Republicans in Florida in both legislative and congressional races is property insurance reform.
Republicans have hailed laws they passed in 2022 and 2023 to address the spiraling crisis for homeowners. Beltran and other members of the GOP point to those laws (such as (SB 2-A) as major tort reform that protects insurance companies from civil lawsuits, which the business community blames for inflating premiums to cover defense costs and raising monetrecoveries.
Those laws restored access to private market coverage, they contend, boasting the state’s Office of Insurance Regulation reported 20 property and casualty insurers entering Florida’s market as of May of this year.
Democrats have called the laws a “bailout” for the insurance companies, claiming that while the legislation extended a $1 billion subsidy to insurance companies, it did little to decrease premiums.
The Castor campaign has said that Beltran took tens of thousands of dollars from insurance companies while many Floridians struggle to find insurance carriers. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has been airing a negative ad  accusing him of going soft on the industry.
He says that’s nonsense.
“They say that I’m in the pocket of insurance companies,” he said at the Tiger Bay forum. “Go ask any insurance lobbyist in Tallahassee which Republican was the biggest pain in their neck in Tallahassee. It was me. I voted against insurance companies more than anyone else in my party.”
As for where the public is on all of this, a public opinion survey published last month by the Public Opinion Research Lab at the University of North Florida in conjunction with the Orlando Sentinel and South Florida Sun-Sentinel found that 55% of respondents saw no sign the homeowners insurance market is improving, with 26% saying it’s getting worse.
Beltran says the vitriol against Republicans on the issue is “preposterous” and that the party would not enjoy supermajorities in the Legislature “if we were doing a bad job.”
Stock trading
Another contentious issue is banning members of Congress from individual stock trading, which overwhelming bipartisan majorities in both parties say they support.
Castor was one of 13 Democrats who voted earlier this year in support of the Stop Insider Trading Act, which would ban members of Congress and their spouses and dependent children from purchasing individual stocks.
In the WMNF radio debate, Beltran alleged that in her two decades in Congress, Castor increased her net worth “by as much as 4,000%.”
“She’s an eight-digit multimillionaire,” he said.
Because members of Congress report their personal finances, assets, and liabilities in broad ranges rather than exact figures, it is difficult to determine how wealthy members of Congress are. Castor’s 2025 financial disclosure form showed she had an estimated net worth of between $7 million and $22 million.
In his financial disclosure form, Beltran reports earning $1.7 million from his legal work in 2025. He has loaned his congressional campaign more than $2 million.
Third-party spending has been considerable, illustrating how badly both parties want this seat.
The Trump-aligned No Going Back PAC has spent over $6 million opposing Castor. That includes an ad alleging Castor is now worth up to $31 million.
All told, third-party groups have spent more than $7 million against Castor and more than $5.25 million against Beltran, according to Midterm Mondays, which totals candidate and independent spending for every candidate running in the United States.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: NorthWestern Energy applies for permit to build another natural gas power plant near Aberdeen
text:
A photo simulation submitted by NorthWestern Energy as part of its application to build a natural gas power plant just south of Aberdeen. (Image courtesy of the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission)NorthWestern Energy wants to build another natural gas power plant just south of Aberdeen.
The proposed Hub City Energy Park would generate up to 131 megawatts of electricity at peak capacity, and is expected to operate at 15% to 25% of capacity annually, generating enough power for about 26,000 homes. The company’s 2025 annual report says the project is expected to cost $300 million.
The utility company applied to the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission for a construction permit on Oct. 1. On Tuesday, the commission approved hiring outside consultants and appointing a local committee to help review NorthWestern’s proposal. 
The plant would sit on 176 acres owned by the company, which has 65,600 electric customers in South Dakota. The site is near its existing natural gas plant, the Aberdeen Generating Station. 

A map of the proposed site for NorthWestern Energy’s 131 megawatt natural gas power plant just south of Aberdeen. (Map courtesy of the Public Utilities Commission)

The new facility would use three natural-gas-fired turbines to generate electricity. The company says the project would help prevent power shortages and improve reliability for South Dakota consumers. 
“The Aberdeen area was selected for the Project based on its (i) robust electric transmission infrastructure, (ii) proximity to a major natural gas interstate pipeline, (iii) proximity to existing NorthWestern facilities and (iv) anticipated minimal impacts on the surrounding communities and environment,” NorthWestern’s application says. 
The company also plans to build a new natural gas pipeline connection stretching a few miles, but it has not yet selected a route. The company does not expect to need eminent domain, which is a legal way of forcing landowners to allow access if negotiations fail.
The plant will need an air quality permit from the state Department of Environment and Natural Resources. NorthWestern’s permit application to the Public Utilities Commission outlines plans for air-quality controls and says the project is expected to result in emissions below National Ambient Air Quality Standards.
Construction could begin in late 2027 or early 2028, according to the company. The plant is expected to begin operating in 2030. The company’s application estimates the facility will employ six to 10 people.
Sioux Falls-based NorthWestern Energy is in the process of merging with Rapid City-based Black Hills Corp., creating Bright Horizon Energy, which would serve about 2.2 million electric and natural gas customers across eight states, according to the companies.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas rotates National Guard members deployed to Washington
text:
Deploying Arkansas National Guard members stand at parade rest during a departure ceremony on Oct. 5, 2025. (Photo by John Oldham/Arkansas National Guard)Eighty members of the Arkansas National Guard have departed for Washington, the guard announced Tuesday, in its sixth deployment to the nation’s capital since President Donald Trump retook office.
Members of the 39th Mobile Brigade Combat Team will be in Washington until Feb. 12 and replace 60 members of the same unit as well as members of the 142nd Field Artillery Brigade, which have spent several months participating in Trump’s “D.C. Safe and Beautiful” task force.
Arkansas has been sending guard members to Washington for the taskforce since Dec. 1, 2025, with 170 members of the guard currently deployed there.
Trump’s use of thousands of National Guard members from multiple states to reduce crime in D.C. has been challenged in state and federal courts.

name: National
title: New home completions are stuck at 2020 levels
text:
Instructor Jeff Karnes teaches plumbing construction techniques at St. Philip's College in San Antonio, Texas, in September 2026. A shortage of skilled workers is one reason housing construction is down. (Photo courtesy of St. Philip’s College)Single-family home completions remain stuck at early pandemic levels as of September as costs, labor supply shortages and high interest take a toll on home builders, especially in the Northeast and South. 
Apartment building was a more mixed picture, down nationally but up sharply in the Midwest (53%) and West (18%). 
New single–family homes dropped to an annual rate of 840,000, the lowest since May 2020, according to new U.S. Census Bureau survey results released Oct. 20. 
Aging workforce, immigration crackdown are depleting skilled workers

Single-family home completions fell in every region, especially in the Northeast (-17%) and South (-15%).  
Builders of single-family homes are stymied by rising mortgage rates, costs for energy and materials, and worsening labor supply, according to an October survey by the National Association of Home Builders. 
More than a third of home builders said immigration enforcement activity caused construction delays and discouraged legal workers from reporting for work, said  Bill Owens, chairman of the home builders group, in a statement. 
Buyer interest in new homes has fallen as costs rise, NAHB chief economist Robert Dietz said, and 43% of builders cut prices in October, the largest share in recent years. 
“Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges,” Dietz said in a statement. 
New apartments came in at an annual rate of 339,000, an increase from August’s 295,000, which was the lowest since 2022. Apartment completions were down 64% in the Northeast and 37% in the South. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Mississippi Today
title: State lawmaker urges Jackson city leaders to support Pearl River casino project
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
A state lawmaker pleaded with members of the Jackson City Council on Monday night to sell city-owned swampland along the Pearl River, a move that could advance a long-sought riverfront casino resort in Mississippi’s capital city.
Rep. Chris Bell, a Democrat from Jackson, expressed his dismay that the council had not yet approved an order allowing LeFleur Development to buy and develop 93 acres within the river’s floodplain.
“We have an opportunity to change the trajectory of the city of Jackson,” Bell said after thanking the council for letting him speak even though the project was not on the council’s work session agenda. 
Further delays, he asserted, would mean the potential loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in much-needed tax revenue for the cash-strapped city. Last year, the city’s tourism arm, Visit Jackson, estimated that the proposed resort could attract over 4 million visitors annually and create more than 6,722 new jobs. 
“I’m not saying we will, but we do not need to fumble a $600 million influx of funds to the city of Jackson,” Bell told the council.
The council had tabled the matter during an Oct. 6 meeting after Ward 1 Council Member Ashby Foote, who represents northeast Jackson and is the body’s lone Republican, had questioned if the proposed selling price of $110,000 was too low. The amount was based on two estimates LeFleur Development obtained from two Mississippi property appraisers.
LeFleur Development is supported by former Gov. Haley Barbour and attorney-developer Robert Gibbs, a key ally of Mayor John Horhn.
Jackson City Council President Vernon Hartley, who represents Ward 5 in west Jackson, told Bell the proposal was not dead but had been referred to a committee for further discussion.
While the council’s support is crucial for advancing the project, the development faces other hurdles.
Despite repeated attempts, Bell has yet to secure passage of the required legislation that would allow a casino to be built in Jackson. His bill faced opposition from lawmakers whose districts already have casinos. 
It also remains to be seen how the Pearl River’s swampy banks will be converted into land suitable for development. In March, the Rankin Hinds Pearl River Flood and Drainage Control District announced that it had approved a plan to widen and develop the river, though federal officials later clarified that no final decision has been made.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Trump renews call for New Mexico name change
text:
President Donald Trump on Sept. 6, 2026, posted on Truth Social images and text that proposed renaming New Mexico, prompting immediate pushback from Democratic officials. (Screenshot image)President Donald Trump on Monday took to social media to renew his call for New Mexico to be renamed New America.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that the state should change its name “immediately” because, “We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!  The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag! Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!”
The post followed Trump’s initial call for the name change in early September, which prompted numerous denunciations by state and federal officials and candidates.
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.), who is in a competitive race for his seat representing the 2nd Congressional District, quickly rebuked Trump and his opponent, former Marine and Albuquerque police officer Greg Cunningham.
“Greg Cunningham’s boss is doubling down on this ridiculous proposal,” Vasquez wrote on social media. “Shouldn’t the President be spending his time figuring out how to lower prices for Americans? Of course he’s not. And Greg will stay silent again — he can’t even defend our state’s name.”
Source NM reached out to Cunningham’s campaign for a comment, but did not receive a response prior to publication. Vasquez and Cunningham had a lively debate on Friday.
Both Democratic and Republican gubernatorial candidates Deb Haaland and Gregg Hull rejected Trump’s call in September. Hull reiterated his opposition on Monday.
“I stand by my original statement — New Mexico does not need a new name,” Hull said in a statement. “Our identity is defined by our rich culture, our beautiful landscape, and the resilience of our people. That identity is never up for negotiation. EVER.”
New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham in a social media post responded similarly. “This tired ‘New America’ bit again?  You have to ask — what policy failure is Trump trying to distract Americans from this time? Let me repeat: New Mexico was New Mexico long before the United States existed and we’ll be New Mexico forevermore.”
Both Lujan Grisham and Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver also rejected Trump’s critique of the state’s elections.
“President Trump continues to push tired and patently false narratives about our voting process in New Mexico,” Toulouse Oliver said in a statement. “He must stop insulting the intelligence of this state’s voters. New Mexicans know that we have repeatedly received high national rankings for administering some of the most secure and accessible elections in the country.”
In April, Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s (MIT) 2024 Elections Performance Index ranked New Mexico’s election administration seventh in the U.S.
New Mexico’s congressional delegation in September called upon major tech companies Apple and Google to commit to ensuring New Mexico retains its name on the companies’ maps.
On Monday, U.S. Sen. Ben Ray Luján responded to Trump’s renewed call with an online statement noting,
“New Mexico’s name dates back hundreds of years, long before the United States even existed. It carries generations of history, culture, and rich traditions that continue to shape who we are. We are New Mexicans. We’re proud of our name, proud of our home, and we’re keeping both. Long after Donald Trump is out of office, we’ll still be New Mexico.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: Election group sues Santa Fe County Clerk Clark for turning away state-confirmed poll observers
text:
A New Mexico consortium of grassroots organizations on Oct. 16 sued Santa Fe County Clerk Katharine Clark alleging she violated state law by requiring additional training for election watchers. (Photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)A New Mexico civic group intending to observe the upcoming general election on Oct. 16 sued Santa Fe County Clerk Katharine Clark alleging she violated state law by denying recognized election watchers access to polling places unless they attended additional training. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Land of Action, which describes itself as a nonpartisan civic association and hub for numerous progressive groups throughout the state, requested among other remedies that the First Judicial District Court require Clark to admit its election watchers. A hearing was slated for Tuesday afternoon in First Judicial District Judge T. Glenn Ellington’s courtroom. 
New Mexico law permits properly designated individuals to serve as challengers, observers and watchers during early voting and on Election Day. Political parties appoint challengers, while observers often come from academic or human rights fields. Groups qualified by the Secretary of State appoint watchers to monitor polling locations. All three must complete a training session provided by the Secretary of State’s office before receiving access to voting centers or polling places in order to observe voting. 
Land of Action had more than 20 of its members complete the required SOS training. Nonetheless, on Oct. 6 — the first day of early voting in New Mexico — the lawsuit alleges Clark turned away one of its watchers from the early voting station at the Santa Fe County Clerk’s office for not completing additional training with the county clerk. The following day, the lawsuit says, Clark turned away two additional Land of Action election watchers for the same reason. 
The group and the additional plaintiffs, which include Land of Action founder Heidi Feldman and several other group members designated as election watchers, seek a temporary restraining order against Clark, who ran in the June 2 Democratic primary for New Mexico Secretary of State, losing to Doña Ana County Clerk Amanda López Askin. The suit alleges Clark’s requirement for additional training violates New Mexico statute.
Gary Reid, a spokesperson for the Santa Fe County Clerk’s office, told Source NM via an emailed statement that the county’s additional training responds to “concerns about unauthorized individuals at polling sites” for the upcoming election, and that the county “is following the law to ensure only legally authorized individuals are present.” He added that 13 individuals from Land of Action, Observe New Mexico and both the Democratic and Republican parties of Santa Fe County have completed the county training.
Feldman confirmed that some Land of Action members completed Clark’s training “under protest.”
SOS spokesperson Lindsey Bachman confirmed via email that Land of Action completed all training required by state statute and said it is one of six election-related organizations registered with SOS for the 2026 general election. 
When asked about the Santa Fe County clerk’s additional training, Bachman told Source NM: “Those wishing to serve in these roles, who have completed the required uniform curriculum provided by the Secretary of State’s Office and followed all other laws for registration and activity, should not be further hindered from that service.”
The lawsuit’s documents also include an Oct. 14 email the Secretary of State’s general counsel sent to Santa Fe County attorney Walker Boyd that says Clark’s actions “result in unlawfully denying” Land of Action’s watchers access, and if Clark does not reconsider her requirement, to “consider this letter to be a cease and desist demand in anticipation of litigation.” 
In addition to a court order admitting appointed election watchers from its organization to polling places in Santa Fe County, Land of Action also requested a declaration that New Mexico election code does not permit county clerks to impose their own training requirements.
“At a time when democracy itself in this country is under siege, we all need to take responsibility — not only for participating in elections by voting, but for participating in election support,” Feldman told Source NM. She added that voters in New Mexico “fear intimidation” and election watching “is a way to lessen their fear and make sure that intimidation efforts are reported.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Little, Pratt vie for Craig’s open seat in south suburban swing district
text:
Matt Little, Democratic candidate for Minnesota's 2nd congressional district, stands with his mother as he talks to supporters at a fundraising event at New Market Township Hall in Lakeville, Minnesota Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)In a TikTok video from January, Matt Little stands a couple feet away from a federal immigration agent sitting in a car with his window open.
“There’s some bad folks that joined to do some bad things,” Little says to the agent, who wears a black neck gaiter covering most of his face and black baseball cap. The two talk briefly. Little had followed the agent in his car, the caption said, joining thousands of Minnesotans who sought to disrupt immigration operations that had become infamous for racial profiling and the killing of two Americans.
In the caption, Little promises to “hold ICE accountable” if he’s elected to Congress.
The 41-year-old attorney, former Lakeville mayor and one-term state senator is running to represent the 2nd Congressional District, which encompasses the south suburbs of the Twin Cities and rural Le Sueur County and has been the state’s most competitive for about a decade. The seat is currently held by U.S. Rep. Angie Craig, who gave it up for an unsuccessful Senate run.
Just a year before Operation Metro Surge, in January 2025, Craig voted in favor of the Laken Riley Act, a punitive immigration bill. Her decision lined up with what she had told MinnPost when she was reelected in 2024: “I really believe that voters want someone who has a moderate, centrist voting record.”
Little has said he wouldn’t have voted for the bill and promises to fight for an “Anti-ICE Bill of Rights” that cuts U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement funding to pre-Trump levels and replaces ICE with another federal immigration agency.
A few weeks out from the election, Little isn’t too worried that his ICE chasing might’ve pushed swing voters into the arms of his Republican opponent, state Sen. Eric Pratt.
“If your politician wasn’t out there trying to help people and protect people, then where are they gonna draw the line?” Little said to the Reformer on Oct. 8.
“Whether it hurt or helped us in this election, I don’t care as much,” he added.
Pratt, Little’s mild-mannered opponent and the top Republican on the Minnesota Senate Finance Committee, has accused Little of “screaming on TikTok” instead of solving problems during the surge.
Pratt’s campaign declined repeated requests for an interview, but he’s struck a more moderate tone on immigration compared to many in his party — the 2024 Republican National Convention featured signs that read, “Mass deportation now.”
“We are a nation of immigrants. We do need to take a look at immigration reform,” Pratt said during an Oct. 9 MPR News debate.
During a September WCCO debate, Pratt said that he told the White House it needed to “back down” during the immigration enforcement surge, and that he began reaching out to decision-makers in both parties after Renee Good was shot and killed by ICE agent Jonathan Ross.
Pratt was also in D.C. when Trump’s “border czar” Tom Homan was sent to Minnesota to replace Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino, signaling the beginning of the end of the surge, Pratt said in the KSTP debate. Little retorted that he was in Minnesota, “doing my best to protect the people I care about and our neighbors.”
The race between Little and Pratt is a barometer of the swift changes in American politics in the past two years. If elected, Little would represent a leftward shift for the swing district that had a streak of voting red until 2018, as well as the possibility that Operation Metro Surge has led to enduring changes in the attitudes of suburban, exurban and even rural Minnesotans on the issue of immigration enforcement.
Pratt and Little debate Trump, healthcare, war
First, however, Little has to beat Pratt, who has managed to avoid getting caught up in Trump-era theatrics, which is no small feat. (When Little’s campaign revealed that Pratt’s field director had posted racist and antisemitic content to social media, Pratt quickly announced his resignation.)
Pratt worked in finance and banking for three decades, most recently at U.S. Bank. He’s touted his experience leading risk management and fraud prevention teams as proof that he’ll effectively cut spending and prevent fraud in government programs, a central issue in Minnesota politics following revelations of widespread fraud in the state’s safety net programs. He also served on the board of St. Gertrude’s, a nursing home.
Pratt was first elected to the state Senate in 2012, overlapping with Little from 2017 to 2021 before Little lost to Republican Sen. Zach Duckworth of Lakeville. In addition to the Finance Committee, Pratt serves on the Senate Jobs and Economic Development Committee and Capital Investment Committee. He chaired the jobs committee during the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic; during a debate, he cited his work with state Rep. Mohamud Noor, DFL-Minneapolis, on a bipartisan $1.6 billion omnibus economic recovery bill as an example of making “real, tough decisions.”
Sen. Eric Pratt, R-Prior Lake, deliberates the aspects of an amendment brought forth by Sen. Jason Rarick, R-Pine City, to an omnibus education policy bill during a floor session Tuesday, April 9, 2024. (Photo by A.J. Olmscheid/Senate Media Services)
Immigration is among several issues Pratt and Little have repeatedly clashed on in public debates leading up to Nov. 3.
Pratt has pitched himself as an “independent voice,” touting his bipartisan bills in the Minnesota Senate, while Little has accused Pratt of “quiet extremism” and being “all in on Trump.” On PBS Almanac, when asked to clarify his stance on Trump, Pratt said: “I don’t agree with my wife on everything, I don’t agree with the president on everything. And I’m not going to be a rubber stamp for anybody’s policy. I’m going to represent the people of the 2nd District.”
Little has said he would vote in favor to end the Iran war, and called the conflict a “complete bungle” and “absolute mess.” Pratt has been more ambiguous: He’s said he doesn’t want the U.S. to be in Iran “any longer than we need to,” and that “the president needs to be more clear on what the objectives are of this war,” but that the U.S. “cannot allow Iran to become a nuclear power.” (Trump claimed after 2025 bombing that the Iranian nuclear program had been “complete and totally obliterated.”)
Little’s stated policy priority is Medicare for All, under which the government would insure all Americans for medically necessary healthcare instead of private health insurance companies. Pratt denounces Medicare for All, and instead proposes “bending the cost curve” and “reducing fraud, waste and abuse” in healthcare, a sector which now comprises more than one-sixth of the American economy. He also advocates for tighter controls on pharmacy benefit managers, which are the opaque middlemen of the pharma business.
To address the impending depletion of the Social Security trust fund, Pratt has said the U.S. needs to look at “gradually increasing the retirement age” and consider giving younger people the opportunity to opt out of the program. Currently, income above $184,500 isn’t taxed by Social Security; Little has said he’d vote to eliminate that cap and make all income taxable by Social Security.
Little has pointed out that Pratt worked at U.S. Bank when it had the practice of opening fake customer accounts to meet sales goals, for which the bank was eventually fined $37.5 million. Pratt said that he wasn’t in the fraud department at the time and was not personally responsible and accused Little of misleading voters with “reckless speech.”
Humor as an ‘offensive tool’
The last time Little lived in D.C., he was in his early 20s and working for the letter carriers union.
“My vantage point and my leverage at that time was minimal,” Little said. “This time, I’d like to build as many relationships as I can within the party, but also try and find some room to work with any Republicans.”
He became Lakeville’s youngest mayor at 27 in 2012, before running for the state Senate in 2016 and winning a Republican district. Little has a private law firm where he sues assisted living homes for abuse and neglect, among other personal injury cases.
In 2020, when running for state Senate reelection, Little gained a large following of Gen Z fans from wielding TikTok and lip-syncing to trending audio clips. Politico published an article titled “Meet the politician who lives on TikTok,” and reported that he was the most-followed American politician on the app, with over 140,000 followers. (Other politicians’ TikToks have since amassed followings of millions.)
Little’s TikTok account, now used for his congressional campaign, still has over 140,000 followers, but his relationship to the app has shifted since 2020, when he was defeated for reelection in a red-leaning, south metro state Senate district.
“I just don’t care for it as much anymore. Honestly, I’m just not that interested,” said Little, who deleted the app from his phone and instead sends clips for his team to post.
On social media, the campaign’s videos are generally either serious (Matt Little confronts an ICE agent) or comedic (Matt Little prepares to break the world record for most hands shaken by a politician). In person, Little shifts smoothly from humor to intensity, often layering the two.
Scott Jensen, a Chaska physician who served with Little and Pratt in the Senate from 2017 to 2021, described them both as respectful colleagues. He said Little “has a sense of humor that’s outside the box.”
“Matt enjoys laughter,” he added.
Little had run into Jensen on Oct. 3 at the GOP booth at South St. Paul’s “On the Road Again” festival, a packed annual affair with thousands of attendees, a classic car show, the self-proclaimed “World Championship Booya” competition, and a handful of campaigning politicians.
Jensen, whose 2022 campaign for governor was hindered by his vaccine skepticism and waffling position on abortion rights, is the GOP nominee for state auditor.
Little had a hard time advancing his bills — his party was in the minority during his tenure — “because of partisanship,” Jensen said.
“I think we’re both at times willing to be mavericks. And I think when you’re a maverick, sometimes people are nervous about it,” Jensen said.
“Yeah, a lot of people call me Tom Cruise,” Little jumped in, with a reference to the blockbuster movies about Naval aviators. “It’s really odd, you know.”
Jensen: “Do you have a need right now to change from serious conversation to humor?”
Little: “Constantly. Yeah.”
Jensen: “Because I thought we were having a serious conversation.”
Little: “Well, we had those in the Senate. But here we’re at the Booya, we’re having a good time,” Little said. “I’m voting Zack Filipovich. Get that on the record,” he added to the Reformer, referring to Jensen’s DFL opponent. Later, Little told the Reformer that he uses humor as an “an offensive tool,” i.e., a political weapon.
It’s a style that’s not without risk — a well-placed quip can also bruise the inflated ego of a colleague. Reflecting on his time in the state Senate, Little said he is “pretty brash” and admitted that he could have built relationships better.
“But that doesn’t mean I’m not gonna fight my ass off for what I’m saying. I’m gonna fight hard for things I believe in that I think would help people, and if I run into walls, I’m gonna try and run through ‘em.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A federal judge lets North Carolina’s new absentee ballot rules stand
text:
Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)A federal court judge ruled against challengers of new absentee ballot requirements, saying the signature and envelope sealing requirements are not undue burdens. 
In a ruling late Monday, Federal District Judge Thomas D. Schroeder wrote that the challengers were not likely to win after a trial and denied their request for a preliminary injunction. 
In a rule the state Board of Elections adopted on Sept. 4 in a party-line vote, ballots that arrive in an unsealed inner envelope or only in a sealed outer envelope are no longer accepted. When county boards of election receive ballots in the outer envelope or in an unsealed inner envelope, they must send voters new ballots. 
The North Carolina Alliance for Retired Americans, North Carolina Asian Americans Together, Down Home North Carolina, and two voters filed a federal lawsuit against the state Board of Elections and elections boards in Guilford and Durham, asking the court to block the rules for the 2026 midterm and future elections. They also challenged a signature verification requirement.
More absentee ballots in NC in danger of being tossed under new directives

Schroeder wrote that the plaintiffs would have counties accept ballots that were clearly not signed by the voter.
“Plaintiffs’ proposed remedy eliminates any verification of the signature, permitting a voter to sign anyone’s name to the certification, even ‘Mickey Mouse,’” he wrote. 
The state board approved the rule the day the first absentee ballots were mailed. The plaintiffs filed their lawsuit 18 days later, a delay Schroeder said was significant. The state board told the court at last week’s hearing that 31,582 absentee ballots had already been cast under the new rules. 
Schroeder said the plaintiffs took too long to sue, and that they were unlikely to win on the merits. 
“[T]he absentee voter who fails to seal his or her ballot correctly has an opportunity to correct a mistake, and is not barred from participating in early voting or voting on election day. Likewise, the voter whose signature is rejected for ‘clear evidence’ that it is not their name has an opportunity to submit another ballot, participate in early voting, or vote on election day,” he wrote.

name: California
title: California state workers are about to strike. What that means for the DMV, EDD, parks and more
text:
In summary
California state government’s largest union is scheduled to strike this week. It could affect services at a number of offices that people visit every day, including the DMV.


Tens of thousands of state government workers are expected to walk off the job Wednesday in a one-day strike that could affect services at the DMV, unemployment offices and more. 
Members of SEIU Local 1000 are protesting what they argue are bad-faith bargaining practices by Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration. The union has been negotiating a new labor agreement since its latest three-year contract expired on June 30, and the strike would be Local 1000’s first statewide walkout in its 44-year history.
The union represents about 100,000 public workers, with members employed in dozens of agencies across California. They’re accountants, government analysts, nurses, IT workers, custodians and more. 
Local 1000 could call off the work stoppage at any time leading up to Wednesday. But if it happens, here’s how the strike could affect you.
Can I still go to the DMV
Yes, you can, but services could be delayed depending on who is participating in the strike. DMV offices might close early, too, a department spokesperson said. The same holds for other public-facing services, including unemployment benefits at the Employment Development Department and food assistance at CalFresh.
State parks could be affected, too, even though rangers are not represented by Local 1000. Hearst Castle in San Luis Obispo County, for instance, adjusted its tour schedule to accommodate people who’ve already reserved spots to see the newspaper magnate’s estate. 
This may not be ideal from a customer service standpoint, but union president Anica Walls urges Californians “to give our employees some grace.”
“If you happen to go to the DMV office and the services are limited, make an appointment for another day,” Walls said. “Realize that we are standing up for 100,000 state workers who have not had a good living wage. … It’s not just about state employees. It really is about the working class.”
Which state workers can’t strike?
Local 1000 represents almost half of the state’s workforce, and 95,000 workers would be able to participate in the strike. The remaining 5,000 workers are legally excluded from the strike, because their absence “would create an imminent and substantial threat to public health or safety,” according to the union. In general, they work in healthcare or public safety.
Eight state agencies and divisions employ workers who are deemed essential. These include workers such as veterans homes nurses, cooks at state prisons, Caltrans dispatchers and others:

Department of Veterans Affairs
Correctional Health Care Services
Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation
Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Division of Adult Parole Operations
Department of Education
Department of Developmental Services
Department of State Hospitals
Caltrans

To see which employees at which worksites are deemed essential, check out this list. 
How did we get here?
Many state workers are frustrated with Newsom, who has demanded wage cuts to help balance the budget in three of the eight years he’s led the state. These cuts essentially negated the last 3% salary increase he gave Local 1000 members. 
Pointing to a $20 billion increase in general fund spending over the past two years, the union wants better pay and more affordable healthcare coverage than the administration has offered. It also wants more flexibility to work from home, pushing back against the governor’s return-to-office mandate for state workers.
But talks have been contentious. In July, the union filed a complaint with the state’s Public Employment Relations Board, accusing CalHR, the state agency that handles labor negotiations, of delaying negotiations and rejecting proposals outright. Last month the labor board sided with the union and concluded that CalHR “refused to meet and confer in good faith.”
Earlier this month, union members authorized the strike. Local 1000 members will hold demonstrations in more than a dozen cities, including Oakland, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego and Sacramento, where members will also hold a march to lawmakers’ offices near the Capitol.
How has the Newsom administration responded?
In response to the labor board’s findings, Angela Musallam, CalHR’s deputy director of communications, said in an email to CalMatters that “the state has been and remains open to negotiation” She added that the state “is prepared to move into mediation to assist the parties in reaching an agreement.” 
CalHR also filed an unfair practice complaint of its own to the board in an effort to stop the strike. CalHR claimed that the strike was unlawful because the union did not initially identify which essential workers would be excluded from the walkout. The union disagreed with CalHR’s interpretation of events, arguing that it did identify these employees. The board sided with the union last week, rejecting CalHR’s request for an injunction.
Could there be another strike?
Both parties are scheduled to meet for mediation talks on Oct. 30. For now the union is planning to only strike on Wednesday, but Walls said that if the Newsom administration continues to engage in bad-faith bargaining, the union will “escalate” its actions. This could include filing another complaint with the labor board, and potentially holding another strike.

name: Mississippi Today
title: These artists are honoring the Mississippi River Basin one piece of glass at a time
authors: Hector Alejandro Arzate, Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk
text:
Libby Reuter watched the creek flow slowly, like she had done dozens of times before.
Mallard ducks rested on stones and cattails sprang out of the creek. The water ran parallel to a street busy with traffic and joggers, pooling behind the art museum in Springfield, Mo. 
Fassnight Creek is hundreds of miles from the banks of the Mississippi River, but that’s exactly what drew Reuter, an artist, there with her creative partner, Joshua Rowan. They wanted to tell a story about the creek and its changing environment. More importantly, the pair wanted to highlight its place in the larger story of the Mississippi River watershed. 
Here in Springfield, Reuter saw “an opportunity to show both the urbanization and the way the natural environment can contribute to it.”
Rowan, meanwhile, studied the scene. As a photographer, he was looking for a composition that could serve as a “gateway” into the themes surrounding water resources — in Fassnight Creek’s case, erosion, flooding. 
“Even in the background, the tall grass is the diversity of vegetation,” Rowan said. “If we can include even this rigid piece of concrete, forming at the far end of the photograph — that goes far to tell the story.”
The pair have followed this process more than 400 times over the past 15 years in states across the Mississippi River Basin, from Iowa to Wisconsin and Tennessee to Louisiana. 
The artists build cairns, which are normally stacks of stones raised to mark trails or a place of significance. But theirs are delicate, fleeting sculptures made out of found glassware, often recycled vases or antique dishes. Each one is custom-made to its location — rivers, creeks and wetlands in the basin — and placed at 40-mile intervals from one another.
The goal is to spark conversation about the state of the watershed and how each location is impacted by both nature and human activity. “There’s the common things,” said Reuter. “About stormwater, about flooding, about the soil and what it supports, and the history of the place.”
Each cairn’s construction and placement is inspired by the story of water the artists uncover there. For example, one of their many cairns sat on top of a levee in Rohwer, Ark., while another stood in the shadow of a grain silo in Warsaw, Ill., rising from an overgrown flowerbed on a no-till farm. In Mississippi, the artists created temporary cairns in Greenville bridge, Coahoma County, Natchez and Vicksburg.
We’re “trying to get a new metaphor of how we’re connected to the water and land and each other,” Reuter said.
Before the cairns are built, the pair meet with local stakeholders to get a better sense of the location’s past, present and future. In Springfield, they talked to Caleb Sanders, a parks supervisor for the city. 
Sanders told them that, before colonization, the area surrounding Fassnight Creek was likely a prairie with a series of buffalo wallows — places where native wildlife could find watering holes and rest. While this creek might not ever return to what it once was, he said, the city is making improvements to help the creek better manage stormwater and protect its soil from washing away. 
“It’s a space that, like an art installation, challenges expectations and norms and really serves to give that same feel that you would have when you’re walking into an art space,” Sanders said.
The Springfield Art Museum commissioned the watershed cairn artists to produce a special series for the city. This cairn was created to spotlight Fassnight Creek, which flows by the art museum, and its place in the Mississippi River watershed.  Credit: Courtesy of Joshua Rowan
That mindset of connecting art and nature is why Joshua Best, museum educator at the Springfield Art Museum, commissioned the artists to create three cairns in a special series for the city. They met last year at an environmental conference and decided to work together on the local project. 
“Naturalization projects have been at the forefront of our civic thinking in Springfield,” Best said. “So it was one way that I saw to connect art with what we’re doing.” 
After viewing the site, the artists headed back to their cargo van. Inside were milk crates and plastic tote bags full of fragile glassware, cushioned with packing paper and styrofoam. The containers were labeled with descriptions like “swirly.” 
With help from Rowan, Reuter unboxed a long cylindrical vase with a small illustration taped to it: blueprints for the cairn that the artists would build.
The final product was a deep blue-green glass tower made of stacked platters and vases, its mismatched pieces evoking an otherworldly tea party set. For a brief moment, it rose from the bubbling Fassnight Creek, marking the many paths that intersected here across time: that of the buffalo, rainwater and visitors to the art museum.
True to the artist’s goal of sustainability, the sculptures are not meant to stay. “The photograph and the sculpture are both capturing a moment, and that moment doesn’t exist beyond that,” Reuter said.
A cairn glows at dusk among recently planted native species. The dark building in the background is the Hotel of Terror, a longstanding haunted house in the city. The “Haunted Hotel” image was commissioned by the Springfield Art Museum in a special watershed cairns series for the city. Credit: Courtesy of Joshua Rowan
After they’re photographed, the artists take the cairns apart, storing the pieces for possible reuse elsewhere in the basin. The artists log each cairn’s location and add the photos to their interactive map.
Occasionally, the glass sculptures might find themselves reconstructed at an art exhibition alongside Rowan’s photographs. In Chicago, the Watershed Art and Ecology Center is hosting the pair’s artwork through Oct. 31.
For Reuter, the connection between each community and the Mississippi River is why they’ve kept this project going.
“That’s what we’re trying to mark with the cairns,” Reuter said. “Not only the biological, ecological, but the history and the dynamics of the place. And the culture — the human culture — and how we all interact. None of it is independent of it.”
This story is a product of the Mississippi River Basin Ag & Water Desk, an independent reporting network based at the University of Missouri.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Democrats ramp up outreach in Va.’s 1st, 2nd and 5th Districts 2 weeks before Election Day
text:
Former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, center, stumps for Democratic congressional candidates in Virginia on Oct. 19, 2026. From left: Elaine Luria, Tom Perriello, Buttigieg, U.S. Rep. Jennifer McClellan, D-Richmond and Shannon Taylor. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)In the final stretch before the pivotal midterm elections on Nov. 3, Democrats at the local, state and national level are ramping up their engagement with voters in Virginia’s 1st, 2nd and 5th Congressional Districts and eyeing potential partisan flips in the competitive contests.
At a rally with the Democratic candidates in the three districts on Monday, former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg said that the road to shifting the U.S. House of Representatives from red to blue runs through Virginia.
“We’ve got enough rubber stamps for Donald Trump in Washington,” Buttigieg said. “It’s time for real leaders who are going to remember who they’re working for. That is the difference between the current Republican one-party control in Washington and a Democratic majority in the House,” Buttigieg said.
With US House control hanging in the balance, Wittman faces Taylor in contentious VA-01 race

Henrico’s chief prosecutor Shannon Taylor is hoping to oust longtime incumbent U.S. Rep. Rob Wittman, R- Westmoreland. The 1st District —  which stretches downward from Westmoreland and wraps around Richmond’s suburbs — has voted reliably Republican in recent years but pundits have marked it as a tossup this year. 
Elaine Luria, who used to represent the Hampton Roads-anchored 2nd, is facing a rematch against U.S. Rep. Jen Kiggans, R-Virginia Beach. The Navy veterans have each held the swingy seat for two terms, with Kiggans first ousting Luria in 2022.
Luria and Kiggans rematch in Va.’s 2nd Congressional District among most-watched races in nation

In the 5th, a GOP stronghold which sprawls from just north of Charlottesville down to the North Carolina border, former congressman Tom Perriello aims to replace U.S. Rep. John McGuire, R-Goochland. 
Former U.S. Department of Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg speaks at a campaign event for democratic congressional candidates in Virginia on Oct. 19, 2026. (Photo by Charlotte Rene Woods/Virginia Mercury)
Perriello is the lone Democrat to have represented the 5th in the past two decades and analysts pinpoint the contest as competitive this year. 
At Monday’s event, Perriello noted the growing healthcare disparities within the district, as rural patients drive further for treatment and various hospitals in Virginia’s South Side lack obstetrics care for expecting parents. 
“We have families struggling across this district who are hopeful for the first time in years,” Perriello said. “(They’re) hopeful that they will have champions who will put up with the process of politics in order to do public service.” 
During his one term in the U.S. House of Representatives, Perriello cast a decisive vote as Democrats advanced the Affordable Care Act, an insurance marketplace for people who’d otherwise have no healthcare options.
Perriello seeks another 5th District upset as McGuire leans on Trump

Perriello lost re-election in 2010 after voting for former President Barack Obama’s flagship policy.
Buttigieg reiterated Perriello’s support for it at the rally, saying the ACA “saved countless lives and is deservedly one of the winning issues for Democrats.” 
He joined the trio of candidates in lambasting President Donald Trump and the Republican majorities in Congress, whom they blamed for rising gas, grocery and healthcare prices amid Trump’s war with Iran. 
Wittman, Kiggans and McGuire have all voted in favor of H.R. 1, a reconciliation bill that puts 300,000 Virginians at risk of losing Medicaid. Virginia hospitals have also trimmed services in the past year in advance of changes to hospital funding mechanisms included in the bill, several citing H.R.1 as a factor. Thirteen rural hospitals have been identified as at risk of potential closure.
Though Wittman was one of 17 Republicans to back extending now-expired ACA subsidies, Taylor took aim at him for siding with his party and Trump on many issues. 
“I’ve spent my career building cases, and I know what it takes to win one: evidence and persistence,” Taylor told the crowd of a few hundred at the Henrico Theatre. “We’ve got nearly 20 years of evidence against Rob Whitman, and now all we need is you.” 
With the 2nd district having the highest concentration of military in the state, Luria criticized Kiggans for her expressed support of the Iran war. 
Congress has not formally approved the conflict that Trump launched in February, a fact the Democrats pressed Monday and in recent months on the campaign trail.
After noting higher gas prices, which Kiggans has admitted are a consequence of the conflict, Luria said “in Hampton Roads, it’s even more personal” because the fight also means constituents there are deploying. 
“We need a leader in Hampton Roads again who is going to stand up for our military, stand up for our veterans, and put a check on this administration,” Luria said. 
In a statement ahead of the rally, RNC spokeswoman Emma Hall emphasized Buttigieg’s failed 2020 presidential campaign and the fact that he went on to work for former President Joe Biden.
With no reference to the Perriello and McGuire matchup, she called Taylor and Luria “desperate” for campaigning alongside a “Biden hack” and criticized the candidates for their records in office.  
With roughly 15 days to go before Election Day, Republican and Democratic candidates statewide are making their final appeals to voters. Early voting is underway and ends Oct. 31. Read The Mercury’s voter guide to learn more about the candidates and races.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware’s pumpkin season serves up 10 fall favorites from Hockessin to the beaches
text:
From savory soups and pumpkin French toast to handmade ice cream and seasonal coffee drinks, Delaware restaurants and bakeries offer plenty of ways to taste autumn.
Oct. 20, 2026
HOCKESSIN, Del. — Pumpkin season in Delaware is about more than carving jack-o’-lanterns and decorating front porches. Across the First State, restaurants, bakeries and ice cream shops are finding creative ways to bring one of fall’s favorite flavors to the table.
Some have made pumpkin a signature dish, while others introduce seasonal treats that disappear when autumn ends.
From a longstanding Hockessin soup to pumpkin-flavored ice cream at the beaches, here are 10 Delaware destinations worth considering this fall. Several offerings are listed on current menus, while others are documented seasonal favorites whose return should be confirmed before visiting.
1. Pumpkin mushroom soup at the Back Burner Restaurant & Tavern — Hockessin
Few pumpkin dishes in Delaware have the staying power of Back Burner’s signature pumpkin mushroom soup. Unlike most seasonal offerings, this Hockessin favorite remains on the menu throughout the year.
The creamy soup combines pumpkin and mushrooms, finished with crème fraîche, croutons and chives. Its popularity has made it a defining dish at the restaurant, attracting customers who return specifically for the soup.
The restaurant’s published menu lists the soup at $10 for a cup and $12 for a bowl. It also is available for takeout, making it an easy fall meal to enjoy at home.
Website: backburner.com
Phone: 302-239-2314
2. Pumpkin crab bisque at Big Fish Grill — Rehoboth Beach
Big Fish Grill has developed a following for its seasonal pumpkin crab bisque, combining the flavor of fall squash with one of Delaware’s best-known seafood ingredients.
The bisque has appeared on past restaurant menus and holiday catering offerings, including a Thanksgiving menu that offered larger quantities for customers to take home.
Its combination of pumpkin and crab has attracted enough attention that regional dining guides have highlighted the soup as a seasonal favorite.
The restaurant’s current website does not establish whether the bisque has returned for October 2026, so diners should call to confirm its availability.
Website: bigfishgrill.com
Phone: 302-227-3474
3. Pumpkin pie cold brew at the Station on Kings — Lewes
The Station on Kings offers a fall twist on coffee with a pumpkin pie cold brew listed on its online ordering menu.
The drink combines cold brew coffee, house-made pumpkin syrup, cinnamon cold foam and Biscoff cookie crumbles. The online menu lists it at $8.
The café has previously offered a pumpkin pecan torte with layers of pecan cake, caramel crémeux and pumpkin Bavarian cream, although that pastry could not be confirmed on the current menu.
With its café, pastry offerings and garden-center atmosphere, The Station provides a pleasant stop for visitors exploring Lewes during the fall.
Website: thestationlewes.com
Phone: 302-645-0300
4. Pumpkin pie praline French toast at Egg — Rehoboth Beach
For breakfast lovers, Egg offers one of the more creative ways to enjoy pumpkin without waiting for dessert.
Its pumpkin pie praline French toast combines pumpkin custard-soaked French toast with a pecan topping, bringing together traditional breakfast ingredients and the flavors of pumpkin pie.
The dish appears on the restaurant’s published menu at $17, making it one of the more clearly documented pumpkin offerings at the beaches.
Egg has also featured fall-inspired cocktails in previous seasons, although those selections may change.
Website: eggrehoboth.com
Phone: 302-227-3447
5. Pumpkin pie and pumpkin roll at Bing’s Bakery — Newark
Delaware’s oldest continuously operating bakery keeps pumpkin season traditional.
Bing’s Bakery in Newark offers a classic 9-inch pumpkin pie and a pumpkin roll filled with cream cheese icing. The bakery’s website currently lists the pie at $17.95 and the pumpkin roll at $20.
Both products are advertised as available through Thanksgiving, giving customers an opportunity to bring familiar seasonal desserts to family gatherings.
For those who prefer traditional baked goods over pumpkin-flavored drinks, Bing’s provides a dependable choice.


Delaware’s Longest Running Bakery


Website: bingsbakery.com
Phone: 302-737-5310
6. Pumpkin bars and seasonal pastries at Dolcé Bakery and Coffee Shop — Milford
In downtown Milford, Dolcé Bakery and Coffee Shop has a history of preparing pumpkin bars and pumpkin rolls alongside its selection of fresh pastries.
Older published menus identify both pumpkin specialties, although the bakery’s current online menu does not specifically confirm that they are available this fall.
The downtown café offers coffee, pastries and a casual atmosphere for visitors exploring Milford’s shops and businesses.
Customers looking for the pumpkin bars should contact the bakery before visiting.
Website: dolcebakery.com
Phone: 302-422-5760
7. Pumpkin spice latte Spark’d Creative Pastry + Coffee — Wilmington
Spark’d Creative Pastry + Coffee brings pumpkin season to downtown Wilmington through its fall beverage menu.
At its I.M. Pei Building location on Market Street, the shop lists a pumpkin spice latte available hot or iced. Customers can also add pumpkin cold foam to customize their beverages.
The current online ordering menu lists the seasonal latte starting at $5.50.
While Spark’d is known for its creative pastry selection, specific pumpkin pies and cheesecakes mentioned in earlier descriptions could not be confirmed on its current online menu.
Website: sparkdcreativepastry.com
Phone: 302-594-3966
8. Pumpkin pie ice cream at Hopkins Farm Creamery — Lewes
Hopkins Farm Creamery offers a distinctly Delaware approach to pumpkin season by combining locally produced dairy products with traditional fall flavors.
The creamery has offered pumpkin pie ice cream as part of its seasonal selection, a flavor documented in regional tourism and restaurant coverage.
Located on Dairy Farm Road, the family dairy operation makes its own ice cream and offers visitors a chance to enjoy a frozen dessert in a farm setting.
The pumpkin pie flavor is historically documented, but its availability for October 2026 has not been confirmed on the creamery’s current website. Its telephone number provides recorded information rather than live customer service.
Website: hopkinsfarmcreamery.com
Phone: 302-645-7163, recorded information line
9. Small-batch pumpkin ice cream at Marigold Creamery — Lewes
One of the clearest current pumpkin finds at the beaches comes from Marigold Creamery, a small-batch ice cream business operating from a truck in the parking lot at The Station on Kings.
Its published flavor list includes pumpkin ice cream, offering another way to experience fall without ordering a traditional pie or pastry.
Marigold’s website lists Oct. 23-25 as its final operating weekend of the 2026 season, giving pumpkin lovers a limited opportunity to visit before the business closes for the year.
Customers interested in purchasing pints can preorder by email, subject to availability and confirmation from the creamery.
Website: marigoldcreamery.com
10. Fall treats, cider doughnuts and pumpkin picking af Fifer Orchards — Camden-Wyoming
For families who want to experience pumpkin season beyond the restaurant table, Fifer Orchards offers a combination of farm activities and seasonal foods.
The farm’s 2026 Fall Festival runs from Sept. 19 through Nov. 7, with pumpkin picking, a corn maze and seasonal attractions.
Visitors can also enjoy the farm’s apple cider doughnuts, kettle corn, cider and other treats.
Although Fifer’s has been associated with pumpkin desserts, its current website does not specifically confirm pumpkin pies or pumpkin rolls. The cider doughnuts and fall activities, however, are advertised as part of the seasonal experience.
It’s an option for visitors who want to make a day of autumn rather than simply stop for a meal.
ite: fifers.com
Phone: 302-697-2141
Fall flavors worth seeking out
Delaware’s autumn food scene offers something for almost every preference, from savory soups and seafood bisques to traditional bakery desserts and small-batch ice cream.
The advantage of living in a small state is that many of these destinations can become part of a fall day trip, whether that means breakfast at the beach, dessert in Newark or a stop at a Kent County farm.
The 10 spots were selected from restaurant reviews on respected apps,  local visitor guides (including Visit Delaware and Visit Rehoboth), Delaware Today and Delaware Online coverage, and restaurant write-ups that specifically praised particular pumpkin dishes. Priority went to items with the strongest reputations—such as cult-following soups, year-round staples, and standout pastries—while also aiming for geographic variety across the state and a mix of savory, breakfast, and dessert options rather than only basic lattes or generic pies. The ranking reflects the depth of that local praise, not a formal tasting or poll.

Where: Hockessin, Wilmington, Newark, Milford, Camden-Wyoming, Lewes and Rehoboth Beach.
