name: Connecticut Mirror
title: These white suburban moms regret voting for Trump but aren’t sold on Dems
text:
This story was originally reported by Grace Panetta of The 19th.  Meet Grace and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
Two years ago, six White suburban mothers were among the more than 77 million Americans who voted to put President Donald Trump back in the White House. Now, they say they regret it. 
In a recent focus group convened by Navigator Research, a Democratic polling and public opinion firm, and shared exclusively with The 19th, the six Trump voters discussed their disappointment with his second term — and their mixed feelings about the upcoming midterm elections. Navigator shared the group with The 19th on the condition that the participants be referred to only by their first names to protect their privacy.     
Chrissy, a 44-year-old woman from Michigan, said that two years ago, she was “lazy” in basing her vote on political ads and discussions with others instead of her own research. 
Now, she’s committed to voting for candidates who will check Trump. 
“He’s pushed the country into an authoritarian playbook,” she said. “And if we don’t do something to stop it right now, it’s unlikely that there’ll be much left.” 
Trump is also losing women who were once among his most committed backers. 
“I was a die-hard supporter, but it’s been a complete backstab since, pretty much, the storming of the Capitol for me,” said Kristen, a 39-year-old woman in Ohio. “That’s when my opinion really started changing about how he is as a leader.”  
Nicole, a 47-year-old in Texas, could relate. She believes Trump “might have his intentions in the right place,” but his second term hasn’t matched his campaign promises. She knows people struggling to afford groceries and turning to public assistance programs to make ends meet, and she thinks things “will get worse before they get better.” 
“I just feel we’re drowning, and it only started when Trump got in office,” she said. “I was fully, like she said, a die-hard fan of Trump. I mean, flag supporter, everything. Now I feel like I regret voting for him, I’ll just be honest.” 
Melissa Toufanian, a managing director at Navigator, said their research has found that 1 in 4 people who voted for Trump in 2024 now regret it. Moms are more likely to regret their votes than dads — and suburban women are a critical election demographic for both parties. 
While all the focus group participants have soured on Trump, they aren’t all sold on Democrats. Several expressed deep disillusionment with politics and doubted their votes could meaningfully change what they see as a broken status quo upheld by both political parties.    
“I do think in a lot of ways that our voice doesn’t matter anymore,” said Gayle, a 47-year-old in Florida. “I think Congress sucks, honestly. I just think it sucks. I don’t think that they’re in it for the people. I think they’re in it for themselves these days, and it’s really on both sides.”
The cost of living consistently ranks as voters’ top concern, and many Democratic candidates are putting affordability front and center in their campaigns. Polling from The 19th and YouGov found that women are more worried than men about paying for groceries, healthcare, housing and retirement. 
Even women who weren’t as personally affected by rising prices saw the war in Iran and the resulting increase in gas and fuel prices as a clear about-face from Trump’s 2024 campaign promises to lower costs. 
“I’m not struggling, but so many people are,” said Denise, a 49-year-old woman from Ohio. “I’m repulsed about the tariffs that we’ve put on our neighbor in Canada, the war, basically picking on other countries and just starting a war for no reason.”  
Of the entire group, Gayle had the most positive assessment of Trump’s second term and the economy. But she said she regretted voting for him because of the war in Iran, which “really messed things up.”
“If you’re looking at the gas prices versus if I’m going to see a nuclear bomb happen, I’m more concerned with my gas prices than I am with the nuclear bomb, to be honest,” she said. 
And it wasn’t just the economy that made the women in the focus group turn against Trump.  
Denise pointed to Trump “taking down history because he’s a narcissist” in tearing down the East Wing of the White House to build a new ballroom.
“It just … that disgusts me,” she said. “He had no right to do that, and that’s one of the big things that pissed me off.” 
Women in the focus group said that while they supported enforcing immigration laws and securing the border, they thought the government had gone too far. 
“I’m not against the deportation, I’m against inhumane treatment in that process,” said Kristen, the 39-year-old in Ohio. 
Brandy, a 43-year-old woman in North Carolina, said she was particularly troubled by federal immigration officials killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minnesota. She said when she posted about Good’s killing on Facebook, she was attacked by her friends who are “extreme Trump lovers.”  
“He just makes people lose their human decency,” she said. 
And they didn’t view other members of the Trump administration much more favorably. They used words like “terrible,” “compromised,” “Trump’s twin,” and “corrupt” to describe Vice President JD Vance. Secretary of State Marco Rubio was called “a liar,” and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.  “uneducated.” Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “should have stayed on TV,” Kristen said. 
But despite the group’s collective distaste for Trump and his inner circle, not all plan to vote for Democrats down the ballot in November. 
Denise in Ohio said she was leaning toward voting for Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio’s race for governor over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, whom she described as “up [Trump’s] rear end,” while Gayle in Florida said she planned to vote for the Republican, Rep. Byron Donalds, in her state’s gubernatorial race.  
Brandy said she didn’t like former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in North Carolina, but was voting for him because of GOP nominee Michael Whatley’s ties to a convicted sex offender who served in several leadership positions in the state Republican Party, something Democratic groups have spent millions highlighting in campaign ads. 
“I’m gonna go for the guy that doesn’t have a buddy that’s a sex offender,” she said. “Even though I don’t like him, he is the lesser of two evils.” 
Toufanian said Democrats have a big opportunity to focus on issues suburban women care about “and to really make some tangible improvements in their lives.” 
Food quality and safety is one of those issues. Nearly all the women cited it as a top concern, but only two had heard of the acronym MAHA, or Make America Healthy Again. 
“I think there’s a real opportunity because it touches on so many of the other issues that are so important in this election cycle, particularly corruption and affordability,” Toufanian said.
Most women in the focus group said they’re taking a wait-and-see approach to the 2028 presidential race. Two, Chrissy and Kristen, said they were open to voting for a Democrat but wouldn’t want to vote for Vance or former Vice President Kamala Harris, the 2024 Democratic presidential nominee.  
Chrissy said she’d primarily evaluate Republican candidates on whether they would further the “cruelty” and “highly polarized” atmosphere cultivated by Trump. 
“I don’t want the country to be identified like that anymore, at all. I don’t even want to be a member. … I don’t want to be a citizen of this country,” she said. “I’m embarrassed on a world stage.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC state rep calls state’s new curbside voting warning signs ‘intimidating’
text:
Curbside voting warning sign seen at an early voting site in Carteret County, N.C., Oct. 18, 2026. (Photo: Rep. Pricey Harrison on X) State Rep. Pricey Harrison, D-Guilford, is concerned about the tone of curbside voting signs outside some North Carolina early voting sites, calling them “intimidating and threatening” and “possibly a violation of state law.”
Rep. Pricey Harrison (Photo: NCGA)
“Come on #SBOE [State Board of Elections], stop suppressing the vote. You can do better,” Harrison wrote in a X post Sunday.
The signs were given to county boards of elections by the state board to use outside polling places near the spaces reserved for curbside voting. 
The signs remind voters that curbside voting is a service for “voters who cannot come inside due to age or disability ONLY.” They also warn that curbside voters must attest that they meet the requirements for curbside voting “under penalty of law.”
Harrison, who saw the sign at a polling site in Carteret County, told NC Newsline that she is concerned the signs might deter people with mental health issues or other non-visible health issues from utilizing curbside voting. 
“I think that maybe the sign’s a little harsher and more intimidating than it needs to be to dissuade folks who abuse the curbside voting option,” Harrison said.
Harrison said she’s worked a lot of polls over “several decades and has never seen signs like this before.” She says she’s also never seen anyone abuse curbside voting.
“I don’t want to second-guess somebody’s need to use the curbside voting lane,” Harrison said. 
N.C. Elections Director Sam Hayes (Photo: State Board of Elections)
But Sam Hayes, the state board’s executive director, defended the signs in an emailed response to questions.
“We have noticed an uptick in curbside voting, and this sign serves as a reminder that it is not intended for those who are truly not in need of it,” Hayes said. “It is not, as the tweet implies, some type of tactic to intimidate or suppress voting.”
Hayes said the signs follow existing law, which already requires people using curbside voting to sign an attestation that they meet the requirements to do so. He said that, given limited resources in some counties, the “use of curbside voting for the able-bodied takes away resources for those [who] are truly in need.”
NC officials express confidence in election integrity as early voting begins

Charlie Collicut, director of elections in Guilford County, said voters sometimes misunderstand curbside voting, so the signs serve as a good reminder that the service is intended for elderly citizens and those who are disabled. 
Collicut said that it’s also important to post accompanying signage indicating that curbside voting is welcome and available at polling sites.
He said counties aren’t required to use the signs provided by the state.
State board officials confirmed that Durham, Nash and Polk counties declined the state signs but added the counties did not express concerns similar to Harrison’s when declining them.
It’s a felony under state law for “any person knowingly to swear falsely with respect to any matter pertaining to any primary or election.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: PACs spend more than $6.2 million in Central Kentucky House district as Election Day looms
text:
Republican Ralph Alvarado, left, and Democrat Zach Dembo, right, are running in Kentucky's 6th Congressional District. (Photos provided by campaigns)Spending by political action committees in Kentucky’s most competitive U.S. House race has reached more than $6.2 million with two weeks to go until Election Day. 
In the 6th Congressional District, PACs boosting Republican Ralph Alvarado have a slight spending edge over those backing Democrat Zach Dembo, according to Federal Election Commission reports Monday. 
The GOP PACs have spent about $1.7 million in support of Alvarado and $1.4 million against Dembo for a total of nearly $3.2 million. The largest bulk of that funding, about $2.6 million, comes from the No Going Back PAC, which is tied to President Donald Trump’s political operation. Other active PACs include MAGA Inc., Americans Ready to Work and Protection Freedom PAC. 
On the Democrats’ side, PACs have spent just about $895,000 in support of Dembo and about $2.2 million against Alvarado. Most of that is $1.7 million from Kentuckians Not Corruption. Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear’s PAC, In this Together, has reported spending $500,000 on ads against Alvarado. Other active PACs include End Citizens United, VoteVets, and the Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates. 
The PAC’s dollars are going toward advertising on TV, digital placements, text messaging and more. 
Alvarado’s campaign is criticizing at least one donation to Kentuckians Not Corruption — $500,000 from Reid Hoffman, the LinkedIn founder who has been linked to former financier and convicted sex offender Jeffery Epstein.  
In a Friday press release, Alvarado said “dirty Epstein Class money fueling Zach Dembo’s campaign” before adding “the least Zach Dembo could do is apologize for dragging the rest of Kentucky into the sewer with him.” 
Trump, who endorsed Alvarado ahead of the primary election, is also mentioned in the Epstein Files. Elon Musk, an ally of Trump who has given to MAGA, Inc. this year, is in the files, too. 
Federal law prevents PACs from coordination with campaigns. 
Olivia Dupree, Dembo’s campaign manager said in a statement “Dembo doesn’t solicit money from shady corporate interests or dark money donors to get elected and will never be beholden to them and their interests.” 
“(Alvarado) has never once spoken up about the terrible actions of Jeffrey Epstein until it became politically convenient to do so, while Zach has been calling for a full release of the files since his first day in the campaign,” Dupree added. “There is only one candidate who has the record and political independence required to stand up for victims of crime, including Jeffrey Epstein’s victims, and that’s Zach Dembo.”
As for the campaigns’ finances, Dembo’s campaign reported $1.4 million in receipts for the third quarter of the year and a total of nearly $2.9 million. Alvarado’s campaign reported more than $666,000 in receipts in the third quarter for a total of nearly $2.2 million.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: En un mitin en Kansas, Trump defiende el historial de Marshall y llama a Hamilton una ‘vergüenza’
text:
El senador estadounidense Roger Marshall, republicano de Kansas, habla junto al presidente Donald Trump durante un mitin el 19 de octubre de 2026 en el Heartland Credit Union Arena de Park City, Kansas. (Foto de Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)PARK CITY — El presidente Donald Trump defendió el lunes el historial del senador estadounidense Roger Marshall y culpó a los jueces y a la ley estatal de la práctica del senador de demandar a pacientes con deudas médicas —lo que llevó a que algunos de ellos fueran arrestados— cuando era médico.
El presidente hizo campaña por Marshall y otros candidatos republicanos durante una visita a Kansas, entre Alaska y las Carolinas. Marshall se presenta a la reelección contra el reverendo Adam Hamilton, pastor de una mega-iglesia del área de Kansas City, quien es demócrata. También en la carrera está David Graham, un libertario de Overland Park.
Trump dedicó los primeros 20 minutos de su discurso de aproximadamente una hora y cuarenta minutos a mencionar apenas a Kansas, Marshall o Hamilton, para llamar al principal oponente de Marshall “mala persona” y “vergüenza”, mientras se centraba en la carrera al Senado de Michigan y condenaba a otros senadores demócratas. Durante todo su discurso, los manifestantes le interrumpieron al menos cinco veces mientras Trump reiteraba las prioridades republicanas de cara a las elecciones de mitad de mandato: fronteras seguras, un ejército más fuerte y costes más bajos.
Anunció un programa de “alivio del combustible de cosecha”, prometiendo compensar a los agricultores por los precios del diésel y la gasolina, que en las últimas semanas han superado los 6 dólares por galón en Kansas.
Trump emprendió una gira por Estados Unidos a principios de este mes, visitando estados tradicionalmente favorables a los republicanos antes de las elecciones de mitad de mandato del 3 de noviembre. Su parada en Kansas fue la primera desde 2018 y la primera vez que un presidente en ejercicio visita el área de Wichita en 20 años.
Calificó a Marshall como “uno de los mejores senadores de nuestro país” y advirtió a los asistentes sobre las consecuencias percibidas de que los demócratas ganaran elecciones de mitad de mandato, incluida la depresión económica.
Pero si los republicanos ganan, dijo: “Os daré dinero en efectivo.”
Trump ha repetido desde septiembre la promesa de 5,000 dólares en efectivo por cada adulto en EE. UU. si los republicanos ganan las elecciones de mitad de mandato para mantener el control de la Cámara de Representantes y el Senado.
Dijo que Marshall es un “tipo duro” y “de alta calidad”. Dijo que Marshall fue “injustamente acusado” por su práctica de demandar y solicitar órdenes de arresto contra personas que le debían dinero por servicios médicos cuando era médico en el centro de Kansas.
Trump culpó de los arrestos a un juez y a la ley, no a Marshall.
“Él no lo hizo”, dijo Trump.
“Te han molestado eso”, le dijo a Marshall.
Llamó a Hamilton “radical de izquierda” y “lunático” que “finge ser un moderado.”
Trump fue precedido en el escenario por siete funcionarios de Kansas que se presentaron a cargos públicos en noviembre, entre ellos Marshall y el músico de rock y entusiasta de la caza Ted Nugent. Cuando el presidente subió al escenario, de los aproximadamente 6,000 asientos del Heartland Credit Union Arena, en las afueras de Wichita, aproximadamente dos tercios estaban ocupados.
El rockero y cazador Ted Nugent posa para un fan en el mitin del presidente Donald Trump, el 19 de octubre de 2026, en el Heartland Credit Union Arena de Park City, Kansas. (Foto de Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Entre discursos, sonaba una lista de éxitos de Another Century y colas de concesiones se extendían por los asientos de un estadio que suele acoger música y eventos deportivos de tamaño medio.
También asistió la secretaria del Departamento de Agricultura de EE. UU., Brooke Rollins, el senador Eric Schmitt, republicano de Missouri, y la piloto de NASCAR Danica Patrick.
Marshall, en su discurso ante Trump, se centró en su oponente. Criticó las posturas de Hamilton sobre la inmigración y dijo que era “el demócrata liberal más radical que jamás haya superado una primaria para el Senado en la historia de Kansas.”
Hamilton se enfrentó a otros 10 candidatos demócratas en las primarias de agosto.
Tyson Brody, portavoz de la campaña de Hamilton, dijo que el mitin del lunes era señal de que la campaña de Marshall se hundía y de que Washington entraba en pánico.
“Están enviando refuerzos para mentir y atacar a Adam Hamilton, con el fin de intentar salvar a Marshall”, dijo Brody. “Pero nada de lo dicho en el mitin puede distraer del hecho de que los habitantes de Kansas están siendo aplastados por el aumento de los precios de la gasolina y el diésel, luchan por acceder a una sanidad asequible y están cansados de la corrupción en Washington.”
Marshall dijo que, si los republicanos pierden la carrera al Senado de Estados Unidos en Kansas, teme que los veteranos senadores demócratas Chuck Schumer de Nueva York, Elizabeth Warren de Massachusetts, Bernie Sanders de Vermont y Cory Booker de Nueva Jersey controlen el Senado de EE. UU.
“Los medios tradicionales quieren complicar demasiado esta carrera”, dijo Marshall.
Medios nacionales y expertos se han aferrado a Kansas en las últimas semanas, ya que la recaudación personal de Hamilton ha superado a la de Marshall, y grupos externos han empezado a inundar los mercados de Kansas con anuncios dirigidos a ambos extremos del espectro político.
El vicepresidente JD Vance visitó Kansas en septiembre y destacó los logros personales y profesionales de Marshall.
Los asistentes respondieron a los puntos de Trump sobre inmigración, género y economía.
“Creo que estas son unas elecciones muy importantes”, dijo Karen Malone, de Manhattan, a poco más de dos horas de Park City.
“Si queremos mantener nuestros valores en nuestro país, tenemos que votar, entusiasmarnos con el voto y escuchar lo que nuestros políticos tienen que decir”, añadió.
Malone dijo que no piensa en Marshall de la misma manera que en Trump. Dijo que aún votará por él, aunque no sea el mejor que los republicanos puedan ofrecer, y que desearía que fuera más vocal. Se presenta bien en las noticias televisivas, dijo, pero no habla lo suficiente sobre las necesidades rurales de Kansas.
El presidente Donald Trump habla durante un mitin el 19 de octubre de 2026 en el Heartland Credit Union Arena de Park City, Kansas. (Foto de Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Donna y Tom McLain viajaron durante aproximadamente dos horas y media desde Lenexa para ver a Trump. Dijeron que votaron por Marshall hace seis años y que planean volver a votar por él. Dijeron que no les molestan los informes sobre sus prácticas agresivas de cobro de deudas médicas ni su historial documental en Florida, donde tenía una segunda residencia hasta hace poco.
“Es política”, dijo Donna McLain. “Lo mismo puede decirse de su oponente.”
El Comité Nacional Republicano del Senado, antes de la visita de Trump a Kansas, expresó su apoyo a Marshall y calificó a Hamilton de “protector pedófilo”, refiriéndose a un voluntario de la iglesia de Hamilton que, en 2005 y 2006, tocó inapropiadamente a niños menores de edad en un campamento juvenil.
Trump y Marshall también mencionaron el incidente.
En informes de Kansas Reflector publicados en mayo y julio sobre las acusaciones de abuso que involucraban a la Iglesia de la Resurrección, con 25,000 miembros, Hamilton dijo que dos empleados de la iglesia llevaron a cabo una investigación interna sobre las denuncias surgidas en 2005. La investigación quedó inconclusa porque los niños no pudieron identificar al agresor, y el voluntario, Scott Moore, fue vetado en la iglesia en 2006, cuando el asunto también fue remitido a la policía. Moore falleció en 2015.
“El presidente Trump y Roger Marshall trabajan al unísono para reducir impuestos, proteger a las comunidades y nivelar el terreno de juego para los agricultores”, dijo Samantha Cantrell, secretaria de prensa regional del Comité Nacional Republicano del Senado.
Hamilton dijo en un vídeo publicado el lunes que las personas que votaron por Trump tienen un lugar en su campaña. Enfatizó su disposición a trabajar con el presidente.
“Cuando el presidente haga algo bueno por Kansas, estaré a su lado y lo diré. Cuando una decisión de Washington perjudique a nuestros agricultores, a nuestros hospitales rurales o a nuestros sueldos, también me enfrentaré a Washington y lo diré. Algunos días estaremos de acuerdo. Otros días no”, dijo Hamilton.
Hamilton y Marshall tienen previsto un debate televisivo el miércoles, del que Graham, el candidato libertario, ha sido excluido.
Graham dijo en un comunicado por correo electrónico que la visita de Trump el lunes era prueba de una contienda reñida.
“Mi porcentaje del electorado es mayor que la diferencia entre mis dos oponentes”, dijo Graham. “La mayor parte de mi apoyo proviene de votantes que simplemente no pueden votar por ninguno de los otros candidatos.”
Dijo que debería ser incluido en cualquier debate en el que participaran sus oponentes.
“Mis oponentes me están ignorando y espero que los votantes también lo hagan”, dijo. “No está funcionando. Soy el único candidato que habla de temas como la reforma de la justicia penal y la transparencia en el gobierno.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Whittier honored for supporting the World War II effort in Alaska
text:
Boats line the harbor at Whittier on Oct. 1, 2026. A new National Park Service designation honors Whittier for its role as a supply and support center for the World War II effort in Alaska. Whittier continues to serve as a najor transportation hub for Alaska, though now in the civilian sphere. It has marine, rail and road connections.  (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The Prince William Sound town of Whittier is sometimes called the “strangest town in Alaska” because nearly all of its roughly 250 residents dwell in a single high-rise building. Now it has another claim to fame: It is designated by the National Park Service as one of the nation’s American World War II Heritage Cities.
 

The 14-story Begich Towers building in Whittier is seen on July 17, 2025. The building is home to most of the town’s residents. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The designation, announced last week, is part of the Park Service’s American World War II Heritage City Program, created in 2019 as part of the John D. Dingell Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act. Under the program, one city in each state or territory can receive the designation.
Whittier was one of 10 cities given the honor last week. Among the others were Charlotte Amalie, U.S. Virgin Islands; Pendleton, Oregon, and Honolulu, Hawaii.
“These designations highlight the enduring legacy of service, sacrifice, innovation, and industrial achievement that helped establish the United States as the “Arsenal of Democracy” and continue to shape our national story,” Jessica Bowron, the National Park Service’s acting director, said in a statement. “The 2026 designations reinforce the role communities played across the country, from manufacturing critical military equipment to hosting strategic training facilities, and their ongoing work to preserve and interpret this history for future generations.” 
 

A sign, seen Aug. 5, 2024, explains the history of the Buckner Building in Whittier. THe building was erected by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers but used for only a few years before being abandoned. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Whittier’s World War II designation stems from its service as a supply and support center for the war effort in Alaska. To put Whittier into use, the Army blasted a tunnel through Maynard Mountain and laid a rail spur connecting the site with the Alaska Railroad. The rail link to the port town was completed in 1943.
Aside from its handy location as a transportation hub — a function the city continues to serve — Whittier had another attribute that attracted the military. Shrouded by tall mountains and near-constant cloud cover, it was well-hidden from enemy eyes.
Whittier’s military service continued for a while after the war. The sprawling Buckner Building, completed by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers in 1953, was considered a city unto itself, with accommodations for 1,000 soldiers and amenities like a theater, bowling alley and hospital. The Corps also completed the 14-story Hodge Building in 1957. It was converted to civilian use and later named for the late U.S. Rep. Nick Begich, D-Alaska, who died in a 1972 plane crash.
 

A sign on a fence at the Buckner Building in Whittier, seen Aug. 5, 2024, warns about the presence of cancer-causing asbestos. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The Begich Towers building remains in use as the home of most residents, but the Buckner Building was shut down after only a few years. Local and state officials are trying to figure out what to do with the Buckner building, which has historic status but is also in extreme disrepair and riddled with asbestos and other dangers.
Whittier’s history extends far earlier than its military era.
The same location that made it strategic to the Army also made it important to Indigenous travelers prior to European contact.
A short hike over Portage Pass connected the Prince William Sound homeland of the Alutiiq people and the Cook Inlet region homeland of the Dena’ina people. Portage Pass’ role as a trade link continued after European contact, with explorers and miners also making the quick trek. In the past, travelers crossed a portion of Portage Glacier, but the glacier has since receded dramatically.
 

A truck emerges from the Anton Anderson Memorial Tunnel on the Whittier side on July 16, 2025, as vehicles are lined up in lanes on the right in preparation to leave Whittier through the tunnel. The tunnel has only one lane, and traffic goes through in shifts. It also accomodates train traffic. The tunnel was built by the Army during World War II as a rail link enabling Whittier to serve as a supply and support center. It was later converted, and began accomodating auto traffice as well as trains in 2000. It is named for the Army engineer who supervised its construction. (Photo byYereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Now part of the Chugach National Forest, Portage Pass remains a popular hiking destination. The modern recreation trail runs about 2 miles from the Whittier trailhead to Portage Lake, still linking the Alutiiq and Dena’ina homelands.
Whittier’s new designation adds to others in Alaska that honor the state’s role in World War II.
Best-known is the National Park Service’s Aleutian Islands World War II Heritage Area. Based in Unalaska, it commemorates the war history in the Aleutians, which includes the 1942 Battle of Attu, the Dutch Harbor bombing and the trauma endured by the Indigenous Unangan people.
A small recreational vessel sails on Oct. 1, 2026, through the Whittier harbor, where the USS Ted Stevens towers over the docked boats. The new U.S> Navy warship is named after the late U.S. Sen. Ted Stevens, a World War II veteran. Whittier was the site of the USS Ted Stevens commissioning on Oct. 3, 2026.(Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Think capping ticket prices will save you money? Think again.
text:
MASSACHUSETTS FANS ARE paying steeper and steeper prices to go to concerts and see their favorite bands.  
It’s a frustratingly common experience: sitting at the computer for hours continually refreshing the window just to get the opportunity to buy a ticket, if they aren’t sold out yet. The lucky few who actually break through have to hand over a small fortune for a ticket – and pay for not just the price of admission, but also service fees and add-ons that drive the cost even higher. 
For too many families, attending a concert has become prohibitively expensive, pricing out entire communities from the experiences that bring people together.  
Gov. Healey is right to look at this issue. Unfortunately, the proposal included in her supplemental budget bill, called “The Great Divide Act,” will likely only make the problem worse. That’s because the policy strengthens the very monopoly that has made ticket buying so expensive: Ticketmaster. 
The Great Divide Act has some smart policies, including a ban on deceptive websites and “speculative” tickets, which are listed for sale before the reseller even owns the ticket. Such policies hold bad actors accountable and should be enacted. 
But consumer concerns stem from the bill’s price cap, which only applies when fans resell tickets. At first glance, capping prices on websites like SeatGeek and StubHub to 10 percent above a ticket’s original cost might sound like it benefits everyone. In reality, it’s really a giveaway to Ticketmaster and its parent company Live Nation. While the monopoly makes more money, fans will be left with the unintended consequences. 
The National Consumer League doesn’t oppose price caps as a matter of principle. But to have any chance of working, they must be backed by robust enforcement and a serious strategy to fight fraud. Sadly, Gov. Healey’s proposal includes neither. 
The Great Divide Act’s price caps will almost certainly result in far fewer tickets being listed on regulated resale marketplaces. While no one likes paying above face value for a ticket, these marketplaces do provide a safe, regulated place for consumers to buy tickets to sold-out events and even find below-face value bargains when events don’t sell out. 
What won’t change if the bill becomes law is that fans’ demand to see their favorite artists and teams will inevitably exceed the supply of tickets. With far fewer tickets available on secondary marketplaces, desperate fans will seek out unregulated marketplaces like Facebook Marketplace, Craigslist, TikTok and other platforms. There will be a huge incentive for scammers to flood these unregulated marketplaces with fraudulent tickets, ripping off an untold number of Massachusetts fans.  
We’ve already seen this play out in Australia and Ireland, where ticket resale price caps are in effect and fraud rates are 400 percent higher than the United Kingdom, which doesn’t have a cap.  
Just north of the border, the same pattern is emerging after Ontario enacted a price cap earlier this year. In Massachusetts, experts ranging from the president of the Boston chapter of the Association of Certified Fraud Examiners to a former State Police sergeant have warned about the wave of fraud this law could unlock. 
Someone who pays a premium for a ticket on a regulated resale platform may be frustrated by the price, but a paper trail exists. There’s a customer service team and a path to a refund if something goes wrong. A fan who sends cash to a stranger on social media through Venmo risks both their money and their ticket, with no recourse. 
Capping resale prices doesn’t just hurt fans through a higher chance of being scammed. It could also lead to higher ticket prices, overall.  
Today, Ticketmaster controls an estimated 86 percent of concert ticket sales, while its parent company Live Nation owns or operates some of the largest concert venues and manages some of the biggest musical acts. That’s why a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general, including Massachusetts AG Andrea Campbell, took the company to court for illegal monopolization — and won.  
If this price cap passes, that 86 percent monopoly then inches closer to 100 percent.  
Fans will have no alternatives to Ticketmaster. A company whose CEO says tickets are “underpriced” and that uses dynamic pricing to increase the cost fans pay in real time can’t be trusted to bring ticket costs down. 
Eliminating the only competitors preventing Ticketmaster from controlling every ticket transaction in Massachusetts—and setting whatever price they want—is not consumer protection. It’s regulatory malpractice. 
During a recent Boston Public Radio segment, Ken Casey of the Dropkick Murphys told Gov.  Healey that Live Nation is “the real enemy in the room.” She should take that message to heart, abandon this misguided resale price cap, and pursue legislation that addresses the monopoly’s predatory pricing practices. 
John Breyault is vice president of public policy telecommunications and fraud at the National Consumers League.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Ticket prices are out of control. Gov. Healey’s bill will make them worse.
text:
FOR YEARS, Massachusetts fans have been struggling with the cost of ticket prices to go see their favorite bands and live acts. 
Now, Gov. Healey has introduced a bill in the Legislature that she claims will rein in concert pricing and save consumers money by targeting platforms that allow people to buy and sell tickets. In September, she included the bill in her $2.24 billion supplemental budget bill. 
But this bill unwittingly hurts concertgoers, especially working-class fans, who often have to choose between a car payment or a rent payment, and paying for a ticket. The unintended consequences will have chilling anti-consumer effects. The very prices it’s intended to lower will actually rise, because this law gives Ticketmaster and Live Nation total control over all ticket pricing in the state. 
I spent decades booking and promoting shows across the country. That’s why I know this bill has a serious flaw that will hurt the very fans it’s meant to help. By setting limits on the price when reselling a ticket on legitimate marketplaces, the law simply makes it easier for Ticketmaster to gouge fans when they try to buy a ticket online in the queue. 
Sixteen years ago, Live Nation targeted me for trying to launch a music festival at the Meadowlands in New Jersey. I never struggled to schedule shows before, but once Live Nation’s threats started coming, musical acts and talent agencies stopped returning my calls. I have been locked in a lawsuit with them ever since. I’ve seen how they operate up close – which is why I support Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s ongoing lawsuit against their monopolistic practices. 
This new bill helps Live Nation and Ticketmaster’s monopoly get even stronger. Here’s why. 
Today, fans who want to go to a concert, a show, or a sporting event buy their tickets online – almost uniformly from Ticketmaster and Live Nation. If the event is sold out, or the tickets are too expensive or unattractive (sitting behind a pole at Fenway Park), fans have the option to visit one of many resale marketplaces – which are like the eBay of tickets. If there’s significant demand for an event, such as a Taylor Swift concert, the resale prices will be higher than the box office. But there are many times where buying the ticket on resale can be cheaper: it just happened in August with BTS at Gillette Stadium, where resale tickets went for as low as $8 while Ticketmaster charged more than $135. 
Gov. Healey’s bill would make big changes.  
The price limits will make it illegal for fans to buy and sell tickets at the best price. This change will backfire, because you can cap prices, but you can’t put a limit on how badly fans want to see a show. That will push ticket sales to social media or to the parking lot behind a venue, where fraud is rampant. Fans face the unfair choice of taking a gamble on the black market or missing out on the once-in-a-lifetime experience of seeing their favorite artist live. 
Ticketmaster and Live Nation already control the venues and ticket sales almost everywhere – an estimated 86 percent of the concert market runs through their monopoly. Gov. Healey’s bill places no restrictions on them. That means Ticketmaster and Live Nation are free to continue using unfair and deceptive tactics that hurt fans, like dynamic pricing. Dynamic pricing is happening across industries – where the price increases on people when they’re literally trying to complete a purchase. It’s wrong, and should be outlawed. 
The US Senate has been investigating Ticketmaster and Live Nation’s unfair practices, and their report from March points to one example in 2021 when Ticketmaster used their dynamic ticket pricing technique on fans who wanted to see Morgan Wallen – it delivered a 94 percent revenue jump. From 2019 to 2022, Ticketmaster saw a 700 percent increase in revenue on dynamically priced tickets. 
The resale price caps would also still allow Ticketmaster to hold back tickets from the general public. The strategy is as simple as it is underhanded: Ticketmaster can declare a show is “sold out,” dramatically increasing demand, and then release more seats that were held back as “platinum” tickets at exorbitant prices. It’s the purest form of price gouging—and completely legal under Gov. Healey’s bill. New Jersey Congresswoman Nellie Pou’s  HOLDBACKS Act is commonsense legislation that would tackle this hidden ticket inventory. 
Gov. Healey’s bill would pour gasoline on an already raging fire. 
So how should this legislation be crafted to actually help working families? It should target Ticketmaster’s predatory pricing approach, while putting reasonable guardrails on the legitimate resale market – not wiping it out entirely. 
For about half of live events, fans can get tickets on resale at prices that are lower than what they’re charged at the box office. This bill would gut that market in Massachusetts. Ticketmaster wins. Fans lose. 
This bill also hurts smaller artists trying to launch their careers and the small, independent venues they play at. Most of us know about the high prices to see Noah Kahan, Bruce Springsteen, and Taylor Swift. But there are an estimated 250,000 artists pursuing music professionally, playing shows at thousands of small independent venues around the country. Cheaper resale tickets fill empty seats, bringing in more fans who buy drinks, purchase merchandise, and come back for future shows. An empty seat does nothing for anyone. 
There are so many working-class fans who buy concert tickets and keep this industry running. I now do door-to-door outreach in Massachusetts, talking to Uber drivers, Dunkin’ workers, construction workers, parents just trying to take their kids to a show. They hate dynamic pricing and can only afford tickets by waiting for resale prices to drop.  
Fans need more choices, not fewer, to lower prices. They need platforms they can actually understand. 
When Live Nation and Ticketmaster sought approval for their merger, their executives told the US Senate it would benefit consumers and wouldn’t raise prices or harm competition. We know how that turned out. Earlier this year, a federal jury found that Ticketmaster violated state and federal antitrust laws in operating as a monopoly.  
We should be fighting against that market domination, not enacting legislation that further enables it. 
Tommy Dorfman is the founder of Juice Entertainment and a former concert and nightclub promoter.

name: California
title: They killed with their big rigs. The DMV routinely did nothing
text:
Trucks and cars drive along Interstate 580 through Altamont Pass on Aug. 18, 2026. Photo by Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters




After Baljit Singh killed a 26-year-old man on a motorcycle with his semitruck, the California Department of Motor Vehicles didn’t suspend his commercial drivers license. 
Eleven months later, he crashed his truck again, killing Jenny Chow, a mother of two on the way home from visiting colleges with her son. The DMV still didn’t take any action. 
It did, however, go after Chow’s widower, Loren. The DMV threatened to seize his home or garnish his wages. The agency said he was late paying his vehicle registration fee on the SUV that was totaled, by the truck driver it allowed to stay on the road.

Loren Chow: “The death was completely avoidable. That accident never should have happened.”

In the latest installment of their License to Kill series, CalMatters investigative reporters Lauren Hepler and Robert Lewis turn their focus to how the state handles the people driving 80,000 pound vehicles up and down the state, and across the country. 
They found that nearly half of all commercial drivers charged with vehicular manslaughter over a recent five-year period still had a valid license. 
“State law empowers the agency to investigate drivers involved in fatal and serious-injury collisions and suspend their licenses,” they write. “But the DMV routinely does nothing.”
You can dig into this story two different ways: 

Read: Why California allows drivers like Singh to stay on the road. 


Watch: Our new documentary with Evident Media to follow along with the reporters as they unravel the story. 




Join CalMatters, AAJA Sac, ABC 10 and The Sacramento Observer for a free VotingMatters event Wednesday in Sacramento. The event enables attendees to learn and discuss the upcoming election and focuses on the ballot propositions and insurance commissioner race. Register here to attend in person.
Other Stories You Should Know


About those bonds on your ballot


Courtyard view of the UCLA Research Park in West Los Angeles on Aug. 19, 2024. Photo by Brian van der Brug, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images




It’s time for you to decide whether California should issue more bonds — debt — for things that could make the state a better place to live. We’re here to help with two new stories today on ballot measures that call for new bonds.

Immunology research: Proposition 38 would allocate up to $8.4 billion for scientific research on diseases and cures concerning the immune system. But a deeper look at the proposal reveals that half that money would go to a single institute — the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy — whose principal funder wrote Prop. 38. The proposition’s language also would exempt the institute from having to comply with state transparency laws. Read more from Mikhail Zinshteyn.


Housing loans: Prop. 37 would allow the state to borrow up to $25 billion to set up a loan program to help people pay for down payments on new homes. Critics argue that the proposal would create a complex lending operation that could also end up reinforcing the state’s existing economic and racial disparities. Read more from Ben Christopher.




Feds allege immigrants voted


Homeland Security Investigations task force officers escort a suspect accused of illegally registering to vote to a processing facility at Federal Building in Los Angeles on Oct. 19, 2026. Photo by Jae C. Hong, AP Photo




Federal officials are charging 28 immigrants with illegally voting or registering to vote in California. They announced the cases just days after the Trump administration sued California and Los Angeles County over allegations of noncitizens registering to vote, writes CalMatters’ Ryan Sabalow.
Prosecutors said the individuals who face charges are lawful permanent residents who are not citizens and are not allowed to vote. Twenty-two are accused of voting in at least one election; five only registered to vote and one submitted a provisional ballot in 2020, prosecutors say.
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Monday that if the suspects are guilty, they should be held accountable, but the charges are not proof that there is widespread voter fraud in California.

Bonta: “Twenty-eight out of 23 million registered voters in California is just … a drop in the bucket numerically. It’s 0.0001% of all the registered voters.”

Read more.



And lastly: Will a blue wave crash in San Diego?


Councilmember Marni von Wilpert (left) and San Diego County Supervisor Jim Desmond. Photos by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters




A former Republican stronghold straddling San Diego and Riverside counties is one of a handful of competitive congressional races in California following the state’s voter-approved redistricting that favors Democrats. The Democratic candidate, Marni von Wilpert, is sticking to her record as a moderate, pro-Israel city councilmember, while her opponent, Jim Desmond, is running as a budget-hawk style conservative. Read more from CalMatters’ Nadia Lathan and Deborah Brennan.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Cheaper manufactured homes could be having a moment, if states can catch up
text:
For decades, manufactured home builders have been working to shed the old image of boxy trailer homes reserved for the outskirts of cities and suburbia. Now, a small change in federal regulations could open the door for architecture welcomed in more neighborhoods.
This summer’s sweeping housing bill, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, removed a 1974 mandate that required every manufactured home to be built on a nonremovable steel frame, known as a chassis. Experts and home producers think the change could help unlock thousands more affordable housing options around the country.
But first, experts say, states have to examine outdated regulations that are blocking the manufactured home industry’s potential. The Pew Charitable Trusts’ housing initiative estimates that 30 states might need to change their regulations to align with the new federal law.
Unlocking manufactured homes from chassis will allow manufactured homes to become multi-family developments, said Stephanie Hawke, associate research director of land use and supply at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at the University of California, Berkeley.
They’ll be cheaper for builders, she noted, and they’ll be easier to stack into two-story and multi-family homes.
“First of all, you were putting a very heavy, expensive thing on the bottom of these homes that is not needed and it is not used, and it’s made out of steel,” Hawke said. “If you’ve got this heavy piece of steel on the bottom of a home, stacking it becomes more difficult.”
Manufactured homes are built entirely in a factory, regulated by U.S. Housing and Urban Development codes, and then trucked to a home site. 
They cost 50% less per square foot than homes built on a site, according to the Manufactured Housing Institute, an industry group. And experts say dropping the chassis could drive down costs by $5,000 to $10,000 per home.
“There’s really the opportunity to stack these manufactured homes to make multi-family developments,” Hawke said. “So it’s unlocking this thing which was primarily used for single-family and it’s making it much more accessible for a multi-family developer, which is great because manufactured housing is far and away the least expensive non-subsidized housing supply in the United States.” 
In a 2026 earnings call, UMH Properties, a publicly traded real estate company that owns and develops manufactured-home communities, said the chassis rule change will allow it to put two-story manufactured homes on existing lots. The company also is considering designs that could combine two stories with duplex units, allowing for smaller, more affordable apartment rentals. 
“You build 2,000 square feet of homes instead of 1,000 square feet on the same piece of land. It’s a very, very important development,” said Eugene Landy, founder and chairman of UMH Properties, on the earnings call. “This is a change that’s gonna help every manufactured home community out in the country.”
Another benefit to removing the chassis, according to Mark Brunner, president of the Manufactured & Modular Home Association of Minnesota, is that manufactured homes can blend more seamlessly into subdivisions because they won’t look too different from other homes.
Under the new law, states are required to certify before July 11, 2027 — or 2028 if their legislatures meet biennially — that they will treat all manufactured homes the same regardless of whether the homes have a chassis or not. So far, at least three states — North Carolina, Tennessee and Texas — have modernized the definition of a manufactured home to align automatically with code updates from HUD.
“If you are not essentially in compliance with this new regulatory framework, then you’re really limited both in using manufactured homes and making them, which is obviously an economic driver for a state,” Hawke said. “North Carolina did an incorporation by reference, essentially saying, ‘We are just going to define this like HUD defines it. Go see HUD’s definition.’ It’s a lot simpler.” 
From temporary housing to mobile home parks
Rachel Siegel, a researcher and policy expert for Pew’s housing initiative, said her research has found that more than 30 states are going to need to update their definition of manufactured housing to remove language about a required chassis.
HUD certification now requires equal treatment of homes with and without chassis, and changes to state laws may not be as easy as striking a few words, she said. References to permanent chassis can appear throughout state statutes in various manufactured home policies.
“States vary completely across the country on how they treat manufactured housing,” Siegel said. “This requirement of permanent chassis is really pervasive.”
A Stateline review found use of the “permanent chassis” language currently written on manufactured housing laws include Virginia, Maine, New York, Missouri, South Carolina, Washington, Nevada and Maryland.
Following World War II, a shift in how mobile homes were being used began forming. No longer reserved as temporary housing, mobile homes were designed to be increasingly more permanent. Mobile home communities sprang up, though many were zoned into rural or suburban areas on a city’s edge.
For decades, manufactured homes — called mobile homes until the early 1970s — have been built in factories and trucked to their new locale. Many were unloaded into mobile home communities, specialized zoning districts where residents own their house but rent the land underneath. 
They are far cheaper than site-built houses: The average sales price of a new manufactured home rose from $81,900 in 2019 to $127,200 in 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau’s Manufactured Housing Survey. 
Those factory-built sales have slowed since a late 1990s boom as fewer manufactured home communities have been built since 2000, a trend largely attributed to restrictive zoning and rising land costs. Still, an estimated 20 million people live in one, most of them on acreage owned by a landlord. 
In the past, a home attached to a trailer or visibly hoisted a few feet off the ground were tells of manufactured housing when they first popped up in neighborhoods. But many modern ones are virtually unrecognizable from site-built homes.
“They have the same walls, ceiling, sheetrock, windows and shingles,” said Dustin Brakemeier, who owns and operates manufactured home communities in Minnesota, South Dakota and Wisconsin. “One’s built in a factory, one’s built outside. They’re the same.’” 
Changing zoning, mortgage rules
Pennsylvania Republican state Rep. Dan Moul, who owns a manufactured home park in Oxford Township in Adams County, recalled in an interview that zoning restrictions kept him from expanding the community into an adjoining parcel a few years ago. The township said the land was zoned exclusively for detached single-family residential housing. 
“The bottom line is they look at mobile home communities as that’s where the poor riffraff lives, and we don’t want any more riffraff,” Moul said. 
One of the big domino effects from the removal of the chassis requirement could be state banning or overriding restrictive local zoning policies that targeted manufactured homes. 
In an analysis of over 6,700 zoning districts in Texas, the National Zoning Atlas found 33% of localities have explicit restrictions on manufactured housing and 11% allowed them via special hearing or permit, but not by-right. 
Last year, Kentucky and Texas banned local ordinances that would unreasonably restrict where manufactured homes could be placed. Kentucky also insisted that local governments cannot impose design standards for manufactured homes that are  higher than those for non-manufactured homes. 
Alex Rodino, a real estate agent in Savannah, Georgia, who sells manufactured homes, said the stigma isn’t just among local governments and stodgy neighborhood groups. Some buyers, he said, are confusing modern manufactured housing with the image of older mobile homes.
“I think (that perception) is slowly changing as construction quality improves and traditional housing becomes less affordable,” said Rodino.
Siegel, of Pew, said that because states must align their manufactured housing laws with HUD’s definition by 2027 – there’s an opportunity for states to take a holistic look at their regulations, including whether states can make it easier to define manufactured homes as “real estate.”
Siegel said states also should revisit laws that classify manufactured homes as personal property — like cars. 
“If you own property that’s personal property instead of real estate, you’re not eligible to get a mortgage,” Siegel said. “That’s not about a person’s financial status or financial credibility, and it’s not even about the quality of the home. It’s just this titling component.”
A Pew analysis touting the potential for manufactured homes shows that a typical $100,000 mortgage for a manufactured home would save a borrower roughly $49,000 over the life of the loan when compared with “home-only” or personal property loans, which are the only options now. 
Some states already are taking action: Laws in Georgia, Maine and New York have made it easier for some manufactured homeowners to convert their homes to real property and gain access to mortgage financing.
“If we’re going to title manufactured homes without a chassis the same way as we’re titling manufactured homes with a chassis, let’s make sure that that process is as streamlined and makes the most sense for what these modern homes are today,” Siegel said.
This story was first published Oct. 20, 2026 by Stateline.

title: State says resident data is safe with state AI tool. Advocates have concerns.
text:
THE PUBLIC IS souring on artificial intelligence, even as it grows more pervasive and widely adopted. High-profile incidents of AI tools involved in hacking banks, tech websites, and even government sites haven’t helped.  
A recent poll from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found a solid majority of Americans — 64 percent — think AI is developing “too fast.” Respondents were most concerned about the need for human control over AI systems and the technology’s potential impact on workers. 
How does that square with Gov. Maura Healey’s push to use AI throughout state government? The Healey administration in February announced a purported first-in-the-nation AI shift: Massachusetts would be the first state to adopt the technology for the entire executive branch — which includes nearly 40,000 state employees — through a partnership with OpenAI.   
The AI assistant can handle resident data like tax records, RMV files, housing and rental information, and benefits documentation. There is “no direct opt-in or opt-out for residents,” according to the tool’s public FAQ, which describes it as strictly internal and not the final word on state decisions. 
Given the recent hacking incidents, CommonWealth Beacon checked back in with state officials to see how they’re protecting the data. Here’s what you need to know:  
A SWIFT EVOLUTION 
In June 2025, members of the Massachusetts congressional delegation were pushing back on a provision in President Trump’s sprawling tax and spend bill that would have blocked states from regulating AI for a decade. Gov. Maura Healey said she was “less focused on regulation of AI” than “leaning into the investments that we’re making here on AI.” 
But, her tone has now shifted.  
“When the people building the most powerful AI systems in the world are telling us there are serious risks, it’s the latest and clearest sign yet that we need more guardrails and protections,” she said in September. “AI has enormous potential, but we cannot let this technology move faster than our ability to keep people safe.” 
Her remarks followed multiple high-profile incidents of AI agents built by major tech companies breaking out of what should have been isolated training environments. The leaders of those companies are now pleading for the federal government to slow them down. 
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published an essay last month calling for more regulation to “police the frontier” of artificial intelligence modeling, by regulating the industry’s advancement before things get further out of hand. 
In September, Healey called on federal officials and state lawmakers to move on AI regulations, some of which are currently being negotiated as part of a sweeping economic development bill in Massachusetts. If passed, provisions in the House and Senate versions would create new obligations for AI companies to plan for and work to prevent major catastrophic incidents. It could also include a first-in-the-nation obligation for the tech companies to cover the cost of independent evaluators to monitor the safety of these systems.   
California, New York and Illinois have enacted laws addressing areas including safety protocols, transparency, and reporting of critical safety incidents. Anthropic and OpenAI, the companies behind Claude and ChatGPT, respectively, say they support independent evaluators. 
Bills in the House and Senate that would limit the way that artificial intelligence or other automated decision making systems could be used by supervisors in government and the private sector made it to both chambers’ Ways and Means committees in late 2025 and never emerged for a vote this year. An amendment to the data privacy bill with the same language was withdrawn. 
These bills would limit “bossware” surveillance and automated decision making technology by restricting the use of employee monitoring tools. The bills would also have restricted the state from rolling out programs that relied on technology that used machine learning or algorithms to make decisions that could impact people unless “specifically authorized in law.” 
STATE CLAIMS SUFFICIENT SAFEGUARDS 
Massachusetts has three-year, roughly $4.3-million-a-year contract with OpenAI for a phased in a plan to roll out the assistant across the executive branch. “Several thousand” employees across all secretariats are currently using the assistant, according to the Executive Office of Technology Services and Security. 
In response to questions from CommonWealth Beacon, the technology office noted its artificial intelligence usage is a far cry from the headline-grabbing security breaches. 
“Recent reports of rogue AI agents have involved testing of AI models in advanced research environments,” a spokesperson said in an email. “These conditions are fundamentally different than the state’s Enterprise AI Assistant, and are not part of our operating environment.” 
Much of the focus on the new risks posed by AI tools has centered on so-called “frontier models,” or the latest and more advanced systems. 
The state “does not use frontier models” and does not integrate the ChatGPT environment into “major systems” like Microsoft365, the spokesperson also said.  
Massachusetts’s technology secretariat “employs a comprehensive, defense-in-depth cybersecurity strategy to protect the state from both traditional and emerging threats, including increasingly sophisticated AI-enhanced attacks,” the spokesperson continued. 
In a conversation with CommonWealth Beacon in April, Technology Secretary Jason Snyder said resident data is also protected by contract. 
“OpenAI is obligated to ensure that our data remains in Massachusetts,” Snyder said, and “if this data were to leave, it would be bad for OpenAI. It would be a public embarrassment. Our data is prohibited from being used to train AI models, and it’s not accessible by other ChatGPT users. It’s not accessible by even other ChatGPT users in the same office. Our data is protected.” 
OpenAI has disclosed multiple data issues in the past year, including a hack in December 2025of one of its data analytics providers that captured “limited customer identifiable information and analytics information.” The company is being sued for allegedly unlawfully scraping data from children who signed up without their parents’ consent. After the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence library, OpenAI disclosed that agents leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users, according to Reuters. 
SAFETY AND USAGE CONCERNS 
The state notes that AI use in Massachusetts is guided by state and federal privacy laws — like the Massachusetts Fair Information Practices Act — which emphasize ethical, secure, and equitable use of emerging technologies.  
All state employees using the assistant must abide by policies like the Enterprise Use and Development of Generative AI Policy and the Acceptable Use of Information Technology Policy, the technology office said. Those guidelines include continuous human fact-checking and using the minimum amount of user data needed for any given task.  
Data privacy advocates are not convinced. 
“The state’s collaboration with OpenAI raises several red flags,” said Kade Crockford, director of technology and justice programs at the ACLU of Massachusetts. 
“There is no state law prohibiting OpenAI from training its proprietary models on the personal data that Massachusetts residents share while interacting with government officials,” Crockford said. “The company’s stated policy is not a sufficient safeguard, as it could be changed at any time.” 
But, unless a resident can prove they were harmed because of a breach, the penalties can be meager. A state holder of data who violates the Massachusetts Fair Information Practices Act must pay at least $100 per violation, plus reasonable costs and attorneys fees, and a court could order them to stop the illegal behavior. 
Advocates warn that forthcoming data privacy and artificial intelligence policy laws are targeted at large commercial entities and are unlikely to have much impact on state actions, and the ChatGPT partnership is a state contract.  
The technology office notes that its policies prioritize human decision-making and that the division is “monitoring the economic development and data privacy bills.” 
“Executive branch policies are a good start, but Massachusetts residents need state laws protecting them,” Crockford said. “Government regulation is essential to safeguard residents’ privacy and ensure AI is never used to unlawfully discriminate against them or deny them due process of law.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Workers’ concerns prompt warning to SC employers about campaign donations
text:
The South Carolina Ethics Commission issued a warning Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, about a prohibition in state law. (iStock/Getty Images Plus)COLUMBIA — The state Ethics Commission wants to make this clear to employers: It is illegal in South Carolina to tell workers they must donate to a campaign and even suggest their job depends on it.
In response to questions received from worried workers this election season, the agency issued an advisory opinion about the state’s 35-year-old ban on providing employees “an advantage or disadvantage” based on their donation or refusal to give.
Questions from callers didn’t involve any particular candidate, the agency’s director, Meghan Dayson, said Monday.
The issue is “employers and their relationships with employees,” she told the SC Daily Gazette.
“Sometimes employers are banking on the imbalance of power in that relationship,” she said. “So, it can cause hesitancy on behalf of employees to say ‘no’ or to report violations to the commission. But we issued this advisory opinion as a warning to all employers in South Carolina.”
State law allows asking employees to donate to a candidate or party, but only if the boss makes clear the request is voluntary.
“An employee’s decision to contribute to political causes must remain free from employment-related coercion, intimidation, reward or retaliation,” reads the advisory opinion approved unanimously by the agency’s governing board last Thursday.
The agency “intends to vigorously enforce” the law, the opinion concludes.
By law, every illegal request can be fined $2,000.
The document issued last week represented the agency’s first formal notice about the prohibition, which is part of the state’s 1991 Ethics Act.
It’s unknown how widespread the problem is. But the agency got enough calls they realized it needed to be addressed, Dayson said, noting it’s rare for commissioners to have a special-called meeting.
“We understood this is something that we needed to get out before the election,” she said.
Without giving specifics about callers or their employers, Dayson said concerned involved employers threatening negative treatment.
For example, “if success at a specific company is tied to being a ‘team player,’ and being a team player is tied to contributing to a candidate, whether or not you actually support that candidate or not,” she said. Those are “the kinds of situations we’re looking at.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Putting food on the table is now even harder for Michiganders
text:
Checkout lane at Meijer store in Howell, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)In Michigan, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) shows up at every kind of table: rural and urban, young families and veterans, working parents and grandparents. Right now, those tables are at risk of looking bare.
In late September, the Michigan League for Public Policy brought together parents, food pantry leaders, a school food service director and a legal aid attorney for a roundtable to discuss concerns around changes to SNAP. The event opened with the data, and it’s hard to hear.
Since the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” passed in July of last year, more than 172,000 Michiganders have lost their SNAP benefits. More than 56,000, or 1 in every 3 of those Michiganders, are children.
With Michigan’s unemployment rate barely moving since last summer (it’s still higher than the national average), the need for SNAP has certainly not decreased. These families are being pushed off because of red tape and heartless restrictions from the federal administration. And what we heard on that call showed the potential impact.
Melissa Miles, a graduate student and mom of a 6-year-old in Hillsdale County, said there’s just not enough time in the day to keep up with everything the new rules require. They change faster than she can track them. Colleen Sadows, a parent and graduate student in Washtenaw County, described being right on the edge of eligibility. If she picks up a little extra income, she loses SNAP, even if that income still falls short of a living wage.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Elly Jordan of the Michigan Poverty Law Program pointed out that these changes are hitting everyone on SNAP, including people with disabilities who are supposed to be exempt from work requirements. Shelters and domestic violence programs are now spending their own limited resources just helping residents keep up with paperwork. And Dan Gorman, who runs the food service department at Montague Area Public Schools, explained that his district qualifies for a federal provision that provides access to free school meals, but that eligibility depends on how many local families qualify for SNAP. As SNAP enrollment drops, schools lose that eligibility and the state has to pick up the extra cost.
Food banks cannot possibly make up for the losses this preventable crisis is causing. Greta Faworski from Kalamazoo Loaves and Fishes told us her pantry has seen a 56% jump in people asking for help. Last November, when the federal shutdown delayed SNAP benefits, they went from serving about 800 people a day to 1,200 a day. That meant adding staff and buying more food when shortages and rising prices made things even harder, especially in northern and rural counties where the percentage of children facing food insecurity is often over 20%.
As of October 1, the federal administration now requires states to pay a larger share of SNAP’s administrative costs. In Michigan, that adds up to $95 million this year alone. By next October, the cost could rise to $400 million a year. Where will we come up with that money? It will mean cuts to something Michiganders need.
But Congress has an opportunity to turn this around for the people they serve. Michigan members of Congress  can protect SNAP and delay these devastating cost shifts by acting by the end of this year. For the sake of every community in our state, we hope they do the right thing.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Westport Museum for History & Culture sends out funding SOS
text:
When the Westport Museum for History & Culture announced a new strategic plan eight years ago, the organization reimagined what Westport’s history could look like. Now, Executive Director Ramin Ganeshram and board members are putting out an emergency fundraising appeal, without which the organization may have to leave its historic building by next year.  
That news came from the museum last week, as it launched a campaign to raise $750,000 by the end of the calendar year, funding that will sustain its already scaled-down operations and let it stay in the Bradley-Wheeler House, a 1795 home out of which it has operated since 1985. The organization itself dates back to 1889, when it was recognized as the Westport Historical Society (it has also operated as the Saugatuck Historical Society and the Westport-Weston Historical Society). 
“I think people don’t realize the value of the institution,” said Ganeshram, a journalist and scholar who stepped into her position in January 2018. “It’s no longer a historical society with a house museum,” but a space with interactive, rotating exhibitions and installations backed by research. 
She nodded to the museum’s tag line, “Making History Whole,” then continued, “Our approach to history is to respect our visitors’ intellect enough to be able to share with them complex ideas.”
The reason for the appeal, and its urgency in this moment, is multi-pronged, Ganeshram said in an interview last week. For years, she and members of the museum’s staff and board have fought the misconception that the organization receives funding from the town of Westport, the municipal hub just a minute away across Myrtle Street.
While the Town of Westport does provide support to civic institutions such as the Westport Public Library, it does not provide operating funds to the museum. In 2022, it regranted $20,000 of Westport’s overall $8.4 million federal American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds to the organization, for project-based funding that has since supported “The Real Revolution,” an exhibition that celebrates and explores the full breadth of America’s semiquincentennial.
Per a series of guidelines that the town implemented around the grants, the museum hired local illustrators and writers, and worked on a ​​”a reusable resource packet for fifth graders,” Ganeshram said. Like many other small museums and historical societies across Connecticut, the Westport Museum for History & Culture also does not receive any dedicated line item funding through the state.    
“We’re completely private,” and reliant on grants, institutional funders, and individual donations to raise a $400,000 annual operating budget, Ganeshram said. Despite small grants from organizations like CT Humanities ($1,000 for a dinner and dialogue last year, for instance, or $2,715.15 for summer youth programming in 2024) and more significant donations from the Daniel E. Offutt III Charitable Trust, that still leaves Ganeshram with hundreds of thousands of dollars to raise each year.   
“I haven’t cracked the code,” Ganeshram said. “Funders, grantmakers, as well as donors believe that Westport has money, and therefore should be funding its institution.” 
When asked Monday, Westport First Selectman Kevin Christie confirmed that the museum, as an independent and private organization, does not receive funding from the town, which has allowed it to maintain “the autonomy that comes from being privately funded and outside the municipal budget process.”
“There have been some informal inquiries about potential Town support, but I have not proposed municipal funding,” he said in an email Monday afternoon, adding that “the museum plays an important role in preserving Westport’s history,” and he does hope it is successful in its emergency appeal. “Any such funding would need to go through the Town’s established budget and appropriation process, including review and approval by the appropriate funding bodies.” 
“With the cost of living an increasing concern for many residents, as well as significant financial obligations and competing priorities facing the Town, we need to be disciplined about the use of taxpayer dollars. That applies to funding requests from any independent organization, including those that make important contributions to our community.” 
The call for funding comes after eight years of growth and transition for the museum, including a name change, several capital improvement projects, a new museological approach that includes rotating exhibitions, new gallery spaces, and historical markers that acknowledge Connecticut’s history of enslavement and its original inhabitants, members of the Paugesset Tribe who stewarded the land for generations.
After her tenure began in 2018, Ganeshram built and streamlined the collections management process, began planning exhibitions that pulled from the museum’s extensive archives, and focused on all of Westport’s residents, including those who had long been pushed to the historical margins (in 2024, she held a formal dedication to the Black and Indigenous residents of Westport, including the Golden Hill Paugussett Tribe, framing the history as one that continues to evolve). 
In 2019, one year after her appointment, the museum opened the exhibition “Remembered: The History of African-Americans in Westport,” an exhibition that received recognition from the Institute for Museum and Library Services (ILMS), American Association for State and Local History, and Connecticut League of History Organizations. 
The mission was not just to bring attention to Connecticut’s history of enslavement, which remained legal until 1848, but also shine a light on the long and sometimes fraught history of Black residents of the town, and the way their local stories intersected with national history. 
Zach Terrillion, who grew up in Westport and worked on the exhibition as a high school intern, remembered the thrill of discovering history through the museum’s archives, and the ways in which the exhibition opened his eyes to facts about Westport that he had missed out on in the city’s public schools. He learned, for instance, that both the civil rights activist Martin Luther King, Jr. and the prophetic Black writer James Baldwin had visited and spoken at Westport’s Temple Israel, next to which he attended elementary school, in the 1960s. 
He, and other visitors to the exhibition, also learned that the state’s history of enslavement was more complicated than it had seemed in school, where slavery was largely framed as something that happened in the American South. In fact, slavery was legal in Connecticut through 1848; the last known sale of enslaved people took place on the New Haven Green in 1825. 
In Westport, Greens Farms Parish records from the eighteenth and nineteenth century indicate almost 250 enslaved people, including children, between 1742 and 1822 — a fact that the museum included in the exhibition, and has since commemorated in a brick walkway that leads up to the historic house. 
“It was this moment of local history connecting to national history” that later informed his decision to study public humanities at Oberlin College, Terrillion said. He added that “understanding those uglier parts of the local history are very very important, but I think the museum touched upon excellency and success” of Black Westport residents in a way that made, and continues to make, him proud.   
During those first years of Ganeshram’s tenure, which coincided with the Covid-19 pandemic and a move to increased digital content, the museum also raised $3 million that allowed it to tackle long-deferred maintenance projects on its grounds and building. That included, for instance, a $500,000 restoration of the 1846 Bradley Wheeler Cobblestone Barn by the Middletown-based company Kronenberger & Sons Restoration, $450,000 in updates to the museum’s grounds, including the addition of free WiFi, and updates to the museum’s collections management systems. 
Ganeshram pointed to the importance of protecting and preserving archives that date back to the 1670s, and are often the foundation for the museum’s exhibitions as staff and volunteers do research, and tie in Westport’s history. She said that another chunk of that funding went toward general operating support, including utilities and building needs that can be as much as $150,000 in a given year. 
In recent years, though, raising funds to keep the museum going has become harder, due in part to a nonprofit landscape in which both state and federal dollars are drying up after an ARPA boom, and individual donors are giving less money, less frequently. In the last year, the museum staff has shrunk from six full- and part-time employees to just three, including Ganeshram and two part-time staffers.
