name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: The summer we lost AI containment: A survey shows Ohio citizens’ thoughts and concerns
authors: Ryan D. King, Stephen M. Gavazzi
text:
A young woman asks AI companion ChatGPT for help. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)In July of 2026, OpenAI disclosed that its AI agents went rogue during an internal test of cyber capabilities. They broke containment, hacked into a machine learning company, and stole private information.
OpenAI later disclosed that its test required lowering some guardrails designed to restrict the AI agents’ access. With the door cracked open, the autonomous agents snuck out.
Notably, this was not an isolated case of an AI model acting autonomously after safety features were temporarily relaxed for testing purposes. We learn of more cases each week.
Such incidents signal a new phase in the evolution of artificial intelligence, one characterized by AI as an autonomous agent rather than a human tool.
This pivot also creates tension with public sentiment in Ohio, as evidenced by the results of a recent survey we conducted.
We fielded a survey of 501 Ohioans about the purpose of AI, along with respondents’ preferences and fears.
As of early May, a majority of Ohioans (65%) generally agreed that AI technologies are safe. A similar percentage (67%) trusted private tech companies to develop safe and responsible AI tools.
Still, Ohioans expressed concerns.
More than a quarter of Ohioans “definitely” believed AI poses a threat to humanity’ s long-term survival, with another 49% answering “possibly.” Fewer than 20% felt that AI presented no threat.
When asked what makes an AI system safe, secure, or trustworthy, a majority emphasized human oversight over critical decisions (72%), and 60% mentioned transparency, defined as understanding how AI-generated results are produced.
More than 7 in 10 Ohioans agreed that, to prevent harm, the government should create new regulations for AI, even if it risks slowing down innovation.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The latter sentiment about regulation and pace is particularly apt in the current moment. The summer of ‘26 may be remembered as the moment that humans lost containment.
Recent events underscore that concern. A former Anthropic researcher publicly resigned, warning that AI companies are “gambling with our lives” as they pursue autonomous systems.
Relatedly, over 1,000 employees from technology companies called for urgent government action to develop the tools needed to pace AI development.
The letter acknowledges that we’re on the doorstep of AI accelerating “beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”
Is the tech sector likely to pull the reins and slow the rate of AI development? Probably not. The competitive pressures incentivize moving faster, not slower. No one wants to tap the brakes in this race unless others must do the same.
Bill Gates and others are making an urgent call for regulation. As he wrote in his essay, “The highest priority is a monumental task: creating a domestic and international framework for dealing with AI.”
Other technologists agree, as reported by Rogé Karma in The Atlantic.
Our survey indicates that most Ohioans agree. They support regulation, even if it slows AI’s advance.
Notably, based on results from our survey, the public’s support for regulation crosses ideological lines, with left- and right-leaning respondents expressing similarly strong backing for government safeguards.
Inaction risks public criticism and perhaps losing votes.
We’re already seeing public displays of disapproval. Commencement speakers have been booed for praising AI, and pro-regulation advocacy groups like Humans in Control are gaining members.
Our survey shows that the public is willing to embrace AI, but not at any cost. They want innovation accompanied by accountability, transparency, and human oversight.
If industry and government do not provide those safeguards, the greatest risk may not be losing control of AI. It may be losing the public’s trust.
Ryan D. King is dean of social and behavioral sciences at The Ohio State University.
Stephen M. Gavazzi is director of the Center for Human Resource Research at The Ohio State University.

 Catching Our Eye

• Special interest money floods the Ohio election. Signal Ohio’s Jake Zuckerman reports, “Ohio insurers, utilities drop millions on governors races.”
Investor-owned electric utilities and insurers that help run Ohio Medicaid gave millions of dollars to groups trying to influence Ohio’s governor’s race and similarly close contests in other states. One Democratic group received $75,000 from the scandal-plagued FirstEnergy Corp. and $10,000 from its CEO.
• NCAA v. DeWine. The Statehouse News Bureau’s Jo Ingles reports, “NCAA files lawsuit over DeWine executive order on college athlete eligibility.”
The NCAA has filed a federal lawsuit against Gov. Mike DeWine over an executive order he signed earlier this week on college athletic eligibility.
DeWine’s order allows students from the high school class of 2022 to have a fifth year of eligibility. It’s something he said is necessary, but the NCAA said it gives Ohio’s schools an unfair advantage.
DeWine’s executive order told the state’s colleges and universities to disregard the NCAA’s new age-based eligibility rule. He said it unfairly denies a fifth season of competition to a small number of students who graduated from high school in 2022, while granting five seasons to others currently playing on college sports teams.
• Lobbyists. The Toledo Blade’s Danny Eldredge reports, “Ohio governor candidates weigh new restrictions on lobbyists.”
As Ohioans continue to name government corruption as a top issue ahead of the November election, all three candidates for governor have discussed ideas to clean up the Ohio Statehouse.
Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy said he is open to prohibiting lobbyists from serving on state boards and commissions…
Dr. Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for governor, said she would issue an executive order addressing corruption on her first day in office.
• Ohioans v. Flock cameras. The Dayton Daily News’ Cornelius Frolik reports, “Ohioans hitting, shooting, stealing and chopping down Flock cameras.”
Some of the backlash against controversial Flock Automated License Plate Readers has crossed the line into criminal territory, as people across Ohio have intentionally damaged, vandalized and stolen cameras that are used by many police departments.
More than 30 Ohio police agencies conducted Flock network searches over the summer related to ALPR cameras that were moved, removed, dismantled, struck, chopped down, rammed with automobiles and covered over with spray paint and bags, according to search audit records and other documents obtained by the Dayton Daily News.
• Ukraine. The AP reports, “Zelenskyy says Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again.”
Russia used ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to launch more attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that Kyiv again received no early warning of the attack from partner countries who in the past have shared that intelligence.
Zelenskyy is grappling with the implications of recent Washington moves benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin, including waiving U.S. sanctions on Moscow and signing a deal to import Russian diesel.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: The most public part of public service
text:
On Oct. 7, Ellington town administrator Matthew Reed was among five people named by the Connecticut Foundation for Open Government as a recipient of the Mitchell W. Pearlman Freedom of Information award. This is the text of his acceptance speech:
Thank you very much. I am truly honored to receive the Mitchell W. Pearlman Freedom of Information Award.
Receiving an award that bears Mitch Pearlman’s name is particularly meaningful. His career represents something that is easy to say but sometimes much harder to practice: that open government is not an inconvenience of public service —it is an essential part of public service.

Matthew Reed

I have had the privilege of viewing Connecticut’s Freedom of Information Act from several different perspectives over the course of my career —as a police officer and police chief, as an attorney with the Freedom of Information Commission, as an attorney, and now as a municipal administrator.
Those experiences have convinced me of something very simple: public records do not belong to us.
They do not belong to the police chief, the town administrator, the department head, the board or commission, or the employee who created them. We are merely their custodians. They belong, ultimately, to the public we serve.
That distinction matters.
An FOI request should never be viewed as a personal attack. A resident should not have to explain why he or she wants a public record, and government should not approach a request by first asking, “How can we avoid providing this?” Our first question should be, “How can we help this person obtain the public information they are entitled to receive?”
Sometimes that means picking up the phone and talking to the requester. Sometimes it means helping someone better define what they are looking for. And sometimes it means acknowledging that producing records can be inconvenient, time-consuming, or even uncomfortable. But transparency is most important precisely when it is inconvenient or uncomfortable.
The same philosophy applies beyond records requests. It means writing agendas that actually tell the public what its government intends to discuss. It means using executive sessions only when the law permits them —not simply because a conversation would be easier behind closed doors. And it means remembering that the public’s ability to observe its government and examine its records is not an obstacle to effective government. It is part of what makes government legitimate.
Connecticut has been fortunate to have a Freedom of Information Commission that, for decades, has served not merely as an enforcement agency, but as an educational resource for public officials and citizens alike. I was fortunate to spend part of my career there, and the lessons I learned during that time have remained with me throughout every position I have held since.
One of those lessons is that compliance with the Freedom of Information Act should be the floor —not the ceiling.
The goal should not simply be to avoid an FOI violation. The goal should be to create a culture in which openness is the default, where public employees understand why transparency matters, and where residents recognize that their government belongs to them.
That requires leadership. It also requires patience, education and occasionally the willingness to tell colleagues something they may not particularly want to hear.
Throughout my career, I have tried to do that.
I am deeply grateful to be recognized for those efforts, and especially humbled to receive an award associated with someone who devoted so much of his professional life to protecting the public’s right to know.
Thank you to everyone responsible for this recognition, to the people I have worked alongside throughout my career, and to the public officials and employees who work every day to make government more accessible and transparent.
And most importantly, thank you to the citizens who continue to ask questions, attend meetings, request records and hold their government accountable.
Open government only works when people exercise the rights the law gives them.
Matthew Reed is the Ellington Town Administrator.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: One city, two newspapers, many memories, many losses
text:
Later, while working at a well-staffed daily in New Haven, I would have the luxury of time to write feature stories and occasional, extended, polished pieces, but it was at the Hartford Times, in Connecticut’s capital, that I learned to write under pressure, a few times dictating a breaking news story from a pay phone as I composed it in my head from notes.
Once, back in the office, I had two editors reading over my shoulder as I typed an article that was going to run on the front page. A newbie, I was amazed that they were literally holding the presses for my piece. It was an exciting, highly competitive, rapid-fire business, and I thrived on it.
American cities used to have multiple daily newspapers, and it was also at the Hartford Times that I learned that most cities were destined to have only one — which today is in itself a challenge. Fifty years ago, on October 20, 1976, only eight months after I started there, the Hartford Times, once Connecticut’s largest and most prestigious newspaper, folded after 159 years. Even its 1962 Pulitzer couldn’t save it.
My first day at the Times, I had been assigned to cover an evening meeting in Bolton, 14 miles outside the city. Late that night, on my way back to Hartford, I came to an emergency scene where 150 firefighters from eight towns were trying to save an almost-300-year-old burning house. Built in 1689 and once a stop on the underground railroad, the house had many historic features, as well as art and antiques.
A photographer from my paper lived nearby and heard about the fire on his police radio; he showed up, so we had photos and the story. Unfortunately, the house was a total loss. The next morning, when the first of several rolling editions of the Times came out, I had my first page one story, at the top of the page, my first day on the job.
The dozens of news stories and personal memories I have from my brief career at the Hartford Times don’t capture the sadness of the passing of a daily newspaper and what a great loss it is to a community. I only lost a job and had another within days. The city, the metropolitan area and the state, lost a newspaper. On the community level, that’s like losing an arm or a leg. I miss the time when just about everyone got a morning or evening paper — and some got both.
The Times was founded in 1817, and a century later, then the largest-circulation and most influential newspaper in the state, it built a grand, Beaux-Art style, six-columned building adjacent to Hartford City Hall. Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy and Johnson would all speak at the top of the dual stairways. After the newspaper closed, the building endured, and a decade ago, keeping the beautiful façade, it was rebuilt and expanded to house the downtown Hartford campus of the University of Connecticut.
A mile away is the nondescript building that once belonged to the Hartford Courant, which was founded on October 29, 1764, America’s oldest newspaper in continuous circulation. I delivered copies of the 200th anniversary issue on my paper route in 1964. About then, the Courant, with a circulation of 137,000, exceeded the Times for the first time, and 12 years later it became the only show in town. During Covid, the severely depleted staff vacated the building to work remotely, and later it was sold.
According to a 2014 New York Times article about the Courant’s 250th anniversary celebration, the paper had peaked in 1993, when Sunday circulation hit 323,892. Then came the internet. By 2000, daily circulation was down to 216,000, and by its big anniversary in 2014, Sunday circulation was down to 180,000 and weekdays were down to 120,000. According to the Sept. 30, 2026, Courant publisher’s statement to Alliance for Audited Media, the Courant’s print circulation is down to 24,948 on Sunday, and 14,695 to about 21,000 on various weekdays; however, paid digital circulation is up to 50,976.
I grew up in a newspaper family. Back in hot-type days, my dad was a linotype operator at the Courant for three decades, my brother worked in the Courant composing room for several years, and I worked there four summers. The Courant had seven editions, and my dad would bring the first one home with him at 1  a.m.
When I was 13, I got a Courant paper route, and delivered it every morning, seven days a week, for over three years. I took over a route with many apartment buildings but barely 30 customers, and I built it to 80 daily and 125 Sunday customers. Little did I know I was contributing to losing my first reporting job a decade later.
Sixty years ago, I got hooked on daily newspapers, and after all this time, there is still no better, more enjoyable way to get news. Even with online options, there is nothing as good as a venerable broadsheet. When daily newspapers reigned, we were a better-informed, more cohesive society. With a common source thoroughly covering our city or town, our state, and nation, we started our day on the same page, and those bent on spreading misinformation and disinformation had a much harder time doing so.
Over the summer, I spent a day in downtown Hartford, the city where my father’s family settled in the 1850s and where my mother’s family arrived in the 1920s, where I grew up, and where I have lasting ties. I visited the former Hartford Times building, which still bears its name on the portico. Without UConn ID, I couldn’t go far beyond the café, where I had lunch, but I didn’t need to go any farther.
Inside, nothing was the same. I was almost as sad as I was the day paper closed.
Tom McKone is a retired teacher, principal, and library administrator in Montpelier, VT.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Report finds birth centers improve outcomes. Mississippi has none
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Despite growing evidence that midwife-led birth centers improve outcomes for mothers and infants, Mississippi remains one of 10 states with no centers. Mississippi is also among the states with the fewest midwives per births in the nation, according to a new report by the Commonwealth Fund, a non-profit research organization focused on healthcare issues. 
Built in the communities they serve, freestanding birth centers employ midwives to care for people with low-risk pregnancies, according to the report released Tuesday. They focus on patient autonomy and cultural responsiveness, which can help reduce pregnancy and delivery disparities for Black and Indigenous communities. Birth centers also may lower unnecessary interventions and increase maternal satisfaction, the report authors said. 
“Birth centers offer the kind of continuous, midwife-led care, shaped around each family’s needs, that can be part of the response to our maternal health crisis,” said Laurie Zephyrin, senior vice president of the Achieving Equitable Outcomes program at the Commonwealth Fund, in a press release. 
Last year, Mississippi health officials declared a public health emergency over rising infant deaths, most of which were Black infants. Experts have said increased access to care is a vital part of the solution. But in February, state lawmakers failed to pass legislation that would have made it easier for midwives to practice without paying a collaborating physician a monthly fee. . Advocates argue these arrangements provide little meaningful collaboration while creating financial barriers that discourage midwives from practicing or opening birth centers. 
Mississippi, along with Louisiana and Alabama, has fewer than 20 midwives per 10,000 births, according to the report. All three states have collaboration agreements for nurse midwives. 
In 2026, the American College of Nurse Midwives sued Mississippi for restricting access to midwives in a place with some of the worst outcomes for mothers and babies. That lawsuit is still pending. 
Beyond collaboration agreements, the Mississippi State Department of Health has regulated birth centers in a way that may put underserved, rural areas at a disadvantage, Zephyrin told Mississippi Today. 
For example, a Mississippi birth center can only open within 30 minutes of a hospital, according to state regulations. Nearly half the counties in Mississippi are maternity care deserts, where there are no obstetric clinicians or birthing facilities. 
“With hospital shortages and maternity deserts, there may not be a hospital nearby,” Zephyrin said, adding that state leaders need to be innovative to address gaps in care. 
The state Health Department did not respond to a request for comment by the time of publication. 
Across the country, access to birth centers remains limited. In addition to the 10 states without birth centers, eight states have only one. 
On the other hand, Texas leads the nation in this health model, with 90 birth centers. Between 2004 and 2024, the model grew significantly, according to the report. However, birth center deliveries still only account for less than one percent of all U.S. births.
Getty Israel, founder of a Jackson-based women’s health clinic called Sisters in Birth, has spent nearly six years trying to open a birth center in the state. She believes the state overregulates birth centers and midwives. She said lawmakers lack the will to integrate midwives and birth centers into the healthcare system. 
Israel said she feels lawmakers don’t pay attention to the growing research that supports midwifery as an integral part of the solution. 
“There’s a lot of evidence about the efficacy of birth centers,” Israel said. “But no one is helping me to build a birth center.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Fact check: President Donald Trump on $5,000 bonus, victory margin, medical debt
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — President Donald Trump renewed during a Kansas political rally a promise to send $5,000 to every adult citizen of the United States if Republicans retained control of the U.S. House and U.S. Senate.
“If the Republicans win, you each will have $5,000 in your pocket,” Trump said. “The only caveat on the $5,000 is that the Trump dividend, you must spend the money in the United States of America.”
He said the cost to the federal government would be “approximately $1 trillion,” but the obligation would be paid with revenue from a “record-setting $22.2 trillion that’s being invested in the United States right now.” He has mentioned use of tariff revenue to pay the bonuses.
Trump, speaking at a Park City rally in support of U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and in opposition to Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, incorrectly portrayed the cost of payments to 240 million to 250 million people. The actual cost would be closer to $1.2 trillion.
And PBS said Trump misstated the level of foreign investment in the United States. Instead of more than $22 trillion, economic data placed the number at $11.2 trillion.
The arrangement outlined by Trump would be off the table if Democrats seized just one of the chambers Nov. 3. Even if the GOP prevailed and held both chambers, there was no certainty the appropriation would clear the House and Senate. Of special concern would be the 60-vote bipartisan margin required in the Senate.
CNN reported infusion of more than $1 trillion in federal payments would increase consumer demand for goods and services and trigger a spike in inflation.
 
Margin of victory
Before boarding a helicopter and the flight to Wichita, Trump spoke at the White House about Marshall’s campaign in Kansas and the midterm struggle of other red-state Republicans.
The president told reporters he anticipated the first-term GOP senator from Kansas would prevail, but he conceded the contest against Hamilton was unexpectedly tight.
“It’s a close race. It shouldn’t be,” Trump said. “As you know, I won by a tremendous amount, like 25 to 30 points. I won by a lot.”
Trump exaggerated his margin of victory in Kansas. He ran for president in 2016, 2020 and 2024 and carried the state of Kansas each time.
In 2016, Trump beat Hillary Clinton by a margin of 20.6 percentage points. In the campaign against Joe Biden, who was elected president in 2020, Trump’s margin slipped to 14.6 points. In 2024, Trump defeated Kamala Harris by a margin of 16.1 points.
Trump earned a low of 56.2% and a high of 57.1% of the vote within Kansas during the three election cycles. Those double-digit victories didn’t equal the Kansas showing by Dwight Eisenhower, Ronald Reagan, Richard Nixon or George W. Bush.
In 1952, Eisenhower defeated Adlai Stevenson by 38.2 percentage points. That contest in Kansas was heavily influenced by Eisenhower having lived in Abilene during his youth.
Reagan crushed Walter Mondale in 1984 by 32.6 percentage points. Nixon outran George McGovern by 29.5 points in 1972, while Bush topped John Kerry by 25.4 points in 2004.
 
Fans cheer as President Donald Trump takes the stage at an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
‘Worst thing they did’
Trump addressed his administration’s immigration agenda and criticized Biden for enabling an avalanche of people without proper documentation to enter the United States.
“The worst thing they did to us is allowing 25 million people into the country totally unchecked, totally unvetted, and many of them were hardcore criminals,” Trump said.
Politifact, a nonprofit project of the Poynter Institute, said the number of immigrants in the U.S. illegally during Biden’s tenure ranged from 11 million to 12 million. Other organizations offered a range between 11 million to 16 million, rather than the 25 million claimed by Trump.
 
Falsehood on debt collections
In a Truth Social post and during the rally, Trump defended Marshall, a former OB-GYN in Great Bend, from criticism initiated by a news report in the New York Times that said Marshall’s attorneys filed lawsuits against hundreds of people for unpaid medical debt. Some of Marshall’s patients didn’t appear in court, leading to the arrest of at least 80 people.
Trump condemned Hamilton, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, for making Marshall’s debt-collection tactics a campaign issue.
Trump’s post in support of Marshall: “He is absolutely great, a wonderful person, given a ‘bum rap’ because he was mandated by law to request money owed from patients. If he didn’t make those requests, he would be breaking the law and subject to criminal liability and arrest.”
Trump’s statement about a mandated duty to seek collection of debt was false. Under federal and state law, no legal requirement exists to obligate a doctor or healthcare provider to pursue patient debt. No provision in law required a debt collector to ask judges to issue arrest warrants for individuals who didn’t appear in court to answer a lawsuit.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: In Kansas rally, Trump defends Marshall’s record and calls Hamilton a ‘disgrace’
text:
U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, speaks alongside President Donald Trump during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)PARK CITY — President Donald Trump on Monday defended U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall’s record and blamed judges and state law for the senator’s practice of suing and arresting patients in medical debt cases when he was a physician.
The president campaigned for Marshall and other Republican candidates in a visit to Kansas in-between Alaska and the Carolinas. Marshall, R-Kansas, is running for reelection against a Kansas City-area pastor, the Rev. Adam Hamilton, who is a Democrat. Also in the race is David Graham, a Libertarian from Overland Park.
Trump spent the first 20 minutes of his roughly one-hour-and-40-minute speech with scant mention of Kansas, Marshall or Hamilton, taking a few moments to call Marshall’s opponent a “bad person” and a “disgrace” while focusing on the Michigan Senate race and condemning other Senate Democrats. Throughout his speech, protestors interrupted him at least five times while Trump reiterated Republican priorities going into the midterm elections: secure borders, a stronger military and lower costs.
He announced a “harvest fuel relief” program, promising to offset diesel fuel prices for farmers, which have exceeded $6 per gallon in Kansas in recent weeks.
Trump embarked on a tour across the U.S. earlier this month, visiting traditionally Republican-friendly states ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. His stop in Kansas was his first since 2018, and the first time a sitting president has visited the Wichita area in 20 years.
He called Marshall “one of the greatest senators in our country,” and warned attendees about the perceived consequences of Democrats winning midterm races, including economic depression.
But if Republicans win, he said: “I’ll give you cash.”
Trump has repeated since September the promise of $5,000 cash for every adult in the U.S. if Republicans win the midterm elections to retain control of the U>S. House and Senate.
He said Marshall is a “tough guy” and “high quality.” He said Marshall was “given a bum rap,” for his practice of suing and arresting people for medical debt when he was a physician in central Kansas.
Trump blamed the arrests on a judge and the law, not Marshall.
“He didn’t do it,” Trump said.
“You got screwed with that,” he said to Marshall
He called Hamilton “radical left” and a “lunatic” who is “pretending to be a moderate.”
Trump was preceded on stage by seven Kansas officials running for public office in November, including Marshall, and rock musician and hunting enthusiast Ted Nugent. By the time the president took the stage, the roughly 6,000 seats in the Heartland Credit Union Arena on the outskirts of Wichita were about two-thirds full.
Rocker and hunter Ted Nugent poses for a fan at President Donald Trump’s Oct. 19, 2026, rally at Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
In-between speeches, a playlist of hits from another century played and concession lines stretched above stadium seats in an arena that typically hosts midsized music and sporting events.
U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, U.S. Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Missouri, and NASCAR driver Danica Patrick also were in attendance.
Marshall, in his speech ahead of Trump, largely focused on his opponent. He criticized Hamilton’s stances on immigration, and he said Hamilton was “the most radical liberal Democrat to ever make it through a Senate primary in the history of Kansas.”
Hamilton faced 10 other Democratic candidates in the August primary election.
Tyson Brody, a spokesperson for Hamilton’s campaign, said Monday’s rally was a sign of Marshall’s campaign sinking and Washington panicking.
“They’re sending in reinforcements to lie and attack Adam Hamilton to try to save Marshall,” Brody said. “But nothing said at the rally can distract from the fact Kansans are being crushed by rising gas and diesel prices, struggling to access affordable healthcare, and are tired of Washington corruption.”
Marshall said if Republicans lose the Kansas U.S. Senate race, he feared longtime Democratic Sens. Chuck Schumer of New York, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Bernie Sanders of Vermont, and Cory Booker of New Jersey would control the U.S. Senate.
“The legacy media wants to make this race so complicated,” Marshall said.
National news outlets and pundits have glommed onto Kansas in recent weeks as Hamilton’s personal fundraising has outdone Marshall’s, and outside groups have begun to flood Kansas markets with targeted ads on both sides of the aisle.
Vice President JD Vance in September visited Kansas, highlighting Marshall’s personal and professional accomplishments.
Attendees responded to Trump’s points on immigration, transgender issues and the economy.
“I think this is a very important election,” said Karen Malone, of Manhattan, a little more than two hours from Park City.
“If we’re going to keep our values in our country, we need to vote and be excited about voting and listen to what our politicians have to say,” she added.
Malone said she doesn’t think about Marshall the same way she thinks about Trump. She said she still will vote for him, even if he isn’t the best Republicans have to offer, and that she wishes he were more vocal. He presents himself well in television news appearances, she said, but doesn’t speak out enough for Kansas’ rural needs.
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)
Donna and Tom McLain traveled roughly two-and-a-half hours from Lenexa to see Trump. They said they voted for Marshall six years ago and plan to vote for him again. They said they aren’t bothered by reports about his aggressive medical debt collection practices and paper trail in Florida, where he had a second home until recently.
“It’s politics,” Donna McLain said. “The same can be said for his opponent.”
The National Republican Senatorial Committee in advance of Trump’s visit to Kansas expressed support for Marshall and called Hamilton a “pedophile protector,” referring to a volunteer at Hamilton’s church, who in 2005 and 2006 inappropriately touched underaged boys at a youth camp.
Trump and Marshall also brought up the incident.
In Kansas Reflector reports published in May and July on the abuse allegations involving Church of the Resurrection, Hamilton said two church employees conducted an internal investigation into claims that surfaced in 2005. The inquiry was inconclusive because the children couldn’t identify the perpetrator, and the volunteer, Scott Moore, was barred from the church in 2006, when the matter also was turned over to police. 
“President Trump and Roger Marshall are working in lockstep to cut taxes, protect communities, and level the playing field for farmers,” said Samantha Cantrell, regional press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee. 
Hamilton said in a video released Monday that people who voted for Trump have a place in Hamilton’s campaign. He emphasized his willingness to work with the president.
“When the president does something good for Kansas, I’ll stand beside him and say so. When a decision out of Washington hurts our farmers, our rural hospitals, or our paychecks, I’ll stand up to Washington and say that too. Some days we’ll agree. Some days we won’t,” Hamilton said.
Hamilton and Marshall are scheduled on Wednesday for a television debate, which Graham, the Libertarian candidate, has been excluded from.
Graham said in an emailed statement that Trump’s visit Monday was evidence of a tight race.
“My percentage of the electorate is greater than the difference between my two opponents,” Graham said. “Most of my support comes from voters who simply cannot vote for either of the other candidates.”
He said he should be included in any debates in which his opponents participate.
“My opponents are ignoring me and hope the voters do, too,” he said. “It’s not working. I’m the only candidate talking about issues, like criminal justice reform, and transparency in government.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: The Chesapeake Bay’s young rockfish are still struggling. It may be the ‘new normal.’
text:
Maryland Department of Natural Resources fisheries biologists sample a site on the Nanticoke River with a seine net as part of the annual juvenile striped bass survey. (Photo courtesy Joe Zimmermann/Maryland DNR)For the eighth straight year, Maryland scientists found well below average numbers of young rockfish in the Chesapeake Bay.
This summer’s survey, released Monday, showed the best results since 2018, the last time that surveyors counted an above-average quantity of juvenile striped bass, or rockfish. But with “young of the year” index of 5.5 this year — compared to a historical average of 10.8 — Maryland scientists aren’t really celebrating.
“The important piece of information is that it is still below average, and it is now the eighth year of low abundance,” said Carrie Kennedy, the Tidal and Coastal Monitoring and Assessment Division director for the Maryland Department of Natural Resources.
Virginia scientists also released their results Monday, showing a slightly better picture. The state’s index was 9.52, a bit above its historical average of 7.77.
In Maryland, it’s possible that these continued low numbers of rockfish at or below 3 inches in length are “the new normal,” Kennedy said. Fisheries scientists believe that changing environmental conditions, including water temperature, could be altering the species’ reproduction in some way. Maryland’s survey has been running since 1954, making it one of the longest-running fish surveys in the nation, according to the DNR.
Bipartisan group of Maryland legislators call for menhaden harvest reductions

“Maybe we need to have a conversation about new reference points and new expectations,” Kennedy said. ”I don’t think that we should expect the population to be where it was in the early 2000s. We have a different Chesapeake Bay. We have a different planet than we had in the early 2000s.”
It isn’t just striped bass, Kennedy said. Low spawning numbers have persisted for other anadromous species, such as white perch and yellow perch — which are born in freshwater, migrate to the ocean to mature, then return to freshwater to spawn.
“They’re all showing similar trends of low recruitment in the last seven to eight years,” Kennedy said. “To me, that’s a pretty good indicator that it’s not just a striped bass situation.”
But rockfish are an iconic species — and fishery — in the Chesapeake Bay region, which serves as a key spawning ground, attracting large adult fish that swim upriver to reproduce in the springtime.
In 2024, Maryland canceled what was known as the spring trophy fishery, when anglers were allowed to catch — and keep — those large fish. Since then, recreational anglers have only bee allowed to catch and release rockfish from Jan. 1 through April 30.
The state has also closed the fishery for the month of August, when warmer water places greater strain on the fish, making them more likely to die after being caught and released.
Despite the lackluster findings, Maryland officials say the numbers are not expected to trigger changes to the state’s rockfish regulations next year. That’s because Maryland is waiting for an assessment of the entire striped bass stock, likely next spring, After that, the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission, which includes Maryland, will decide on new fishing restrictions coastwide.
The commission declared Atlantic striped bass overfished in 2019, and the species is subject to a plan that requires the stock to be rebuilt by 2029. The new stock assessment will provide a progress update.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Either it’ll say, ‘Hey, you met your rebuilding target,’ or it’ll say, ‘Nope, you have a ways to go.’ Or the board will say, ‘Maybe we need new targets based on this information,’” Kennedy said.
After the commission decides, Maryland could add more stringent rules of its own. But they wouldn’t likely arrive until the 2029 season, Kennedy said.
There are reasons for “cautious optimism” about the overall stock assessment, Kennedy said, with recent figures showing that adult rockfish could be at a healthy population.
Last October, the commission’s striped bass board declined to move forward with a proposed 12% cut in fishery removals, after preliminary data through June 2025 showed the recreational catch throughout the Atlantic region was lower than expected.
But as below-average classes of baby fish reach maturity, the adult population will look smaller and smaller, Kennedy said.
“It generally takes seven to eight years for a fish to become mature enough to spawn,” Kennedy said. “So now, we’re really at the point where we’re going to start seeing it and feeling it in the adult population.”
Eight years of poor survey results “paints a bleak picture,” said Allison Colden, Maryland executive director of the nonprofit Chesapeake Bay Foundation.
“What happens in the Chesapeake Bay is a prediction for striped bass’s future up and down the Atlantic Coast. Roughly 80 percent of the coastwide striped bass population spawn here in the Bay,” Colden said in a statement.
Sturgeon are full of surprises, including that they’re here

The foundation is “encouraged” by DNR’s recent seasonal changes, including closing the fishery in August, Colden said.
“But striped bass need coastwide commitment and action from ASMFC if we want this beloved fish to have any chance to rebound,” she added.
For ths summer’s survey, biologists repeatedly sampled at 22 sites in four Maryland rivers known to be striped bass spawning areas. On each visit, the scientists cast a 100-foot seine net twice from the shore, and counted the small striped bass they collected. The index is the average number of juveniles counted in one sweep of the net.
Maryland officials believe the slightly stronger numbers this year could be due to weather conditions. Cold winters tend to be favorable for the species, as can a large amount of melting ice and snow, which improves water flow, Kennedy said. But drought conditions, which have been an issue for much of the state this year, can lower river flows, reducing areas the fish can reach to spawn, and causing other harms.
This year, the best results came from the upper Chesapeake and the Choptank River, according to the DNR.
In total, the surveyors caught nearly 72,000 fish of 62 species in their nets this year. Atlantic menhaden — the fish at the base of the bay food chain that is the subject of hot debate heading into the Atlantic States commission’s meeting next month — had a strong showing, Kennedy said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Rob Sand withdraws from Wednesday debate after brother-in-law’s death
text:
Democratic candidate for governor Rob Sand speaks with Carolyn Scott, a resident at Frank W. Smith Retirement Center in Des Moines on Sept. 3, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) Rob Sand, the Democratic nominee for governor, has withdrawn from a debate scheduled for Wednesday with Republican candidate Zach Lahn following the death of his brother-in-law.
Sand and Lahn were scheduled to meet for a debate on “Iowa Press” on Iowa PBS Oct. 21, the third of four planned debates between the two candidates competing to become Iowa’s next governor. However, the Sand campaign announced it was withdrawing from the debate Monday as the candidate focuses on his family.
“Rob Sand is focused on his family during this difficult time,” Emma O’Brien, Sand’s deputy campaign manager, said in a statement. “… We are in contact with the Lahn campaign on rescheduling, and appreciate their willingness to work with us. We will have more updates soon.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Walter E. Lauridsen II, 42, died Thursday in a traffic incident near Lucas, according to the Iowa State Patrol. A vehicle going east on U.S. Highway 34 moved into the westbound lane to pass Lauridsen’s vehicle, which was parked on the east side of the highway. Lauridsen had walked into the westbound lane and was struck by the SUV. He was the brother of Sand’s wife, Christine Sand, the CEO at Lauridsen Group, Inc.
Sand said Friday in a statement on social media, “We are heartbroken by the tragic loss of Walter, who died last night. This is an extremely sad and devastating time for all who knew and loved him.”
“Walter lived with mental health complexities. While this is a difficult and painful time for all of us, we know he is now at peace,” Sand wrote. “As we begin the difficult task of making funeral arrangements, we ask that you keep all of us in your prayers and respect our privacy as we grieve. We will share additional information when plans are finalized.”
Lahn’s campaign released a statement Monday announcing the change to the planned debate and calling for Iowans to pray for Sand and his family.
“We have been informed by Iowa PBS that Rob Sand has withdrawn from Wednesday’s debate,” a campaign spokesperson said in a statement. “We completely understand and are supportive of his decision. We will work with the station on rescheduling.
“We urge all Iowans to join us in continued prayer for Rob and his family at this difficult time. Some things are bigger than politics.”
In addition to a potential rescheduled debate on “Iowa Press,” the two gubernatorial candidates are set to debate at 6:30 p.m., Oct. 27 in Cedar Rapids at an event hosted by KCRG-TV9 and the Cedar Rapids Gazette.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho legislator selected to serve as state’s next U.S. attorney after Davis retires
text:
State Rep. John Shirts, R-Weiser, speaks from the floor of the Idaho House of Representatives on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)An Idaho legislator has been tapped as the state’s next U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho after former U.S. Attorney Bart Davis announced his retirement earlier this month.
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed Rep. John Shirts, R-Weiser, as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, effective Sunday, according to a press release from the U.S. Department of Justice. Shirts was sworn in Sunday by U.S. Chief District Judge Amanda K. Brailsford in a private ceremony, the release said.
Idaho US Attorney Bart Davis announces retirement from Justice Department

“I am honored to serve as Idaho’s next U.S. Attorney,” Shirts said in the DOJ release. “Our office will remain focused  on upholding the rule of law and protecting the rights of citizens by prosecuting terrorism, drug trafficking, violent crime, human trafficking, illegal immigration offenses, and fraud. The safety of Idahoans and their communities is paramount. Those who commit federal crimes in our state will be held accountable and brought to justice.” 
Shirts, who ran against a GOP primary election opponent in May and won with 75% of the vote, is running unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election. The DOJ press release did not mention whether Shirts has stepped down from his Idaho House seat, but the deadline has passed to remove his name from the general election ballot, a spokesman from the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office confirmed.
As U.S. attorney, Shirts is considered the top-ranking federal law enforcement official in the state. The position has prosecutorial responsibility over Idaho’s 44 counties, encompassing more than 83,000 square miles and a population of nearly 1.5 million people.
He leads three staffed offices located in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Pocatello with 65 employees, including 33 attorneys. The  office is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in the district, including crimes related to immigration, terrorism, public corruption, child exploitation, firearms and narcotics. The office also defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States.
 John Shirts is a University of Idaho grad, former law clerk and former US Air Force JAG officer

Shirts is a fifth-generation Idahoan who grew up in Weiser, according to the press release. He represented Legislative District 9 and served as the vice chairman of the House’s Agricultural Affairs Committee. 
From 2018 to 2024, Shirts served as an assistant U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, prosecuting criminal cases in the Pocatello and Boise offices. 
Shirts was raised and worked on his family’s ranch, according to the press release. His great-great-grandfather homesteaded in Washington County in the 1880s.
Shirts attended Weiser High School and attended the University of Idaho, the press release said. After college, he graduated from the University of Colorado Law School. Shirts then clerked for Jonathan P. Brody, an Idaho district court judge in Rupert.
Following his clerkship, Shirts earned a commission in the U.S. Air Force as a JAG officer. During his active-duty service, he served in Korea as an adviser to the 51st Fighter Wing on Osan Air Base, according to the press release.
 Later appointed to the Air Force’s Special Victims Unit, he prosecuted sexual assault cases at 30 Air Force bases around the world, from Germany to Hawaii. His military decorations include the Air Force Commendation Medal and the Korean Defense Service Medal. After leaving active service to join the U.S. Attorney’s Office, he continued to serve as a prosecutor in the U.S. Air Force Reserve.
Shirts is married to Mercedes Shirts, a high school teacher.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Supreme Court takes Montgomery County magnet school admission policy case
text:
Students at their lockers on Aug. 28 at Montgomery County's Argyle Middle School. Argyle is not one of the magnet middle schools included in a case the U.S. Supreme Court said it will hear. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)The U.S. Supreme Court agreed Monday to hear a challenge from a group of Montgomery County parents who claim that the county’s lottery system for admission to middle school magnet programs decreases the number of Asian American students in the programs.
The case has been dismissed by lower courts, that said the parents had not proved that the policy “disparately impacts Asian American students” or that it was created with discriminatory intent.
But in agreeing Monday to hear the case, the high court said it would consider whether the parents “challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory must establish that the targeted racial group suffered an aggregate disparate impact relative to its share of the applicant pool” for their case to proceed.
The case was filed by the Association for Education Fairness challenges the lottery system used for admissions at four county middle schools that offer magnet programs focused on the humanities and STEM – science, technology, engineering and math. A student’s grades and test scores are another component of selection.
The association, which is mostly comprised of Asian Americans parents, filed suit in 2020 concerning the policy that took effect in the 2021-22 school year.
“If you institute a policy intended to increase the enrollment of some groups at the expense of others, you’re discriminating against the group that you are doing it at the expense of,” said Chris Kieser, a senior attorney at Pacific Legal Foundation, which is representing the association.
“You’re using, in this case, geography as a proxy … to get the racial results that you want, and that’s exactly what the Supreme Court said that you can’t do in students for fair admissions,” Kieser said in an interview Monday.
Keiser said there are four magnet middle schools affected: Takoma Park and Eastern are considered in the downcounty area; and Roberto Clemente and Martin Luther King Jr. in the upcounty area.
Montgomery County schools, parents reach settlement in suit over LGBTQ+ books in classes

Liliana López, a spokesperson for Montgomery public schools, said in an email Monday afternoon the court is strictly addressing a “purely legal question and decide what plaintiffs who challenge race-neutral admissions criteria on their face must establish to demonstrate discrimination.”
“Montgomery County Public Schools (MCPS) remains committed to providing equitable access to rigorous opportunities for all students. This commitment will continue uninterrupted as the judicial process proceeds,” her statement said.
But a number of outside groups, such as The Buckeye Institute, based in Columbus, Ohio, and Mountain States Legal Foundation in Lakewood, Colorado, filed legal briefs supporting the association and opposing the county’s policy.
“No State shall … deny any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws. Students must be treated based on [their] experiences as an individual — not on the basis of race,” they wrote in their brief.
‘Reforms opened doors’
Several other organizations filed briefs in support of the school’s policy, which they said expanded access to the program to previously underserved groups.
In 2018, for example, there were fewer that 10 Black and Latino students in magnet programs at the upcounty schools, Clemente Middle and MLK Jr. Middle. In the first year of the lottery, Black and Latino students accounted for 33% of admissions to MLK Jr. and 41% of magnet program students at Clemente.
Numbers similarly rose in the downcounty schools, where Black and Latino students made up 23% of Takoma Park Middle and 31% of Eastern Middle magnet admissions. By 2021, those numbers had risen to 37% and 40%, respectively.
Four groups – the Montgomery County Branch of the NAACP, Montgomery County Progressive Asian American Network (MoCoPAAN), We Are CASA, and AALEAD (Asian American Youth Leadership Empowerment and Development) released a joint statement on the case Monday.
“These reforms have opened doors for students who too often have been left out of opportunities designed to help them thrive,” the groups said. “A child’s future should not be determined by the poverty level at the school they happen to attend, their family’s knowledge of the admissions process, or how much or little access they have to resources that help them prepare for the future.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The county’s school board was successful in getting the case dimissed by U.S. District Court Judge Paula Xinis in July 2022, a ruling that was upheld in February by a three-judge panel of the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
But in its reply last month to the county’s filing urging the Supreme Court to reject the case, the association argued that Montgomery County’s policy violates the Equal Protection Clause of the Constitution. They also claim that there is a split between circuit courts on the issue that the Supreme Court must step in to resolve.
“Whether intentional racial discrimination receives strict scrutiny should not depend on the circuit in which it occurs. Only this Court can resolve the conflict once and for all,” the association’s lawyers wrote.
The Pacific Legal Foundation defended plaintiffs in a similar magnet-school admissions case the Supreme Court declined to hear in February 2024. The plaintiffs in that case claimed a policy by the Fairfax County, Virginia, school board would reduce the number of Asian American students attending Thomas Jefferson High School, one of the nation’s top-ranked high schools.
Two of the conservatives on the court, Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, said in a joint dissenting opinion that the Fairfax case should have been heard.
“The Court’s willingness to swallow the aberrant decision below is hard to understand. We should wipe the decision off the books, and because the Court refuses to do so, I must respectfully dissent,” Alito wrote.
The Montgomery County middle school case is the second case from Montgomery schools the court has taken up in two years. In June 2025, the court ruled 6-3 in Mahmoud v. Taylor that parents should be allowed to opt their children out of classes that teach LGBTQ+-themed books in classrooms.
No hearing date has been set for the latest case, Association for Educational Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Center for Intellectual Freedom head accuses officials of unlawful obstruction
text:
Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. De Castro in his annual report to the General Assembly outlined actions by board and university officials that he believes undermined the center's efforts. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The interim director of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa alleged in a report to lawmakers that university and Iowa Board of Regents officials broke the law in attempts to obstruct the center’s development.
The 409-page report details more than a year of tug-of-war between center staff and advisors and the Iowa Board of Regents and university for control of its operations and offerings.
University of Iowa Center for Intellectual Freedom Interim Director Luciano I. de Castro. (Photo courtesy of the University of Iowa)
Luciano de Castro, the center’s interim director, made numerous allegations in the center’s first Legislature-required annual report, submitted Oct 12 to the governor, General Assembly and Board of Regents. De Castro had been a candidate for the permanent director but said in the report he would no longer want the job permanently even if he was still being considered for it.
In the report, he states the center is on the path to becoming a “lost opportunity” for true reform, with its opponents stymying its independence in day-to-day operations and exerting a level of control he believed wasn’t lawful.
“University of Iowa administrators have used their influence over the Board of Regents to hinder the Center’s operations at nearly every stage of its development,” de Castro wrote as his central finding in the report.
Established in a law signed by Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds in June 2025, the center has put on discussions and guest speaker events throughout the previous and this academic year, offered two courses this past spring, introduced an organizational plan and is about to select a new permanent director.
It has also recently lost nearly half of its advisory council membership, and all activities beyond the guest speaker series and director search have been paused as the 2028 requirement to offer general education courses creeps closer. A three-person board of regents committee led by Regent Christine Hensley now oversees the center, with Hensley having approval authority over travel and certain expense decisions.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
De Castro in the report called House File 2800, which sets the civic education requirements, the center’s “greatest opportunity,” but one he believes won’t be realized since “the required courses will be shaped by a director operating under close control by a Board that has consistently followed the University administration’s preferences.”
Hensley, in a statement sent via email by Iowa Board of Regents Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman, said the board has received the report and is reviewing it. The University of Iowa when asked for comment directed inquiries to the board of regents.
The board will meet Oct. 20 to interview three center director finalists and select a new director, with one finalist having dropped out for personal reasons, Lehman said in the email. De Castro himself applied for the director position, but the advisory council’s executive committee didn’t move his application ahead, he stated in the report. His tenure as interim director will end Oct. 22, according to a letter from the board.
“The Board of Regents wants the Center to be successful, and we will be interviewing finalists tomorrow for the director’s position,” Hensley said in her statement Monday. “We will continue to provide support to the Center to help meet its goals of providing scholarship on the intellectual foundation of free societies, as well as the principles, ideals and institutions of the American constitutional order, and the foundations of responsible leadership and informed citizenship.”
De Castro alleges unlawful actions
Multiple actions taken by the board of regents office “in coordination with University administrators” were described by de Castro in the report as “illegal, or at least contrary to the spirit of the law that created the Center.” Those include delaying hiring, campus invites and report releases, adding director search requirements and a timeline and interfering with the center’s efforts to be an independent academic entity.
De Castro said in the report many of these details have already been shared with state officials during a meeting in April.
Board Executive Director Mark Braun tried to have de Castro postpone a visit by now-former advisory council member Richard Lowery in fall 2025 to the point where de Castro paid for the visit with his own money, according to the report. This led de Castro to believe that UI Executive Vice President and Provost Kevin Kregel, who contacted Braun about the visit, was “attempting to undermine the center” since other expenses were approved without issue.
House File 437, which establishes the center, states the director “shall have the authority to invite guest speakers to the university on behalf of the center.”
The law also states that the director “shall have the sole and exclusive authority to manage the recruitment and hiring process,” but de Castro said in the report he was barred by Braun and through Kregel from hiring temporary faculty in October 2025, which led to restrictions on how courses could be developed since the center had no instructors and de Castro was beholden to his faculty responsibilities in the university’s business college.
Establishment of bylaws was left in the law to the center with required approval from the board, a process which took place in October and November 2025. De Castro said in the report he wrangled with board staff over inclusion of certain provisions.
De Castro wrote that he didn’t want a provision granting authority for approval of expenditures to the executive director of the board of regents. While it didn’t end up in the bylaws, he said in the report nothing was added giving that authority to the center director instead and Braun still handled expense approvals.
Other actions de Castro listed as potentially violating the law include the board of regents setting finalist requirements and a search timeline for the center director selection. He also objected to the center’s advisory council debating director applicants in closed session. No votes were taken on finalists in open session, he said in the report, and while de Castro made no requests to have his application discussed in closed session, the comparison between him and other candidates did not take place in an open meeting.
The center, through the law, was to be established at the UI as an “independent academic center,” which de Castro said in the report Kregel pushed back against. The report included a March 17 email from Kregel to center Administrative Services Manager Collin Sawyer about exploring the process for the center to become authorized to offer courses independently. Kregel said in the email because the center is a board of regents entity, “it cannot function as an academic unit within the University of Iowa” and recommended working with Braun on course offerings.
“The Provost’s email therefore effectively denies the Center the ability to fulfill its lawful obligation,” the report stated.
Proposal to reorganize
In April 2026, de Castro reported he submitted a proposal for reorganization to board of regents members that would put the center “on par with the University College and University Libraries,” with memorandums of understanding to let the center offer its own courses instead of ones temporarily through the University College or under the university’s control and to have the center receive administrative services.
“The proposal was not taken up; the framework later adopted by the Board was developed by the Board Office and the University without the Center’s participation,” de Castro wrote.
He said in the report that Hensley told him in August that Braun had sent out a draft plan for reorganizing the center, but de Castro wouldn’t get to see it until it she finalized it with Cramer, Regent Steve Lacy and Braun.
There were many instances where de Castro said he was left out of conversations about the center he felt he should be included in because of his position, including pay changes for staff, updates on questions he had for the university and board and center framework planning.
Despite sending messages to Hensley and Board President Robert Cramer about Braun leaving de Castro out of emails and discussions about things he had a direct hand in, de Castro said in the report things didn’t change.
The organizational plan, which received board approval at its September meeting, places Hensley, the board Center for Intellectual Freedom committee chair, in “an executive role” for the center through her required approval of expenditures and director travel, a position de Castro questioned in the report given her governing role on the board of regents.
“In particular, rather than vesting expenditure and travel approval in the Chair of the CIF Committee, the Center should be permitted to hire its own personnel to review its expenditures, an arrangement equivalent, in function, to the chief financial officer of a university,” the report stated.
Recommendations 
De Castro offered recommendations in the report for the center to reach “true reform” despite the obstacles and challenges it has faced, including suspending the permanent director search and picking a different interim director. He proposed having the General Assembly decide the center’s future and develop an independent academic council of academics who “have no stake in the administration of Iowa’s public universities” to advise the board of regents.
He also included information on his approach to the director role, mistakes he made during his tenure and lessons he learned. De Castro described the center’s status as “a defeat,” as the legislation seems to not matter much when “the university bureaucracy retains effective control over every decision.”
“The experience of the past year does not show that such centers are unnecessary or that they cannot succeed. It shows that they require far more resolve than was anticipated, from the legislators, regents, and civic patrons who support them, to persist in the face of opposition from university administrators and faculty,” de Castro wrote. “Where that resolve exists, as other states have shown, such centers can flourish. Where it does not, they become a pretense. The choice now before Iowa’s leaders is which of these the Center for Intellectual Freedom will be.”

name: VTDigger
title: Lewis M. Holmes
text:
Born: 04/16/1938
Troy, New York
Died: 10/17/2026
South Burlington
Details of service:

Lewis Meredith Holmes lived an engaged life as both a scientist and a humanist, with respect for the mind, the earth and the many people with whom he shared his life. He worked professionally in research, editing and teaching in Europe and the United States.
Lewis was born on April 16, 1938, in Troy, New York to Lynn C. and Caroline Kosegarten Holmes and grew up in Fairport, a suburb of Rochester, with older brothers Paul and Lawrence. He received a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering from Cornell University in 1960.
He married Madelyn Jamison in 1970 and together with their beloved daughter, Amanda, lived an international life starting in New Jersey, then moving to Copenhagen, Zurich, Norwich and Stevenage in England, Belmont and Acton in the Boston area and Washington D.C. They retired to Burlington, where Lewis took up an interest in gardening, and also lived part-time in an apartment in Montreal, enjoying the city’s international culture.
Lewis earned a Ph.D. degree in condensed-matter physics from Harvard University and a master’s degree in European literature from the University of East Anglia in England. He conducted research at Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey, and at universities in Denmark and Switzerland. Later he served as Editor-in-Chief of the trade publication Laser Focus World and as Editor of the American Institute of Physics journal Computers in Physics. He published over forty research papers and many magazine articles, as well as four books
His intellectual and cultural interests were wide-ranging. He became fluent in German and started a small publishing company, CEK Publishing, named after his mother Caroline Elizabeth Kosegarten, who was of German heritage. In retirement he wrote three books on the life and works of Ludwig Gotthard Kosegarten, an eighteenth-century German poet, and was an independent scholar in the German department at the University of Vermont. He became interested in music history while researching the musical settings of Kosegarten’s poems.
In addition to a lifelong fondness for Western classical music, while teaching English in China, Lewis learned to play the sheng, a three-thousand-year-old musical instrument. Afterwards he wrote The Mystery of Music: An Exploration Centered on the Lives of Thirty Ancient Musicians.
He is survived by his wife Madelyn, daughter Amanda, her husband Nicolas Gulino, grandchildren, Nathaniel and Caroline; brother-in-law, Andrew Jamison and nieces Emily and Klara and their children; and niece and nephews of deceased brother Lawrence Holmes: Jeffrey, Brian, Douglas, Steven, and Laura Binetti.
He passed away peacefully at the Residence at Quarry Hill with his wife and daughter at his bedside.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Jackson will skip this weekend’s Trump rally in Macon
text:
Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, speaks alongside President Donald Trump at a rally in Dalton on Friday, Oct. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderRepublican candidate for governor Rick Jackson will skip President Donald Trump’s upcoming rally in middle Georgia this weekend, opting instead to campaign in suburban Atlanta as the virtually tied race enters its final stretch.
The decision comes after Jackson on Friday joined Trump on stage at a rally in Dalton after taking part in a tele-rally with the president the previous Sunday. Now, Trump will head to Macon on Saturday for another push to turn out his  supporters for the midterms.
A Civiqs poll finds Trump at 33% approval in Georgia, the lowest since his second term began. A new poll from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution also shows that 55% of likely Georgia voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance.
Since Jackson won the GOP nomination in June, the Republican who once said he would be “Trump with a Southern tone” has sought to align himself more with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. But a spokesperson with the Jackson campaign downplayed his absence from the upcoming Trump rally, framing it instead as a strategy to increase Republican voter turnout elsewhere in the state.
“Rick will be serving as a force multiplier and rallying Republicans in Cherokee County to turnout,” said spokesperson Garrison Douglas in a statement.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive and a self-described political outsider, is running against Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, in a race that’s rated a toss-up according to the Cook Political Report. And despite Jackson pulling ahead of Bottoms in recent polling by a couple percentage points, the race remains within the margin of error.
Bottoms’ campaign argued that the Trump-endorsed Republican nominee remains closely aligned with the president.
“Donald Trump is coming back to Georgia again in an attempt to elect his ‘great friend’ Rick Jackson, because Slick Rick Jackson would do whatever Donald Trump wants as governor,” said Tharon Johnson, campaign manager for the Bottoms campaign.
Kennesaw State University political science professor Jason Shepherd, who previously chaired the Cobb County Republican Party, said that despite the president’s low approval rating, Jackson’s absence doesn’t necessarily mean that the Republican nominee is trying to distance himself from Trump. Shepherd added that since Trump is already attempting to turn out voters in middle Georgia, it makes sense that Jackson will try to mobilize voters in another region.
“You have the president rallying Republicans to get out to vote in Macon. Rick Jackson needs to be rallying Republicans to get out the vote in someplace else, and other candidates as well. It’s all one team working together over a very big state,” Shepherd said.
And the Democratic Party of Georgia was quick to suggest Jackson’s campaign statement implies that he is still working closely with Trump, with spokesperson Jake Strickland saying that Jackson “will never be able to run away from his long record of fighting for Trump over what’s in the best interest of Georgia families.”
“It’s beyond clear that Slick Rick is a Trump-obsessed billionaire who will do anything to suck up to the president,” Strickland said.
