name: Source New Mexico
title: In New Mexico, US Sen. Elizabeth Warren praises universal childcare, Dem governor nominee Haaland
text:
Former Democratic presidential candidate U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), left, joins New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, right, for an Oct. 19, 2026, tour of an Albuquerque childcare facility to promote the state's first-in-the-nation universal childcare program. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)During a tour of an Albuquerque childcare facility Monday afternoon, U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) hearkened back to 2019, when she and Deb Haaland, then a member of Congress, introduced a bill that would have established universal childcare for millions of American families.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Seven years later, Haaland, now the Democratic nominee to be New Mexico’s next governor, is running on a platform to expand the state’s first-in-the-nation universal childcare program, which went into effect late last year.
“As a nation, we invest in infrastructure and roads and bridges and clean water and electricity so that you can go to work,” Warren told reporters gathered at Corazoncitos Felices Academy in southwest Albuquerque Monday. “Childcare is infrastructure. It’s infrastructure for working parents, it’s infrastructure for the businesses that want to hire those parents.”
The program Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced in 2025 makes every New Mexico family eligible for tuition-free childcare. A bill passed in this year’s legislative session requires that the state implement co-pays for high-earning families amid economic downturns.
Warren said she wants the federal government to be a strong partner to New Mexico and hopes to see the program replicated across the nation, particularly as inflation and affordability have become key issues ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
“The world has changed since we first introduced this” in 2019, she said. “We first introduced this and a lot of people were like, ‘Eh, here come the girls again.’ This has become a more urgent, more visible problem.” 
Some providers and parents across the state have advocated for the state to boost capacity, citing lengthy waitlists for children to gain admittance to childcare facilities.
New Mexico childcare providers struggle as demand, waitlists increase

As Warren and Haaland toured the childcare facility Monday, toddlers and children showed off their bilingual education. One teacher, holding up a flash card depicting zoo animals, quizzed her class: “¿Qué es esto?”
Giggling in unison at the picture of a monkey, the children in class responded: “¡El mono!”
Haaland, who served as a national co-chair on Warren’s 2020 presidential campaign, previously told Source NM that she’ll work to increase capacity statewide if elected, with a particular focus on making sure rural areas have the same childcare access as New Mexico’s major cities.
Gregg Hull, the Republican nominee facing Haaland in the Nov. 3 general election, has criticized the program for serving New Mexico’s highest-earning families and has said that if elected, he’d like to re-examine the failed proposals to mandate co-pays for families with high household incomes.
A group of children at Albuquerque’s Corazoncitos Felices Academy sing, dance and shake tambourines for New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) on Oct. 19, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)
Haaland, who on the campaign trail has often cited her experience as a working single mother, said she will work to strengthen and expand the program if elected.
“I know what it’s like to not afford childcare and to have to clean up my child’s preschool so that I could actually afford the tuition bill,” she said Monday. “I want to see whatever we can do to make sure that we can keep it available. In my opinion, early childhood education should be public school. It’s that important.”
After their tour, Haaland and Warren took turns reading picture books to a group of children and participated in a panel discussion moderated by Olga Grays, a Las Cruces-based childcare provider and state representative for the National Association for Family Child Care.
While Grays praised the universal childcare program, she said childcare professionals across the state have complained that it has not done enough to boost wages for early childhood educators across the state.
Haaland said she’s focused on issues related to affordability and believes that strengthening the early childhood education workforce will have a ripple effect by allowing more parents to work outside the house.
“Let’s be clear: Universal childcare is an economic driver for our state. It creates jobs, it allows parents to have the jobs that they need to have,” she said. “Everyone deserves to have a living wage.”
Former U.S. Interior Secretary and New Mexico Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, right, and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), left, read picture books to a group of children at Albuquerque’s Corazoncitos Felices Academy on Oct. 19, 2026. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)

name: Daily Montanan
title: Some state lawmakers want to legalize gun suppressors, short-barreled weapons
text:
An unloaded Glock 19X handgun sits next to a magazine and 9 mm ammunition at a gun range. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)Three Republican legislators announced they’re preparing bills for the opening of the 2027 Legislature in January that would allow more types of firearms and firearm accessories.
Gun suppressors (sometimes referred to as silencers) would become legal under proposed legislation, which would additionally allow for short-barreled shotguns and rifles, sometimes colloquially referred to as “sawed-off” weaponry.
Sound suppressors and short-barreled rifles and shotguns had previously been banned at the federal level, and state law currently prohibits their usage. However, the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms, Tobacco and Explosives recently said it was no longer going to enforce certain aspects of federal law related to suppressors and short-barrelled firearms after an August decision in a court case in North Texas.
The ATF said it was “working as quickly as possible to issue new regulations to authorize federal firearms licensees” to transfer short-barreled rifles and shotguns under the Gun Control Act of 1968, a foundational piece of gun control legislation. The agency said in the meantime it won’t enforce the provisions.
“I have been working with ATF for months to issue guidance to Montanans and all Americans regarding the sale, transfer and manufacture of suppressors and (short-barreled guns) following a federal district court ruling striking down the National Firearms Act registration requirements on these items,” Montana Attorney General Austin Knudsen said in a Facebook post. “We still have law changes necessary at Montana state level, but I’m confident we’ll get this done in the 2027 session.”
A nonprofit focused on reducing gun violence said suppressors make firearms “uniquely dangerous,” but Montana Republican legislators said they’re looking to push the legislation quickly.
“We never want to see the feds get ahead of Montana on protecting Second Amendment rights, so we’re going to axe these unnecessary regulations as fast as possible,” Sen. Wylie Galt, a Martinsdale Republican, said in a press release.
Galt requested drafts for the legislation in September and Sen. Carl Glimm, a Kila Republican, as well as Rep. Braxton Mitchell, a Flathead Republican, agreed to carry them during the 2027 session.
“This policy is especially beneficial to hunters as we eliminate the paperwork and fees standing between them and using a suppressor to protect their hearing,” Galt said in a press release. “As hunters head out into the field this fall, they can be confident that this is the last season with unnecessary restrictions and taxes on their ability to use suppressors.”
Contrary to popular culture, suppressors do not fully “silence” a weapon. They cool and redirect gas created by firing a weapon; that process is responsible for most of the sound of a gun being fired.  
Many hunters and shooting sports enthusiasts wear ear protection to preserve hearing.
Drafts for the two bills — one will be introduced in the Senate and the other in the House — are identical in an effort to fast track the legislation. They would trim certain parts of the law related to silencers, or suppressors, and eliminate a section about short-barreled weapons.
“We’ve all been chomping at the bit to get this done for Montana sportsmen and hunters since the court ruling,” Glimm said in a press release. “With the ATF’s new guidance making it clear that the only thing standing between shooters and freedom is Montana law, we’re going to update those laws immediately.” 
But suppressed weapons can be more difficult to track, according to GIFFORDS, an organization dedicated to reducing gun violence in the United States. The nonprofit was founded by former Arizona Congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords who was herself a victim of gun violence. 
“These devices don’t actually reduce the sound by enough decibels to really protect someone’s hearing,” said Lindsay Nichols, the policy director at GIFFORDS Law Center. “What they do do is make it hard for a law enforcement officer or a witness to determine where the gunshot is coming from and to identify it as a gunshot. So that makes them uniquely dangerous because they can be used in ambushes and situations where a shooter wants to evade law enforcement.”
Montana had 247 gun deaths in 2024, with 212 of those ruled suicides, according to Johns Hopkins data. Additionally, Montana had the third-highest gun deaths via suicide and the highest highest gun death rate in the country overall among American Indian/Alaska Native people.
Republicans indicated in the release the bills also included work with Democratic leadership. Requests to legislative Democrats for comment on their inclusion in the process were not returned.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington panel eyes ways to ease hurdles to rebuilding homes destroyed by wildfires
text:
A Cal Fire firefighter works amid the remains of homes destroyed in the Old Trails Fire on Aug. 6, 2026 in Spokane, Washington. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)Under pressure from Gov. Bob Ferguson, the Washington state Building Code Council is wrestling with how far it can bend residential energy codes to speed up rebuilding homes destroyed by wildfires this summer.
Ferguson issued an emergency proclamation in August directing the council to identify state laws, rules or code requirements “that may be waived or suspended” if enforcing them strictly would hinder replacement of nearly 700 homes lost in blazes, most in the vicinity of Spokane in eastern Washington.
Earlier this month, the governor asked the council to adopt an emergency rule allowing owners of homes built before 2015 to rebuild in line with less restrictive residential energy codes adopted in 2015. For homes constructed after 2015, the governor is pushing for owners to be able to rebuild to the energy code that was in effect when their residence was first constructed.
“Newer building codes can increase construction costs and create delays as builders, designers and permitting staff adapt to new requirements,” he wrote in his Oct. 8 letter. “For homeowners rebuilding after a wildfire, those added costs and delays can be significant barriers to returning home and can prolong displacement and increase recovery costs.”
On Friday, Oct. 16, in their first meeting since receiving the letter, council members said they want to support the community’s recovery but flagged several concerns and challenges. After two hours, there appeared to be a path that would provide homeowners an option without ceding ground on existing standards. The full council could act by the end of the month after the approach is scrutinized by a subcommittee.
Some members are concerned about the precedent. Any change of building code standards through code waivers can have broad impacts and unintended consequences, they said.
There are statutory realities: an emergency rule to allow use of the older codes would only last 120 days and could expire before many owners are ready to rebuild.
There are political realities: Controversial code changes drawn up since 2015 are geared to get new homes built with electric heat pumps rather than natural gas, an idea widely disfavored on the east side of the state. In Friday’s meeting, several people expressed concern that homeowners would be deterred from rebuilding if required to install a heat pump.
Pam Stone, Ferguson’s senior housing adviser, told the council the intent is to provide flexibility for those who owned the home at the time of the wildfire. If the properties are sold, the new owners would need to comply with the most current codes.
“This is targeted relief. This is not a rollback,” she said. “Time matters just as much as cost. We fear that if we don’t take swift action, which is what we hope the council will do, we are going to lose some deeply important members of our community.”
Washington’s building code contains energy efficiency requirements for residential and commercial construction. It establishes a scoring system used in the approval of building permits based on the size of a home and construction options. 
In recent years, Washington has pushed to wean the state off its dependence on natural gas to heat homes. Changes drawn up in 2023 offer builders greater incentives in the permitting process for choosing electric heat pumps — which provide both heating and cooling in the same unit — instead of natural gas furnaces. The appliances are more energy efficient and result in less pollution.
Rep. Suzanne Schmidt, R-Spokane Valley, and Sen. Shelly Short, R-Addy, sent a letter to the council strongly endorsing the governor’s request.
Schmidt told the council on Friday that most of the roughly 700 structures destroyed were built 40 to 60 years ago. Building codes concerning safety and energy efficiency have been updated multiple times since then so any homes that are rebuilt will be better from an environmental standpoint under the 2015 or 2018 codes.
“We’re still improving on what existed prior to the fires,” she said.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Charting a path
Ferguson’s August proclamation required the Building Code Council to submit a report within 30 days assessing potential options.
What the council turned in Sept. 9 expressed little interest in what the governor is now seeking.
“While the State Building Code Council considered blanket code rollback and more targeted relief, it does not yet support waiver of a specific current code provision for wildfire recovery,” reads the opening line of the central conclusion.
The council pointed out that providing relief in this situation far exceeds suspending or waiving a single building code. 
“The near-term universe of current-owner total-loss rebuilds is only a subset of all affected properties,” the report reads. “Partial-loss repair, local permitting practice, insurance, financing, debris removal, utilities, and contractor availability, may affect more households than a broad new construction code waiver.”
Complicating the process is that the council is in the final weeks of formally adopting its 2024 standards that would take effect in May 2027. Members generally don’t want to see the timetable disrupted.
One option outlined Friday will get more study in the coming days.  
It would involve rule-making to amend current standards to give owners of older homes flexibility when complying with the energy codes. Secondly, new provisions would be tacked into the 2024 codes giving cities and counties the ability to deal directly with owners seeking to rebuild. It would allow local governments to be more surgical with how the property owners’ needs can be addressed. 
The council is on course to adopt those 2024 codes in December, which means any new language would need to receive a public hearing and council vote very soon.
“I am interested in finding a permanent pathway that allows for this to be available for users that are affected by this disaster,” said Dustin Curb, the council’s managing director. “I also think that this is a good opportunity for the council to envision ways to have something memorialized for future disasters that may come down the line.”
The council is aiming to take action on an approach by the end of the month.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: School board members can be deposed for removing library books, federal court rules
text:
Books in a Florida high school library. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)A years-long legal battle over book removals in Escambia County has a new chapter. A federal appeals court ruled school members may be deposed about why they removed library books and classroom material.
The lawsuit was brought by book publishers, parents, and the PEN American Center in 2023 after Escambia County officials voted to remove, at the request of a teacher and the superintendent, library books deemed to have “‘extreme sexual content,’ ‘LGBTQ agenda,’ ‘race-baiting,’ ‘graphic rape scenes,’ and ‘language,’” the suit explains. 
School board members claimed legislative privilege to avoid depositions. The appeals court agreed with the trial judge: Board members acted as administrators and not legislators when removing books and do not enjoy legislative privilege in this case. 
Three judges of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit oversaw the appeal. Two agreed with the district court — Jill Pryor and Andrew Brasher. Chief Justice William Pryor dissented. 
Brasher, writing for the majority, wrote that the school board’s decisions on the books resembled “nothing about” “what a legislator does i.e., the ‘proposal, formulation, and passage of legislation.’”
“We have explained an act is ‘more apt to be administrative in nature’ if ‘the facts utilized in making a decision are specific, rather than general, in nature,’” Brasher wrote, referencing 11th Circuit precedents.  
First, an internal committee advised keeping the books, while an appeal to the school board ended with the books being removed, Brasher wrote. 
“Our decision today is a narrow one. We do not address whether other privileges or discovery rules may warrant quashing these subpoenas, curtailing the depositions, or the like,” Brasher continued. 
“Nor do we suggest that every decision to stock or remove a book is administrative in nature. Legislative privilege serves important interests in preserving legislative independence and protecting legislators from compelled inquiry into legitimate legislative acts. Those interests warrant robust protection.”
But he added: “Our dissenting colleague’s independent research may have been comprehensive. But we respectfully suggest that his resort to unraised arguments about far-flung authorities merely underscores that this Court’s precedents (which we have obviously addressed in depth) do not support his position,” Brasher wrote. 
Pryor had cited, in the majority’s words, “an obviously distinguishable 1880 decision from California.”
“But the majority prefers to base its decision on our recent precedents about disparate contexts like personnel and zoning decisions that look nothing like an elected school board having to decide a political issue like removing a controversial book from school libraries,” Pryor wrote. 
Pryor viewed the board’s vote as “of a public character” in setting “a prospective and generally applicable Board policy.”
“Because the members of the Escambia County School Board exercise discretion over a matter of public policy when voting to remove books from school libraries, the majority wrongly strips them of their privilege to avoid testifying about those votes. In doing so, it ignores the common law that the Supreme Court has explained defines the privilege. It misreads our precedents too,” Pryor wrote. 
Had the board members acted on their own initiative, as opposed to reacting to parental and superintendent actions, Pryor argued, the majority would have views that as legislative, not administrative.
Backstory
Last year, Chief Justice Allen Winsor of the U.S. District Court in Tallahassee sided with the county, saying the school district had not violated students’ First Amendment rights in keeping from them a book about two male penguins raising a chick together.
Escambia County’s library policy has accumulated a long legal history, including disagreements about whether a 7-year-old student should be deposed. The district argued the student should be, and he was deposed.
Judge: Escambia County did not violate First Amendment by removing same-sex penguin book

In August 2025, a federal judge in Orlando ruled the state law banning school library books was “overbroad and unconstitutional.” That case was appealed to the 11th Circuit. Oral arguments were held in April.
Meanwhile, Henry Mack, Florida’s education commissioner, who started in that position this summer, sent a memo telling all districts “to identify deficiencies in how some districts are discharging those duties” of reviewing instructional and library materials. The duties are prescribed by the 2023 law.
“Districts must follow Florida law and State Board of Education rules by providing only materials that are age- and developmentally appropriate. Unfortunately, parents continue to find a shocking amount of material that fails that test. Again, that is unacceptable,” Mack wrote.
“Several districts, including Clay, Escambia, and Nassau, have already removed or discontinued substantial numbers of titles following review. Delaying until a district becomes the subject of the next public controversy is not an acceptable approach,” Mack added, adding that he holds authority to investigate noncompliance with the law.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: McKee extends pause deadline on Flock cameras indefinitely
text:
Rhode Island Gov Dan McKee has decided to keep a pause on the installation of new Flock Safety license plate readers in place. Questions surrounding oversight of the technology have led to backlash in communities across 49 states. (Photo courtesy of Flock Safety)Rhode Island’s pause on new automated license plate reader installations, originally set to end Monday, has been extended indefinitely after Gov. Dan McKee announced he would leave it to the General Assembly to establish binding statewide safeguards for the surveillance technology.
But the governor’s announcement Monday afternoon came with a framework crafted by the Rhode Island State Police to guide local departments’ use of the technology during the interim.
“Automated license plate readers can be a valuable tool for law enforcement, but we need to make sure they’re being used responsibly and that people’s privacy is protected,” McKee said in a statement.
McKee on Aug. 18 directed Rhode Island’s Department of Public Safety to conduct a 60-day “comprehensive review” of automated license plate reader systems amid growing resistance to Flock Safety cameras over concerns about privacy and how police are using the surveillance technology.
Rhode Island State Police Superintendent Col. Darnell Weaver completed the review and presented his recommendations to McKee’s office at 10 a.m. The governor’s office made the announcement at 4:08 p.m.
McKee’s August order tasked Weaver with consulting the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association, the League of Cities and Towns and other stakeholders. But privacy advocates criticized the review for shutting them out of the process.
Flock camera opponents say they were left out of state-led policy review

The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Rhode Island said in a statement that an initial review of the guidance raised “fundamental concerns,” though officials in the organization said they had not yet had time to thoroughly analyze the policy.
Under the proposed guidelines, police departments would need to delete license plate data within 30 days unless the information is being preserved for an investigation. Privacy advocates had called for state law to limit data retention to seven days in a letter sent to Weaver on Oct. 9, noting that Flock Safety, the company behind the network, had reduced the limit from 30 days to seven in August.
The policy Weaver recommended disallows cameras from being used for federal immigration enforcement, traffic violations, outstanding fines, civil infractions or investigations involving conduct not criminalized under Rhode Island law. Additionally, the camera technology could not be used to infringe on First Amendment rights or to discriminate against protected groups or interfere with reproductive rights.
Police could still access the camera data when a criminal investigation warrants reasonable suspicion of a state or federal crime. Advocacy groups had called for restricting camera use to specific serious offenses, including stolen vehicles, missing persons and violent crimes.
“This model policy establishes clear, consistent standards for how this technology should be used, how information is accessed and shared, and how agencies are held accountable,” Weaver said in a statement. “Our goal is to ensure that law enforcement can use this technology effectively and responsibly.”
Rhode Island municipalities and state police have contracted independently with Flock since 2021, creating a patchwork network of at least 280 cameras statewide, according to an ACLU estimate. Some communities have since moved to cancel their contracts over concerns about data access and use — including Providence, where city councilors recently proposed ending the city’s relationship with Flock.
“Not every community will choose to use automated license plate readers, but it is important that all municipalities have access to a consistent set of standards if they decide to adopt this technology,” Michael Correia, chief of the Barrington Police Department and president of the Rhode Island Police Chiefs Association, said in a statement.
Spokespeople for House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski and Senate President Valarie Lawson did not immediately respond to request for comment.

name: VTDigger
title: Local businessman donates $4 million to financially ailing Brattleboro Memorial Hospital
text:
The Brattleboro Memorial Hospital campus on Belmont Avenue. Photo by Kevin O’Connor/VTDigger

Brattleboro Memorial Hospital, seeking to recover from a multimillion-dollar budget deficit, announced Monday that a local businessman has offered a $4 million infusion.
Willy Buhlmann, who emigrated from Switzerland in 1970 to found and recently sell his Swiss Precision Turning machine shop, is donating the money to the southeastern Vermont healthcare hub’s depleted investment account, the hospital reported.
“I’m glad I made Brattleboro my home, and I wanted to give something back,” Buhlmann said in a statement. “The hospital is important to this community, and I wanted to do something meaningful to help ensure that people can continue to receive care.”
The Windham County facility, operating on a $130 million annual budget, has forecast a $7.1 million deficit for the 2027 fiscal year that began Oct. 1. That would follow a $33.6 million operating loss for the fiscal years 2017 through 2025, and an estimated $9.5 million shortfall for the 2026 fiscal year that ended Sept. 30, it reported in a state filing.
The hospital has blamed recent deficit spending on past administrative and accounting problems. To cover the losses, it has tapped reserves of cash, investments and unrestricted assets that collectively have dropped from $53.3 million in FY 2021 to a projected $19.7 million for FY 2027, the state filing shows. 
“Willy’s gift is an extraordinary investment in Brattleboro Memorial Hospital and in the future of health care in our region,” interim CEO David Sanville, the former chief financial officer of Windsor’s Mt. Ascutney Hospital and Health Center, said in a statement.

Willy Buhlmann, center, stands at Brattleboro Memorial Hospital with interim CEO David Sanville and fundraising head Gina Pattison. Provided photo

Last month, state regulators at the Green Mountain Care Board adopted current spending plans for the state’s 13 other general acute-care hospitals, only to level-fund the Brattleboro facility as it works to further clarify its finances.
Buhlmann founded Swiss Precision Turning in 1990 and sold it to Geokon, a New Hampshire-based engineering and manufacturing company, in 2023.
The $4 million gift comes a dozen years after 92-year-old Ronald Read, a former gas station attendant and janitor, left the hospital $4.8 million upon his death in 2014.
Buhlmann said of his own contribution: “I wanted to make this donation while I’m still alive and can see its impact.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Corruption, affordability are themes Democrats highlight in U.S. Senate race
text:
U.S. Sen.Bernie Sanders (L) with Democratic U.S. Senate hopeful Angie Nixon (R) in Tampa Saturday. (Photo via Bernie Sanders'  FaceBook page)A Florida Democrat hasn’t held a seat in the U.S. Senate since 2019, but 42-year-old Democrat Angie Nixon is working to reverse that trend in her push to defeat incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody in the general election Nov. 3.
To accomplish her goal, Nixon is hitting her opponent hard on connections to the Hope Florida story involving grand jury’s finding that the DeSantis adminstration steered $10 million intended for Medicaid through the nonprofit before it would its way through two other nonprofits to a political committee fighting a ballot initiative on marijuana.
Similarly, no Democrat has held the Governor’s Mansion since the 90s — Lawton Chiles was elected in 1991 and died in office in 1998. Democrat David Jolly hopes to move in next year.
The weekend events unspooled as early voting was about to kick off Monday in 34 of Florida’s 67 counties. Byron Donalds, the Republican candidate for governor, and Moody began the day early by speaking to dozens of supporters in Moody’s hometown of Plant City in eastern Hillsborough County.
More than 833,000 Florida voters had already cast ballots by mail as the early voting opened in more than half of the state. All 67 Florida counties will be open for early voting by Saturday.
Speaking a few minutes after 8:30 a.m. in the parking lot of Fred’s Market Restaurant, Moody blasted the platform of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the left-leaning organization Nixon joined earlier this summer.
“Sometimes, I feel like I am being punked because I’m running against a self-proclaimed card-carrying socialist who has outright said she wants to join up for an agenda that would do away with the Constitution, do away with the executive as we know it — the judicial branch — they would want to kneecap the military. Defund the police. Let non-citizens vote. This cannot happen in this country, but definitely not in the free state of Florida that we love,” Moody said.
Nixon has stated on several occasions that she does not fully align with the DSA platform, saying specifically that she does not support defunding the police or prisons or drafting a new Constitution. She does embrace other parts of its platform like Medicare for All and abolishing ICE.
Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody in Tampa on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)
The Hope Florida debate
The Hope Florida saga has triggered multiple legal battles, the latest involving the Republican Party of Florida’s attempt through a lawsuit to force off the air a Florida Democratic Party television ad that mentions the charity, which helps divert the needy from state assistance to churches and charities also offering help.
In speeches in Tampa and Tallahassee over the weekend, Nixon repeatedly jabbed at her Republican opponent as “lying, cheating, scamming, thieving Ashley Moody.” She referred to the fact that as attorney general Moody let the Hope Florida transfer transpire. Later, Gov. Ron DeSantis placed Moody in the Senate seat once held by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Crowds in Tallahassee and Tampa cheered.
“Unlike Ashley Moody, I wasn’t appointed as a ‘thank you’ for my loyalty to a corrupt system. I was elected to fight that corrupt system and that is exactly what I’ve been doing in the state House,” Nixon said in Tampa Saturday. 
“She works for the corrupt and the powerful to advance herself and put millions in her own pocket. But I know who I work for. I work for you. I fight for you. And when I get to the United States Senate, working people will have a senator focused on putting more in your pocket, not lining their own pockets.”
Accompanied by U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders from Vermont, Nixon staged a four-city blitz across Florida dubbed “Fighting Oligarchy.” She made appearances Saturday in Tampa and Melbourne and Sunday in Gainesville and Tallahassee.
Sanders only half jokingly told the Tallahassee crowd gathered at The Moon, a concert venue about 1.5 miles away from the Florida Capitol, “I can’t keep up with this woman. She doesn’t stop.”
Crowd response
The weekend rallies were packed with people who ran the gamut in age, with some acknowledging that Sanders was the attraction, not Nixon.
Florida State University students Tracy Caballero, 22, and Adayn Cao, 23, outside the “Fighting Oligarchy” campaign event in Tallahassee Oct. 18, 2026. (Photo by Christine Sexton/Florida Phoenix)
For others, though, such as Florida State University students Tracy Caballero, 22, and Adayn Cao, 23, Nixon, a mother of five, was the star. They arrived an hour before the rally was scheduled to start but were forced to watch her speech outside in the parking lot, part of an overflow crowd.
They both emigrated from Cuba when they were children — she was 11 and he was 8. They are now U.S. citizens and both intend to vote for Nixon.
“We are both very saddened about what’s going on in the country right now, and we want to support politicians who are fighting with us,” Caballero told the Phoenix. 
“She is very much anti-ICE, which I love, and she just wants to do what is actually best for everybody.”
Immigration and ICE also weigh on Cao’s mind. Even though he’s a citizen, Cao acknowledged “there’s an element of fear” because he’s seen ICE agents around campus.
“I have a couple of friends that have been deported, or like family that have been deported because of the situation that’s right now,”  he said. “A lot of Cubans, they come here seeking asylum. You know, starting a life here and then being in fear that you’re gonna be kicked out. Again, it’s difficult.”
Moody has more money on hand than Nixon, but in a sign that her underdog campaign is not forlorn she edged Moody in the most recent fundraising quarter. Nixon’s campaign has also attracted visits by national Democratic figures and well-regarded progressives such as Sanders.
As the race enters the final stretch, Nixon has persisted despite initial predictions her progressive record would make it easier for Moody to prevail.
The RealClearPolitics average has the Republican up by an average of 7 points over Nixon, 50%-43%.
The GOP’s case
Moody and other Florida Republicans have derided Nixon as a radical or socialist because of her recent alliance with the DSA. Moody sharply criticized Sanders and Nixon in weekend social media posts for voicing opposition to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included tax cuts.
She also noted that Sanders had once praised programs put in place by Cuban leader Fidel Castro (although Sanders also called Castro an authoritarian).
“Floridians whose families fled Castro’s socialist regime don’t need a lecture on it,” Moody posted on X. “They came here for freedom, and I’ll never let the radical Democrat Socialists like my opponent bring that misery to the USA.”
Nixon took time to respond to the “socialist” moniker and during her weekend campaign swing leaned into it.
“If believing that a mother working two jobs should earn enough to put food on the table is radical, then call me radical,” she said to growing cheers at the Tampa event held Saturday afternoon at the Cuban Club in Ybor City
 “If believing that a senior who works their entire life should be able to retire with dignity is radical, then call me radical. If believing that a child with cancer should get treatment whether their parents can afford it or not is radical, then call me radical. If believing that no family should go bankrupt [who] got sick is radical, then call me radical!.”
Nixon’s association with the DSA has excited some Democrats, like 30-year-old Tallahassee resident Natahsa Junkermeier, who said she supports “progressive Democrats” and has been a fan of Sanders since his presidential campaign in 2016. 
Junkermeier said she voted for Nixon in the primary because she was, drawn to her “no b—” attitude. Junkermeier said she was confident, even when the pundits weren’t, that Nixon would edge her Democratic opponent Alex Vindman in the August primary.
“I feel it’s so important to get as many progressives and Democrats in office as possible to even have a chance of stopping the more terrible things that are coming down the pipeline,” she said. 
Sanders’ draw
While it’s Nixon’s name on the ballot Nov. 3, Sanders drew people to the events. While critics fear the “socialist agenda” would bankrupt the country, Sanders countered that money would be better spent building up Americans than on the war in Iran, which the Associated Press reported last month has cost U.S. taxpayers more than $43 billion.
He mostly focused on Nixon, though.
“What this campaign is about is looking [Elon] Musk and his friends in the eye, and saying your day has come and it’s over. This country belongs to all of us. We’re going to create an economy that works for all of us, brothers and sisters. And I say this with absolute sincerity,” Sanders said. 
“What you do in the next 16 days can change the course not only of American history but of world history because what happens in America obviously impacts the whole world. If we can elect Angie is the next senator from Florida. If we can end Republican control over the House and the Senate.”
Moody was introduced Monday morning by House District 69 Republican Rep. Danny Alvarez, running against a DSA-backed Democrat in Ashley Herrmann in Hillsborough County, who warned against socialism.
“Openly talking about the dismantling of the American system as if something that you should be proud of. Openly talking about getting rid of everything that has made us Florida,” he said. “Everything that has made us the great state and the free state of Florida and getting rid of everything that makes us Americans.”
Donalds spoke for just six minutes and refrained from discussing socialists or his Democratic opponent, Jolly. His message was short and succinct: That Florida is the “best state in all of America,” and that Republicans need to go the polls now to make sure their voice is heard.
The Donalds bus tour was scheduled to make stops in the Villages and Jacksonville Beach later Monday.

title: Clement “Ted” Meunier
text:
Born: 04/06/1937
Burlington, VT
Died: 10/12/2026
Richford, VT
Details of service:
A service to honor Ted’s remarkable life will be held on October 25, 2026 at 1:30 p.m. at the Fairfax United Church in Fairfax, Vermont. Following, there will be a military remembrance held at the Underhill Rod and Gun Club, refreshments provided, starting at 3 p.m.

Clement “Ted” Meunier, beloved husband, father, grandfather and great-grandfather, passed away peacefully on October 12, 2026, with his devoted wife by his side. Born on April 6, 1937, in Burlington, Ted was the adored son of the late Clement Meunier and Edith Allen Meunier.
Ted’s life was a testament to love, commitment and adventure. On June 22, 1957, he married the love of his life, Margaret “Peggy” Patton. Together, they shared an extraordinary 69-plus-year journey filled with laughter, love and countless cherished memories. As devoted parents, they raised three wonderful children: Wendy Meunier Wood, Linda Meunier Cota and Melanie Meunier.
A proud graduate of Burlington High School in 1955, Ted soon dedicated his service to the U.S. Naval Air from 1955 to 1959, continuing in the reserves and retiring after 20 years of honorable service. His professional life included a fulfilling career as a computer analyst at IBM, where he worked for over 19 years before embarking on various entrepreneurial ventures. Ted’s endeavors included North Country Oil & Construction, Fixed Base Operator of the Franklin County State Airport in Highgate, and Meunier Real Estate.
Ted was an active participant in community service wherever they lived. He was a member of the Masons, served on the Fairfax School Board, and served on the Select Board in Franklin. He was the President of the Underhill Rod & Gun Club, and the Vermont delegate to the National Skeet Shooting Association, where his passion for skeet shooting flourished. He was a skeet shooting instructor for Remington and he also taught his wife to be a competitive shooter and shared his love for the sport with his children and grandchildren, creating treasured family memories.
Ted was actively involved with skiing, boating, golfing and hunting with the entire family. In pursuit of his dream of flying, Ted became a pilot, flight instructor and earned his mechanics license, sharing the skies with his family. He and Peggy traveled the country, finding joy and adventure at skeet shoots and the cockpit, inspiring a love for flying in the future generations.
Ted’s life was characterized by his quiet demeanor, yet his robust laugh and zest for life were unmistakable. He approached each day with enthusiasm, pursuing dreams and nurturing his family’s shared adventures.
Ted is lovingly survived by his wife, Peggy; his children, Wendy (Jonathan Wood), Linda (Kerry Caldwell) and Melanie; his grandchildren, Christopher Cota (Ashley Cota), Emily Cota Dallier, Curtis Cota (Jessica Cota), Julia Nuzzo (Chris Campbell) and Isobel Nuzzo; and his great-grandchildren, Autumn and Ryleigh Dallier, Ella, Cavin and Ciara Cota.
A service to honor Ted’s remarkable life will be held on October 25, 2026 at 1:30 p.m. at the Fairfax United Church in Fairfax, Vermont. Following, there will be a military remembrance held at the Underhill Rod and Gun Club, refreshments provided, starting at 3 p.m. (located off the Allen Irish Road). In lieu of flowers, the family kindly suggests donations be made to the Underhill Rod & Gun Club, in memory of Ted’s generous spirit and love for his community. The family wishes to thank the staff of Our Lady of the Meadows Ave Maria Community Care Home and Bayada Hospice for their thoughtful and compassionate care.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ lawmakers weigh AI regulations amid industry and safety expert clash
text:
Assembly lawmakers considered a four-bill package Monday that would implement various regulations on AI. Business groups warned of overreach. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Business groups urged New Jersey lawmakers Monday to avoid erecting regulations on artificial intelligence over fear of creating patchwork enforcement, while AI safety experts and others want the state to adopt strong safeguards amid federal inaction on the issue.
The discussion before the Assembly Science, Innovation, and Technology Committee could help determine how closely New Jersey follows other states, like New York and California, that have enacted more stringent AI regulations, and whether the state will allow large AI firms to escape liability for harms their technology causes, as some industry officials urged Monday.
Large model creators like Meta and Anthropic should be shielded from liability for harms spurred by a user because those firms could test their products but would be unable to prepare for every possible instance of abuse, said Matt Lenz, public policy director for Meta.
“We go through an exhaustive list to make sure that the models we release are safe and won’t cause any catastrophic harm. I don’t think we can predict use cases of everything, but making sure that that liability is on the appropriate downstream user so that we can still release open source models, I think, is really important,” he said.
AI safety has become an increasing focus for lawmakers after numerous AI researchers at industry-leading firms raised concerns about the technology.
Recent incidents like Hugging Face — where AI agents run by OpenAI broke free of their training environment and hacked Hugging Face, an unrelated AI firm — have redoubled legislators’ concern that the industry cannot safeguard its own technology.
Some witnesses told the committee that while AI represents a tectonic shift in computation and capability, it is still a man-made product that could be regulated the same as any other.
“We should start with the baseline principle that these are human-engineered products. We have human ways to control it, and if they’re not appropriately responding to our human-level controls, that’s a problem on whoever’s deploying the product,” said Mihir Kshirsagar, director of Princeton University’s Tech Policy Clinic. “It shouldn’t be the problem for society to then adapt to whatever that reality is.”
The panel discussed, without votes, four bills that would place limits on artificial intelligence or give residents new rights that could limit its use.
One bill would give New Jerseyans an exclusive property right over their name, image, likeness, and voice and would allow them to enforce that right through a civil action for damages and attorney fees. Violations of that right would also be prosecutable as disorderly persons offenses.
Jack Ramirez, a lobbyist for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association, warned that allowing individuals to recover attorney fees in this area would prompt a surge of lawsuits. The proposed criminal penalties are unusual, and firms should be provided an opportunity to remove offending content before facing legal liability, he said.
A separate bill would require disclaimers on AI-generated content in plain English and as computer-generated marks that could be used to verify a file was generated by AI.
“One of the biggest challenges our country faces is the proliferation of artificial digital objects created by artificial digital intelligence and the ability to understand if something’s real or not,” said Rob Eleveld, founder of the Transparency Coalition, which lobbies for AI safety regulations.
Ramirez warned that the bill’s fines, set at $5,000 per violation per day, would be too much for small and mid-sized AI firms to bear. He raised similar concerns over a separate bill that would make generative AI platforms civilly liable if their products are used to further a crime or create child sexual abuse material.
That measure would allow firms to make an affirmative defense that they made “reasonable efforts” to prevent their product from being used for a prohibited purpose. Ramirez said lawmakers should be clear on what qualifies as reasonable effort and again warned steep fines could bankrupt smaller AI companies or push some products out of New Jersey altogether.



Quotation







One of the biggest challenges our country faces is the proliferation of artificial digital objects created by artificial digital intelligence and the ability to understand if something’s real or not.


– Rob Eleveld, founder of the Transparency Coalition


Assemblyman Andrew Macurdy (D-Union), who is sponsoring the four-bill package, argued fines need to be large to affect the behavior of AI behemoths like Anthropic, which is valued at close to $1 trillion.
The final bill in the package would require large AI developers to disclose their safety procedures for frontier models to the New Jersey attorney general. It would also allow the attorney general to audit large AI firms both directly and through contracts with private entities.
Witnesses said strong oversight of the most cutting-edge models is needed even if those models are still in testing phases. They urged lawmakers to take steps to prevent regulatory capture, a phenomenon where firms effectively control their regulators, including by making regulators dependent on the companies they oversee.
“We’ve known from any number of places that we don’t want to trust someone to grade their own homework,” said Kshirsagar. “On the other hand, if you don’t actually empower anybody else to do it, then you’re going to get a set of captured entities that go out and do that work.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: As Iowa harvest picks up, state officials urge farmers to vote early
text:
A combine harvests soybeans in western Iowa. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Corn and soybean harvest in Iowa is about 20 percentage points behind the five-year average pace, but is progressing after a wet September that stalled field work. Officials urged farmers Monday to fit voting into their busy harvest-season schedules. 
According to the latest crop progress and conditions report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, 57% of soybean acres and 26% of corn acres have been harvested as of the Oct. 12 through Oct. 18 reporting period. The calculated five-year normal for the state shows 74% of soybeans and 50% of corn have typically been harvested by this mid-October reporting period. 
Soil moisture conditions remain consistent with the previous reporting period. According to the report, 24% of topsoil and 21% of subsoil rated as having surplus moisture conditions during the reporting period.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Climatologist Justin Glisan said the statewide average precipitation amount, at 0.86 inch, was above the normal of 0.62 inch for the period. Most of the state received some rainfall during the reporting period. 
Iowa had its first “widespread” frost and freeze event of the season, according to Glisan, who said lows fell below 30 degrees Fahrenheit at multiple weather stations in the state during the reporting period.
Despite the lows, overall temperatures across the state averaged more than 5 degrees above the climatological norm for the period. The statewide average temperature was 56.9 degrees. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said that while farmers are about two weeks behind schedule, the mostly warm and dry conditions during the reporting period and in the forecast should give farmers the opportunity to “keep harvest moving.” 
“As activity picks up, I remind drivers to watch for farm equipment, slow down and be patient,” Naig said in a statement. “A successful harvest means everyone gets home safely at the end of the day.”
Farmers encouraged to make a plan to vote
Naig joined Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate at a news conference Monday to get out the vote and urge farmers to take advantage of early voting options as delayed harvests are making for busy schedules. 
Republicans Naig and Pate are running for reelection to their seats – Naig against water quality activist and researcher Chris Jones and Pate against Democrat Ryan Peterman.
The secretaries join officials and activists on both sides of the aisle in pushing Iowans to take advantage of early voting options. On Saturday, participants in the No Kings protests across the country, including events in Iowa encouraged voters to request their absentee ballots. The deadline to request an absentee ballot by mail was 5 p.m. Oct. 19, but voters can request absentee ballots in person at county election offices or satellite voting locations until Nov. 2. 
Naig said that with farmers behind schedule for harvest, he wanted to remind farmers to “have a plan.” 
“Take advantage of the opportunity to vote early when you’re running to town for parts or something else, or you have a rainy day,” Naig said. “Go ahead and get over to the courthouse and cast your vote. And certainly, if you are not able to do that, have a plan to vote on November 3.” 
According to Pate’s office, more than 210,000 Iowans had requested absentee ballots as of Oct. 16, and just over 61,000 absentee ballots had been returned. Absentee ballots must be returned to the appropriate county auditor’s office by the time the polls close at 8 p.m. Nov. 3. 
Pate, speaking at the news conference Monday, encouraged Iowans who have requested a ballot to return them early. 
“Today we are 15 days out until the Election, and we want to make sure all Iowans have a plan to be successful in voting,” Pate said. “Particularly, our farm friends and their families, and all the people associated with the ag community.” 
Voting information including a county auditor list, polling locations, voter registration and absentee ballot information can be found on the Iowa Secretary of State’s website.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Vance touts $858M in Helene relief funding for Western North Carolina
text:
HENDERSONVILLE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 19: U.S. Vice President JD Vance delivers remarks at a campaign rally at Hyder Warehouse on October 19, 2026 in Hendersonville, North Carolina. Vance is headlining a midterm campaign rally organized by the Trump 47 Committee Inc. to support Republican candidates ahead of the upcoming elections. (Photo by Kenny Holston-Pool/Getty Images)Vice President JD Vance promised $858 million in additional disaster relief funding from the U.S. Department of Transportation during a campaign stop in Hendersonville, North Carolina on Monday.
Vance’s event is part of the White House’s push to encourage GOP turnout this election cycle in what polls show is a challenging political environment for Republicans. President Donald Trump will hold a rally in Greenville, N.C. on Tuesday.
The vice president stumped for Michael Whatley, as well as U.S. House candidates Jennifer Balkcom and Laurie Buckhout. 
In the U.S. Senate race, Whatley is running against Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper. With 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independents, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip control of the chamber. Cook Political Report rates the race as “likely Democratic.”
“We are going to rebuild eight major corridors destroyed by Hurricane Helene, including the I-40 and Pigeon River Gorge,” Vance told supporters in Hendersonville.
The U.S. Department of Transportation announced $873 million on Monday in Helene relief funding for North Carolina. 
Last month, Trump jokingly claimed at a campaign rally in Gastonia that he would withhold Helene relief funding unless Whatley won the Senate race. 
Vance joked that U.S. Senate candidate Michael Whatley, former chair of the Republican National Committee and North Carolina Republican Party, “would not shut up” about Helene relief in Western North Carolina. 
Whatley was named Trump’s “recovery czar” in January 2025, but has been accused by his critics, including some in his own party, of doing little to help secure federal resources.  
Trump heads to Greenville as NC Republicans struggle with early voter turnout

Public records show just six text messages and five phone calls totaling 38 minutes between Whatley and a state official helping coordinate recovery efforts over the course of roughly one year, according to Asheville Citizen-Times. 
But at the rally, Whatley said it was Cooper who had failed the region. 
“He was totally unprepared for the disaster and completely failed to respond after the skies had cleared,” Whatley claimed. “Roy Cooper even vetoed a bill that would have delivered key disaster relief to communities who were affected by the storm.”
Whatley was referring to a 131-page bill that, although branded as Helene relief, shifted power away from Democrats elected to office. Cooper referred to the legislation as a “sham” in his veto message. 
“Roy Cooper led North Carolina through several major catastrophic storms, activating emergency resources, keeping families safe and securing significant state and federal funding for recovery,” a Cooper campaign spokesperson told NC Newsline. 
During Vance’s speech, a protester behind him on the stands yelled out, “Release the Epstein files!”
Vance turned around to look at the protester, a man of color. As security dragged the man away, Vance suggested the protestor was an illegal immigrant. “I said that we have had zero illegal border crossings in the United States of America, but one isn’t bad, right?”
The crowd booed the protester and cheered for Vance. 
Balkcom, a state lawmaker representing Henderson County, is facing Democrat Jamie Ager in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. The NCGOP chose her to replace incumbent U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards in August after he dropped out.
Though Hendersonville is her hometown, Balkcom gave a short speech of about three minutes. 
Her primary accomplishment so far in the state legislature, where she’s served since 2023, has been sponsoring a bill banning transgender athletes from competing in women’s and girls’ sports. She and several other speakers at Monday’s rally emphasized that issue.
Last month, Balkcom and Ager both aired ads aiming to appeal to rural voters. Ager’s ad showed him hosting a barn dance at his farm. 
“My opponent, Jamie Ager, likes to have barn dances and drag queen shows,” Balkcom said. “The only thing I know around this area that we like to have in our barn is either crops, hay, tools, or tractors.”
In Balkcom’s ad, she revealed her mom taught her to be strong, and that Balkcom’s mother shot a home intruder. Buckhout and fellow Republican state auditor Dave Boliek referenced the moment during their speeches. 
“She’s as tough as they come,” Boliek said. “When she was growing up, when a guy tried to break into her house, her mom shot the guy. So I know where she gets the resolve from, and she brought that with her to Raleigh.”

name: Daily Montanan
title: Nearly 12% of absentee ballots returned, according to Montana Secretary of State’s Office
text:
Montana's new "I voted" sticker. (Secretary of State's Office photo)Montana voters already are turning in their general election ballots — 60,329 as of Monday, according to the Montana Secretary of State’s Office.
That’s 11.6% on average of the 520,035 absentee ballots sent, according to the Secretary of State’s ballot counts tracker. Montana has more than 780,000 registered voters.
People who haven’t registered to vote may still do so, and details are available on the Secretary of State’s website.
In Cascade County, election administrator Terry Thompson encouraged people who need to register to do so sooner rather than later.
“Register early,” Thompson said Monday. “Come down and register so that we don’t have long lines on Election Day.”
Thompson said a steady flow of people have been registering, and her staff are ready to help so voters don’t have to wait at this point.
“It’s all hands on deck with my team,” Thompson said.
As of Friday night, Thompson said her team had processed 5,530 ballots, and the drop boxes had been filling up since then.
“We probably have 2,000 to process tonight,” Thompson said.
As of Monday, Hill County had the highest portion of ballots back so far, 18.47%, or 1,029 out of 5,571. Pondera, Toole and Sweet Grass counties also had an estimated 18% each.
In a couple of the most populous counties, Yellowstone and Missoula, voters have turned in more than 16% of absentee ballots. 
Missoula County Elections Administrator Bradley Seaman said Monday of the 64,000 ballots the county mailed out, voters have turned in more than 10,000.
“We are rocking and rolling on the election,” Seaman said in a voicemail.
He also said county employees are working hard to contact voters who have undeliverable ballots.
One race in particular is heating up in western Montana.
Last week, political analysts shifted the U.S. House race in district No. 1 to a “toss up” between Republican Aaron Flint and Democrat Sam Forstag.
Saturday, Montanans at No Kings rallies said they were motivated to vote to counteract U.S. President Donald Trump’s policies.
They said high gas prices and unaffordable health care were driving their decisions on the ballot.
Trump himself also visited Montana last week to rally his base before the Nov. 3 general election.
Thompson said not everyone has figured out that they don’t have to fill out their birth year on their absentee ballots anymore — a judge found the requirement to be unconstitutional — and ballots won’t be rejected based on that issue.
She also reminded voters that at least in Cascade County, the elections office has extended hours. It’s open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Monday through Friday through Oct. 30, and 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. this Saturday and on Halloween.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: ‘Night and day’ difference revealed after restoration in South Dakota Capitol rotunda
text:
A view of the restored rotunda dome in the South Dakota Capitol building on Sept. 14, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/101926-Rotunda-Restoration-Done-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story produced by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
PIERRE — Scaffolding stood in the center of South Dakota’s Capitol building for six months, but now the work is done and the reviews are coming in.
Pierre resident Mary Keeler, who works for the state Bureau of Finance and Management, stood looking up into the dome recently while admiring the restoration work.
“It has always been a beautiful building,” she said. “But this is pretty spectacular.”
Refreshed paint, brighter details and new lighting have made the interior dome more vibrant, she said.
“Just wow,” Keeler said. “And the lighting, it just really makes it even more special than it has been. I think they did a fabulous job.”


Philip Atilano, the project foreman, has years of experience as a professional restorer for Conrad Schmitt Studios in Wisconsin. He told South Dakota Searchlight earlier this year, before completing the restoration, that his team’s focus was restoring the faded wall paint, decorative details and artwork. The lighting had become less visually appealing over time, too, he said.
“It was so dark and dreary in here, initially, for a rotunda. It just didn’t scream ‘state Capitol’ as much as it will now,” Atilano said then. “What we’re doing now, it’s going to blow people’s minds. I think people that were used to it before, now they’re going to see it, and it’s just, I think it’s going to be night and day.”
Restoration artists craft ‘the next phase of history’ in the South Dakota Capitol rotunda

The state paid for the work out of a $3 million pool of money approved last year by state lawmakers for the restoration, maintenance and repair of historic areas and objects within the Capitol.
Since 2019, lawmakers have provided a total of $13 million for various Capitol projects including the dredging of Capitol Lake, plaster and paint restoration work, and to begin saving for a full restoration and renovation that could cost more than $150 million, including updated wiring and utilities. That prediction comes from the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the Capitol.
The next steps toward a full restoration are being evaluated. The last full restoration was conducted ahead of the 1989 state centennial, nearly 40 years ago. Construction of the Capitol was completed 116 years ago in 1910.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Clinic union certified, but Rogers Behavioral declines to say it will start bargaining
text:
A National Labor Relations Board official has certified the National Union of Healthcare Workers as the official representative for employees at the West Allis clinic (above) of Rogers Behavioral Health. The union was previously certified at Rogers' Madison location. (Rogers Behavioral Health media photo)A federal official has affirmed the pro-union vote at a West Allis mental health clinic, rejecting challenges to the outcome lodged by Rogers Behavioral Health.
The decision, issued Oct. 15 by National Labor Relations Board regional director Jennifer Hadsall, certifies the National Union of Healthcare Workers as the official representative for employees at the Rogers West Allis clinic.
Hadsall also rejected a series of challenges that Rogers management made in connection with the election, held April 22, when employees voted 53-4 for union representation.
The union was previously certified to represent employees at Rogers’ Madison clinic, where employees voted 26-4 in favor of the union, also on April 22.
Rogers Behavioral Health, based in Oconomowoc, operates a network of mental health hospitals, residential treatment clinics and outpatient clinics in 10 states. Employees at three clinics in California and one in Pennsylvania organized with the National Union of Healthcare Workers starting a few years ago.
In a statement issued Monday, Rogers acknowledged the union had been certified at both Wisconsin locations but declined to respond to questions about the organization’s next steps, including whether it would begin bargaining with the union.
The organization’s statement said Rogers was “unable to comment further on pending legal proceedings related to these certifications.”
A certification order can be appealed to the full National Labor Relations Board in Washington, D.C. Rogers declined to answer directly when asked if the organization’s management was appealing the certification decisions to the board.
The West Allis certification order rejected a series of objections to the election outcome, including claims that three fired employees trespassed on the day of the vote. An administrative law judge upheld the right of the fired employees to vote and found no evidence of trespass, and the new order upheld those findings.
The certification order follows a finding, also issued by Hadsall, a week earlier that Rogers violated federal labor laws before, during and after the election, including by firing six employees involved in the union organizing campaign. A hearing on the NLRB complaint is scheduled for December.

name: VTDigger
title: ICE looks to boost staffing at intelligence hubs in Vermont
text:
A Department of Homeland Security office off Industrial Avenue in Williston on Tuesday, October 7, 2025. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement could hire more workers at its offices in Vermont as part of a $100 million plan to boost intelligence-gathering for the branch of the agency that carries out arrests and deportations, federal records show. 
The plan, which is not final, calls for 24 positions evenly split between ICE’s Law Enforcement Support Center and its National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center, both of which are in Williston. They’re among 142 total positions proposed for ICE offices around the country, all of which would be staffed by a government contractor. 
The workers would provide “intelligence research and analytical support” for ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations division, often abbreviated ERO, according to a contracting document published online last month. That includes “understanding emerging trends, identifying potential threats, recognizing intelligence gaps, assessing relationships and patterns” and a number of other duties.
The contractors would work with a mix of classified and unclassified information, and at least some of them would need “top secret” government security clearance, according to the document. ICE estimates the total cost of the nationwide plan, called ERO Overwatch and National Security Enforcement, would be more than $100 million, according to another federal record published last month.
The government has been “conducting market research” for the plan and issued a request for information to potential contractors, which was due late last month, according to the published records. A final contract could be awarded around February, the magazine The American Prospect reported last week, citing intelligence contracting experts.
One of the Williston centers, the Law Enforcement Support Center, is located on Harvest Lane. It operates a round-the-clock service for police nationwide to get information on a person’s immigration status, as well as a tip line for the public. Workers there also generate leads for immigration enforcement agents and process biometric data for other federal law enforcement agencies including the U.S. Secret Service, according to ICE’s website.
Less than a 10-minute drive away on Industrial Avenue, the National Criminal Analysis and Targeting Center also develops leads for ICE operations, using an array of digital tools to provide “critical investigative support for daily arrest efforts” according to an agency webpage.
Together, the centers are a major node in ERO’s national intelligence-gathering network. Another key facility, the Pacific Enforcement Response Center, is located in Southern California. That center would get nine contract workers under the plan outlined last month.
The plan marks at least the third time ICE has considered increasing its staffing at Vermont’s facilities since President Donald Trump took office a second time last year, but the agency has disclosed little information publicly about those earlier efforts.
Both Vermont centers have been regular sites for protests in Trump’s second term. Some of those demonstrators have been arrested and are now facing trespassing charges.
The demonstrations in Vermont have been a far cry from the violent clashes that have erupted between protesters and federal agents in other parts of the country. Earlier this month, protesters wrote anti-ICE messages with chalk on the facade of the Law Enforcement Support Center and blocked the road in front of the building using garden beds.
ICE did not immediately respond to a request for more information Monday about its plans for the facilities in Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ICE looks to boost staffing at intelligence hubs in Vermont.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: U.S. Department of Agriculture argues it’s not required to enforce Animal Welfare Act
text:
A male Australian shepherd with significant dental health issues was photographed by USDA inspectors in 2021 at Steve Kruse's Stonehenge Kennels in West Point, Iowa. (USDA photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji)Less than two weeks after the head of the U.S. Department of Agriculture said the agency was stepping up enforcement of the federal Animal Welfare Act, the USDA’s lawyers are arguing in court that it’s not required to enforce that law.
The American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals filed a lawsuit against the USDA in September 2024, challenging its past decisions to license three Iowa dog breeders — Steve Kruse, Brian Lichirie and Wuanita Swedlund.
The lawsuit, which is still pending, alleges the USDA has pursued an informal policy of failing to enforce the federal Animal Welfare Act. As evidence, the ASPCA cites the USDA’s decision to repeatedly renew Kruse’s license, despite a history of animal-welfare violations, and by licensing two of his associates, Lichirie and Swedlund.
As a result, the ASPCA claims, hundreds of Kruse’s dogs have cycled through Kruse’s associates as part of a puppy-laundering scheme intended to conceal the role Kruse plays in supplying puppies to out-of-state retailers.
More recently, the ASPCA has noted in court filings that within days of Kruse’s license being canceled in September 2025, the USDA approved a license for another individual, Christine Snakenberg, at 2345 Highway 16 in West Point — the same address as Kruse’s Stonehenge Kennels, which Kruse still owned at the time.
All of that, the ASPCA contends, points to the USDA’s informal policy of refusing to enforce the Animal Welfare Act.
In response to those allegations, the USDA is arguing that the agency is not required to enforce the law — stating that none of the enforcement provisions of the Animal Welfare Act are mandatory, and that decisions on enforcement are entirely at the agency’s own discretion.
The USDA also argues that nothing in the ASPCA’s lawsuit “suggests that this imagined ‘policy’ of non-enforcement even exists.”
Rollins: ‘Those days are over.’
On Oct. 6, 2026, U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins appeared at the Animal Rescue League of Iowa and publicly announced the agency was stepping up its enforcement efforts related to inspections — called “surveys” by the agency — and penalties.
“This USDA, over the last year and a half, is very different than prior USDAs,” Rollins said. “We have really stepped up enforcement … The prior USDAs, they would come in, they’d survey, they may fine, and then they would leave. But those days are over. We are now in the active process of shutting down these puppy mills.”
In court, the USDA is arguing that the ASPCA’s lawsuit centers on four Iowa breeders — Kruse, Swedlund, Lichirie and Snakenberg. The first three have voluntarily surrendered their licenses or allowed them to expire, the USDA alleges, and Snakenberg fits the agency’s “regulatory criteria for licensure.” Because of that, the USDA argues, the lawsuit should be dismissed as moot.
The ASPCA’s lawsuit cites the licensing of Snakenberg as evidence that the USDA’s “ongoing policy of non-enforcement persists to this day,” and so the lawsuit should not be dismissed as moot.
Swedlund, whose USDA license expired on July 14, 2026, has since been criminally charged with 34 counts of animal neglect. She has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. A trial is now scheduled for Dec. 18, 2026.
As the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported in 2024, a USDA inspector visited a dog-breeding kennel in the Van Buren County town of Cantril in late 2023. The business was located on property owned by Kruse but operating under a license held by Swedlund. During the inspection, USDA officials reported six puppies at the facility appeared to have frozen to death.
USDA records showing that in 2025 and 2026, Swedlund repeatedly denied federal inspectors access to her Van Buren County facilities.
On June 25, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice obtained a temporary restraining order against Swedlund and then inspected her business, cataloging 20 violations. A few days later, the Van Buren County sheriff seized Swedlund’s 32 dogs, which led to the filing of the criminal charges.
