name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Security breach reveals some healthcare data of Kentuckians
text:
Technology is making it easier to pull off financial crimes, and the U.S. is lacking a central agency to track them, experts say. (Getty Images)Kentucky’s Cabinet for Health and Family Services says a vendor’s recent security breach exposed some health plan information for nearly 4,000 people. 
According to a Monday notice, Gainwell Technologies experienced security breaches on March 26, April 16 and April 21 and learned about them in August. 
During the breaches, “an unauthorized third party had gained access to some provider payment accounts on the KY Health-Net Provider Portal and downloaded files containing Kentucky Medicaid member information.” the cabinet said. 
Notifications to the estimated 3,816 “potentially impacted individuals” started on Oct. 16, the cabinet said. 
The breach did not expose electronic health records, Social Security Numbers or financial account information, according to the cabinet. 
Other information that may have been exposed, according to the cabinet’s notice, include: 

Full names
Identification numbers associated with the provider’s account or Medicaid claims
Dates of medical services
Information about services received and how they were billed
Payment information, including amounts paid
Information about applicable non-Medicaid health insurance, including policy and group numbers. 

“Immediate action took place upon discovery and steps were taken to secure the information portal,” the cabinet said in its Monday notice. “Law enforcement was notified and a thorough investigation was completed. It is believed the unauthorized caller was seeking access to provider payment information rather than patient information.” 
Gainwell has a nearly $34 million, two-year contract with the state to perform various reviews for the Medicaid program. 
According to the cabinet, the company “has implemented specialized training for call center staff on validating individuals requesting new or revised provider portal access” and “is implementing security enhancements while coordinating with the Department for Medicaid Services, Division of Program Integrity on suspected bad-actor investigations.”

name: Delaware
title: Proposed FOIA overhaul raises concerns about new limits on public access
text:
Supporters call it modernization. But new authority to reject records requests raises questions about government transparency and accountability.
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE News
DOVER, Del. — A sweeping proposal from State Senate Majority Leader Bryan Townsend to rewrite Delaware’s Freedom of Information Act could expand access to some government records while giving public agencies new authority to reject requests they consider overly broad, burdensome or abusive.
For advocates of open government, the proposal raises a fundamental question: Should government agencies have greater discretion to decide when citizens have asked for too much information?
The legislation, Senate Bill 355, was introduced Oct. 5 by Townsend, D-Newark, with State Rep. Cyndie Romer, D-Newark, as a co-sponsor. It is intended to generate public feedback rather than win immediate legislative approval. Its sponsors anticipate considering revised legislation during the General Assembly’s 2027 session.
The proposal could represent one of the most significant overhauls of Delaware’s public records law in decades.
While the bill includes substantial transparency improvements, provisions allowing agencies to reject certain requests have raised concerns about whether the changes could weaken an important tool for holding government accountable.
Who decides when a request goes too far?
Freedom of information laws exist because citizens cannot effectively oversee government without access to records documenting how public officials conduct business.
Delaware’s existing law generally focuses on whether requested records are public or exempt from disclosure.
The proposed legislation would also establish specific grounds for denying requests based on their scope, the burden they impose or the requester’s conduct.
Under SB 355, public bodies could deny requests determined to be unreasonably broad, unduly burdensome, disruptive to essential government functions or abusive.
The legislation defines an unreasonably broad request as one using sweeping terms without connections to specific records, dates, individuals or subject matter.
An unduly burdensome request would involve an unreasonable volume of records or require an unreasonable commitment of government resources.
Supporters of such restrictions argue that processing extensive or repetitive requests can consume taxpayer-funded staff time and divert resources from essential government services.
The public-accountability concern is that complicated, time-consuming requests are sometimes necessary to uncover waste, misconduct, conflicts of interest or policy failures.
Giving agencies additional grounds to reject such requests could make it more difficult for citizens to obtain information about controversial government decisions.
The legislation includes safeguards. Agencies would have to provide factual explanations for denials, and requesters could challenge those decisions through the Delaware attorney general’s office or the courts.
However, those protections also raise a practical question: How many citizens have the time or resources to challenge a government agency’s refusal to release records?
Why journalists are paying attention
For news organizations, extensive public records requests are often necessary when investigating government spending, personnel decisions, contracting practices, law enforcement activity or public health issues.
A routine request might seek a single document. Investigative reporting can require hundreds or thousands of pages of emails, invoices, reports or other government communications.
Those requests can be burdensome, but they can also reveal information that would otherwise remain outside public view.
One provision deserving particular scrutiny is the proposed definition of an abusive request, which considers patterns of conduct, including previous interactions between the requester and a public body.
That raises concerns about whether frequent requests from journalists, advocacy organizations or citizen watchdogs could eventually become grounds for denying access.
The concern is not necessarily that agencies would reject ordinary requests. Rather, the new authority could make obtaining sensitive or politically uncomfortable information more difficult.
The proposal’s safeguards against arbitrary denials will be particularly important as lawmakers evaluate the legislation.
Transparency gains could be significant
The proposal also contains several reforms intended to improve public access to information.
Among the most significant is the removal of broad public records exemptions covering the University of Delaware and Delaware State University.
The universities would become subject to expanded disclosure requirements, although exemptions would remain for certain confidential educational, research, fundraising and donor records.
The legislation would also narrow the broad exemption covering investigatory files compiled for civil or law enforcement purposes. Agencies would have to identify specific harms that could result from disclosure rather than automatically withholding records under the existing exemption.
Other changes include reducing the deadline for an initial agency response from 15 business days to 10 and extending FOIA eligibility to people who do not live in Delaware.
The proposal also addresses fees associated with processing records requests, including exemptions for certain news media, scholarly and scientific research requests.
Those changes could significantly improve transparency in areas where Delaware’s public records law has historically limited disclosure.
Balancing government efficiency with public oversight
The debate ultimately centers on how to balance the legitimate cost of complying with public records requests against the public’s right to scrutinize government.
Townsend’s proposal recognizes that processing large volumes of records can create substantial administrative burdens. The legislation attempts to establish standards for identifying requests that go beyond reasonable public oversight.
But those same standards could create opportunities for disagreement over what constitutes an unreasonable request.
From a limited-government perspective, the question is whether agencies responsible for producing public records should also have expanded authority to determine when requests for those records become excessive.
The bill’s provisions for written explanations and independent review are important protections, but their effectiveness would depend on how agencies apply the new standards.
Why it matters to Delawareans
Public records laws are often discussed as legal and administrative issues, but they affect anyone seeking answers about government decisions.
FOIA requests can help citizens examine school district spending, local government contracts, police department policies, public employee conduct and the use of taxpayer dollars.
When access becomes more difficult, residents may lose opportunities to identify problems or challenge decisions affecting their communities.
Conversely, clearer disclosure requirements and broader access to previously exempt records could strengthen public oversight.
As lawmakers consider the future of Delaware’s FOIA law, the central issue will be whether the proposed changes expand meaningful public access without giving government agencies excessive discretion to deny requests.
For citizens and journalists alike, the ultimate measure of reform will not simply be how quickly agencies respond, but whether the public can obtain the information necessary to hold government accountable.
TO GO

What: Senate Bill 355 proposes a major rewrite of Delaware’s Freedom of Information Act.
Sponsors: State Sen. Bryan Townsend and state Rep. Cyndie Romer, both Newark Democrats.
Status: Introduced Oct. 5, 2026, to solicit public feedback ahead of potential revised legislation in 2027.
Supporters’ argument: The proposal modernizes FOIA, expands access to previously exempt records, shortens response deadlines and establishes safeguards against abusive or excessively burdensome requests.
Accountability concern: New authority to deny broad, burdensome or abusive requests could make it harder for journalists and citizens to investigate government operations.
Why it matters: FOIA is a primary tool Delawareans use to examine government spending, decisions and accountability.
More information: Delaware General Assembly, Senate Bill 355.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ‘It’s shameful’: New Mexico veterans increasingly turn to food banks after SNAP rollbacks
text:
New Mexico food banks report serving more people with less food after federal rollbacks to SNAP and an emergency food assistance program. (A food drive at Holloman Air Force Base in June 2025. Photo courtesy of The Food Depot)New Mexico food bank officials told lawmakers recently that federal rollbacks to food assistance programs have impacted veterans’ food security, and left food banks across the state struggling to provide more help with fewer resources. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Previously, veterans received an exemption from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program’s work-requirement rule. Under the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” signed into law last year, veterans now must prove they are working, volunteering, participating in job training or looking for work for at least 80 hours a month to keep their food assistance benefits beyond three months.
“We see more veterans seeking assistance at food banks and our network of food security partners than we have in the past because they can no longer access the SNAP program,” Jill Dixon, executive director of The Food Depot, a northern New Mexico food bank, told lawmakers on the interim Military and Veterans’ Affairs Committee during its Oct. 16 meeting. Veterans living in rural areas in New Mexico, she continued, have been “disproportionately affected” by the federal changes.
Roadrunner Food Bank, whose distribution area includes both Cannon and Kirtland Air Force bases, saw a “shocking” 40% to 60% increase in the number of people seeking help this year, Katy Anderson, Roadrunner’s vice president of strategy, partnerships and advocacy,  told the committee.
“Folks are telling us they’re struggling to make things work with the cost of groceries, the cost of fuel,” Anderson said. She added that Roadrunner received 50% less food from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Emergency Food Assistance Program compared to two years ago, while at the same time spending 70% more on fuel to transport food compared with last year. 
Roadrunner stocks food for the Veteran Integration Services’ food pantry in Albuquerque, where veterans in need can receive a bag of dry and canned goods and a bag of frozen produce. Cedric Smith, who helps operate the food pantry, told Source NM that the pantry can’t provide as much as it used to for veterans.
“We barely have enough to get us from week to week,” Smith said. The pantry serves more than 70 veterans and their families weekly, and Smith estimated approximately 70% are senior citizens.
The change in SNAP requirements also has changed the clientele.
“Before it used to be a lot of homeless or low-income families. Now we get people that are working, but they’re not making enough money to buy the amount of food that their family might need,” Smith told Source NM.
New Mexico lawmakers did not mince words when presented on the status of food banks and veteran food insecurity in the state: “It’s shameful. This isn’t a partisan issue — this is a humane issue,” Sen. Gabriel Ramos (R-Silver City) said.
State Rep. Art De La Cruz (D-Albuquerque) added that the issue of veteran food insecurity in New Mexico is a “number one priority” that state lawmakers should urge New Mexico’s congressional delegation to address in Washington. 
“It seems unconscionable to me that you are or have been fully employed by the federal government, serving in a capacity that we all respect and honor, yet there would be some service members and veterans that can’t afford food,” De La Cruz said.

name: VTDigger
title: Fewer Vermont retailers are accepting food assistance benefits. Here’s why.
text:
This commentary is by Johanna Doren, the direct markets and local food access director at the Northeast Organic Farming Association of Vermont. 
In 2025, 619 Vermont food retailers accepted Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits from customers. By August 2026, just 574 were authorized to do so. Data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture shows that the number of Vermont retailers that can accept SNAP declined during this period at more than double the rate of the previous five years.
This trend is not isolated to Vermont. It’s a pattern seen across the country as retailers contend with hurdles designed to make it difficult to accept SNAP — known as 3SquaresVT in our state — which is our nation’s first line of defense against hunger. 
In July 2025, Congress passed H.R.1, or the “One Big Beautiful Bill.” It included historic cuts to SNAP, including $187 billion over the next decade, in exchange for permanent tax breaks for the wealthy and big corporations. Nationally, more than 5 million people lost SNAP benefits between the passage of H.R.1 in July 2025 and June 2026. In Vermont, more than 5,000 people have lost their benefits — an 8% decline. 
While the federal government chips away at people’s ability to buy food, less talked about is the simultaneous damage to stores, farmers markets and farms where community members spend their SNAP dollars. 
The USDA claims it is focusing on rooting out rampant “fraud, waste, and abuse” of SNAP, but fraudulent use of SNAP is incredibly uncommon and not addressed by the USDA’s new efforts. 
Losing SNAP retailers means low-income Vermonters have fewer affordable places to buy food, and reduced sales threaten stores’ business viability. If the federal administration successfully cripples this program, we may see lasting impacts on retailers, vulnerable Vermonters and our local economy. 
SNAP retailers are being targeted through two main channels: overly burdensome requirements for authorization and eligibility, and increased surveillance and harsher enforcement.
The already onerous SNAP retailer authorization process has recently added more hoops for applicants to jump through. The USDA’s Food and Nutrition Service has been requesting a wide variety of additional materials beyond the application itself, on tight timelines. The agency cut more than 30% of its staff in 2025, making it harder to confirm whether follow-up paperwork has been received. If a SNAP retailer authorization application is not completed within 30 days, the applicant must start over. 
Compounding these application hurdles, the USDA announced tougher retailer stocking standards earlier this year. Starting Nov. 4, SNAP-authorized retailers must stock a wider variety of foods to maintain eligibility. Ostensibly, this looks like an effort to increase healthy food options for SNAP customers. In reality, small food retailers, general stores and some farmers markets will find it harder to maintain SNAP eligibility if they cannot meet new requirements. The USDA estimates 5,000 retailers nationally will lose authorization because of this rule.

READ MORE

The federal administration’s pressure on food retailers does not stop there. The USDA has urged states to apply for legally dubious food restriction waivers to further limit what SNAP shoppers can buy with their benefits. This harms the autonomy of SNAP shoppers and creates a costly logistical nightmare for businesses. 
A national trend of increased retail oversight has affected Vermont as well. In 2025, three Vermont farmers markets received unexpected visits from third-party SNAP field reviewers, which is atypical outside the authorization process. Secret shoppers — a more pernicious tactic — have also been active in stores, trying to sting cashiers by using benefits to purchase items not eligible for SNAP. One such sting happened in Cambridge in November 2025. Entrapping stores and revoking authorization is particularly concerning in rural areas, where a store stripped of its SNAP authorization may be the only nearby place to buy food.
During economic downturns, every $1 in SNAP benefits generates up to $1.80 in economic activity. Currently, $11.3 million in SNAP flows into the Vermont economy every month, down from $12.4 million per month a year ago. Losing the ability to accept SNAP as tender, combined with the shrinking number of community members receiving SNAP, means that small businesses lose an important income source.
We need to know that our taxpayer dollars are invested in programs with integrity. Time and time again, SNAP has proven to be an effective anti-poverty tool and economic stimulus, with systems that keep fraud negligible. 
Slashing this program, both for participants and retailers, unfairly complicates business operations for Vermont’s farms and food retailers and cruelly strips away basic support for children, older adults and folks with disabilities — with the only clear beneficiaries appearing to be the billionaires receiving tax cuts through the same bill that slashes SNAP. 
Our state and federal governments should be finding every way possible to make SNAP simpler, not more complicated, so that the people who live, work, grow food and eat here can thrive.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland officials announce dramatic decrease in teacher vacancy rate
text:
Rachel Bayer, a former federal worker, working as a student teacher with elementary students on April 22, 2026. (Photo by Alexander Taylor/Capital News Service)The number of teacher vacancies fell from 2,145 in the 2022-23 school year to roughly 572 for the current school year, state officials announced Monday, a 70% drop that was attributed to programs to expand recruitment and retention of teachers.
The drop — from about 3.4% of teaching positions in the 2022-23 school year to about 0.9% for the 2026-27 year — was announced by Gov. Wes Moore (D), State Superintendent Carey Wright and state Board of Education President Joshua Michael at Hillsmere Elementary in Anne Arundel County.
The announcement was held in that county based on this statistic: Teacher vacancies decreased from 283 in 2022, which was Superintendent Mark Bedell’s first year in the district, to 16 on the first day of school in August this year.
“The hard work to reduce teacher vacancies has many pieces to it,” Bedell said. “Compensation and training programs are certainly huge factors, but so is creating supportive cultures where every teacher feels a sense of belonging. We are very proud of the work we have done in all of those areas.”
State officials attributed a few programs to the drop in teacher vacancies in a state with more than 64,000 educators.
The state’s Grow Your Own initiative not only focuses on expanding teacher and staff pipelines, but also boosting diversity in the profession and establishing apprenticeships.
School officials celebrate drop in chronic absenteeism, but are still shy of goal

As part of the initiative, the governor announced in August nearly $15 million in grants to support 845 educators who focus on high-need areas such as special education and early childhood. The first round of grants, announced last December at $19 million, sought to slice vacancies nearly in half from more than 1,600 to 886 last year.
“Our administration has tackled barriers to entry and strategically invested to create opportunities for passionate educators to pursue their dream of teaching,” Moore said in a statement Monday. “We are proud of the historic progress we’ve made, and we won’t stop until every vacancy is filled to deliver the world class education our students deserve.”
Another statewide push to decrease the vacancy rate comes from TEACH Maryland, a program that allows aspiring educators or those seeking a career change to seek out a teaching career. With Maryland being one of the states hardest hit by federal layoffs and job reductions in the first years of the second Trump administration, some federal workers were left looking for employment elsewhere, including teaching.
One continued initiative to improve teaching in the classroom is the statewide teacher development program.
The General Assembly approved $14.2 million during this year’s 90-day legislative session toward the program to hire more than five dozen educators who will act as instructional coaches for literacy and math teachers for this school year. The Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Accountability and Implementation Board, which oversees the 10-year education reform plan, recommends the legislature continue to allocate funding.
Wright is a major supporter of the program known as “coaching,” which she has said helps to ensure stronger teachers, but also produces better students.
“These results show that targeted investments and partnerships are making a measurable difference for students and schools across the state,” she said. “We will continue advancing strategies that attract, prepare and support excellent educators for every classroom.”

title: Conservation and government build ‘starter homes’ for beavers
authors: by Brittany Peterson, The Associated Press
text:
GREEN RIVER—On Jackson Ramsay’s family ranch late in the summer, there were few signs it had just weathered the worst-ever winter snowpack and record-setting heat.
Water twisted unhurriedly through the land, splayed into various branches that rejoined to form pools behind mounds of piled sticks. Young willows stretched from the bank across an expanse roughly the length of a football field, fed from moisture below.
Then a familiar brown head emerged from a deep pool: a beaver.
“They’re thriving here,” Ramsay said, beaming at the creature. “They benefit us, and hopefully we benefit them.”
The Ramsays’ ranch in southwest Wyoming is one of many areas embracing the semiaquatic rodents as nature’s engineers. Conservation groups and government agencies are increasing their use of “starter homes” made of wood and brush to encourage the creatures to move in and expand upon the initial structures. Beaver dams slow moving water in a way that promotes localized year-round availability, creates habitat for native fish and provides a natural break that slows wildfires.
Proponents hope that by increasing active beaver dams, the ecosystem will grow more resilient. This is increasingly vital as climate change and overuse make the American West drier, experts say.
“In their blood, they have one thing and that’s to dam streams up and make deep water habitat so they can survive,” said Nick Walrath, a project manager for the nonprofit Trout Unlimited. He first pitched the idea to Ramsay, who now proudly hosts more than 100 human-made beaver dams in addition to natural ones.
Build it, and they will (hopefully) come
Walrath has overseen construction of some 500 “starter homes” for beavers across snow- and spring-fed streams — including Trout Creek on the Ramsay ranch — that form the headwaters of the Green River, the largest tributary to the Colorado River. The materials are simple: several raw posts jammed vertically into streambeds, branches loosely woven around the posts and mud to pack it down.
The structures, known as beaver dam analogs, are typically built near existing beaver families to encourage them to “move in” and customize them. The ultimate goal is to cultivate thriving beaver populations in key watersheds across both public and private land in the western U.S.
Workers build a beaver dam on Spring Creek on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, near Rock Springs, Wyo. (AP Photo/Brittany Peterson)
“Beavers are uniquely positioned as our allies in the battle against climate change,” said Samantha Miller, senior carnivore campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity.
Without beavers, water can also move so fast that it erodes the bank.
“Where the water is held there, sediment builds up, the soils build, vegetation takes off and really makes it lush,” Ramsay said. “They’re really beneficial when they build where you want them to, but they can be a nuisance when they build where you’re trying to divert water.”
Not everyone wants a dam
Flooding caused by beaver dams may be a boon for ecosystems, but can present problems for homes and infrastructure built near streams.
Utah State University operates the state’s beaver relocation program that takes unwanted beavers from private property and moves them to remote streams where they’re needed. It uses live-trap cages and quarantines the beavers at a facility, aiming to keep families together and prevent the spread of invasive species, before re-releasing them in wilder areas. The program has moved approximately 100 beavers each year since 2019.
Water sits in Trout Creek on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, near Rock Springs, Wyo. (AP Photo/Brittany Peterson)
The state bans lethal beaver trapping along key watersheds where it is trying to grow the population. It also pays trappers to live-trap beavers to hand over to trained experts for relocation.
Aquatic ecologist Nick Bouwes, a Utah State faculty member who helped launch the program, said he received countless requests to get rid of the furry creatures that had caused a nuisance for property owners. But before moving them, he’d recommend solutions to coexist. There’s a flexible tube known as a pond leveler that runs through a beaver dam and acts as an overflow drain, as well as “beaver deceiver” cages that protect drainage pipes from damming and fencing for tree base protection.
Still, if beavers are unwanted, nonlethal means are worth the effort because the animals can benefit other water bodies, Bouwes said.
Beaver populations still need protecting
Beaver populations have made a strong recovery since fur trappers nearly caused their extinction in the 19th century, but protection is still needed because of their role in preserving scarce water resources in the American West, Miller said.
Oregon and Wyoming limit commercial beaver trapping, while California has banned it altogether.
A beaver sits in the Green River on Thursday, Aug. 20, 2026, near Green River, Wyo. (AP Photo/Brittany Peterson)
Walrath and other advocates for beaver expansion understand that a lot more work is needed to make a meaningful difference across the Colorado River basin.
“It’s a drop in the bucket,” he said of the work they’ve done so far. But after the worst snowpack ever measured, followed by record-setting summer heat, any effort is “much more meaningful.”
On a recent August morning, Walrath and his crew were putting up several “starter homes” on private grazing land along Spring Creek in western Wyoming. Water rose several feet across the dry, eroded bank in a valley thick with sagebrush shortly after the structures were erected.
“If we can replicate that a hundred, a thousand times over the entire Colorado River basin, we can have a much larger impact to the system itself,” he said.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware HB 59: Protecting the accused or limiting the public’s right to know?
text:
New Law passed by the Democrats in the General Assembly limits information on what the police can release about adults charges with a crime. Image was created on 10/19 using AI.
New Delaware law restricts release of arrest information, raising public safety concerns
Taking effect Oct. 21, HB 59 aims to protect the presumption of innocence, but questions remain about police transparency, community awareness and the public’s right to know.
DOVER, Del. — A new Delaware law taking effect Wednesday will significantly restrict the information police departments can release about people charged with crimes, creating a new balance between protecting the rights of the accused and keeping communities informed about criminal activity.
House Bill 59, signed by Gov. Matt Meyer on July 23, prohibits law enforcement agencies from releasing the names or photographs of adults charged with crimes unless they face felony charges and police determine that releasing the information is necessary to protect public safety.
The legislation, sponsored by state Rep. Sean Lynn, D-Dover, expands privacy protections previously reserved primarily for juveniles to adults charged with criminal offenses.
Supporters say the law reinforces a fundamental principle of American justice: People are presumed innocent until proven guilty and should not suffer unnecessary damage to their reputations simply because they have been arrested.
But the new restrictions also raise questions about government transparency, the ability of residents and businesses to monitor criminal activity in their communities, and the role of law enforcement in providing information to the public.
Protecting the accused before conviction
Lynn, a practicing criminal defense attorney, has argued that publishing arrest photographs and identifying information can create a presumption of guilt long before a criminal case reaches court.
Even when charges are dismissed or defendants are acquitted, photographs and arrest announcements can remain accessible online indefinitely, potentially affecting employment, housing opportunities and personal relationships.
The new law seeks to reduce that damage by limiting when police can identify people charged with criminal offenses.
Under HB 59, police generally will no longer be permitted to release the name or photograph of an adult charged only with a misdemeanor.
For felony offenses, police must determine that disclosure is necessary for public safety before releasing identifying information. Both conditions must be satisfied.
The law applies to law enforcement agencies, including their public websites and social media accounts. It does not directly prohibit independent news organizations from publishing legally obtained information or eliminate public access to criminal court proceedings.
Existing protections for juveniles remain in place. Police generally may identify juveniles only when they are charged with violent felonies and disclosure is necessary to protect public safety.
Public safety and the right to know
While the law addresses legitimate concerns about protecting innocent people from unnecessary public exposure, it also changes how Delaware residents may learn about criminal activity in their communities.
Police announcements traditionally have provided details about arrests involving theft, assault, fraud, drug offenses and other crimes. In addition to informing the public, those announcements can help residents and businesses recognize patterns of criminal activity.
Under the new law, police will generally be prohibited from identifying adults charged with misdemeanors, even when the incidents involve offenses of particular concern to local communities.
For example, residents may learn that police arrested someone for a series of misdemeanor thefts but may no longer receive the person’s name or photograph from the investigating agency.
Similarly, a business owner concerned about repeated thefts or fraudulent activity may have fewer opportunities to learn the identities of those charged through routine police announcements.
The restrictions do not prevent police from sharing appropriate information directly with victims during an investigation or pursuing criminal charges. However, the law does not expressly establish detailed procedures for informing affected businesses or community members when disclosure may serve a legitimate safety interest.
Another question involves the discretion police departments will have in determining when identifying someone charged with a felony is necessary to protect public safety.
HB 59 does not establish detailed criteria for making that determination, potentially leaving different agencies to adopt different standards.
That could create inconsistencies between Delaware State Police, county police departments and municipal law enforcement agencies.
Republican concerns led to significant changes
The legislation encountered substantial opposition when it first reached the House floor earlier this year.
The original proposal would have also restricted police from releasing photographs and identifying information about adults suspected of crimes but not yet charged.
Republican legislators argued that provision could interfere with criminal investigations by preventing police from asking the public to help identify suspects.
State Reps. Shannon Morris, R-Harrington, and Valerie Jones Giltner, R-Georgetown, were among those who raised concerns about the potential effect on police investigations.
The original version passed the House in May by a 23-11 vote without Republican support.
Following those objections, Lynn agreed to remove the provision restricting publication of information about adults merely suspected of crimes.
The revised legislation subsequently passed the House 31-8 in June, gaining bipartisan support.
House Republican Leader Tim Dukes, R-Laurel, welcomed the change.
“I appreciate Rep. Lynn taking this action,” Dukes said in a statement issued by House Republicans following the amendment. “With the amendment, I was comfortable voting in favor of the bill.”
House Republican Whip Jeff Spiegelman, R-Townsend, also praised the compromise.
“Rep. Lynn has given me some hope that there are still some instances where we can overcome party tribalism and reach consensus on good policy,” Spiegelman said.
The compromise preserved an important investigative tool: Police can still release images of uncharged suspects when seeking the public’s assistance in identifying them.
However, once an adult is charged with a misdemeanor, the new restrictions on publishing that individual’s identity apply.
That distinction could create an unusual situation in which police publicly circulate a suspect’s photograph during an investigation but cannot identify that person in a subsequent misdemeanor arrest announcement.
Transparency and police accountability
Beyond individual criminal cases, the legislation raises broader questions about government transparency and public oversight.
Public access to arrest information allows journalists and community members to examine how police departments enforce laws, whether criminal activity is increasing in particular neighborhoods and how the justice system responds to repeat offenses.
Routine identification of defendants can also help connect arrests to subsequent court proceedings, allowing the public to follow cases from the initial police investigation through prosecution and resolution.
Restricting police disclosure does not eliminate those opportunities, but it may make obtaining and connecting information more difficult.
The distinction is particularly important because information about crime serves purposes beyond identifying individual defendants.
Residents use police reports to understand neighborhood safety. Businesses monitor theft and fraud. Victims and community organizations look for patterns of criminal behavior. Journalists evaluate police performance and prosecutorial decisions.
The challenge for policymakers is determining how to preserve those public interests without unnecessarily damaging the reputations of people who have not been convicted.
How will police implement the new law?
With the law taking effect Wednesday, one of the immediate questions is how Delaware’s law enforcement agencies will change their public information practices.
Police departments routinely distribute news releases announcing arrests, identifying suspects and describing criminal charges. Many agencies also publish photographs on social media.
Those practices will now require closer consideration of whether the charges and circumstances satisfy the law’s disclosure requirements.
Among the questions facing law enforcement are how public safety will be defined, who will authorize the release of identifying information and whether departments will establish written policies to ensure consistent decisions.
Another issue involves how agencies will communicate information about misdemeanor arrests to victims, businesses and residents who have legitimate reasons to be concerned about possible ongoing criminal activity.
The legislation also leaves questions about how existing public records laws and court information systems will interact with the restrictions on police announcements.
The law directly governs law enforcement agencies, rather than making all arrest or court records confidential. However, its practical effect on access to police records and routine public information will depend in part on how agencies interpret and implement the new requirements.
Finding the balance between privacy and public safety
HB 59 reflects two principles that are not necessarily in conflict.
The justice system should protect individuals against unwarranted damage to their reputations before guilt has been established. At the same time, government agencies have a responsibility to provide the public with meaningful information about crime, law enforcement and potential threats to community safety.
The bipartisan amendment demonstrates that lawmakers recognized the importance of preserving police access to the public during criminal investigations.
Whether the final law achieves an appropriate balance between personal privacy and public safety will become clearer as departments begin operating under its restrictions.
There is no established evidence that HB 59 will lead to increased crime or prevent police from solving cases. But the law does introduce new limits on the information police can make available, creating practical questions about transparency and community awareness.
For residents, businesses and news organizations, the issue is not simply whether the names of arrested individuals should appear in police reports.
It is whether Delaware can protect the presumption of innocence while continuing to provide the public with the information necessary to understand crime and evaluate the performance of its criminal justice system.

To-Go Box: What Delaware’s new arrest information law means
Law: House Bill 59, signed July 23, 2026.
Effective date: Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026.
What changes: Police generally cannot release the names or photographs of adults charged with misdemeanors. Information about adults charged with felonies can be released when necessary to protect public safety.
What remains permitted: Police may continue releasing images and identifying information about uncharged adult suspects to seek public assistance in investigations.
Who is affected: Delaware law enforcement agencies and the public that relies on police announcements for information about criminal activity.
Why supporters favor it: To protect the presumption of innocence and prevent unnecessary reputational damage before a criminal conviction.
Primary concerns: Public safety, government transparency, consistent police disclosure standards and access to information about crime in local communities.
