name: California
title: Mataron gente con sus camiones y California les permitió seguir conduciendo
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Loren Chow miró por el espejo retrovisor y tuvo una terrible revelación.
Nos van a chocar. 
 No hay nada que pueda hacer para salir de esta.
El tráfico en las afueras de Fresno había disminuido. Un camión de carga pesada transportando fertilizante procedente de Missouri, que circulaba a 105 kilómetros por hora, no lo había hecho. Cuando el conductor, Baljit Singh, frenó, ya era demasiado tarde. Un camión de gran tamaño completamente cargado que viaja a esa velocidad necesita casi la longitud de dos campos de fútbol para detenerse.
 En junio de 2022, Chow, su esposa y su hijo de 17 años regresaban a casa tras una visita a una universidad. El camión Freightliner rojo de Singh chocó contra la parte trasera de su SUV y la volcó. Jenny Chow falleció. Las autoridades indicaron que Singh provocó el accidente por conducir a exceso de velocidad.
 Loren Chow no puede hablar sobre los detalles de la colisión debido a una demanda en curso contra Singh, las compañías de transporte y los fabricantes de vehículos. Pero los documentos judiciales, los informes policiales y los registros de conducción conducen a una conclusión simple:
 Si el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados de California hubiera hecho su trabajo, Jenny Chow todavía estaría viva.
 Eso se debe a que en julio de 2021, 11 meses antes de matar a Chow, Singh dejó que su camión se saliera de la carretera y cruzara la mediana en Merle Haggard Drive en el condado de Kern, cuando se dirigía a un centro de distribución de Amazon, matando a un hombre de 26 años que iba en motocicleta.
 El informe del accidente revela que la policía encontró páginas de un libro de registro, destinado a controlar las horas de conducción de Singh, “rotas en pedazos” en un compartimento superior. Los investigadores de la Patrulla de Carreteras de California alegaron que Singh estaba fatigado en el momento del accidente tras haber conducido más de las 12 horas permitidas y recomendaron que se le imputara el delito de homicidio vehicular.
 Pero si bien el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) estaba al tanto del accidente mortal anterior y tenía la autoridad para suspender el permiso de conducir de Singh, le permitió seguir conduciendo un camión de gran tonelaje hasta que volvió a causar la muerte.
 “La muerte era totalmente evitable. Ese accidente nunca debería haber ocurrido”, dijo Chow, apenas conteniendo el dolor durante una entrevista en la sala de estar de su casa en el Área de la Bahía, que está repleta de fotos sonrientes de Jenny y sus dos hijos. 
 Loren Chow sostiene una foto de su esposa, Jenny, en la casa que compartían en Los Altos. Skeeter, el perro de la familia que adoptaron poco después de la muerte de Jenny, se acurruca junto a él. Foto de Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters. 



Izquierda: El coche de Jenny Chow tras la colisión con el camión de Baljit Singh. Captura de pantalla vía KGET. Derecha: Un altar dedicado a Jenny Chow, quien falleció después de que el coche familiar fuera embestido por un camión. Foto de Anna Hoch-Kenney, CalMatters.
 “Todavía tendría a mi pareja. Seríamos una familia de cuatro. Jenny habría visto a Dylan y Tyler graduarse de la preparatoria”, dijo Chow. “Habría visto tantas cosas si el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados hubiera hecho lo que cualquier persona en su sano juicio habría hecho: suspender la licencia”.
 Una investigación de CalMatters descubrió que el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV, por sus siglas en inglés) a menudo permite que conductores profesionales con un historial de comportamiento peligroso al volante permanezcan en la carretera y conduzcan vehículos de gran tamaño (autobuses llenos de pasajeros, camiones con remolque cargados de mercancías y camiones cisterna cargados de productos químicos peligrosos) incluso después de un accidente mortal.
 Según la ley de California, un camionero condenado por homicidio involuntario queda inhabilitado para conducir camiones de gran tonelaje durante 12 meses. Además, cualquier conductor condenado por homicidio vehicular grave generalmente recibe una revocación de licencia de tres años. Sin embargo, los casos penales pueden prolongarse, a veces durante años. Singh no fue condenado por homicidio involuntario en los condados de Kern y Fresno hasta 2024. Fue entonces cuando el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) le retiró la licencia. Singh y su abogado no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios.
 La ley estatal faculta a la agencia para investigar a los conductores involucrados en colisiones con víctimas mortales o lesiones graves y suspenderles la licencia, con o sin condena. Pero el DMV habitualmente no hace nada al respecto. 


 Incluso cuando la agencia actúa, los registros muestran que puede tardar años en hacerlo. Examinamos los expedientes judiciales y los registros del DMV de más de 130 titulares de licencias comerciales acusados de homicidio vehicular entre 2019 y principios de 2024 tras un accidente fatal ocurrido en el trabajo o fuera de servicio en un vehículo particular. Casi la mitad tenía una licencia válida de Clase A o Clase B a finales de mayo. Esto incluye a una docena de conductores que recibieron una multa por conducción peligrosa en un vehículo comercial después de haber causado la muerte de una persona. 
 Además, el homicidio vehicular debería conllevar una penalización de tres puntos para un camionero, pero en casi todos los registros del DMV que revisamos, figuraba con dos puntos, la sanción para un conductor particular. En un comunicado escrito, la agencia indicó que depende de que los tribunales le notifiquen cuando una condena involucra un vehículo comercial para poder determinar la cantidad de puntos correspondiente.
 A pesar de estos ejemplos de indiferencia burocrática, sí encontramos un área de aplicación de la ley en la que el DMV es enérgico: asegurarse de que la gente pague las multas.
 En 2023, meses antes de que la agencia finalmente suspendiera la licencia de Singh, comenzó a enviarle cartas a Loren Chow amenazándolo con embargarle el sueldo, confiscarle sus propiedades y poner un gravamen sobre su casa.
El Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) indicó que no había pagado por el registro del auto que quedó destruido debido a las acciones del conductor del camión al que permitió seguir circulando.
 Aviso del DMV que Loren Chow recibió advirtiéndole sobre el impago de las tasas de matriculación del vehículo implicado en el accidente mortal. Composición gráfica de Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters. 
 ‘Vas a matar a alguien’ 

La inacción del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) contra los camioneros comerciales es aún más grave debido a los claros riesgos que representan. Conducir camiones es un trabajo agotador que implica largas jornadas y recorridos enormes. Un semirremolque completamente cargado puede llegar a pesar 80,000 libras, 20 veces el peso de un automóvil. Un semirremolque a exceso de velocidad no solo causa pequeños choques, sino que los destroza.
 “Si algo sale mal, vas a matar a alguien”, dijo Joe Rajkovacz, propietario y operador de larga trayectoria y defensor de la Western States Trucking Association.
 Entre 2015 y 2024, la década más reciente para la que se dispone de datos federales , murieron alrededor de 4.000 personas en accidentes con camiones de gran tamaño en California. 

 Las decisiones de California sobre la concesión de licencias tienen repercusiones más allá de las fronteras del estado. Los camiones de gran tamaño, que durante mucho tiempo han sido la columna vertebral de nuestra economía, transportan miles de millones de dólares en alimentos desde las granjas del estado y pedidos en línea desde puertos repletos de actividad hasta destinos en todo el país.
 Tami Friedrich, presidenta de la Coalición para la Seguridad de los Camiones, un grupo nacional de defensa de los conductores, afirmó que por eso los reguladores deben hacer más para identificar a los camioneros que no deberían estar en la carretera. Se involucró en temas de seguridad vial después de que su hermana, su cuñado y sus dos hijos —Kris, Alan, Anthony y Brandie— fallecieran en un accidente con un camión de gran tonelaje poco después de la Navidad de 1989.
 “Existe un cierto nivel de responsabilidad que va más allá del de un conductor de coche normal y corriente, y que deberían cumplir”, dijo Friedrich.
 Los casos que hemos examinado sugieren que California no les está exigiendo ese nivel de exigencia.
 En 2023, un camionero mató a un hombre de 55 años en Bakersfield, cuatro años después de que, según consta en los registros judiciales, presuntamente hiriera a una mujer con su camión en un accidente en Sacramento. No hay constancia en su historial de conducción de que el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) tomara ninguna medida al respecto. En 2025, sufrió otro accidente con su camión. 

Un conductor fue declarado culpable de manejar de manera temeraria y de darse a la fuga tras un accidente, sufrió una colisión en el condado de San Joaquín en 2023, no se presentó ante el tribunal en Sacramento por una multa de tráfico y causó la muerte de una persona mientras conducía en el condado de Amador. Este mismo año recibió una multa por exceso de velocidad en Sacramento y tuvo otro accidente en Amador. El Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) no le suspendió la licencia de conducir comercial hasta septiembre, después de que consultáramos sobre el caso.
 Otro conductor con cinco colisiones previas —incluida una en 2021 en la que se desvió hacia el arcén con un camión y mató a una persona en el condado de Riverside— pudo renovar su licencia el año pasado y casi de inmediato acumuló dos multas por exceso de velocidad en un vehículo comercial. Tenía una licencia de camión válida hasta septiembre.
 Si bien los conductores particulares pueden conducir fácilmente con la licencia suspendida, es poco probable que una empresa de transporte asigne un camión cargado a un conductor sin una licencia comercial válida, según los expertos. Esto significa que la intervención del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) sería aún más significativa. Sin embargo, la agencia suele actuar solo cuando está legalmente obligada a hacerlo y no utiliza su inmenso poder discrecional para garantizar que los conductores peligrosos sean retirados de las carreteras.
 La postura permisiva del DMV se produce en un momento de gran agitación para el sector del transporte por carretera. Los expertos afirman que la proliferación de operadores y escuelas de formación fraudulentas ha socavado los estándares de seguridad y ha impulsado una competencia a la baja en las condiciones de conducción. Al mismo tiempo, la administración Trump ha alegado que California está otorgando indebidamente licencias comerciales a personas que no cumplen con los requisitos de inmigración o de idioma. Los expedientes judiciales y los registros del DMV que revisamos no incluyen el estatus migratorio de los conductores.
 Enviamos al Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) una lista de conductores comerciales junto con preguntas para este artículo. La agencia rechazó la solicitud de entrevista y no quiso hacer comentarios sobre casos específicos, pero poco después tomó medidas contra una docena de conductores, como la suspensión de licencias o la revocación de sus privilegios de conducción comercial. 

 En un correo electrónico, el portavoz del DMV, Jonathan Groveman, escribió que la agencia actualizó recientemente la forma en que maneja los accidentes fatales y las condenas por homicidio involuntario.
 Según el correo electrónico de Groveman, “durante este proceso de modernización, el DMV identificó algunos casos que no habían sido revisados previamente y que ahora han sido procesados o están siendo procesados actualmente”.
 También escribió que las fuerzas del orden y los tribunales deben informar a la agencia de manera oportuna para que el DMV pueda actuar. 
 ‘¿Qué demonios?’ 

 Jon Israel sabía el daño que podía causar un camión de gran tonelaje completamente cargado. Solía conducir uno. Y como operador de grúa en el extenso Inland Empire de California, había pasado años remolcando los restos destrozados de accidentes en uno de los corredores de transporte de camiones más transitados del estado.
 Así pues, Israel habría sido precavido una mañana de verano de 2018, cuando detuvo su grúa sobrecalentada a un lado de la Interestatal 10 y se bajó para revisar el líquido del radiador, mientras el tráfico pasaba a toda velocidad.
 Pero no hay mucho que puedas hacer cuando un camión se desvía hacia ti.
 Según el informe policial, Marco Rodríguez dejó que su camión se desviara hacia el arcén. El enorme espejo retrovisor lateral golpeó a Israel, quien falleció en la carretera que había patrullado durante tanto tiempo.
 El historial de Rodríguez en el Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) muestra que siguió conduciendo vehículos comerciales incluso después del accidente fatal, por el cual finalmente fue declarado culpable de homicidio involuntario. La policía lo sorprendió conduciendo a exceso de velocidad en vehículos comerciales en tres ocasiones distintas entre 2022 y el año pasado, y le impuso una multa más por una infracción de carril.
 A pesar de sus antecedentes —una condena por homicidio vehicular, además de cuatro multas por conducción peligrosa en vehículos comerciales—, la agencia renovó la licencia de camionero de Rodríguez en marzo, negándose a usar su discreción para impedirle conducir. 
 Jon Israel con una de las grúas que usaba para patrullar el extenso Inland Empire de California. Foto cortesía de Maxine Israel.
 —¿Qué demonios? —dijo Maxine Israel, la viuda de Jon—. ¿Acaso esperan a que mate a alguien más?
 El abogado defensor de Rodríguez, Mukund Arun, calificó el accidente fatal como “un incidente muy desafortunado y trágico” y recalcó que su cliente solo fue acusado de un delito menor. Los fiscales pueden imputar el homicidio vehicular como delito grave o menor, y el cargo más grave generalmente implica conductas extremas como conducir bajo los efectos del alcohol o exceso de velocidad.
 Maxine Israel proviene de una familia de camioneros. Se perdió su graduación de la preparatoria para acompañar a su padre en un viaje en su camión. Durante años, ella y Jon vivieron cerca de un puesto de control del condado de Riverside, conocido por su estricta vigilancia, donde la Patrulla de Caminos de California (CHP) pesaba los camiones y los conductores podían comprar camisetas con la leyenda: “Sobreviví a la báscula de Banning”.
 Pero con el tiempo, ella y su esposo notaron que los camioneros parecían ser cada vez más jóvenes. Conducían rápido y a menudo desviaban la vista de la carretera. Lo que más comentaban ella y Jon era cómo, a diferencia de otros estados, aquí los camioneros a menudo no reducían la velocidad ni cambiaban de carril para adelantar a los peatones que circulaban por el arcén.
 “Antes, en California eran muy, muy estrictos con los camiones grandes”, dijo Israel. “Pero ahora, es como si no les importara”.
 Han pasado más de seis años desde que Rodríguez fue declarado culpable del asesinato de Jon Israel. En julio, después de que CalMatters consultara al Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) sobre el caso, la agencia finalmente le retiró a Rodríguez la licencia para conducir vehículos comerciales.
 Los registros del Departamento de Vehículos Motorizados (DMV) indican que se trata de una prohibición de un año; debería poder volver a conducir camiones el próximo verano.
 Investigación judicial realizada por Robert Lewis, Lauren Hepler, Anat Rubin, Sergio Olmos, Cayla Mihalovich, Ese Olumhense, Ko Bragg, Andrew Donohue y Jenna Peterson.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Governor’s husband, Kevin Reynolds, diagnosed with cancer recurrence
text:
Kevin Reynolds, left, and Gov. Kim Reynolds  and family members walk out of the Iowa House chamber after the governor's Condition of the State message on Jan. 16, 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Iowa governor's office)Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds’ husband, Kevin Reynolds, is recovering from a surgery to remove a brain tumor after being diagnosed with a recurrence of cancer, the governor’s office announced Monday.
The governor’s husband, 68, was first diagnosed with lung cancer in 2023. The governor said that year Kevin was in treatment using an oral immune therapy drug and highlighted the “great progress” her husband saw in his treatment and recovery with the medical team at John Stoddard Cancer Center at UnityPoint Health in Des Moines.
But after three years of remission, Kevin Reynolds was diagnosed with a recurrence of cancer. After recovering from surgery to remove a tumor from his brain, he will begin radiation therapy, the governor’s office said in a news release.
“We deeply appreciate the prayers of Iowans during this time. And our prayers for healing are with every family facing cancer,” Gov. Reynolds said in a statement.
“Kevin and I are a strong team,” she said in the statement. “Through 44 years of marriage, we have faced life’s trials together and overcome them. And now, with the strength and support of our family, we will face this fight together just as we have the others—with faith, hope, and love.”
Kevin Reynolds, born in Osceola, became the first to hold the title of first gentleman when his wife became governor in 2017. The couple has three daughters and 11 grandchildren.
The governor’s family struggle with cancer comes as the state of Iowa grapples with high cancer rates. In 2026, the state had the second-highest rate of cancer incidences in the country, and was one of only three states with a rising rate, according to the Iowa Cancer Registry.
“Our family is like many others who experience the highs and lows of navigating a cancer diagnosis over time,” Gov. Reynolds said. “We have been incredibly blessed with an excellent medical team since Kevin was first diagnosed in September 2023, and we are grateful that they remain at our side as we begin this next phase of treatment.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: As Alaska fuel costs spike, this state agency chose three tiny villages for $25,000 relief checks.
text:
The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, which shares offices with the Alaska Energy Authority, is leading development of the Ambler mining road. (Nathaniel Herz/Anchorage Press)Amid a global spike in fuel costs, the tiny Northwest Alaska villages of Shungnak and Ambler reported some of the most eye-watering prices at the pump in the past few months — more than $25 per gallon for gas in both communities, located on the Kobuk River.
Enter the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, or AIDEA. That’s the state-owned economic development corporation that hopes to build a mining road across the remote area where the villages are located, over the objections of conservation groups and some regional grassroots opposition.
In recent weeks, the authority has written $25,000 assistance checks to Shungnak, Ambler and a third village in the area, Kobuk, according to documents obtained by the Anchorage Press through a public records request.
[Read the documents]
The city government of Ambler, population 275, will discuss how to allocate the cash at a council meeting this week, the city clerk said Wednesday. In Shungnak’s case, the contribution went toward buying each household 42 gallons of gas or heating fuel, said Billy Lee, a member of the village’s tribal council, the entity that accepted the check.
That’s a little less than a small rural home might use during a month in the winter.
Up until AIDEA’s donation, Lee said, gas prices were so high that “none of us could even leave town to do any hunting or fishing or anything like that — we were kind of landlocked.”
“People were able to go out and get some fish and maybe a moose or two,” Lee said in a phone interview. “The feeling that I get is it was a real good gesture on AIDEA’s behalf.”
Lee said he didn’t know whether the contribution was initiated by AIDEA or a request from Shungnak. Fuel prices in the village have fallen sharply in recent weeks after a barge delivery, he added.
In Kobuk, a resident said the assistance money was divided between 33 households. Each received a credit for some $750 in fuel; diesel stove oil in the village is currently $15.45 a gallon.
Lawmakers, during Alaska’s annual legislative session earlier this year, took action to blunt the impact of higher fuel prices, offering support to school districts and $200 in supplemental oil-wealth payments to each resident.
Nonetheless, communities across the state beyond Kobuk, Ambler and Shungnak are facing painfully high prices and elected leaders have saidthey’re worried residents may struggle to get through winter.
Lower on the Kobuk River, residents of the village of Kiana pay $8.76 a gallon for gas and $9.53 a gallon for heating fuel, according to data collected by the Northwest Arctic Borough; villages farther south, in the Bristol Bay region, have reported fuel prices as high as $15 a gallon.
An AIDEA spokesperson said the agency’s executive director, Randy Ruaro, was traveling Wednesday, and he didn’t respond to emailed questions from the Press — including about who decided to issue the payments. The agency is a self-funded state corporation, meaning that while its assets belong to the public, its finances are technically separate from Alaska’s main operating fund and the Legislature’s budget process.
Information in the documents released by AIDEA to the Press shows that the money for Kobuk and Ambler came from an agency account dedicated to development of the mining road; that account data was not included in the payment records for Shungnak.
News of the assistance from AIDEA rippled across Northwest Alaska in recent weeks, in part because of the narrow scope and broader political implications of the donations from an agency with a statewide mandate.
Ambler, Shungnak and Kobuk are the three villages in the area of the upper Kobuk River — a remote region that happens to hold rich deposits of copper, zinc and cobalt. Mining companies have eyed the area for decades and one, Ambler Metals, earlier this year applied for a key permit to build a $1.3 billion mine.
The project is proposed in an area that’s more than 150 miles from Alaska’s road system.
Getting its valuable copper and zinc concentrate to market would require construction of a new 200-mile haul road across undeveloped land and part of Gates of the Arctic National Preserve — connecting Alaska’s Dalton Highway with the Upper Kobuk region.

Walker Lake sits at the headwaters of the Kobuk River. The proposed Ambler road project would pass just south of the lake. (R.D. Karpilo Jr., National Park Service)
AIDEA is leading development of the road project and spent the summer doing fieldwork to collect environmental data; construction has not started and litigation over permitting has been ongoing for years.
Its development efforts have support from the administrations GOP Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy and President Donald Trump, who mentioned the road at a Tuesday rally in Wasilla. Proponents say the project would bring employment and cash income to an area where full-time jobs are otherwise scarce — and could also lower prices of shipped-in goods like groceries and fuel.
Across the Northwest Arctic Borough, which extends 150 miles west of the Upper Kobuk to the Chukchi Sea coast, residents’ and elected leaders’ opinions about the road and mining projects are mixed and often nuanced — balancing potential economic benefits against risks posed by road construction and possible spills to the region’s longtime culture of subsistence harvests.
There are also strong pockets of grassroots opposition, with multiple local, Indigenous and conservation groups that have fought AIDEA’s plans for the road.
Observers who learned of AIDEA’s assistance contributions to the Upper Kobuk villages in recent weeks said the political implications were obvious.
“I’m sure there’s goodwill that’s intended to be built, but I’m fine with that,” said Craig McConnell, the borough Assembly president. “If the opposing side wants to make a contribution, they can do so and build the same goodwill. My interest is: Let’s help our people.”
While the whole borough is facing steep prices for fuel amid the global crunch, McConnell said the three Upper Kobuk villages are among those that most urgently need support — though he noted a fourth community, Noatak, could use help, too.
Noatak, population 570, is in a different watershed from the Upper Kobuk villages and wouldn’t be directly affected by the proposed road and mine. But its gas price is just as high: It was $24.95 a gallon this week, according to an employee at the store where it’s sold.
The village has not received any assistance from AIDEA, according to Tristan Ashby, Noatak’s tribal administrator. Community members there recently learned the agency had supported the other villages, Ashby said.
The high prices in Noatak, he added, have meant that some people who typically hunt in the fall haven’t been able to go out — or have waited to hunt by snowmachine instead of by boat so that they’ll use a little less gas.
“There are other villages that are in crisis,” Ashby said. “If there’s any assistance, we greatly appreciate that for reducing the cost or assisting those in need.”
Max Graham contributed reporting.
This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Rochester state Senate candidate ends campaign over residency requirement concern
text:
The New Hampshire Senate chamber on June 17, 2026. (Photo by Maya Mitchell/New Hampshire Bulletin)Cecil Abels, a Rochester Democrat running for state Senate, announced he is ending his campaign over concerns he may not meet New Hampshire’s residency requirement.
Cecil Abels
New Hampshire requires state Senate candidates to live in the state for seven years before they can be elected. Abels said that in 2020, he spent nine months living in Kittery, Maine, a town just across the border.
“That may put me just short of the requirement,” he said in a video posted to Facebook. “I’ve spent more than 14 of the last 15 years in New Hampshire, and I’ve never stopped thinking of myself as a Granite Stater.”
Abels, a barbecue restaurant owner, was seeking to unseat incumbent Sen. James Gray, a Republican and chairman of the Senate Finance Committee. Abels’ name will be on the ballot during the Nov. 3 election, but he said if he is elected he will not accept the seat.
“I signed a filing saying I met the requirements and I should’ve checked first,” he said. “The moment I realized this requirement exists, I raised my hand and I sought legal advice. The requirement is the law and I respect it.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin DNR to assess data center environmental impacts as part of settlement agreement
text:
Residents of communities across Wisconsin have opposed the construction of hyperscale data centers. (Henry Redman | Wisconsin Examiner)The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and a group of environmental organizations announced a settlement agreement Monday that would require stricter environmental impact assessments of future data center developments and initiate a statewide review of how data centers use the state’s resources. 
In June, the Sierra Club and Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the DNR in Ozaukee County court, arguing that the agency approved the permits for Vantage’s massive data center currently under construction in Port Washington without conducting a proper environmental impact statement. 
“AI data centers are massive, thirsty, energy hogs and have popped up all over Wisconsin,” Elizabeth Ward, director of the Wisconsin chapter of the Sierra Club, said in a statement. “They could completely change our landscape and use unprecedented amounts of water and energy. Wisconsinites and our regulators need to understand the impacts and opportunities to reduce harm before allowing data centers to move forward. Wisconsinites deserve an informed, transparent process for decisions that could shape their communities and environment for decades.
A report this summer by the state Public Service Commission found that the Port Washington data center and data centers being built by Microsoft in Mount Pleasant and Meta in Beaver Dam are set to be responsible for a 40% increase in statewide energy demand over the next six years. 
As part of the settlement agreement in the lawsuit, the DNR will conduct full environmental impact statements of individual data center proposals moving forward and complete a statewide strategic analysis of how data centers consume resources. 
State law and the DNR’s administrative rules allow the agency to conduct such an analysis when conflicts arise over resource demands for a  “complicated or complex issue; an issue that is new to the state; an issue or policy that will likely lead to future department actions that will require an environmental impact statement; issues for which there is a high potential for legislation or new department policy and the planning and development of controversial resource-oriented projects.”
“What started as a lawsuit over the environmental review of one data center has become an opportunity to address the data center issue on a much bigger scale,” MEA attorney Michael Greif said. “Looking at these impacts holistically is important because the impacts of data centers are statewide. State regulators will now have to examine the cumulative impacts of data center development across Wisconsin.”
Wisconsin will become one of a few states assessing the statewide impacts of data centers on their resources. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order that initiated a similar analysis and last December, the Maryland Legislature enacted a law that requires a number of state agencies to study “the likely environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Federal appeals court allows mold lawsuit against Women’s Huron Valley prison to proceed
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceAn Oct. 15 ruling by the 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals will allow a lawsuit to proceed against the Michigan Department of Corrections and nine of its employees alleging that pervasive mold at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility has seriously harmed three incarcerated women and violated their Eighth Amendment rights.
The three plaintiffs in the case — Paula Bailey, Krystal Clark and Hope Zentz — allege in the complaint that they experienced severe health complications and were told by nurses that their symptoms were likely caused by mold exposure. The complaint describes black mold dripping in the showers at Women’s Huron Valley and a refusal of facility staff to address concerns raised.
“This lawsuit attempts to address some pretty fundamental structural deficiencies at the facility that are exposing women to really unsafe conditions,” said Channing Robinson-Holmes, a lawyer for the plaintiffs. “Whether it’s the ventilation itself being inadequate, which can lead to a host of problems, including dangerous levels of mold in the facility, there very well could be other unsafe conditions that are associated with inadequate ventilation, and we know that the structure of the facility itself is outdated.”
The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan in November 2019. The case reached the appeals court in July 2025 after a district judge rejected immunity claims by defendants from the Department of Corrections.
The appeals court, in an opinion authored by Judge Richard Allen Griffin, upheld the district court decision for nine of the fourteen defendants — eight of whom were denied both qualified and governmental immunity and one, Michigan Department of Corrections Director Heidi Washington, was denied qualified immunity. The other five were granted immunity, though a partial dissent from Judge Ronald Lee Gilman argued that none of the defendants should have been granted this immunity.
For years, Clark has alleged that black mold at Huron Valley has made her sick. She said she has struggled to breathe and developed rashes, swelling and headaches. (Jay Love/Survivor Speaks)
Besides Washington, the eight other defendants not granted either form of immunity were all those who would have been directly present at Women’s Huron Valley, in positions including warden, deputy warden and physical plant supervisor.
In order to overcome the bar of qualified immunity, the opinion explains, plaintiffs must show that defendants violated a constitutional right and that the law was clearly established that a reasonable person would know that the conduct violated that right.
“Defendants argue that plaintiffs might have ‘experienced discomfort’ from the presence of mold in Huron Valley, but nothing rising to the level of an Eighth Amendment violation,” the opinion states, but says that none of the precedents provided by defendants convinced the judges. “The standard is whether the alleged conditions violate the ‘concepts of dignity, civilized standards, humanity, and decency that animate the Eighth Amendment.’ And contemporary standards of decency do not tolerate prolonged exposure to mold so pervasive and serious that it allegedly drips onto inmates regularly, exceeds healthy airborne levels, and causes severe respiratory conditions, rashes, and seizures.”
Robinson-Holmes described the defendants’ characterization of the conditions as mere discomfort as “like gaslighting their experience entirely.”
“It’s always damaging to minimize someone’s lived experience, and I think that there is a tendency to do that even more so in the context of folks who are incarcerated than maybe other contexts, which is in no way appropriate,” she said. “To do that was just really a minimization of what these women have experienced.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As for governmental immunity, Michigan law states that government officers and employees are immune from liability in a situation like this if their “conduct does not amount to gross negligence that is the proximate cause of the injury or damage.”
“The complaint unquestionably alleges that harmful mold proliferated throughout the facility and that each plaintiff suffered serious injuries as a result,” the opinion explains as to why the eight defendants were not granted governmental immunity. “Further, as recounted above, the complaint alleges that these eight defendants knew of the pervasive mold in Huron Valley, either concealed the mold or refused to eradicate it, and, in many instances, received complaints about the mold’s harms.”
Lucas Verran, a spokesperson for the Department of Corrections, wrote to the Michigan Advance, “The department is aware of the opinion released yesterday and legal counsel is actively reviewing it. In regard to content, MDOC is not commenting on pending litigation at this time.”
Conditions in Women’s Huron Valley have been the subject of criticism from lawmakers and from advocates for years, especially when five women incarcerated at the facility died in less than three months.
“If the facility itself is defunct, you’re going to have all kinds of issues there,” Robinson-Holmes said. “When something happens like a death there, that raises concerns about what is happening at the facility, and if it is linked to the conditions of the facility itself.”
The department has repeatedly denied any issues with mold at the facility and released findings of independent environmental testing done by a private contractor, which concluded the facility did not have dangerous systemic black or toxic mold conditions. 
But at a hearing of the Michigan House Oversight Committee in February, legislators agreed in a rare bipartisan fashion that the problem of mold in the facility did need to be addressed and that department leadership should testify before the state legislature.
Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) told Clark’s story dealing with mold in that hearing, describing that she “has visible mold growing in her ears, and has developed other health issues, including a facial droop and severe swelling in her arms, while incarcerated.”
State Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) testifies to the House Oversight Committee on health and sanitation concerns at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. Feb. 24, 2026. | Screenshot.
In a July protest demanding the closure of the facility and access to better healthcare for women incarcerated in MDOC custody, Clark’s mother, Izora Clark, said, “At the end of the day, I didn’t even recognize my own child.”
Izora Clark said her daughter has mold in her hair and her ears, allegations also raised by Krystal Clark’s attorneys in an emergency motion to have her removed from the prison, citing what they described as her medical deterioration from toxic mold exposure. Krystal Clark was transferred to Duane Waters Health Center in Jackson after the motion was filed.
Michigan Department of Corrections spokesperson Jennie Riehle said at the time that Clark’s attorneys’ allegations “are not supported by the medical evidence or facts known to the department. Ms. Clark is not experiencing any emergent medical condition that warrants transfer from the facility.”
“The incarcerated women there do not deserve to live in unsafe conditions. Really, what the lawsuit is hoping to do is to remedy those conditions and get the attention of the state so that they’re investing in this facility,” Robinson-Holmes said, emphasizing the need for adequate care for people in MDOC custody. 
She continued on to describe last week’s opinion as a victory for Eighth Amendment claims in general, solidifying that in the 6th Circuit, there are claims to be made for inadequate ventilation or dangerous exposure to mold in prison facilities, an area where previous lawsuits have often failed.
“Now we’re seeing that this has been successful, and which will hopefully help other litigants as they try to pursue justice for similar circumstances, which is really critical,” she said.
However, she noted that the discovery and remainder of the lawsuit process in district court may still take years for judges to make a final decision on the question.

name: VTDigger
title: Rural Vermont needs the young to choose this place
text:
This commentary is by Neil Ryan, a third-generation Vermont farmer and consultant helping brands and nonprofits in Corinth.
Vermont is bleeding its young. A University of New Hampshire poll in July found that almost two-thirds of Vermonters ages 18 to 34 plan to leave this state. In September, Vermont Public asked Vermonters what they’d tell an 18-year-old about building a life here. About half said the young should move away.
This is a tragedy. And it is a disgrace. Our state government should have stopped everything and said, “We will look at every policy choice we’ve made and commit to doing everything possible to reverse this.” That hasn’t happened in part because our Legislature is uniquely responsible for a cascade of exclusionary policy choices over the last three decades.I thought back to my 18th summer in the 1990s. I can still recall the feel of the sun on my face back then, running hay between our neighbor’s dairy farm and our farm. Vermont seemed bountiful. Optimistic. I remember being surrounded by young people doing similar things. And I remember knowing I wanted nothing more than to be in Vermont working with livestock and the land.
Fewer young people feel that way about Vermont today. We’ve made it too hard for them to get started. 
Thomas Jefferson wrote, “The care of human life and happiness, and not their destruction, is the first and only legitimate object of good government.”
At the very end of this past legislative session, a few legislators worked compulsively to put conditions on new exemptions for accessory on-farm activities. The justification was, in effect, that absent Act 250, young people might start noisily getting married on farms all over the place. This even as evidence mounted that young people were turning away from Vermont and rural Vermont was hollowing out.Who here doesn’t hope for a Vermont where young people meet each other, fall in love, marry on a farm and perhaps — please! — choose a life of farming for themselves? Apparently, enough legislators primarily fixated on speculative nuisance concerns.
When I was 18, and young people were still plentiful, we had a farm party. Around 10 p.m., a neighbor walked over to tell us to turn down the stereo. We did. Today, we have senators convinced Act 250 permitting is necessary to corral that.Vermont now has the most regulations per capita in the entire country. Vermont not coincidentally has the worst economic momentum of all 50 states. For the last five to 10 years, our Legislature has passed a cascade of sweeping land-use policies that, intentionally or not, position rural Vermont as a quiet, lifeless, scenic amenity for the affluent, and more difficult for everyone else. 
I say to our current crop of legislators: You cannot have equity when investment and relief flow only to the winners you already chose, and everyone else gets crushed by ever-expanding layers of regulation. Wendell Berry said, “If we want to save the land, we must save the people who belong to the land.”
If you are a city mouse, more power to you. Vermont deserves thriving downtown centers. If you are a country mouse, your life, your work and your aspirations are every bit as valid as anyone else’s. It’s time that our state government ran on that understanding.
Vermont must have a rural economy so that rural Vermont is alive with the young. It must be alive with the young so our land has farmers, our farms have markets, our forests have stewards and our wood becomes things of use and value. Vermont must have a diverse rural economy, not one met with suspicion or objection by the Legislature and state agencies at every creative turn.Rural Vermont’s future, should Montpelier choose to embrace it, is a full constellation of enterprises that spring from our agrarian foundation to reconstitute rural life that makes people happy. This must once again be the beckoning country for the young, and they must be trusted to live as they see fit, not forced into a narrow land-use vision shaped and lobbied for to an undue degree, particularly by the Vermont Natural Resources Council. In recent years, Legislative committees have shut out individual rural Vermonters. Instead, committee chairs relied on their favored lobbyists for testimony.

READ MORE

Our Statehouse is the people’s house, and individual Vermonters have a right and responsibility to appeal to their legislators. This fall, rural Vermonters have presented a lengthy list of policy suggestions: Grow What’s Good Here, aimed at easing the burdens on Vermont’s working lands practitioners and rural families. If the past year has signaled anything, it is that legislators and Vermont’s special-interest infrastructure must start listening to Vermont’s farmers, loggers, homesteaders, small-business owners and young families instead of ignoring them, disparaging them or talking down to them. 
Vermonters are about to vote. Whatever one’s politics, we all have an urgent responsibility to evaluate who is actually taking the collective issues raised by rural Vermonters seriously. After voting, all Vermonters must hold their leaders to account. It’s incumbent upon us to stay committed to our land, our homes, our state and better governance. 
Many of us chose to move to Vermont or chose to stay when we were young. By virtue of our choices and our dreams made real over time, we have contributed to making Vermont, Vermont. Rural Vermonters have done it despite the state’s posture and policies. Imagine if our state government empowered more young people to bring their vision of Vermont to life.We can heal this place, grow its food, work its forests, build its businesses, fill its schools and create something better than what we have today. But to get there, we must begin removing the barriers to vitality that are driving the young away. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont needs the young to choose this place.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico utility regulatory officials pave the way for PNM acquisition hearings to continue
text:
A crowd of approximately 100 people protest a private equity firm's proposed takeover of PNM outside the electric company's downtown Albuquerque office building on April 30, 2026. State hearing examiners on Oct. 16, 2026, issued two orders that pave the way for acquisition hearings to continue. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)Hearing examiners for New Mexico’s utility regulators on Friday issued two rulings that pave the way for proceedings to continue in the pending private equity takeover of the state’s largest electric provider.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
New Mexico Public Regulation Commission hearing examiners denied a request to investigate a $200 million stock sale between PNM’s parent company and New York-based investment firm Zimmer Partners. 
Commissioners earlier this year found that a $400 million stock sale between TXNM Energy Inc. and an affiliate of Blackstone Infrastructure, the private equity firm seeking to acquire it, violated state law because the company’s did not first secure the commission’s approval.
Critics of the proposed acquisition had long argued that the transaction was tied to the merger and should therefore be undone — and PRC members agreed in a 2-1 vote in July.
New Energy Economy and the New Mexico Consumer Protection Alliance, both Santa Fe-based advocacy groups, subsequently asked the commission to investigate the stock sale to Zimmer. 
However, hearing examiners in their Friday order wrote that the Zimmer transaction was “fundamentally different.” 
“The present record does not demonstrate comparable evidence that Zimmer participated in the acquisition process” or bought the stock shares as part of a merger, they wrote. 
The hearing examiners also approved a request from TXNM and Blackstone to revise the terms of their proposed acquisition.
The companies in September announced that they were seeking permission to revise the merger application.
At the time, the companies announced that a revised application would include $220 million in direct customer rate credits; $40 million for workforce and economic development initiatives; $25 million for virtual infrastructure upgrades; and $15 million for PNM’s Good Neighbor Fund, which provides bill payment assistance to low-income households.
“These enhanced commitments put real dollars back in customers’ pockets, protect the people who do this work every day and keep PNM locally managed and locally rooted — while giving us the capital to build the grid New Mexico needs,” Don Tarry, PNM and TXNM president and CEO, said in a statement at the time.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Libertarian US Senate candidate Kyle Austin pitches himself as an alternative for voters
text:
Kyle Austin is pictured on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Kyle Austin, the Libertarian candidate for the open U.S. Senate seat in Montana, calls himself “the alternative Republican” as he bids to upend the four-way race and give voters a second conservative choice in the election.
Austin has twice ran in Republican primary races for the U.S. House of Representatives, losing to Matt Rosendale in 2022 and Troy Downing in 2024. This year, he faces off against Republican Kurt Alme, Democrat Alani Bankhead and independent Seth Bodnar. 
He’s fed up with Republican politics, he said, which was why he switched his political affiliation to Libertarian. He added that it would be “too far off home base for me” to switch to the Democratic Party, saying it’s bent too far to the left.
“Republicans used to be all about small government,” Austin said in an interview with the Daily Montanan. “They’ve really shifted away from that.”
Austin has not been immediately welcomed by some longtime members of the state Libertarian Party. But Austin won their primary in June. 
The Libertarian Party in Montana is concerned that if it doesn’t hit a minimum threshold of votes in the race, it could lose major party status from the state, and its candidates wouldn’t automatically appear on the ballot. But Austin said voters will follow him to the ballot box.
“I’m not campaigning as a Libertarian. I’m actually campaigning like I’m an independent. I’m a candidate for all Montanans,” Austin said. “People will follow me to the polls because I’m not like the others … I’m not a politician. They’re politicians. They’re bureaucrats. They’re bought and paid for. I’m running on my own energy, my own two feet.”
A platform built on healthcare reform
Born and raised in Havre, Montana, Austin said he grew up helping his grandfather farm and still owns agricultural land in that area. He also owns and operates Pharm406, a pharmacy serving Billings, Laurel and Butte.
He’s been a pharmacist for 18 years.
Improving Montanans’ healthcare is foundational to his campaign pitch. He said the problem starts with licensing — as it stands, medical licences are handled by the states, not the federal government. 
“Healthcare professionals should be licensed on a national level, and they should be free to go state to state without restriction,” Austin said.
He advocates for shorter training programs for doctors, nurses and pharmacists. These programs take far too long, he said, specifically pointing to issues with finding workers for his own business. 
Being a licensed pharmacist takes significant schooling, which can run anywhere from four to eight years. Doctors, who get extensive training in various aspects of the discipline, can be in training for around a decade.
“Should doctors be forced into a 10-year program?” Austin said. “No, get them in, teach them what they need to know. Get them out into the workforce. I learned most of my pharmacy knowledge after graduating in the workforce, on-the-job training, and that I think would be more appealing for young generations to enter the healthcare industry again.”
He’s also expressed frustration with mail-order pharmacy offerings being pushed by large pharmaceutical companies, which is not only hurting his business, Austin said, but is a similar issue for national brands like Walmart and CVS. He said it amounts to an unfair trade practice.
Seth Bodnar, Kurt Alme, Alani Bankhead and Kyle Austin attend a debate for U.S. Senate candidates in Bozeman on Oct. 11, 2026. (Screenshot via CSPAN)
Austin said he’s also pushing for “rolling deductibles” that start a 12-month clock when a person begins to use their health insurance, as opposed to it resetting on a certain date each year.
“Ninety percent of the people won’t meet their deductible till December, and then when they do, guess what? It starts over Jan. 1,” Austin said. 
While he’s not a supporter of Medicare for all, he said that he would push to create a private nonprofit organization, funded by taxpayers, that would consolidate Medicare, Medicaid, Tricare and other government healthcare programs “under one roof.” He’d then seek to have that program offered to businesses and individuals.
Through that, he said, they would “rewrite the rules and level the playing field” for U.S. healthcare.
Other issues
Gun owners’ rights and agricultural concerns form the rest of Austin’s main pitch to Montana voters.
He’s a gun owner and said he believes that Americans should have unrestricted access to firearms. He likes to shoot, he said, and it’s one of his hobbies while he is out on his late grandfather’s farm.
Austin expressed frustration with recent federal policy decisions that resulted in tariffs and trade problems.
“President Donald Trump really hurt farmers and ranchers over the last couple years with his tariffs, especially when it comes to fuel prices, when it comes to fertilizer prices, and when it comes to our exports,” Austin said. “Tariffs are really just a tax on the consumer, and it’s just raised the rates on things.”
He said he’d be in support of giving ranchers more leeway to kill bears and wolves in defense of their livestock. He’s also advocating for mandatory country-of-origin labeling, and for the federal government to be more hands-on with farm loans.
“Some big banks in Montana grow because when times are tough, farmers and ranchers lose their farms to the bank, and the banks turn around and sell that land and get bigger and bigger,” Austin said. “Let’s take that fear away from the farmers and ranchers.”
Land, who owns it, and what happens on it are also major topics of this election, particularly around public access. Austin is a supporter of U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke’s A River Runs Through It Act that has been panned by some environmentalists. Concerns have been raised about the legislation largely due to a potential increase in logging, roads and motorized recreation on federal land.
Logging is an important industry, Austin said, and he doesn’t believe America’s forests are being managed properly. He says the lack of logging has led to higher costs in the building industry and wildfires causing health impacts via smoke pollution.
“What I’ve seen over my generation is the pendulum has swung too far to the left with the environmentalists,” Austin said. “And what I mean by that is we’ve killed our logging industry, we’ve killed our mill industry.”
He’s also in favor of building more dams, he said, expressing worry that Montana needs to retain more of its water.
“I do believe that if we just let water go downstream, and it ends up in the ocean, we wasted it,” Austin said.
A little more on Austin
Austin is nearly entirely self-financing his Senate campaign and has put in more than $250,000 of his own money.
Austin is a University of Montana graduate — he graduated from pharmaceutical school — and lives by himself in Billings with his dogs.
Austin has said he’s primarily connecting with voters at fairs and other events around the state.
Michael Hummert, who lost in the Democratic Senate primary, says he’s been impressed with Austin, and he’s a person that will change his mind after a good argument. Austin has said he’d debate any Senate candidate.
“He’s not tied to his dogma,” Hummert said. “He’s a conservative person, but he’s not tied to the dogma of conservatism or liberalism. So that’s an important thing in a person that’s running a diverse country like ours is being able to actually be flexible in your thought and willing to listen to other points of view that you don’t agree with.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: In races for Congress, CT Dems have money edge over GOP rivals
text:
Democratic lawmakers from Connecticut maintain a significant fundraising advantage over their Republican challengers just a few weeks before the midterm elections, when the balance of power in Congress is at stake.
While the midterms are historically challenging for the party in power, Republicans have had a cash advantage at the national level. But a number of Democratic candidates have vastly outraised and outspent their Republican opponents, and that trend extends to Connecticut.
Democrats are expected to have a good electoral prospects nationally, with their eyes on both the House and Senate majorities, though the odds look better in the former. The same applies to Connecticut, where all five of its House seats are up and likely to stay blue. The most competitive race is in the western 5th Congressional District.
Candidates for federal office file quarterly reports with the Federal Election Commission. The most recent one covers fundraising and spending from July through the end of September. They are some of the last snapshots candidates will provide of the money race before Election Day.
Four of the five Democratic candidates in Connecticut are incumbents and have the duel advantage of official and campaign events to reach constituents with their message. Plus, sitting members are big beneficiaries of contributions from political action committees that represent a range of special interests that come before Congress.
Luke Bronin, the Democrat who defeated U.S. Rep. John Larson in the primary, also has a well-funded campaign coming out of his competitive four-way race in August. After outside groups contributed in the 1st District Democratic primary, spending from national committees and super PACs isn’t expected to materialize in Connecticut’s general elections.
Without the necessary funds, candidates who are raising little money won’t be able to go up on the airwaves with advertising and have to get more creative to try to break through. They are instead focusing on the ground game, with door-knocking and other less costly get-out-the-vote efforts.
Here’s a breakdown of the fundraising in each race: 
1st Congressional District
Bronin, who was a fundraising powerhouse during the Democratic primary, continues to raise and spend a lot of his resources. The former Hartford mayor faces Republican nominee Amy Chai, a physician, and Green Party nominee Mary Sanders on Nov. 3. All three will debate on Oct. 22 in West Hartford hosted by the League of Women Voters of Greater Hartford. Mark Stewart Greenstein is running as a write-in candidate.

Former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, Democratic candidate for the 1st Congressional District, speaks during a rally with members of Carpenters Local 326 and the Uniformed Professional Firefighters Association in Manchester on Sunday, August 9, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

His quarterly haul covers the last few weeks of the primary campaign. Bronin went on to defeat Larson and two other candidates on Aug. 11. He’s now favored in the general election because the Hartford-based district is one of the most Democratic in the state. He said in a recent interview he doesn’t take the race for granted and described the midterm elections writ large as “turning the political tide for years to come.”
One of the main themes of that primary focused on who contributed to the top two candidates. Bronin pledged not to accept donations from corporate political action committees, which were a large portion of Larson’s contributions. But they sparred over the wealthy donors funding both campaigns.
In his recent fundraising quarter, Bronin raised about $629,000, spent $872,000 and still has $357,000 left in his campaign account as of the end of September. Similar to previous fundraising, it’s a mixture of individual contributors who are giving smaller-dollar donations as well as a wealthier network of donors from private equity and other businesses.
He once again spent money on polling and advertising. Outside of his own campaign, he made contributions to other Democratic House candidates including Stefany Shaheen in New Hampshire and Manny Rutinel in Colorado, who both won their respective primaries. Bronin transferred money to the Connecticut Democratic State Central Committee and $50,000 to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), Democrats’ main committee focused on flipping the House.

Amy Chai, Republican candidate in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, talks with Laurie Wojculewicz, of Bristol, during a candidate Meet and Greet at the Bristol Senior Center on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Chai, meanwhile, is far behind on fundraising. Throughout her campaign, she raised a total of nearly $21,000 and spent about $16,000 as of the end of June. After her most recent report, she didn’t add much to her haul, raising another $445 and spending about $137. She has $307 left in the bank after Sept. 30.
The group U.S. Term Limits sent out a voter education mailer earlier this year, thanking Chai for signing a pledge to support a resolution for two terms in the U.S. Senate and three terms in the U.S. House. The nonpartisan group acknowledges when candidates make the pledge but hasn’t endorsed anyone.
Chai said Republican candidates seeking federal office in Connecticut aren’t getting much help from the party. She said she doesn’t have the money to hire others. To lighten the workload, she said, she programmed bots to help with some tasks.
“I’m doing literally aspect of the campaign exclusively by myself,” she said in a recent interview, noting her work on graphics, bot programming and door knocking.
2nd Congressional District

Congressman Joe Courtney, center, speaks with Maryam Elahi, President and CEO of the Community Foundation of Eastern Connecticut, and Commissioner Seila Mosquera-Bruno, of the Connecticut Department of Housing, before  a roundtable discussion to discuss the  21st Century ROAD to Housing Act at the New London Community Recreation Center on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

In the eastern part of the state, U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney continues to hold a cash advantage, but the Democratic congressman and his Republican challenger George Austin spent similar amounts over the past three months.
Courtney raised $168,000 — half from individual contributors (like Electric Boat employees) and the other half from various political action committees that give to sitting members — and spent $137,000 between July and September. He ended that month with nearly $630,000 cash on hand. He made a contribution to a fellow colleague, U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez, who’s seeking a third term in New Mexico. 
Austin, a contractor from Suffield, raised nearly $30,000 and spent $105,000 during that same three-month period. He has $124,000 left to spend on the campaign. Nearly all of his donors are from Connecticut, including state workers, construction workers, an Electric Boat employee, and eight local Republican Town Committees. U.S. Rep. Pete Sessions, R-Texas, also made a donation to Austin.

George Austin, Republican candidate in the 2nd Congressional District, talks with customers as he campaigns at Sarapes Mexican Restaurant in Enfield on Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Austin has spent money on radio, magazine and Facebook advertising as well as text messages and campaign merchandise like banners, signs, magnets and shirts.
Since the launch of the campaign, Austin’s total fundraising haul surpasses $314,000, but much of that comes from a $240,000 in loans that he gave to his campaign.
The candidates will participate in at least two forums, including a meet-the-candidates event in Storrs on Monday night.
3rd Congressional District

Representative Rosa DeLauro listens to a speaker during a press conference regarding home heating assistance at the Community Action Agency of New Haven on Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

The longest-serving member of Connecticut’s delegation, U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro continues to bring in a sizable haul as she seeks a 19th term in Congress. She faces Republican Chris Lancia in the race for the New Haven-based district.
In the past three months, DeLauro raised nearly $410,000 and spent over half a million. She ended September with $193,000. She brought in about $1.5 million over the course of the 2026 campaign. 
Similar to Courtney and the other Democratic incumbents, about half of her haul comes from PACs. The bulk of DeLauro’s spending went toward contributions to the DCCC as well as the Connecticut Democratic State Central Committee.

Chris Lancia, a Republican running for election to the U.S. House to represent Connecticut’s 3rd Congressional District, talks with District 100 State Representative Republican Candidate Susan Manke at the Middletown Republican Town Committee Pasta & Politics fundraiser at The Cantina in Middletown on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Lancia, a Coast Guard veteran and former federal law enforcement officer employed as a manager at TNI, a provider of fiber networks, is the Republican nominee running against DeLauro.
His most recent quarterly report did not appear in the FEC system in time for this story. Since the start of his campaign, he raised nearly $15,000 and spent about $4,500. He had $4,000 cash on hand as of June 30.
Given the scant resources, Lancia said in a recent interview, his focus has been on meeting voters where they are, especially through door knocking. He said he’s “been to so many towns every day” and still goes to the homes of Democratic voters, noting his past voter affiliation from years ago before he became a Republican. He argued that candidates are too focused on fundraising, saying it doesn’t guarantee a win.
No debate or forum appears to be planned for the 3rd District race. Tom Egan is a candidate endorsed by the Independent Party of Connecticut and Andrew Rice, who failed to make the Democratic primary ballot, is running as a write-in candidate.
4th Congressional District
U.S. Rep. Jim Himes has been one of the most prolific fundraisers of the incumbents and has the largest campaign account of all the Connecticut Democrats: $2.4 million cash on hand.

Rep. Jim Himes, D-Conn., speaks to reporters following votes at the Capitol, Thursday, March 5, 2026, in Washington.  Credit: Allison Robbert / AP

Himes raised nearly $299,000 and spent $387,000 in the last three months. His contributors consist of PACs and individual contributors. His spending includes fundraising events, donations to a local group in Bridgeport and contributions to the state and national party apparatuses, like his colleagues. Himes also made multiple contributions to more than a dozen members of Congress seeking reelection.
He represents the southwest corner of the state, which was the last congressional district that Republicans held in Connecticut. Himes flipped it in the 2008 election. While it has trended blue since his first election, the congressman argued that the “nature of the district hasn’t changed that much” and that the Republican Party as well as independent voters themselves have shifted since then.
His Republican challenger, Michael Goldstein, raised more than $11,000 and spent nearly $27,000. He went into the final weeks of the campaign with about $25,000 in the bank. He’s received a mixture of individual contributions from inside and outside Connecticut. And he spent on things like SMS advertising and yard signs.

Michael Goldstein, a doctor and attorney, is running in the Republican primary for Connecticut’s 4th Congressional District. A Republican hasn’t won the district since 2006. Credit: Courtesy of Michael Goldstein

Goldstein is a doctor and attorney who has previously run for the 4th District. He lost the Republican primary in 2022 but became the GOP nominee in 2024, eventually losing to Himes. This summer, Goldstein won a two-way primary for the nomination.
“I think they’ll get support from their towns, but they’re not getting it from the state party at all. That is one of the issues that we all think about and wonder about,” Goldstein said in a recent interview. “I think that a more engaged Republican Party would probably be much better for the candidates. But this has been this way for a while. I don’t see it changing soon.”
Himes, Goldstein and Independent candidate Benjamin Wesley will square off in a debate on Monday night in Westport hosted by the League of Women Voters.
5th Congressional District
The sprawling 5th District in the western part of the states remains the only competitive federal race in Connecticut. U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes had a nail-biter reelection race in 2022 but won by a larger margin in 2024.
This cycle, election analysts who rate federal races moved it closer to Democrats because the party in power historically faces headwinds in a midterm election.

U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes joins other officials in Danbury, Conn. on Aug. 26, 2026 to condemn the actions of ICE, which detained dozens of people Monday and Tuesday.  Credit: Ryan Caron King / Connecticut Public

From July through September, Hayes brought in her largest haul of the 2026 cycle and outraised Republican opponent Chris Shea. But the two candidates spent similar amounts over the past three months.
Hayes raised $371,000 and spent $260,000. Less than half of her individual contributions come from PACs. She got money from individuals as well as from national and local political committees like EMILY’s List, the DCCC and the Sharon Democratic Town Committee. She also made a transfer of $6,000 to the Connecticut Democratic State Central Committee. Hayes has about $1.2 million left for the remainder of the campaign.
Shea, meanwhile, raised about $129,000 and spent $224,000 during that same time period. He’s received a number of small-dollar donations from around the state but has also been able to secure much larger contributions, such as one from Old Lyme businessman John David Kelsey. Some of that fundraising also comes through his joint fundraising committee, which allows candidate committees, PACs and political parties to raise money together.
His campaign spent on mailers, texting, digital advertising and campaign apparel and signs. He also made a political donation to the Connecticut Republican State Central Committee. Shea has $145,000 cash on hand as of Sept. 30.

Chris Shea in his campaign video. Credit: Chris Shea campaign

Shea is a North Haven firefighter and retired Navy SEAL. He founded the nonprofit Hero to Hero, which encourages military veterans to consider a second career as first responders.
Because he faced a primary, Shea had to file separate reports: a pre-primary report that covered July 1 through July 22 and another one that ran through Sept. 30.
Hayes and Shea squared off last week in the only debate of the 5th District campaign. They shared contrasting views on Trump administration policies, immigration and the war in Iran.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Bayh, Engling split over whether other secretary of state candidates should get debate invite
text:
Four candidates for Indiana Secretary of State squared off on Aug; 26, 2026 in downtown Indianapolis. From left to right, Max Engling, Lauri Shillings, moderators Dan Spehler and Lesley Weidenbener, Greg Ballard and Beau Bayh. (Photo By Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Democrat Beau Bayh wants all four Indiana secretary of state candidates to participate in a televised debate later this week.
Republican Max Engling’s campaign, however, argues that Bayh is trying to avoid a direct matchup by pushing for Lincoln Party candidate Greg Ballard and Libertarian Lauri Shillings to also take part.
Bayh, Ballard and Shillings issued a joint statement Monday asking TV stations FOX59/CBS4 in Indianapolis to reconsider the decision to exclude Ballard and Shillings from Thursday’s debate.
“We believe all candidates on the ballot deserve the opportunity to make their case to voters, particularly in an election where the results will determine whether political parties gain statewide ballot access for the next four years,” the statement said. “More voices in the conversation make for a healthier democracy. No party has a monopoly on good ideas, and competition increases accountability. Hoosiers deserve to hear from everyone in this debate.”
The stations cited debate participation standards set by their parent company Nexstar that include reaching at least 10% support level in nonpartisan polling.
A Free Press Indiana poll released Friday found Bayh with 43% support and Engling at 35%. Shillings had 6% support, with Ballard at 5% and 11% undecided.
Engling’s campaign said Bayh’s stance “looks like an effort to avoid facing Max Engling one-on-one.”
“A crowded stage gives Beau fewer questions to answer and more opportunities to dodge accountability,” the campaign said. “Max is more than ready to lay out his plans for Indiana. Why isn’t Beau?”
Bayh’s campaign didn’t immediately reply to a question from the Capital Chronicle on whether he would still participate in the debate without Ballard and Shillings.
The joint statement argued for an exception to the stations’ polling standards, citing Indiana law that uses secretary of state election results to determine ballot status for the next four years.
A candidate receiving at least 2% in the race secures automatic ballot status for his or her party. A candidate topping 10% gets state-administered primaries for the party.
When asked whether the decision to invite only Engling and Bayh was being reconsidered, the stations’ news director, CJ Hoyt, replied: “We look forward to hosting the two qualified candidates to our debate Thursday evening.”
All four candidates took part in an Oct. 7 televised debate sponsored by the nonprofit Indiana Debate Commission, as well as an August debate put on by the Indy Chamber.
The next debate is scheduled for 7 p.m. Thursday and is set for broadcast on several Indiana stations.
